Ion, Epigram.

The Phaeacians of Homer

THE PHAEACIAN EPISODE
OF
THE ODYSSEY

AS COMPRISED IN THE
SIXTH, SEVENTH, EIGHTH, ELEVENTH, AND
THIRTEENTH BOOKS

WITH
INTRODUCTION, NOTES, AND APPENDIX

By AUGUSTUS C. MERRIAM, Ph.D.
COLUMBIA COLLEGE, NEW YORK

ILLUSTRATED

NEW YORK
HARPER & BROTHERS, FRANKLIN SQUARE
1880

Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1880, by
Harper & Brothers,
In the Office of the Librarian of Congress, at Washington.

PREFACE.

Since the usual curriculum of the American college requires that some portion of the Iliad shall be read by candidates for admission, the Odyssey comes, in natural sequence, within the first year's course after entrance. The present edition of the Phaeacian Episode is the outgrowth of several years' experience in teaching classes in such a course, and the aim throughout has been to meet the needs which this experience has demonstrated. To lay a foundation of grammatical knowledge upon which the student could tread firmly and securely in his subsequent course has been deemed the first essential. For this purpose, constant reference to the grammars has been made, and occasional questions introduced to direct attention to particular points. Road-building is as indispensable as it is laborious; but it must not be forgotten that the adjacent regions may be full of interest, profit, and delight—indeed, that the former is only a means to an end; the latter offer the real fruit to be gathered day by day as the work goes on. This is especially true of the Homeric field, where we wander beside the fountains from which such copious floods stream down through the centuries along all the highways of civilization to our own day. After all the diversity of opinion concerning the date of the Homeric poems, most scholars have regarded them as substantially the product of a single age, and "contemporary evidence for the phenomena of primitive Greek civilization;" as such they are treated in the accompanying notes. Like the poet's own Calypso's isle, they present a region so fair

vi PREFACE.

that even a god might stay his steps to gaze in delight upon it, as it lifts itself on high, the omphalos of a sea of time that stretches on through many a generation, with scarce a resting-place for the foot of the adventurous traveller, till the shores of historic Hellas emerge into view. These many generations, now so dark to us, teemed with the ferment of change that was fraught with momentous consequence to later days. Looking upon the poems as standing thus remote and apart, at the very gate of our dawn, how manifold are the questions with which the student may turn his inquiring gaze towards the resplendent Eos, coming to announce its light unto men! Rightly to understand historic Greece, the inquirer must know all the nooks and corners of this Dawnland; and rightly to search these out, he must take the poems as his main authority, and not confuse the later with the earlier, but recognize once and always the wide expanse that lies between dawn and midday, the rosy-fingered and the bright serene. To train the student in these methods of investigation, to set before him the means of becoming familiar with the ways of thinking, feeling, acting, in that wondrous Dawn Age, and of making his work a real literary study—these are some of the aims embodied in the notes. That the student in college has both time and inclination for work of this kind is fact, not theory.
   In preparing the notes, I have had constantly before me the commentaries of the Scholiasts and Eustathius, of Nitzsch, Ameis, Faesi, and Düntzer, of Hayman, and of Merry in his school edition of the first twelve books of the Odyssey. Merry's large edition did not appear until the notes on the Sixth, Seventh, and the larger part of the Eighth Book were completed, so that little use was made of it. To these authorities are to be added especially Gladstone's Studies on Homer and the Homeric Age, and his Juventus Mundi, the first two volumes of Mure's Critical History of Greek Literature, the

PREFACE. vii

Realien of Friedreich and of Buchholz, Seiler's Homerisches Wörterbuch, and the Index Seberi, that marvel of patient toil. From these sources and many others information has been freely drawn whenever it came within the scope of my plan. To work upon the materials gathered by our predecessors is the privilege and the duty of a later day. It is not easy to say anything new on the subject of Homer. The field has been dug to the lowest subsoil. Yet there is something still left to a close study of the text and the purpose of the poet. To any who may differ with me on questions of mere opinion, I can only say with the ancient poet,

"Let these things seem right to you; to me, let these other things seem so."

As to matters of fact, I have labored hard to eliminate errors; doubtless many will be discovered still by keener eyes. We all strive after accuracy; it is a hard thing to attain.
The text followed is that of Dindorf, with a few changes mentioned in the notes.
I take pleasure in acknowledging the courteous permission extended me by General di Cesnola to use the plates from his "Cyprus," and my thanks are also due to Messrs. Charles Scribner's Sons for a similar favor in the case of the "Troy" and "Mycenae" of Dr. Schliemann. The cuts from these recent and valuable sources for Homeric illustration will, I think, add largely to the value of this work.

Augustus C. Merriam.

Columbia College,
May, 1880.

INTRODUCTION.

I.

AN OUTLINE OF THE HOMERIC QUESTION.

In it is strife, in it is valor, in it is the chilling pursuit.

The people of Colophon say Homer was their own citizen; the Chians claim him as theirs; the Salaminians demand him back; the Smyrnaeans actually confirm that he was theirs, and have even dedicated a shrine to him in their city. Very many others besides dispute and contend among themselves over the matter. — Cicero, Pro Archia 8.

This familiar passage well represents the uncertainty that prevailed in antiquity regarding Homer's birthplace. As for the dates likewise assigned to him, we find a range of some 450 years, from before 1104 BC to 684 BC. Lycurgus is said to have brought the poems from Asia Minor or Samos to Sparta, and we hear of their recitation by rhapsodists at Sicyon around 600 BC; soon after, Solon introduced improved regulations for their recitation at Athens. Peisistratus is credited with a revised edition of the poems, carried out under the editorship of Onomacritus, Conchylus, Zopyrus, and Orpheus of Croton. Their contemporaries Xenophanes of Colophon and Theagenes of Rhegium wrote commentaries on the text. Subsequently many editions were produced, among them one by Aristotle for Alexander the Great, and numerous changes were made to the text, until it came into the hands of the Alexandrian grammarians, who fixed it in the form we now possess, aiming as far as possible to return to the Peisistratean recension.

In early times, several poems of the Epic Cycle circulated under the name of Homer, until critics rejected all of them as spurious except the Iliad and the Odyssey. These were attributed to Homer by

x INTRODUCTION.

the consentient voice of antiquity, save of a few who were called
Chorizontes, or Separatists, of whom two only are named, Xenon
and Hellanicus. They thought that the two poems were by separate authors; but in this they were controverted by the Alexandrian School, notably by Aristarchus, with such arguments that the subject appears to have been laid at rest, and Homer sat like a god unshaken on his throne till modern days. Vico, Casaubon, Bentley, Hedelin, first cast doubts on the authorship of the poems, but theirs were conjectures thrown out at random, without any sound arguments to support them. But, soon after the Venetian Scholia on the Iliad were discovered and published, F. A. Wolf, of Halle, put forth his famous Prolegomena, or Introduction to Homer, in 1795. In this he undertook to show that the Iliad and Odyssey were not two complete poems, but small, separate, and independent epic songs, celebrating single exploits of heroes, and written down and united as the Iliad and Odyssey for the first time by Peisistratus. This position, supported as it was by arguments both plausible and acute, startled the whole literary world by its boldness and apparent novelty, and it not only won for itself many converts, but excited strong opposition. War was soon declared between the two camps, and the struggle has raged with varied tide of success up to the present day.

The arguments of Wolf may be classed under four heads:

1. Without the art of writing, these poems are too extensive and complicated to be either composed or transmitted; and throughout their whole extent everything is calculated to be heard, and nothing to be read. No epitaphs nor any other inscriptions are mentioned, and coins are unknown. When the Greek heroes are casting lots for a champion to engage in the single combat with Hector (H 181-89), that of Ajax, which leaps forth first, has to be handed round by the herald till it comes to Ajax himself before it is recognized. Wolf says that if this had been anything like writing, the herald would have read it aloud at once. So the "folded tablet" of Z 169 contained certain marks or signs, not a true written script. Hence writing was entirely unknown at the time of the Trojan War, and could

AN OUTLINE OF THE HOMERIC QUESTION. xi

not have been common when the poems were composed ; indeed, it only came into vogue with the introduction of prose composition. (Prolegom. xix, xx.)
To this it has been answered :
Writing is not indispensable to the composition of the Iliad and the Odyssey. Long poems have been known to be composed and kept in mind for some time without being committed to writing, and the lays of the Icelandic skalds were preserved for more than two hundred years by oral transmission. One of the songs of the Kalmuk Tartars sometimes lasts a whole day. Again, this could be done much more easily in times when the artificial aid of writing was absent and the memory was more carefully trained and exercised. Indeed, there were Greeks of the historic period who knew the poems by heart, as Niceratus in Xenophon's Symposium. But it is at least open to doubt whether Wolf's view of the late introduction of writing into Greece is not overstated.

2. The bard would have no inducement to compose works so extensive, since they could not be read, and the only opportunity for their being heard would be at banquets and festivals, at which it would be possible to recite but a small portion. (Prolegom. xxvi.)
To this it has been answered :
Musical contests were wont to be held, connected with great national festivals, at which thousands assembled, anxious to hear and patient to listen. The Athenians could hear at one festival in succession nine tragedies, three satyric dramas, and as many comedies. Nay, such masterpieces would be sufficient of themselves to gather such an audience.

3. Before the time of Peisistratus the poems did not exist as a whole. (Prolegom. xxxiii.)
To this it has been answered :
An Iliad certainly did exist before the First Olympiad. The regulations of Solon presuppose a certain definite form for both poems. The task of Peisistratus was restoration, not creation. He did not produce a combination that had not existed previ-

Page xii of the Introduction. The passage continues a discussion of Homeric authorship. It notes that someone re-established the Homeric text after it had been disrupted by the uncertainties of oral transmission, and that this act was more political than literary in nature. Point 4 raises the objection that both the Iliad and the Odyssey lack unity, showing signs of later interpolations and the stitching together of different parts, along with many contradictions and inconsistencies (referring to Prolegomena, chapters xxvii–xxxi). The response to this objection is that many of the greatest critics have praised the structure of both epics as displaying the kind of unity that only the highest art can achieve. Contradictions and discrepancies can speak as much in a poet's favor as against him; we accept them in Virgil, Dante, and Shakespeare, whose works were set down in writing from the very beginning. A poet is swept along by his own thought and cannot attend to every minor detail. While it is impossible to view the Homeric poems as patchwork, it is quite possible that during transmission individual lines or whole scenes crept in or were deliberately added. Those swayed by the list of discrepancies fail to appreciate the remarkable uniformity and consistency running through the characters across both poems wherever the same figures appear. It is not denied that Homer drew on tradition and existing songs, but weaving that material into a harmonious epic with such fine characterization is the work of supreme genius. One great epic poet is a nation's crowning glory; if many authors jointly produced the Iliad and Odyssey, such a collaboration would be marvelous, unparalleled, and incredible. The page closes by introducing Lachmann, who took Wolf's position to its logical conclusion, doing the work Wolf left unfinished despite living a comparatively long life after publishing his Prolegomena.

AN OUTLINE OF THE HOMERIC QUESTION. xiii

tect in the Iliad eighteen separate and independent lays, by different authors and without any mutual connection. Each lay, originally complete in itself, was afterwards expanded, till, after many years of oral transmission (greatly facilitated by the work of the Homeridae and other guilds of poets and reciters), the whole was thrown into its present shape by the recension of Peisistratus.
Though the Odyssey has been treated somewhat similarly, the patches have been deemed larger, and therefore less numerous. Hennings finds in it two distinct epic poems, pieced more or less closely together, i. e. a Telemacheia and an Odysseia. Kirchhoff discerns an original and early nucleus of considerable extent, describing the return of Odysseus. This was added to by a later poet of less power who preceded the first Olympiad. A third poet, about the thirtieth Olympiad, added the parts relating to Telemachus, and considerable other matter.
Grote was of opinion that the two poems were by different authors, but were to be assigned to the same age. While he has no doubt about the unity of the Odyssey, he advances the theory that the Iliad is composed of an original Achilleid, which consisted of Books I., VIII., XI.–XXII. About this were built Books II.–VII., X., XXIII., and XXIV., like additions to a house, forming the Iliad proper; but the entire edifice was constructed within the same generation, whether by the same or different hands. The Ninth Book, however, was an unsuitable and later addition.
Since then, Paley has attempted to show that our Iliad and Odyssey are later than Peisistratus, and, in fact, must have been put into their present shape in or about the time of Pericles.
Still more recently, Geddes, in his "Problem of the Homeric Poems," taking the theory of Grote as his ground-work, seeks to prove that the Achilleid is an older poem, composed by a Thessalian bard, while the remaining books of the Iliad and all the Odyssey are the work of an Ionian, "none other than the Homer whom all ages have conspired to reverence."
Among other names that may be classed with the followers of the Wolfian theory, with its various modifications, may be mentioned F. Schlegel, Heyne, W. Müller, Thiersch, Hermann,

xiv INTRODUCTION.

Ritschl, Köchly, Düntzer, G. Curtius. In the opposing camp are found Goethe, Schiller, Kreuser, Voss, K. O. Müller, Welcker, Nitzsch, Ameis, Coleridge, Clinton, Thirlwall, Mure, Blackie, Hayman, Gladstone. In our own country, Dr. Charles Anthon, towards the close of his life, was a cautious Wolfian; President Felton a pronounced believer "that the Wolfian theory has not an inch of ground to rest upon."

II.
SUMMARY OF THE ODYSSEY.

a.

The poet invokes the Muse to tell of the hero who, after ten years spent far from home in the siege of Troy, and ten years of wanderings in distant seas, winning knowledge of cities and men, is still an exile on the island of Calypso, where he has been detained for the last seven years, and where he is weeping his life away in longing for the dear native land he cannot reach. Poseidon is his enemy, because of the blinding of Polyphemus, and it is during his absence among the Ethiopians that Athena declares, in the council of the gods, that the fated time has come for the return of Odysseus, and urges Zeus to send Hermes to Calypso with an order for his release. She goes herself to Ithaca, where nothing has been heard from the absent king since his departure from Troy, and where all but the steadfast Penelope and her son Telemachus, whom Odysseus had left as a mere infant at his departure, have abandoned every hope of his return. For three years one hundred and eight young nobles of Ithaca and the surrounding islands have been daily frequenting the palace as suitors for the hand of Penelope, growing more insolent with every refusal of the queen to choose among them. There Athena comes in the guise of Mentes, an old guest-friend of Odysseus, and, after being entertained by Telemachus, tells him to call a public assembly and lodge a protest against the oppression of the suitors, and then undertake a journey to Pylos and Sparta to seek news of his father. She then disappears, Penelope descends for

SUMMARY OF THE ODYSSEY. xv

a moment from her upper chamber to entreat the bard Phemius to stop his mournful song of the Woe of the Achaeans, and Telemachus surprises the suitors by his bold words among them. The day comes to a close; the suitors depart into town for the night; and Telemachus retires to rest, pondering the great event of his projected voyage.

Book II.

On the following morning, Telemachus calls an assembly, in which he makes his maiden speech, denouncing the suitors and requesting a ship for his voyage. Antinous and Eurymachus, the leaders of the suitors, justify their own conduct by throwing the blame on Penelope, who, after authorizing the wooing by a promise to select a husband on completion of her pretended web, had treacherously failed to keep her word. They carry everything before them in the assembly, and refuse the request of Telemachus for a ship. Athene, however, in the guise of Mentor, borrows one for him from Noemon, and gathers a crew at evening. Telemachus visits the store-room, where he discloses to the old nurse Eurycleia his intended departure, but enjoins secrecy upon her, procures provisions for the journey, and sets sail in the evening with Athene-Mentor as his guide.

Book III.

He arrives in the morning at Pylos, and finds Nestor and his people on the sea-shore offering a hecatomb to Poseidon. Nestor recounts the fate of the heroes of Troy, all of whom had either perished or resettled in their native lands, except Odysseus, of whom he has heard nothing since they came as far as Tenedos together, on his way home, but there parted ways. Athene, disappearing, is recognized by Nestor, and he offers her a rich sacrifice on the following day. He advises Telemachus to visit Menelaus at Sparta, supplies him with horses and a chariot for the journey, and sends his youngest son, Peisistratus, as his companion. They rest the first night at Pherae.

Book IV.

Late the next day they reach Sparta, where they find Menelaus celebrating the marriage of his daughter Hermione with Neoptolemus. Menelaus had returned home after eight years of wander-

xvi INTRODUCTION.

ing about Cyprus, Phoenicia, Egypt, and Libya, gathering such wealth of presents that his palace was marvellously adorned. While he is entertaining the guests, Helen enters the hall in great state, and immediately recognizes Telemachus by his likeness to his father. Next day, Menelaus relates his travels, and acquaints Telemachus with what he had heard from Proteus, the prophetic sea-god, of Odysseus' detention in the island of Calypso, and he urges his remaining at Sparta for a time, promising gifts. Here the scene shifts to Ithaca; and the suitors learn, for the first time, of the voyage of Telemachus from Noemon, who asks them when Telemachus will be back. They thought him out in the country visiting his farm. Antinous proposes to waylay him on his return, and they all assent. He accordingly fits out a vessel for that purpose, and takes his station at the island Asteris in the channel. Penelope, informed by the herald Medon of the plot against her son, is wild with grief, till comforted by a dream sent by Athene.

Book V.

Athene again, in the council of the gods, reminds Zeus of the detention of Odysseus, and he now dispatches Hermes to Ogygia, where he commands Calypso to send the hero on his way homeward. She reluctantly furnishes Odysseus with implements to build a vessel, which he constructs within the space of four days, and then sets sail. For eighteen days he voyages the vast deep with a favorable breeze, till he sights the land of Scheria in the distance, when he is espied by Poseidon, who is just returning from the Ethiopians. The deity, in his wrath, raises a storm that scatters the timbers of the vessel like chaff upon the threshing-floor. Odysseus, stripping off his garments, swims on for two days, aided by the magic scarf of the sea-goddess Ino, till at last he makes land at the river-mouth, at some distance from the city of the Phaeacians. Here he falls fainting from utter exhaustion. When he revives, he seeks a neighboring covert, and falls asleep ensconced in a heap of leaves.

Book VI.

Nausicaa, daughter of Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, warned by Athene in a dream, descends in the morning, with her damsels,

SUMMARY OF THE ODYSSEY. xvii

to the river-mouth, to wash the family vestments. Odysseus,
roused by their voices, awakes and implores her protection. She
supplies him with food and raiment, and instructs him to follow
her to a grove near the city, where he is to remain till he thinks
she must have arrived at the palace.

Book VI (η).

The princess, reaching home, proceeds to her chamber, and
Odysseus, entering the town, is met by Athena in the guise of a
girl, and conducted to the palace, where he is hospitably received
by Alcinous, and promised an escort home. The queen, Arete, recognizes
the garments given him by Nausicaa, and questions him
about them. He relates his voyage from Ogygia, his shipwreck,
and the help given him by Nausicaa.

Book VII (θ).

On the following day he is generously entertained with song and
games, is presented with rich gifts, which Arete packs in a chest,
and is told by Alcinous that he must reveal his name and native
land, so that the remarkable ship, already prepared to escort
him, may take him to his destination.

Book IX (ι).

The hero complies with the request, and relates his departure
from Troy, his attack on the Ciconians of Thrace, his being seized by
storm-winds when rounding Malea, whence he is swept off
course to the land of the Lotus-Eaters, and his adventures in
the cave of Polyphemus, from which he escapes after blinding
the monster.

Book X (κ).

Odysseus next describes his arrival at the island of Aeolia, and
his hospitable reception by the Keeper of the Winds, who at
parting gives him the adverse gales secured in a bag. The good
intentions of Aeolus are frustrated by the foolishness of the crew, who
open the bag, and the fleet is driven back to the island. They
then sail on to the port of the Laestrygonians, by whom the
whole fleet is destroyed, with the exception of the hero's own

xviii INTRODUCTION.

vessel and crew. He next arrives at the island of the enchantress Circe, where, after baffling her magic arts by the aid of Hermes, he is entertained a whole year.

λ.

By the advice of Circe, Odysseus proceeds to the realm of Aïdes, to consult the seer Teiresias regarding his future destinies. After sailing for a day from Circe's isle, he arrives at the mouth of Oceanus, near which he finds the entrance to the underworld, whence the spirits of the dead are sent up to be seen and questioned. First comes Teiresias, then the ghosts of heroines of the past; among them his mother, who tells him of her death through heart-sick longing for him. After he has told how these passed before him, the hero pauses; but, being urged to proceed, he relates his dialogue with Agamemnon and Achilles, and how he saw Ajax, Heracles, and other heroes, until, terrified lest he might see the Gorgon, he retreats to his ship and returns to Circe's abode.

μ.

Leaving there with directions from Circe as to his homeward route, he sails past the Sirens and the Cyanean Rocks, between Scylla and Charybdis, which he escapes with the loss of six men devoured by Scylla, and reaches at last the island Thrinakia, where the Sun-god pastured his cattle. Odysseus had been warned by Circe not to slaughter any of these, and so he informed his companions; but they, long wind-bound and hungered, one day in his absence, commit the sacrilegious act. The flayed skins crept about of their own accord, and the flesh lowed upon the spits. On again setting sail, the vessel is destroyed by Zeus, and Odysseus alone escapes and is carried to the island of Calypso. Here his story ceases.

ν.

Next morning more presents are given him, and he is feasted through the day. At nightfall he embarks on the galley, whose speed is that of thought, and at early dawn is set ashore fast asleep in a harbor of Ithaca, together with his valuables. As the Phaeacian galley is entering the harbor on its return home,

SUMMARY OF THE ODYSSEY. xix

Poseidon smites it into a rock. Odysseus, awaking, is accosted by Athene, who informs him of his son's absence in Sparta, and of the ambush of the suitors. She promises her assistance in his schemes of vengeance, and, transforming him into an aged beggar, she bids him proceed to the steading of his swineherd, Eumaeus, while she goes to Sparta to send Telemachus home.

Book XIV.

Odysseus, on approaching the steading of Eumaeus, is attacked by the dogs, but is protected and hospitably entertained by the swineherd, who still faithfully and lovingly remembers his lord, but despairs of ever seeing his face again. The beggar assures him with an oath that Odysseus will return shortly, and relates a series of fictitious adventures, in the course of which he claims to have just heard of Odysseus in Thesprotia.

Book XV.

Athene warns Telemachus to return home, avoiding in his voyage the ambush of the suitors; and, on reaching Ithaca, to visit the swineherd first. Accordingly, after receiving presents from his host and hostess, he retraces his former route with Peisistratus, and arrives at Pylos. When about to embark, he is accosted by the seer Theoclymenus, a fugitive from Argos on account of homicide, to whom he affords a passage to Ithaca. The vessel escapes the ambush by a circuitous course. That same evening Eumaeus relates how he was kidnapped in early boyhood from his father's palace in Syrie, sold to Laertes, and brought up in the family. At dawn Telemachus lands, sends on his galley to the city, and proceeds directly to the swineherd's dwelling. Theoclymenus, before parting, prophesies the speedy restoration of the affairs of Odysseus.

Book XVI.

Telemachus finds Odysseus at breakfast with Eumaeus, whom he sends to apprise Penelope of his return. Odysseus, restored by Pallas to his natural form, reveals himself to his son, and they make plans for the destruction of the suitors. In the meantime, the vessel of Telemachus enters the port of Ithaca, and soon after the suitors' galley, having failed in its object, re-

xx INTRODUCTION.

turns. Antinous proposes a fresh attempt on the life of Telemachus, but is dissuaded by the less depraved Amphinomus. Penelope, informed by Eumaeus of the arrival of Telemachus, reproaches the suitors for their designs against her son's life. Eumaeus, in the course of the evening, rejoins Telemachus and Odysseus, now retransformed by Athene into a beggar.

Book XVII (ρ).

Telemachus walks into town the next morning, takes Theoclymenus to the palace, and repeats to his mother what he had heard from Menelaus. Theoclymenus renews his prophecy of the hero's speedy return. Eumaeus and Odysseus set out later in the day for the town; and at the fountain the hero is insulted by Melanthius, one of his own goatherds. Arriving before the palace, Odysseus is recognized by the old hound Argus, who dies for joy at the sight. Within, as he begs among the suitors, he is insulted and struck by Antinous. Penelope hears the blow, inquires about the stranger from Eumaeus, learns that he claims to bring tidings of her husband, and arranges a meeting with him for that evening.

Book XVIII (σ).

The public beggar Irus appears and seeks to drive Odysseus away. He is urged on by Antinous to fight Odysseus, and receives a frightful punishment at the hero's hands. Penelope, counselled by Athene, makes her appearance to scold the suitors for courting her without bringing gifts. Her words and her beauty win rich gifts, which are presented on the spot. Eurymachus, mocking Odysseus, is met with words so bold that he becomes enraged and hurls a stool at him, but it strikes the cup-bearer instead. Telemachus calms the uproar and sends the suitors home for the night.

Book XIX (τ).

Odysseus and Telemachus, when left alone, remove the weapons from the palace hall. Penelope appears, and her maid Melantho treats Odysseus with contempt, but is sternly rebuked by her mistress. The queen explains to him her stratagem of the web, and he wins her confidence by claiming to have entertained

SUMMARY OF THE ODYSSEY. xxi

her husband in Crete on his way to Troy, and by describing the garments he wore. She orders a foot-bath for him, and this is given him by his old nurse Eurycleia, who recognizes him by a scar received in his youth from the tusk of a boar when hunting on Parnassus; but, warned by Odysseus, she conceals the discovery. Penelope resolves to entertain the suitors on the following day with a contest of archery, shooting with the bow of Odysseus between the horns of twelve double-bladed axes, the winner to have a prior claim to her hand.

υ.

Odysseus, resting in the corridor, is enraged to see some of the serving-women going out to meet their lovers among the suitors; but he still holds back and bides his time. The next morning being the feast of Apollo and the New Moon, the suitors' revels begin again at an early hour. Melanthius, the goatherd, and Philoetius, a loyal cowherd, arrive with cattle for the daily feast. The murder of Telemachus is once again proposed in the suitors' council, and once again dropped at the urging of Amphinomus. Ctesippus hurls an ox-hoof at the head of the king in disguise. Theoclymenus warns them of their coming doom in the sublime language of prophetic vision, but is mocked by Eurymachus, and withdraws to the house of Peiraeus in the town.

φ.

Penelope brings the bow of Odysseus out of the storeroom and challenges the suitors to the contest in the hall. Not one of them is able even to string it. The hero reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius outside the palace by means of the scar that Eurycleia had noticed. Returning to the hall, he asks leave to try the bow. The suitors object, but when Penelope withdraws, Eumaeus, at Telemachus's command, brings the bow and arrows to his master, and orders Eurycleia to keep all the women in their rooms. Philoetius secures the doors of the hall, and Odysseus, stringing the bow with a master's ease, shoots his arrow cleanly through the line of axe-heads. Zeus thunders from on high, and Telemachus takes his place at his father's side with weapons in his hands.

xxii INTRODUCTION.

X.

Thus supported by Telemachus, and by Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Athene, Odysseus assaults the suitors. His first arrow strikes down Antinous as he is raising the wine-cup to his lips, and the next lays Eurymachus low. Telemachus slays Amphinomus, and supplies his party with fresh weapons from the armory. Melanthius, detected in a similar attempt, is caught by Eumaeus and Philoetius, and bound fast. In the end, the whole suitor crew are destroyed, except Phemius the bard and Medon the herald, both having been secretly faithful to the interests of the family, amidst an apparent adherence to the suitors. Melanthius and twelve of the women are hanged in the court-yard.

Book 23 (ψ).

Eurycleia informs Penelope of the return of Odysseus, of the death of the suitors, and of her recognition of the hero by the scar on his leg. Penelope descends to the hall, and, though at first incredulous, is finally convinced of the identity of her husband by his describing the construction of his bed, which was known only to herself, Odysseus, and one trusty servant. The hero, anticipating a tumult among the relatives of the suitors, resolves to withdraw at daybreak to the farm of his father, Laertes, and take further measures for the re-establishment of his authority. On retiring to rest, he recapitulates his past adventures to Penelope, with the mysterious prophecy of Teiresias relative to his future destiny.

Book 24 (ω).

Hermes conducts the souls of the suitors to Hades. Odysseus, on arrival at the farm of Laertes, finds him working in his garden, and reveals himself to him. The friends of the suitors, instigated by the father of Antinous, march to avenge the death of their patrons. Odysseus and Laertes, together with his trusty slave Dolius and his sons, attack and defeat the rebels; and, through the interposition of Athene, peace and royal authority are restored.

ODYSSEY, BOOK VI.

The Arrival of Odysseus among the Phaeacians.

So there he lay sleeping, that much-enduring, noble Odysseus,
worn out by sleep and weariness; but Athena
went to the land and city of the Phaeacian men,
who had once in former times dwelt in spacious Hypereia,
near the Cyclopes, those overbearing men,
who used to plunder them, being stronger by force.
From there godlike Nausithoos roused and led them away,
and settled them in Scheria, far from men who eat bread,
and drove a wall around the city, and built houses,
and made temples to the gods, and divided up the farmland.
But he had by now been conquered by his fate and gone down to Hades,
and Alkinoos was then their king, wise with the counsels of the gods.
To his house went the goddess gray-eyed Athena,
planning the return of great-hearted Odysseus.
She went to the richly decorated chamber where a girl slept,
like the immortal goddesses in form and beauty —
Nausikaa, daughter of great-hearted Alkinoos,
and beside her two handmaids with beauty given by the Graces,
one at each doorpost; the shining doors were shut.
Like a breath of wind she swept over the girl's bed,
and stood above her head, and spoke a word to her,
in the likeness of the daughter of Dymas, famed for his ships,
who was of the same age as Nausikaa and dear to her heart.
Likening herself to her, gray-eyed Athena spoke:

2 ODYSSEY, BOOK VI.

"Nausicaa, how could your mother have raised you to be so careless? Your fine, shining clothes are lying there uncared for, yet your wedding is close at hand, when you must yourself be beautifully dressed and provide the same for those who will escort you. It is from such things that a good reputation spreads among people, and your father and honored mother rejoice. Come, let us go washing at dawn's first light; I will go along with you as a helper, so that you may be ready as quickly as possible, since you will not remain a maiden much longer. Already the noblest men among all the Phaeacians, whose people are your own, are courting you. Come then, at early dawn urge your noble father to have the mules and wagon made ready, to carry the sashes and robes and gleaming coverlets. And it is far better for you yourself to ride this way rather than go on foot, since the washing pools are a long way from the city."

With these words gray-eyed Athena departed to Olympus, where they say the gods' seat stands forever secure: it is not shaken by winds, nor ever drenched by rain, nor does snow come near it, but a clear, cloudless brightness spreads all around, and white radiance runs over it; there the blessed gods delight all their days. There the gray-eyed goddess went, once she had spoken her message to the girl.

At once came fair-throned Dawn and woke Nausicaa of the lovely robes. She marveled at the dream straightaway, and went through the halls to tell her parents — her dear father and her mother. She found them both inside. Her mother was sitting by the hearth with her serving women, spinning sea-purple yarn on the spindle. Her father she met at the door as he was going out to join the renowned kings in council, where the noble Phaeacians had summoned him. She went up close to him and spoke to her dear father:

"Papa dear, won't you have the high wagon with good wheels made ready for me, so that I may take the fine clothes

ODYSSEY VI. 3

to wash at the river the garments that lie soiled before me;
and it is fitting for you yourself, who are among the foremost men, 60
to take counsel with clean clothing on your body.
Five dear sons have been born to you in the palace,
two of them married, and three still in the bloom of youth as bachelors;
and these always wish to go to the dance
wearing freshly washed garments—all of this is my concern." 65
So she spoke; for she was ashamed to mention the thought of marriage
to her dear father. But he understood everything and replied:
"I do not begrudge you the mules, my child, nor anything else.
Go; and the servants will make ready for you a high wagon,
well-wheeled, fitted with a rail above." 70
So saying, he called out to the servants, and they obeyed.
Some outside made ready the smooth-running mule-cart,
brought up the mules and yoked them beneath the wagon;
and the girl brought out from her chamber the shining garments.
She placed them in the well-polished wagon, 75
and her mother put in a chest all manner of food to satisfy the heart,
and set in delicacies, and poured wine
into a goatskin flask; and the girl climbed up into the wagon.
Her mother gave her golden oil in a flask,
so that she and her handmaidens might anoint themselves. 80
She took the whip and the gleaming reins
and struck to drive; the mules clattered forth;
they strained without stopping, carrying the clothes and the girl herself,
not alone, for the other handmaidens walked along with her.
When they reached the beautiful stream of the river, 85
where the washing-pools were always full, and much fine water
flowed up abundantly, enough to cleanse even the most soiled things,
there they unhitched the mules from the wagon,
and drove them along the eddying river
to graze on the sweet grass; and from the wagon 90
the women lifted the garments with their hands and carried them into the dark water,
and trod them in the pits, swiftly competing with one another.

4 ODYSSEY, BOOK VI.

But when they had washed and cleaned away all the dirt,
they spread the clothes in a row along the shore, where the sea
washed the pebbles up onto the beach most.     95
Then they bathed and anointed themselves with rich olive oil,
and took their meal along the banks of the river,
and waited for the sun's rays to dry the clothes.
But when she and her handmaids had their fill of food,
they began to play with a ball, having thrown off their headbands.     100
Among them white-armed Nausicaa led the song.
As Artemis the arrow-shooter goes along the mountain,
either over towering Taygetus or over Erymanthus,
taking joy in boars and swift deer,
and with her the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus,     105
play in the fields; and Leto rejoices in her heart;
high above them all she holds her head and brow,
and is easily recognized, though all are beautiful—
so the unwedded girl stood out among her handmaids.
But when she was about to harness the mules and go home,     110
having folded the fine clothes,
then the goddess grey-eyed Athena devised another plan,
that Odysseus might wake and see the lovely-faced girl,
who would guide him to the city of the Phaeacian men.
So the princess threw the ball toward one of her maids,     115
but missed her, and threw it into the deep current,
and they cried out loudly. Then noble Odysseus awoke,
and sitting up he pondered in his heart and mind:
"Alas, to the land of what mortals have I come this time?
Are they insolent, wild, and without justice,     120
or are they hospitable, with a god-fearing mind?
A cry like that of women has come around me—
of nymphs, who haunt the steep peaks of mountains
and the springs of rivers and the grassy meadows.
Or am I somewhere near people of human speech?     125
Come, let me go and find out for myself."

ODYSSEY VI. 5

So speaking, noble Odysseus crept beneath the bushes,
and from the thick wood he broke with his heavy hand a branch
full of leaves, to cover the private parts of his body.
Then he went forth like a lion bred in the mountains, confident in his strength, 130
who goes out in rain and wind, his eyes
blazing; and he goes after cattle or sheep,
or after wild deer; his belly drives him
to make an attempt on the flocks and enter the stout fold—
so Odysseus was about to approach the girls with their lovely hair, 135
naked as he was; for necessity had come upon him.
He appeared terrible to them, crusted with sea-brine,
and they scattered, one here, one there, along the jutting headlands;
but the daughter of Alcinous alone stood her ground, for Athena
put courage in her heart and took the fear from her limbs. 140
She stood facing him and held her ground; and Odysseus deliberated
whether to clasp the knees of the lovely girl in supplication,
or to stand apart and speak to her with gentle words
[entreating her to show him the city and give him clothing].
As he pondered, it seemed to him better 145
to stand apart and address her with gentle words,
lest the girl take offense in her heart if he clasped her knees.
Immediately he spoke a winning and crafty word:
"I am at your knees, queen—are you a goddess or a mortal?
If you are one of the gods who hold the wide heaven, 150
then to Artemis, daughter of great Zeus,
I liken you most nearly in beauty, stature, and form.
But if you are one of the mortals who live upon the earth,
three times blessed are your father and your honored mother,
three times blessed your brothers; their hearts must always 155
warm with joy on your account,
watching such a blossom enter the dance.
But most blessed of all beyond others in his heart
is the one who shall weigh you down with gifts and lead you home as his bride.
For I have never yet seen with my eyes such a mortal, 160

— neither man nor woman: awe comes over me as I look at you.
Once, at Delos, beside the altar of Apollo,
I noticed a young shoot of a palm tree springing up —
for I went there too, and a great company followed me,
on the journey that was to bring me so much grief — 165
and just as then, when I saw that, I stood amazed in my heart
for a long while, since never before had such a thing risen from the earth,
so I marvel at you, lady, and am struck with wonder and dread exceedingly
to touch your knees; yet hard grief comes upon me.
Yesterday — the twentieth day — I escaped the wine-dark sea; 170
all that time the waves and the swift storms carried me
away from the island of Ogygia; and now a god has cast me here,
so that I may perhaps suffer some new evil here, for I do not think
it will stop — the gods will still bring much to pass before then.
But, queen, have pity; for it is to you first that I have come 175
after suffering many sorrows, and of the others I know no one
among the people who hold this city and land.
Show me the town, and give me some rag to throw about me,
if you had any wrapping for the clothes when you came here.
And may the gods grant you all that your heart desires — 180
a husband and a home, and may they bestow on you
noble harmony of mind; for there is nothing stronger or better
than when a man and wife, with one accord in their thoughts, keep house together;
many griefs it brings to their enemies,
and joy to their well-wishers — and they themselves know it best." 185
Then white-armed Nausicaa answered him:
"Stranger, since you seem to be neither a bad man nor a foolish one —
it is Olympian Zeus himself who dispenses fortune to men,
to the noble and the base, as he wills, to each one —
and he has surely given you this lot, and you must endure it nonetheless — 190
but now, since you have come to our city and our land,
you shall not lack for clothing or for anything else
that rightly belongs to a hard-pressed suppliant who comes before us.
I will show you the town, and I will tell you the name of the people.

The Phaeacians hold this city and this land,
and I am the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous,
from whom the Phaeacians derive their strength and might."

So she spoke, and gave orders to her fair-haired handmaids:
"Stop, my handmaids — where are you running off to at the sight of a man?
Do you think he is one of our enemies?
There is no mortal man alive, nor will there ever be,
who would come to the land of the Phaeacians bringing war,
for the gods love us greatly.
We live apart in the sea with its many waves,
at the world's edge, and no other mortal people mingle with us.
But this man is some wretched wanderer who has come here,
and we must take care of him now; for all strangers and beggars
come under the protection of Zeus, and a small gift is still a dear one.
So, handmaids, give the stranger food and drink,
and bathe him in the river, where there is shelter from the wind."

So she spoke, and they stopped and called to one another,
and they led Odysseus to a sheltered spot, as Nausicaa,
daughter of great-hearted Alcinous, had commanded.
They laid beside him a cloak and a tunic to wear,
and gave him liquid olive oil in a golden flask,
and told him to wash himself in the river's streams.
Then noble Odysseus spoke to the handmaids:
"Handmaids, stand back a little way, so that I myself
may wash the brine from my shoulders and anoint myself
with the oil; it has been a long time since my skin has known it.
But I will not bathe while you are watching; for I am ashamed
to undress among girls with their lovely hair."

So he spoke, and they withdrew and told the girl.
Then noble Odysseus washed the brine from his skin in the river —
the brine that covered his back and his broad shoulders —
and from his head he scrubbed the scurf of the barren sea.
And when he had washed himself all over and anointed himself with oil,
he put on the clothing that the unwed girl had given him,

Athena, born of Zeus, made him appear taller and broader, and from his head she made his hair flow in thick curls, like the hyacinth flower. As when a craftsman skilled in his art — one whom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught every kind of craft — overlays silver with gold and produces graceful work, so she shed grace upon his head and shoulders. Then he went apart and sat down on the shore of the sea, radiant with beauty and charm; and the girl gazed at him. Then she spoke to her fair-tressed handmaids:

"Listen to me, white-armed handmaids, while I say something. Not without the will of all the gods who hold Olympus does this man come among the godlike Phaeacians. Before, he seemed base and wretched to me, but now he resembles the gods who hold the wide heavens. If only a man like this were to be called my husband, living here and content to remain. But come, handmaids, give the stranger food and drink."

So she spoke, and they listened to her and obeyed. They set food and drink beside Odysseus, and the much-enduring noble Odysseus drank and ate eagerly, for he had long been without nourishment.

But white-armed Nausicaa turned her mind to other things. She folded the clothes and placed them in the fine wagon, yoked the strong-hoofed mules, and climbed up herself. She urged Odysseus on and spoke to him, calling him by name:

"Rise now, stranger, and let us go to the city, so that I may escort you to my wise father's house, where I tell you you shall meet all the best of the Phaeacians. But do this — you seem to me to be no fool: as long as we are traveling through the fields and the farmlands, walk quickly with my handmaids behind the mules and the wagon; I will lead the way. But when we reach the city, which a wall surrounds,

ODYSSEY VI. 9

It is tall, and on either side of the city there is a fine harbor,
with a narrow entrance; curved ships are hauled up
along the road, for each man has his own boathouse. 265
There too is their assembly place, around the beautiful precinct of Poseidon,
fitted together with hewn stones set deep in the ground.
There they attend to the tackle of their black ships,
cables and sailcloth, and there they smooth their oars.
For the Phaeacians care nothing for the bow or the quiver, 270
but only for masts and oars and well-balanced ships,
in which they delight as they cross the gray sea.
It is that ill-sounding rumor I would avoid, lest someone
blame me afterward; for the people are very arrogant throughout the town,
and some baser man who met us might say: 275
'Who is this tall and handsome stranger following Nausicaa?
Where did she find him? He will surely be her husband.
Either she has taken in some wanderer from his ship,
a man from a distant land, since there is none near here,
or some god she prayed to has come down to her from heaven 280
and will keep her for all time.
Better so, if she has gone and found herself a husband
from elsewhere; for she looks down on the Phaeacians here in the town,
the many fine men who court her.'
That is what they will say, and it would bring shame upon me. 285
And indeed I would blame another woman who did such things—
one who, against the will of her dear father and mother,
consorted with men before coming to an open marriage.
Stranger, take heed of what I say, so that you may quickly
win escort and homecoming from my father. 290
You will find a splendid grove of Athena near the road,
of poplar trees; a spring flows within it, and meadows lie around it.
There is my father's estate and his flourishing orchard,
as far from the city as a man's voice carries when he shouts.
Sit there and wait for a time, until we 295
have come into the city and reached my father's house.

But when she thinks we have reached home,
then go with the Phaeacians into the city and ask for
the house of my father, great-hearted Alcinous.
It is easy to recognize, and even a young child could guide you,
for nothing like it has been built among the people
of the Phaeacians, such is the palace of the hero Alcinous.
But when the halls and courtyard have enclosed you,
pass quickly through the great hall until you reach
my mother; she sits by the hearth in the firelight,
spinning sea-purple yarn — a wonder to behold —
leaning against a pillar, and her handmaids sit behind her.
There my father's chair is set close beside her,
and he sits there drinking his wine like an immortal.
Pass him by and throw your arms about my mother's knees,
so that you may see your day of homecoming
rejoicing swiftly, even if you come from very far away.
[If she looks on you with kindness in her heart,
then there is hope that you will see your dear ones and reach
your well-built home and your own native land.]"

With these words she struck the mules with her shining whip,
and they quickly left the streams of the river.
They trotted well and stepped nimbly with their feet,
and she drove them carefully, so that the attendants on foot
and Odysseus could keep pace; she applied the whip with skill.
The sun set, and they reached the famous sacred grove
of Athena, where noble Odysseus sat down.
At once he prayed to the daughter of great Zeus:
"Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone!
Listen to me now at last, since you never heard me before
when I was being destroyed, when the famous earthshaker struck me.
Grant that I come among the Phaeacians as one loved and pitied."

So he spoke in prayer, and Pallas Athena heard him.
But she did not yet appear to him face to face, for she stood in awe
of her father's brother, who raged fiercely
against godlike Odysseus until he reached his homeland.

ODYSSEY, BOOK VII.

The entry of Odysseus to Alcinous.

So there much-enduring, noble Odysseus prayed, while the strength of the mules carried the girl toward the city. And when she reached her father's glorious house, she stopped the mules in the gateway, and her brothers, like immortals in appearance, gathered around her and unharnessed the mules from under the wagon and carried the clothing inside. She herself went to her chamber, where an old woman, the chambermaid Eurymêdousa from Apeirê, kindled a fire for her — the curved ships had once brought her from Apeirê, and she had been chosen as the prize of honor for Alcinous, since he ruled over all the Phaeacians and the people listened to him like a god. She had raised white-armed Nausicaa in the palace, and now she lit the fire and prepared supper within.

At that same moment Odysseus set out to go into the city. Athena, looking kindly upon Odysseus, shed a thick mist all around him, so that none of the great-hearted Phaeacians, meeting him, might taunt him with words and ask him who he was. But just as he was about to enter the lovely city, the goddess gray-eyed Athena met him, taking the form of a young girl carrying a water jug. She stood before him, and noble Odysseus asked her: "My child, could you guide me to the house of the man Alcinous, who rules as king among this people? For I am a stranger who has come here after much suffering,

12 ODYSSEY, BOOK VII

from far away, out of a distant land; I know none
of the people who inhabit this city and tend its fields."
Then the goddess gray-eyed Athena answered him:
"Very well then, father stranger, I will show you the house you ask me
to point out, since it stands close to my own blameless father's home.
But come, walk in silence; I will lead you on the way,
and do not look at any of the people, or question them.
For these folk do not readily welcome strangers,
nor do they greet with friendship one who comes from elsewhere.
They trust in their swift ships and cross the great
gulf of sea, for the Earth-Shaker granted them this gift;
their ships are as swift as a wing or a thought."
So she spoke and led the way, Pallas Athena,
swiftly; and he followed in the goddess's footsteps.
The Phaeacians, famed for their ships, did not notice him
as he moved through the city among them; for Athena,
the fair-tressed, dread goddess, would not allow it, and she shed
a wondrous mist about him, with kindly thought in her heart.
And Odysseus marveled at the harbors and the well-trimmed ships,
and the assembly places of the heroes themselves, and the long walls,
high and fitted with palisades — a wonder to behold.
But when they reached the glorious palace of the king,
the gray-eyed goddess Athena began to speak:
"Here it is, father stranger — the house you asked me
to point out. You will find the god-nurtured kings
feasting inside. Go in, and let your heart
feel no fear; a bold man fares better in all
his endeavors, even if he comes from somewhere far away.
First you will find the lady of the house in the great hall;
her name is Arete, and she is descended from the same parents
who also gave birth to King Alcinous.
Poseidon the Earth-Shaker first fathered Nausithous
on Periboea, finest in beauty among women,
the youngest daughter of great-hearted Eurymedon,

ODYSSEY VII. 13

who once was king over the proud-hearted Giants.
But he destroyed his reckless people and was himself destroyed, 60
and Poseidon lay with her and fathered a son,
great-hearted Nausithous, who ruled over the Phaeacians;
and Nausithous begot Rhexenor and Alcinous.
Rhexenor Apollo of the silver bow struck down
while still a bridegroom in his hall, leaving behind a single child, 65
Arete; and Alcinous made her his wife,
and honored her as no other woman on earth is honored,
of all the women who today keep house under their husbands' rule.
Such is the honor she has had and still has at heart,
from her dear children and from Alcinous himself, 70
and from the people, who look upon her as a goddess
and greet her with words whenever she walks through the city.
For she herself is not lacking in good sense;
she resolves quarrels even for men toward whom she is well disposed.
If she looks upon you with kindness in her heart, 75
then there is hope that you will see your dear ones and reach
your high-roofed home and your native land."
  So speaking, grey-eyed Athena departed
over the barren sea, and left lovely Scheria,
and came to Marathon and broad-streeted Athens, 80
and entered the sturdy palace of Erechtheus. But Odysseus
made his way toward the glorious halls of Alcinous; his heart
stirred greatly as he stood there, before he reached the bronze threshold.
For a radiance like that of the sun or moon
shone through the high-roofed hall of great-hearted Alcinous. 85
Bronze walls ran along either side,
from the threshold to the inner room, with a frieze of dark blue enamel around them;
golden doors enclosed the well-built house within;
silver doorposts stood upon the bronze threshold,
and a silver lintel above, with a golden handle. 90
On either side were dogs of gold and silver,
which Hephaestus had fashioned with his cunning craft

to guard the house of great-hearted Alcinous,
being immortal and ageless all their days.
And along the walls, set here and there from threshold to inner chamber, were thrones,
over which fine, well-spun cloths were laid, the handiwork of women.
There the leaders of the Phaeacians would sit     95
drinking and eating, for they had abundance year-round.
Golden youths stood upon well-built pedestals,     100
holding in their hands blazing torches,
giving light through the night to the feasters in the hall.
And fifty serving women in the palace —
some grind the golden grain on millstones,
others weave at the loom and ply their distaffs     105
as they sit, like the leaves of a tall poplar tree;
and the liquid oil drips from the finely woven cloth.
As much as the Phaeacians surpass all men
in driving a swift ship upon the sea, so too their women
excel at the loom; for Athena has granted them above all     110
knowledge of beautiful crafts and noble minds.
Outside the courtyard, close to the gates, is a great orchard
of four acres, and a fence runs around it on both sides.
There tall trees grow in abundance,
pear trees and pomegranates and apple trees with gleaming fruit,     115
sweet figs and thriving olive trees.
Their fruit never perishes or fails,
in winter or summer, through the whole year; but always
the West Wind, breathing gently, causes some to bud and others to ripen.
Pear ripens upon pear, apple upon apple,     120
cluster of grapes upon cluster of grapes, and fig upon fig.
There too a flourishing vineyard is rooted,
one part of which, a level threshing-floor in an open spot,
is drying in the sun, while other grapes men are harvesting,
and others they are treading; in front are unripe grapes     125
that are shedding their blossom, while others are turning dark.

There, well-ordered garden beds grow along the lowest row,
blooming in abundance of every kind.
And two springs are there: one scatters its water
throughout the garden, while the other flows beneath the courtyard threshold
toward the great house, from which the townspeople draw water.
Such were the glorious gifts of the gods in Alcinous's palace.

There the much-enduring, noble Odysseus stood and marveled.
When he had gazed upon everything to his heart's content,
he quickly stepped over the threshold and went inside the house.
He found the leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians
pouring libations from their cups to the keen-sighted Slayer of Argus,
to whom they would pour the last libation when they thought of sleep.
Then through the hall went the much-enduring, noble Odysseus,
wrapped in a thick mist which Athena had shed around him,
until he reached Arete and King Alcinous.
Odysseus threw his arms around the knees of Arete,
and at that moment the divine mist that had surrounded him dissolved.
The people in the hall fell silent at the sight of a man,
and gazed in wonder; but Odysseus made his supplication:
"Arete, daughter of godlike Rhexenor,
I come to your husband and to your knees, after much suffering,
and to these guests at your feast — may the gods grant them
prosperity in their lives, and may each one pass on
his wealth in the halls to his children, along with whatever honor the people have given him.
But for me, urge on my escort so that I may reach my homeland
more quickly, since I have long been suffering far from those I love."

So saying, he sat down on the hearth in the ashes,
beside the fire; and all of them fell completely silent.
At last the old hero Echeneus spoke up,
who was the most senior among the Phaeacian men
and excelled in speech, knowing many things from times past;
with good will he addressed them and said:
"Alcinous, this is neither fitting nor proper,
for a stranger to sit on the ground by the hearth in the ashes —

16 ODYSSEY, BOOK VII

and these men are waiting here, eager to hear your word.
But come now, seat the stranger on a silver-studded throne,
raising him up, and bid the heralds mix wine,
so that we may pour libations to Zeus who delights in thunder,
who attends upon suppliants together with the revered— 165
and let the housekeeper give the stranger supper from what is within."

When the mighty spirit of Alcinous heard this,
he took the resourceful, crafty-minded Odysseus by the hand
and raised him from the hearth and seated him on a shining throne,
making his own beloved son Laodamas rise, 190
who had been sitting closest to him and was his most cherished.
A handmaid brought water for the hands and poured it from a beautiful
golden pitcher over a silver basin,
for him to wash; and beside him she spread a polished table.
The revered housekeeper brought bread and set it before him, 175
placing many foods, giving freely of what was at hand.
And the much-enduring noble Odysseus ate and drank.
Then the mighty spirit of Alcinous spoke to the herald:
"Pontonous, mix a bowl of wine and serve it
to all throughout the hall, so that we may pour libations to Zeus who delights in thunder, 180
who attends upon suppliants together with the revered."

So he spoke, and Pontonous mixed the honey-hearted wine
and served it to all, going around with the cups.
And when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their hearts desired,
Alcinous addressed them and spoke among them: 185
"Hear me, leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians,
so that I may say what the spirit in my breast bids me.
Now, after feasting, go home to take your rest;
but at dawn let us summon more of the elders
and entertain the stranger in our halls, and to the gods 190
offer fine sacrifices, and then we shall think also of his escort,
so that the stranger may reach his homeland
joyfully and swiftly under our convoy, without toil or hardship,
even if he comes from very far away,

and let him suffer no evil or harm in between
until he sets foot on his own land; and there afterward
he shall endure whatever Fate and the heavy Spinners
spun into his thread of life at his birth when his mother bore him.
But if some immortal has come down from heaven,
then the gods are planning something different from before. 200
For always in the past the gods have appeared plainly
to us, whenever we offer glorious hecatombs,
and they feast beside us, seated where we sit.
And even if a lone wayfarer meets one of them,
they make no concealment, since we are close to them, 205
just as the Cyclopes are, and the wild tribes of Giants."

Then resourceful Odysseus answered him and said:
"Alcinous, let that be no concern of yours in your mind; for I
am not at all like the immortals who hold the wide heavens,
neither in body nor in build, but rather like mortal men, 210
those among men whom you know best as bearing the greatest
misery — with them I could match myself in suffering.
And I could tell of still more hardships beyond,
all that I have toiled through by the will of the gods.
But let me eat my supper, grief-stricken as I am; 215
for nothing is more shameless than the hateful belly,
which forces a man to remember it under compulsion
even when he is worn out and has sorrow in his heart.
So I too have sorrow in my heart, yet my belly
always bids me eat and drink, and makes me forget 220
all that I have suffered, and commands me to fill it.
But do you stir yourselves at the first light of dawn,
so that you may set me, wretched as I am, upon my homeland,
much though I have suffered; and even at the sight of it let life
leave me, my possessions, my serving-women, and my great high-roofed house." 225

So he spoke, and all of them praised his words and urged
that the stranger be escorted home, since he had spoken fittingly.
And when they had made libation and drunk as much as their hearts desired,

18 ODYSSEY, BOOK VII

The others went homeward each to his own bed,
but godlike Odysseus remained in the hall, 230
and beside him sat Arete and godlike Alcinous,
while the handmaids cleared away the gear of the feast.
Among them white-armed Arete was the first to speak,
for she had recognized the cloak and tunic when she saw them—
fine garments she herself had made with her handmaidens— 235
and she addressed him with winged words:
"Stranger, I myself will ask you this first:
who are you, and where are you from? Who gave you these clothes?
Did you not say you came here wandering over the sea?"

Then Odysseus of many counsels answered her:
"It is hard, my queen, to recount my sorrows without end, 241
since the gods of heaven have given me so many.
But this I will tell you, what you ask and inquire about.
There is an island called Ogygia, far off in the sea,
where the daughter of Atlas, crafty Calypso, dwells— 245
she of the lovely hair, a dread goddess. None
mingles with her, neither gods nor mortal men.
But me, unhappy wretch, some god brought to her hearth
alone, for Zeus had driven and shattered my swift ship
with a bright thunderbolt in the middle of the wine-dark sea. 250
There all my other noble companions perished,
but I, throwing my arms around the keel of the rolling ship,
drifted for nine days. On the tenth dark night
the gods brought me to the island of Ogygia, where Calypso
dwells, she of the lovely hair, a dread goddess, who taking me in 255
cared for me warmly and fed me, and promised
she would make me immortal and ageless all my days.
But she never persuaded the heart within my breast.
There I stayed seven full years, and always
I soaked with tears the immortal garments Calypso gave me. 260
But when the eighth year came rolling round,
then she urged me and bade me go on my way—

ODYSSEY VII. 19

by a message from Zeus, or her own heart turned to it.
She sent me on my way on a well-bound raft, and gave me many things,
bread and sweet wine, and clothed me in immortal garments, 265
and sent a warm and harmless wind to speed me.
For seventeen days I sailed across the sea,
and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains
of your land appeared, and my heart rejoiced—
poor wretch that I was! For I was still to meet with great misery, 270
which Poseidon the earthshaker stirred up against me.
He drove the winds against me and blocked my path,
and roused the sea to a boundless fury, nor did the waves
allow me to ride on my raft, as I groaned again and again.
Then the storm scattered the raft, but I myself 275
swam across this gulf, until the wind and water
brought me near and drove me to your shore.
There as I tried to land the waves would have hurled me
against the great rocks in a joyless place,
but I drew back and swam again, until I came 280
to a river, where the place seemed best to me,
smooth of rocks, and sheltered from the wind.
I fell out, gasping for breath, and divine night came on.
Moving away from the heaven-fed river,
I lay down to sleep in the bushes, and heaped leaves 285
around me; and a god poured sleep over me without measure.
There among the leaves, with a heavy heart,
I slept through the night and into the dawn and midday;
the sun was setting when sweet sleep released me.
I noticed the handmaids of your daughter playing 290
on the shore, and she herself was among them, like a goddess.
I made my appeal to her; and she showed no lack of good judgment—
more than you would expect from someone so young who met you;
for the young are always thoughtless.
She gave me enough bread and gleaming wine, 295
and washed me in the river, and gave me these clothes.
This is the truth I have told you, grieved though I am."

20 ODYSSEY, BOOK VII

Then Alcinous answered him and spoke:
"Stranger, in this my daughter showed no proper judgment,
in that she did not bring you with her handmaidens 300
to our house; yet it was to her you first made supplication."
Then the resourceful Odysseus answered him and said:
"Hero, do not blame your blameless daughter on that account;
for she did tell me to follow with the handmaidens,
but I was unwilling, from fear and also from shame, 305
lest somehow your heart too might take offense at the sight;
for we are a jealous race, we tribes of men upon the earth."
Then Alcinous answered him and spoke:
"Stranger, my heart within my breast is not the sort
to grow angry without cause; all that is fitting is better. 310
Would that it were so — O Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo —
that you, being such as you are, sharing my own thoughts,
might take my daughter and be called my son-in-law,
staying here; and I would give you a house and possessions,
if you were willing to remain; but against your will no one 315
among the Phaeacians shall detain you — let that not be dear to Father Zeus.
And the escort I now appoint, so that you may know it well,
for tomorrow; during that time you shall lie subdued by sleep,
while they row over the calm sea, until you reach
your native land and home, and wherever is dear to you, 320
even if it is much farther away than Euboea,
which those of our people who saw it say is the farthest land,
when they carried fair-haired Rhadamanthus
to see Tityus, son of Gaea.
And they went there and accomplished the journey without hardship 325
on that very same day and returned home again.
And you yourself shall know in your heart how far the best
my ships and young men are at tossing up the brine with the oar."
So he spoke, and much-enduring noble Odysseus rejoiced,
and praying he spoke a word and addressed him: 330
"Father Zeus, may Alcinous bring to fulfillment all that he has said,

Alcinous: his fame upon the life-giving earth
would be undying, and I myself would reach my homeland."

So they spoke such things to one another,
and white-armed Arete commanded her handmaids 335
to place a bed beneath the portico and spread
beautiful purple blankets upon it, and lay rugs on top,
and place thick cloaks above to wrap around oneself.
The maids went from the hall holding torches in their hands,
and when they had busily spread the close-laid bed, 340
they stood beside Odysseus and urged him with words:
"Rise and come, stranger; your bed has been prepared."
So they spoke, and to him sleep seemed most welcome.
So there godlike, much-enduring Odysseus slept
on his corded bed beneath the resounding portico, 345
while Alcinous lay down in the inner chamber of his lofty house,
and beside him his lady wife arranged their bed and couch.

ODYSSEY, BOOK VIII

The introduction of Odysseus to the Phaeacians.

When early-born, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
the sacred might of Alcinous rose from his bed,
and up rose also the god-born sacker of cities, Odysseus.
The sacred might of Alcinous led them
to the Phaeacians' place of assembly, which had been built for them near the ships.        5
They came and sat down on the polished stones,
close together. Meanwhile Pallas Athena went through the city
in the likeness of the herald of wise Alcinous,
devising a return for great-hearted Odysseus,
and standing beside each man she spoke these words:        10
  "Come now, leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians,
go to the assembly, so that you may learn about the stranger,
who has lately come to the house of wise Alcinous,
having wandered over the sea, his form like that of the immortals."
So speaking, she stirred the spirit and heart of each one.        15
Quickly the meeting places and seats were filled
with men gathering together. Many marveled as they looked
upon the son of Laertes, the wise one. For Athena
poured wondrous grace upon his head and shoulders,
and made him appear taller and more broad,        20
so that he might be dear to all the Phaeacians
and inspire awe and respect, and accomplish the many
contests by which the Phaeacians were about to test Odysseus.
But when they were gathered and had come together,
Alcinous addressed them and spoke among them:        25

ODYSSEY VIII. 23

"Hear me, leaders and rulers of the Phaeacians,
that I may say what my heart bids me speak.
This stranger — I do not know who he is — has come wandering to my house,
whether from the peoples of the east or of the west;
he urges his escort and begs that it be guaranteed. 30
Let us, as we have done before, make ready his convoy.
For there is no one else who comes to my house
and lingers here in grief long for want of an escort.
Come then, let us drag a black ship down to the bright sea
for her maiden voyage, and let two and fifty young men 35
be chosen from the people, whoever have proved best before.
Let all of you lash the oars well to the thwarts
and step ashore; then come quickly to prepare a fine feast
at my house, and I will provide well for all.
These are my orders to the young men; but as for the rest of you, 40
you sceptered kings, come to my beautiful halls,
so that we may entertain the stranger in the palace;
let no one refuse. And summon the divine singer,
Demodocus; for the god has granted him above all others the gift of song,
to give delight in whatever way his spirit moves him to sing." 45
So speaking he led the way, and the sceptered kings followed with him;
and a herald went to fetch the divine singer.
The two and fifty chosen young men
went, as he commanded, to the shore of the barren sea.
And when they had come down to the ship and the sea, 50
they dragged the black ship down into the deep water,
and set up the mast and the sails in the black ship,
and fitted the oars in their leather oar-loops,
all in due order; and they spread the white sails.
They moored her high in the harbor; then afterward 55
they went to the great house of wise Alcinous.
The colonnades and courts and rooms of the men
were filled with people gathering; there were many, both young and old.
And for them Alcinous sacrificed twelve sheep,

Eight white-tusked boars and two cattle with shambling gait— 60
they flayed them and prepared a delightful feast.
A herald came close, leading the beloved bard
whom the Muse loved above all others, and had given him
both good and ill: she robbed him of his sight,
but gave him sweet song.
Pontonoos set a silver-studded chair for him 65
in the midst of the feasters, leaning it against a tall pillar,
and hung the clear-toned lyre from a peg
above his head, and showed him by hand where to reach for it.
The herald placed a fine basket and a table beside him,
and a cup of wine to drink whenever his spirit moved him. 70
The guests reached out their hands to the good things set before them.
When they had satisfied their desire for food and drink,
the Muse moved the bard to sing of the glorious deeds of men,
from a song whose fame at that time reached the wide heavens:
the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles, son of Peleus, 75
how once they had clashed at a rich feast of the gods
with violent words, and Agamemnon, lord of men,
rejoiced in his heart that the best of the Achaeans were fighting—
for so Phoebus Apollo had told him it would be
at holy Pytho, when he crossed the stone threshold 80
to consult the oracle; for then the beginning of suffering began to roll
upon Trojans and Danaans alike, through the plans of great Zeus.
This, then, the famous bard sang. But Odysseus,
taking his great purple cloak in his strong hands,
drew it down over his head and covered his handsome face; 85
for he was ashamed to let the Phaeacians see him weeping under his brows.
Whenever the divine bard would pause in his singing,
Odysseus would wipe his tears and draw the cloak from his head
and, taking the two-handled cup, would pour libation to the gods.
But whenever the best of the Phaeacians urged the bard to sing again, 90
delighting in his words,
Odysseus would cover his head again and weep.
There he shed tears unnoticed by all the others,

ODYSSEY VIII. 25

Alcinous alone noticed and perceived him
sitting close beside him, and heard him groaning heavily. 95
At once he addressed the oar-loving Phaeacians:
"Listen, leaders and rulers of the Phaeacians:
we have now satisfied our hearts with the equal feast
and with the lyre, which is the companion of a rich banquet;
now let us go out and make trial of all 100
the contests, so that the stranger may tell his dear ones
when he reaches home, how much we surpass others
in boxing, wrestling, leaping, and in footracing."
So speaking he led the way, and they followed after him.
The herald hung the clear-toned lyre back on its peg, 105
and took Demodocus by the hand and led him from the hall;
and he guided him along the same path that the other
nobles of the Phaeacians had taken, eager to watch the contests.
They went to the assembly-place, and with them followed a great crowd,
countless thousands; and many fine young men stood up. 110
Acroneus rose, and Ocyalus, and Elatreus,
Nauteus and Prymneus, and Anchialus and Eretmeus,
Ponteus and Proreus, Thoon and Anabesineus,
and Amphialus, son of Polyneus son of Tecton;
and Euryalus rose too, equal to Ares the destroyer of men, 115
son of Naubolus, who was the finest in beauty and build
of all the Phaeacians after noble Laodamas.
And the three sons of noble Alcinous stood up:
Laodamas, Halios, and godlike Clytoneus.
These first made trial in the foot-race. 120
From the starting point the course was laid out; and all together
they flew swiftly along, raising the dust of the plain.
Among them in running blameless Clytoneus was far the best;
as great a space as a pair of mules can furrow in a fallow field,
so far he drew ahead and reached the crowd, while the others were left behind. 125
Then they made trial of painful wrestling;
and there in turn Euryalus surpassed all the best men.

In the long jump Amphialus surpassed everyone; in the discus Elatreus was by far the best of all, and in boxing Laodamas, the noble son of Alcinous. When they had all delighted their hearts with the contests, the son of Alcinous, Laodamas, spoke among them:

"Come, friends, let us ask the stranger whether he knows and has learned any sport. His build at any rate is not poor — his thighs and shins, and both his hands above, his sturdy neck and great strength. He lacks nothing of youth, but has been broken by many hardships. For I say there is nothing worse than the sea to shatter a man, however strong he may be."

Then Euryalus answered him and said: "Laodamas, you have spoken this word very fittingly. Go yourself now and challenge him, and put the matter before him."

When the noble son of Alcinous heard this, he stepped forward into the middle and addressed Odysseus: "Come now, stranger father, try the contests yourself, if you have learned any; and it seems fitting that you should know sports.
