For there is no greater glory for a man as long as he lives than what he achieves with his feet and his hands. Come, make the attempt, and drive the sorrows from your heart. Your journey will not be delayed much longer — your ship is already hauled down to the sea and your crew is ready."

Then the man of many counsels, Odysseus, answered him: "Laodamas, why do you urge me to this, mocking me? Sorrows weigh on my heart far more than contests — I who have suffered greatly and toiled greatly before now, and sit here in the midst of your assembly longing for my homecoming, entreating your king and all the people."

Then Euryalus answered him in turn with a taunt: "No indeed, stranger, I would not take you for a man skilled in the contests such as are common among men, but rather for one who travels back and forth on a many-benched ship,

ODYSSEY VIII. 27

— neither captains of sailors nor traders,
mindful of cargo and overseers of profitable
and lucrative ventures; nor do you look like an athlete."

Then resourceful Odysseus, looking at him from beneath his brows, replied:
"Stranger, what you said was wrong — you speak like a reckless man.     166
So it is that the gods do not give all their gifts together
to men: neither handsome form, nor wisdom, nor eloquence.
For one man is lesser in appearance,
yet a god crowns his words with beauty, and those who look upon him     170
are delighted; he speaks with steady confidence
and gentle respect, and stands out among those assembled,
and as he walks through the city they look on him as a god.
Another again is like the immortals in appearance,
yet no grace is woven around his words,     175
just as in your case: your form is outstanding, and not even
a god could improve upon it, but your mind is hollow.
You have stirred the heart within my breast
by speaking without judgment. I am no stranger to contests,
as you claim, but I reckon myself to have been     180
among the first, for as long as I trusted in my youth and my hands.
Now I am held back by hardship and suffering; for I have endured much,
passing through the wars of men and the bitter waves.
But even so, having suffered much, I will try the contests;
for your words have bitten deep — you have provoked me by speaking."     185

He spoke, and leaping up, still in his cloak, he seized a discus,
larger and thicker, considerably heavier
than the one with which the Phaeacians were competing among themselves.
Whirling it around, he sent it flying from his powerful hand,
and the stone hummed; the Phaeacians, those men of the long oars,     190
famed for their ships, crouched down to the ground
under the rush of the stone; and it flew beyond all the markers,
speeding swiftly from his hand; and Athena set the marks,
taking the likeness of a man, and spoke these words:
"Even a blind man, stranger, could distinguish your mark,     195

handling it; for it is not at all mixed in with the crowd,
but far the best. Now take courage for this contest:
none of the Phaeacians will match or surpass it."

So he spoke, and much-enduring godlike Odysseus was glad,
rejoicing because he saw a friendly companion in the contest. 200
And then he addressed the Phaeacians in a lighter tone:
"Come up to this now, young men; and soon I think another
will fly as far, or even farther yet.
As for the rest, whoever his heart and spirit urge him,
let him come here and try, since you have angered me greatly, 205
whether in boxing or wrestling or in running — I refuse no one —
among all the Phaeacians, except Laodamas himself.
For he is my host: who would fight with one who befriends him?
Foolish indeed and worthless is that man
who challenges his host to a contest of games 210
among a foreign people; he cuts short his own advantage.
Of all the others I refuse and slight no one,
but I am willing to see and make trial face to face.
For I am no poor man in any of the contests men have.
I know well how to handle a well-polished bow; 215
I would be first to shoot a man with an arrow in the crowd
of enemy warriors, even if very many companions
stood close beside me and were shooting at men.
Only Philoctetes surpassed me with the bow
among the Trojan people, when we Achaeans used to shoot. 220
But of all others who now live as mortals upon the earth
eating bread, I claim to be far the best.
With men of former times I will not choose to compete,
neither with Heracles nor with Eurytus of Oechalia,
who even rivaled the immortals with the bow. 225
That is why great Eurytus died swiftly, and did not reach
old age in his halls; for Apollo slew him in anger,
because he challenged him to a contest of archery.
With a spear I can throw as far as another man shoots an arrow.

ODYSSEY VIII. 29

Among the Phaeacians I fear that someone may outrun me on foot — for I was broken too shamefully by many waves, since provisions aboard the ship were not plentiful, and so my limbs have grown weak." 230

So he spoke, and they all fell into hushed silence; but Alcinous alone answered him and said: 235

"Stranger, since you have not spoken these words among us without cause, but wish to show the excellence that attends you — being angry that this man stood beside you in the contest and taunted you, as though no mortal who knew how to speak sensibly could ever disparage your excellence — 240 come now, take heed of my words, so that you may tell them to another hero when you are feasting in your halls beside your wife and children, remembering our excellence, and what deeds Zeus assigns to us continually, as he did to our fathers before us. 245 For we are not faultless boxers or wrestlers, but we run swiftly on foot and are the best with ships; the feast is always dear to us, and the lyre and dancing, fresh changes of clothing, warm baths, and bed. 250 But come, all you Phaeacians who are the best dancers, make sport, so that the stranger may tell his friends when he returns home how much we surpass all others in seamanship, in running, in dancing, and in song. Let someone go at once and fetch the clear-toned lyre for Demodocus, which lies somewhere in our halls." 255

So spoke godlike Alcinous, and a herald rose to fetch the hollow lyre from the king's house. The chosen stewards — nine in all, public officials who set everything in order at the games — rose up and smoothed the dancing floor and cleared a fine broad space. 260 The herald came near carrying the clear-toned lyre for Demodocus; and he then moved to the center, and around him stood young men in the first flower of youth, skilled in dancing,

30 ODYSSEY, BOOK VIII.

They struck the sacred dancing floor with their feet. But Odysseus
watched the flickering of their feet and marveled in his heart. 265
And the lyre-player struck up and began his beautiful song.

* * * * * * *

So the renowned bard sang these things; and Odysseus
took delight in his heart as he listened, as did the others,
the Phaeacians of the long oars, men famed for their ships.
Alcinous ordered Halius and Laodamas 370
to dance alone, since no one could compete with them.
So when they took the beautiful ball in their hands,
the purple one that skillful Polybus had made for them,
one of them would hurl it toward the shadowy clouds,
bending back; and the other, leaping high from the ground, 375
would catch it easily before his feet touched the earth again.
And after they had tried throwing the ball straight up,
they danced close together on the bountiful earth,
exchanging it rapidly; and the other young men
standing along the arena beat time, and a great clapping arose. 380
Then noble Odysseus spoke to Alcinous:
"Alcinous, mighty lord, most distinguished of all your people,
you boasted that your dancers were the best,
and so it has proved to be; I am filled with wonder as I watch."
So he spoke, and the sacred strength of Alcinous rejoiced, 385
and he quickly spoke among the Phaeacians who love the oar:
"Hear me, leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians:
this stranger seems to me a man of great good sense.
Come then, let us give him a guest-gift, as is proper.
For twelve distinguished kings rule as lords 390
throughout our land, and I myself am the thirteenth;
let each of them bring a fresh-washed cloak and tunic
and a talent of precious gold.
Let us quickly bring everything together, so that the stranger
may go to dinner with these gifts in his hands, rejoicing in his heart. 395

ODYSSEY VIII. 31

Let Euryalus make amends to him in person, with words
and with a gift, since he spoke words that were not fitting."

So he spoke, and they all approved and urged it,
and each man sent a herald to bring the gifts.
Then Euryalus answered him and said:          400
"Alcinous, lord, most distinguished of all your people,
then indeed I will make amends to the stranger, as you command.
I will give him this all-bronze sword, on which there is
a silver hilt, and a scabbard of freshly-sawn ivory
fitted around it; it will be worth a great deal to him."          405

So saying, he placed in his hands the silver-studded sword,
and spoke to him with these winged words:
"Hail, father and stranger; and if any harsh word has been spoken,
may the storm-winds snatch it up and carry it off at once.
May the gods grant you to see your wife and reach your homeland,          410
since you have long been suffering hardships far from your dear ones."

Then resourceful Odysseus answered him and said:
"And you too, my friend, fare very well; may the gods grant you happiness,
and may you never hereafter feel the want of this sword
which you have given me, making amends with your words."          415

So he spoke, and slung the silver-studded sword about his shoulders.
The sun set, and the splendid gifts were brought to him;
the noble heralds carried them to Alcinous's palace,
and the blameless sons of Alcinous received them
and laid the beautiful gifts beside their revered mother.          420
The sacred strength of Alcinous led them,
and coming in they sat down on the high-backed chairs.
Then the mighty Alcinous spoke to Arete:
"Come, wife, bring the finest and most splendid chest;
place in it a well-washed cloak and a tunic.          425
Heat bronze over the fire for him, and warm some water,
so that after he has bathed and seen all the gifts
laid out in order, which the blameless Phaeacians have brought here,
he may take pleasure in the feast and in hearing the song of the bard."

32 ODYSSEY, BOOK VIII.

"And I will give him this beautiful cup of mine, 430
golden, so that remembering me all his days
he may pour libations in his hall to Zeus and to the other gods."
  So she spoke, and Arete told her handmaids
to set a great cauldron over the fire as quickly as possible.
They set the bathing cauldron over the blazing fire, 435
poured water into it, and brought wood to kindle beneath it.
The fire wrapped around the belly of the cauldron, and the water grew warm.
Meanwhile Arete brought out from the storeroom a beautiful chest for the stranger,
and placed inside it the splendid gifts—
the clothing and the gold which the Phaeacians had given— 440
and she herself placed in it a fine cloak and a tunic,
and spoke to him with winged words:
  "Now see to the lid yourself, and quickly tie a knot upon it,
so that no one may do you harm along the road, when again
you sleep your sweet sleep aboard the dark ship." 445
  When much-enduring noble Odysseus heard this,
he at once fitted the lid and quickly fastened the knot upon it,
the intricate one which lady Circe had once taught his mind.
Then the housekeeper straightway bade him go to bathe,
stepping into the tub; and he gladly saw with his heart 450
the warm bath, since he had not been accustomed to such care
since he had left the house of Calypso of the lovely hair;
but there his care had been constant, as though from a god.
When the handmaids had bathed him and anointed him with oil,
and thrown a fine cloak and a tunic around him, 455
he stepped out of the bath and went among the men at their wine.
And Nausicaa, who had beauty given by the gods,
stood beside a pillar of the well-built hall,
and gazed at Odysseus with wonder in her eyes,
and spoke to him with winged words: 460
  "Farewell, stranger, so that even when you are in your homeland
you may remember me, since it is to me first that you owe your life's ransom."
  Then in answer to her spoke Odysseus of many counsels:

ODYSSEY VIII. 33

"Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous,
may Zeus now grant it — the thundering husband of Hera —
that I reach home and see the day of my return;
then even there I would pray to you as to a goddess
all my days forever, for you gave me life, my girl."
So he spoke, and sat down beside king Alcinous.
They were already dividing out portions and mixing wine. 470
A herald came near, leading the beloved bard
Demodocus, honored among the people; he seated him
in the midst of the feasters, propping him against a tall pillar.
Then resourceful Odysseus spoke to the herald,
cutting off a portion of the back — and there was still more left — 475
of the white-tusked boar, rich with fat on either side:
"Herald, take this piece of meat and give it to Demodocus
to eat, and I will greet him, grieved as I am.
For among all people on the face of the earth, bards
deserve honor and reverence, because the Muse 480
has taught them the paths of song and loved the race of bards."
So he spoke, and the herald carried it and placed it
in the hands of the hero Demodocus, who received it and was glad at heart.
The others reached out their hands to the ready food set before them.
But when they had put away their desire for drink and food, 485
then resourceful Odysseus addressed Demodocus:
"Demodocus, I praise you above all mortal men;
either the Muse, daughter of Zeus, taught you, or Apollo.
For you sing very truly of the fate of the Achaeans,
all they did and suffered and all they toiled through, 490
as if you had been there yourself or heard it from one who was.
But come now, change your song and sing of the building
of the wooden horse, which Epeius made with Athena's help,
the trick which noble Odysseus once brought up to the citadel,
having filled it with the men who sacked Troy. 495
If you tell me this tale in its proper order,

"I shall straightway tell all people
how a god in his grace granted you the gift of divine song."
So he spoke, and the bard, moved by the god, began, and unfolded his song,
starting from the point where the Argives, having set fire to their huts,
were sailing away on their well-benched ships, 500
while others by then were sitting around the renowned Odysseus
in the assembly of the Trojans, hidden within the horse—
for the Trojans themselves had dragged it up to the citadel.
So it stood there, and the people sitting around it
debated at length without resolution; three courses pleased them: 505
either to split the hollow timber with pitiless bronze,
or to drag it to the cliff's edge and hurl it down the rocks,
or to leave it standing as a great offering to appease the gods—
which is indeed what was destined to come to pass in the end.
For it was fated that the city should perish once it enclosed 510
the great wooden horse, within which sat all the best
of the Argives, bearing death and destruction to the Trojans.
He sang how the sons of the Achaeans sacked the city,
pouring forth from the horse, abandoning their hollow ambush.
He sang how different men sacked different quarters of the steep city, 515
and how Odysseus went, like Ares, to the house of Deiphobus,
together with godlike Menelaus.
There, he sang, Odysseus dared the most terrible battle
and won it in the end through the aid of great-hearted Athena.
These were the songs the famous bard was singing; but Odysseus 520
was melting, and tears wet his cheeks beneath his eyelids.
As a woman weeps, throwing herself over her dear husband
who has fallen before his city and his people,
warding off the pitiless day from his city and his children—
she sees him dying and gasping, 525
and clinging to him she wails aloud; but men behind her,
striking her back and shoulders with their spears,
lead her away into slavery to endure toil and misery—
her cheeks waste away with the most pitiful grief; 530

So Odysseus shed a pitiful tear beneath his brows.
He was shedding tears there, unnoticed by all the others,
but Alcinous alone perceived and noticed him
as he sat close beside him, and heard him groaning heavily.
At once he addressed the Phaeacians, lovers of the oar: 535
   "Hear me, leaders and counselors of the Phaeacians:
let Demodocus now set aside his clear-toned lyre,
for not everyone here is delighted by what he sings.
Ever since we began our supper and the divine singer arose,
our guest has not once ceased from his sorrowful lamenting; 540
surely grief has come over his heart and encompassed his mind.
Come then, let the singer stop, so that we may all take pleasure alike,
hosts and guest together, for that is far better;
for all these things have been arranged in honor of the worthy guest —
the escort and the dear gifts that we give him out of affection. 545
A stranger and a suppliant is treated as a brother
by a man who has even a little understanding in his heart.
So do not now hide in crafty thoughts
what I ask you; it is better for you to speak out plainly.
Tell me the name by which your mother and father called you there, 550
and all the others in your city and those who dwell around it.
For no one among men is wholly nameless,
neither low nor noble, once he is born into the world,
but parents give a name to all, once they have brought them forth.
Tell me your land, your people, and your city, 555
so that our ships may convey you there, guided by their own minds.
For the Phaeacians have no helmsmen,
nor any rudders such as other ships possess;
but the ships themselves know the thoughts and minds of men,
and they know all the cities and rich farmlands 560
of mankind, and they cross the gulf of the sea most swiftly,
wrapped in mist and cloud; and never is there
any danger to them of suffering harm or being lost.
But this is what I once heard my father say:

of Nausithous, who said that Poseidon was angry
with us, because we are escort guides, safe for all.
He said that one day he would shatter a fine ship of the Phaeacians
as it returned from an escort through the misty sea,
and would bury our city beneath a great mountain.
So the old man spoke; and the god may bring it to pass,
or leave it unfulfilled, as his heart sees fit.
But come, tell me this and recount it truthfully:
where were you driven off course, and what lands of men
did you come to — both the peoples and their well-inhabited cities —
as many as were harsh and savage and unjust,
and those who were hospitable, and had a god-fearing mind.
Tell me why you weep and grieve within your heart
when you hear of the fate of the Argive Danaans and of Ilium.
The gods brought that about, and spun destruction
for men, so that it might be a song for those yet to come.
Or did some kinsman of yours die before Ilium,
a noble man — a son-in-law or father-in-law, those who are
closest to us after our own blood and kin?
Or perhaps some companion, a man of dear understanding,
a good man? For a wise companion
is no less dear than a brother."

"I could not tell of all of them, nor name them,
all the wives and daughters of heroes that I saw;
for before that the immortal night would pass away. And now it is time    330
to sleep, whether going to the swift ship among my companions
or staying here; the escort shall be the concern of the gods and of you."

So he spoke, and they all fell into hushed silence,
and were held spellbound throughout the shadowy hall.
Among them white-armed Arete began to speak:    335

"Phaeacians, how does this man appear to you
in looks and stature, and the balanced mind within him?
Moreover, he is my guest — though each of you shares in the honor.
Do not be hasty to send him away, and do not cut short the gifts
for one who has such need; for many treasures    340
lie stored in your halls by the grace of the gods."

Then among them spoke the old hero Echeneus,
who was the most senior of the Phaeacian men:

"Friends, the wise queen does not speak wide of the mark or contrary to our reputation; do obey her.    345
But from Alcinous here depends both the deed and the word."

And Alcinous in turn answered him and said:
"This word shall indeed be so, as long as I
live and rule over the Phaeacians, lovers of the oar.
But let the stranger endure, much though he longs for his homecoming,    350
to remain nonetheless until tomorrow, until I can complete the full

38 ODYSSEY, Book XI

I will complete the gift of honor; and the escort will be the concern of all the men, and most of all of me, for the power in this land is mine."

Then the man of many counsels, Odysseus, answered him:
"Lord Alcinous, most distinguished of all people, even if you were to bid me stay here for a full year, and were to urge on my escort and give splendid gifts, even that I would choose, for it would be far more profitable to arrive in my dear homeland with a fuller hand; I would be more respected and more beloved by all the men who see me when I return to Ithaca."

Then in turn Alcinous answered and addressed him:
"Odysseus, when we look at you, we do not in the least take you for a cheat and a deceiver, such as the dark earth breeds in abundance among men scattered far and wide, who fashion lies from which no one could see through; but you have beauty of words upon you, and within you a noble mind, and you told your story with skill, as a singer would, the bitter sorrows of all the Argives and of yourself as well. But come, tell me this and recount it truly: did you see any of your godlike companions who followed you to Ilion and met their fate there? This night is very long, beyond all measure, and it is not yet time to sleep in the hall; tell me of your wondrous deeds. I could hold out until bright dawn, if only you would be willing to tell me your sorrows here in the hall."

Then the man of many counsels, Odysseus, answered him:
"Lord Alcinous, most distinguished of all people, there is a time for many words and a time for sleep as well; but if you are still eager to listen, I would not begrudge you that, nor refuse to tell you things yet more pitiable: the sorrows of my companions who perished afterward, those who escaped the grievous war-cry of the Trojans, but died on their homeward journey through the wickedness of an evil woman."

ODYSSEY, BOOK XIII.

The departure of Odysseus from the Phaeacians and his arrival at Ithaca.

So he spoke, and they all fell into hushed silence,
held spellbound throughout the shadowy hall.
Then Alcinous answered him and said:
"Odysseus, since you have come to my bronze-floored house,
with its high roof, I do not think you will wander    5
astray again before you reach home, however much you have suffered.
And to each one of you men I give this charge,
all who in my halls forever drink the deep red wine
of the elders and listen to the singer:
already the stranger's clothing lies in a polished chest,    10
along with intricately wrought gold and all the other
gifts that the counselors of the Phaeacians have brought here;
but come, let us each give him in addition a great tripod and a cauldron.
We will then recoup ourselves by a collection through the people,
for it is hard for one man to give freely without return."    15
So spoke Alcinous, and his words pleased them well.
Then they went off each to his own home to sleep,
and when early-born, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
they hurried to the ship, carrying the bronze that makes men strong.
The sacred might of Alcinous himself went aboard    16
and stowed it well under the benches, so that it would not hinder
any of the crew as they pulled hard at their oars.
Then they went to the house of Alcinous and prepared a feast.

For them the sacred strength of Alcinous sacrificed an ox
to Zeus, the dark-clouded son of Cronus, who rules over all. 25
They burned the thigh-pieces and feasted on a glorious banquet,
taking their pleasure; and among them sang the divine singer,
Demodocus, honored by the people. But Odysseus
kept turning his head toward the radiant sun,
eager for it to set, for he was longing to be on his way. 30
As when a man longs for his evening meal, one for whom all day
a pair of wine-dark oxen have dragged the jointed plow through the field,
and the light of the sun sets welcomingly for him
to go to his supper, and his knees ache as he walks—
so welcomingly did the light of the sun set for Odysseus. 35
At once he addressed the Phaeacians, lovers of the oar,
and spoke his words especially with an eye to Alcinous:
"Alcinous, lord, most distinguished of all your people,
pour a libation and send me on my way unharmed, and farewell to you yourselves;
for now all that my heart has desired has been accomplished— 40
an escort and loving gifts; may the gods of heaven
make these gifts a blessing to me; and may I find my blameless wife
at home when I return, with my dear ones safe and sound.
And may you, staying here, bring joy to your wedded wives
and your children; may the gods grant you excellence of every kind, 45
and may no evil fall upon your people."
So he spoke, and they all approved and urged
that the stranger be given his passage, for he had spoken fittingly.
And then the strength of Alcinous addressed the herald:
"Pontonous, mix a bowl and serve wine 50
to all throughout the hall, so that with a prayer to Zeus the Father
we may send the stranger on his way to his own native land."
So he spoke, and Pontonous mixed the honey-hearted wine
and served it round to all in turn; and they poured libations
to the blessed gods who hold the broad heaven, 55
right from where they sat. And noble Odysseus rose up,
placed the two-handled cup in Arete's hands,
and addressing her with winged words, spoke to her:

ODYSSEY XIII. 41

"Farewell to you, my queen, forever, until old age
and death come, as they come to all people.
But I am going home; take your joy in this house
with your children and your people and King Alcinous."

So saying, godlike Odysseus crossed over the threshold.
The strength of Alcinous sent a herald along with him
to lead him to the swift ship and the shore of the sea; 65
and Arete sent along with him slave women,
one carrying a freshly washed robe and tunic,
and another she sent to carry the sturdy chest;
yet another brought bread and red wine.

When they had come down to the ship and the sea, 70
the noble escorts quickly received these things
and stowed them in the hollow ship, all the food and drink;
and for Odysseus they spread a rug and a linen sheet
on the deck of the hollow ship's stern, so that he might sleep without waking,
and he himself went aboard and lay down in silence. 75
The others sat down at the oarlocks, each in order,
and loosed the cable from the pierced stone.
Then, leaning back, they churned the sea with their oars,
and over his eyelids fell a sweet sleep,
most deep and pleasant, very like death. 80

And the ship, as four stallions on a plain
all spring forward together under the strokes of the whip,
rearing high and swiftly covering the course—
so the ship's stern rose, and behind her
the great dark wave of the roaring sea surged. 85
She ran steadily and without faltering; not even a hawk,
the swiftest of winged creatures, could have kept pace with her.
So she sped swiftly, cutting through the sea's waves,
carrying a man whose mind was like the gods',
who had before suffered many griefs in his heart, 90
enduring the wars of men and the cruel waves of the sea—
but now he slept in peace, forgetting all he had suffered.

42 ODYSSEY, BOOK XIII

When the brightest star rose up, the one that comes
to herald the light of early-born Dawn,
at that moment the sea-faring ship drew near to the island. 95
There is a harbor of Phorcys, the old man of the sea,
in the land of Ithaca; two jutting headlands
project into it, sheer cliffs that slope down toward the harbor,
which shelter it from the great waves of the harsh winds
on the outside; within, well-benched ships 100
can ride without mooring lines, once they reach the proper anchorage.
At the harbor's head there is a long-leafed olive tree,
and nearby a lovely cave, shadowy and dim,
sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads.
Within it are mixing bowls and two-handled jars 105
of stone; there too bees store their honey.
And there are long stone looms, where the nymphs
weave sea-purple robes — a wonder to behold —
and there are ever-flowing waters. It has two doors:
one facing north, by which men may descend, 110
the other toward the south, more divine; no men
enter by that one — it is a path for immortals.
There they rowed in, knowing the harbor well; the ship then
ran up on the beach as far as half her length,
driven hard, for the arms of the oarsmen urged her on. 115
The crew stepped out of the well-benched ship onto the shore
and first they lifted Odysseus from the hollow ship,
still wrapped in his linen sheet and the shining coverlet,
and laid him on the sand, overcome with sleep,
and unloaded the treasures that the noble Phaeacians 120
had given him on his homeward way, through great-hearted Athena's will.
These they piled together at the foot of the olive tree,
off the path, lest some passing traveler
might come upon them and do harm before Odysseus awoke.
Then they themselves sailed for home. But the Earth-shaker 125
did not forget the threats he had first made
against godlike Odysseus, and he sought the counsel of Zeus.

ODYSSEY XIII. 43

"Father Zeus, I shall no longer be held in honor among the immortal gods, since mortal men pay me no regard — the Phaeacians, who are themselves of my own lineage. 130 For I said that Odysseus, after suffering many hardships, would reach home; I never entirely robbed him of his return, since you first promised it and nodded your assent. But they carried him asleep on a swift ship over the sea and set him down in Ithaca, and gave him boundless gifts — 135 bronze and gold and woven clothing in plenty, more than Odysseus would ever have carried off from Troy, even if he had come home safely with his fair share of the spoils."

Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered him:
"What is this, wide-ruling Earthshaker, that you have said! 140 The gods show you no dishonor; it would be a hard thing to assail with dishonor the eldest and the best. But if any man, trusting in his own strength and power, refuses to honor you, you have your revenge always, now and hereafter. Do as you wish, whatever pleases your heart." 145

Then Poseidon the Earthshaker answered him:
"I would act at once, as you say, dark-clouded one, but I always stand in awe of your will and avoid provoking you. Now I wish to smash that beautiful ship of the Phaeacians as it comes back from its escort, out on the misty sea, 150 so that they may stop escorting men henceforward, and to cover their city with a great mountain."

Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered him:
"Dear friend, here is what seems best to my mind: when all the people from the city are watching the ship 155 as it comes rowing in, turn it into a rock near the shore, in the shape of a swift ship, so that all men may marvel at it, and cover their city with a great mountain."

When Poseidon the Earthshaker heard this, he went to Scheria, where the Phaeacians dwell. 160 There he waited; and the seafaring ship came very close,

swiftly as it sped along; and the Earth-shaker drew near to it,
and turned it to stone and rooted it fast to the sea-bed
with a flat blow of his hand; and then he went away.
  And the Phaeacians, oarsmen of long blades, men famed for their ships,
spoke winged words among themselves.     165
And one would say, looking to his neighbor:
  "Ah me, who has now chained the swift ship on the sea
as it was heading home? And yet it was in full view just now."
  So one would speak; but they did not know how it had been done.
Then Alcinous addressed them and spoke among them:     170
  "Well now, truly the ancient oracles of my father come upon me,
who said that Poseidon would be angry with us,
because we are safe escorts for all men.
He said that one day a beautiful ship of the Phaeacians,
returning from an escort on the misty sea,     175
he would shatter, and would cover our city with a great mountain.
So the old man would say; and now all of this is being fulfilled.
But come, let us all obey as I shall say:
cease from giving escort to mortals, whenever anyone comes
to our city; and to Poseidon let us sacrifice twelve     180
chosen bulls, in hope that he may take pity on us,
and not cover our city with a towering mountain."
  So he spoke, and they were afraid, and made ready the bulls.
Thus the leaders and counselors of the Phaeacian people
were praying to lord Poseidon,     185
standing around the altar.
