NOTES.

BOOK VI.

'Οδυσσείας Z, "the Zeta of the Odyssey." This is more fully expressed as "The Z Letter of the Odyssey," or "The Z Rhapsody of the Odyssey."

The Iliad and the Odyssey were first divided into their twenty-four books by the greatest of the ancient editors of Homer, Aristarchus, who flourished B.C. 222. He assigned as titles to the several books of each poem the letters of the alphabet in succession from Alpha to Omega. Hence a book was named "letter" (gramma); but often the term rhapsody (rhapsodia) was employed, which in earlier days had represented so much of the poem as a rhapsode or reciter assumed to himself or was allotted at the great festivals. Before the division by Aristarchus, there was no method of citing particular parts of the poems except by titles indicative of their contents, such as "The Tale of Alcinous" (Aristotle, Plato) for Odyssey Books 9–12, and this method was not infrequent later. Such titles, called epigraphai, are still prefixed to each book, but are seldom used in citation. The system followed in the notes below is that of naming the books of the Iliad by the capital letters of the Greek alphabet, and those of the Odyssey by the small letters.—"Of Odysseus, beginning..."—this is the epigraphe of the book. Eustathius says that each rhapsody had two titles, one prosaic, the other in metre. The metrical title of this rhapsody is,

"Zeta: Nausicaa conveyed Odysseus to Scheria."

1. The word ὣς (with accent) must be carefully distinguished from ὡς (without accent): the former is the demonstrative adverb, "in this way," "thus;" the latter is the relative conjunction, "in which

48 NOTES.

"way," "how," "as," etc. The word ὥς is very frequent in Homer; but when its pronoun ὁ, lapsing into the article, passed out of use as a demonstrative in prose except in a few set phrases, such as ὁ μέν, ὁ δέ, καὶ τόν, and when οὗτος took its place, ὥς also disappeared, except in the formulae καὶ ὥς, οὐδ' ὥς, μηδ' ὥς, and οὕτως became its substitute. — ὁ, as a demonstrative meaning "he," to which Odysseus stands as appositive; H. 500 d; G. 140, Note 2. This construction lays the foundation for the development of ὁ from demonstrative to article, through the gradual approach of subject and appositive until they stand in juxtaposition. For the process, compare η 230, 21, ζ 117, 141, "the long-suffering Odysseus," K 231; on η 55. — ἔνθα, "there," beneath the sheltering thicket of the olive-trees, described at the close of the Fifth Book; see the Summary of the Odyssey, and on ζ 127, 138. — πολύτλας is an exclusive epithet of Odysseus, used 5 times in the Iliad and 35 times in the Odyssey. This preponderance in the Odyssey is due to the difference of subject and the greater prominence of the hero and his sufferings. It here carries especial emphasis, following as it does directly upon the point where the poet has reduced his protagonist to the lowest degree of exhaustion and suffering to which he is subjected. From this point on, his fortunes improve. Related to πολύτλας are τλήμων and ταλασίφρων. Patient endurance is a prime virtue in Homer, and Odysseus is its fullest embodiment. — δῖος; see on ζ 117.

2. ὕπνῳ . . . ἀρημένος, "mastered by sleep and weariness." For the figure in ὕπνῳ, see on η 289. — ἀρημένος is an isolated form of unknown origin. Perhaps its nearest relative is the Ionic ἀραιρημένος, from αἱρέω. It is a close synonym of δεδμημένος, as shown by the parallel passage ξ 318, where Odysseus, having arrived in Ithaca and appearing in his beggar's disguise at the hut of Eumaeus, tells a fabricated story of his wanderings — how he had been cast ashore on the Thesprotian coast, just as he was here on the Scherian coast, and how the son of the king, just as here the daughter, having found him "worn out by exposure and toil," led him to the palace. Cf. η 318, ν 119. — αὐτὰρ was originally ἀϜτὰρ, in which the digamma is sometimes vocalized to υ and sometimes dropped, even in Homer, as at ζ 69. αὐτάρ is epic only; ἀτάρ occurs among the Attic poets, and rarely in Plato and Xenophon, who were fond of many poetic words.

3. βῆ: what is Homer's practice with respect to the omission

BOOK VI. 49

of the augment, and how does it compare with that of the later poets? H. 307 D. — Homer uses ἐς and εἰς at will, and the tragic poets imitate him. Herodotus has ἐς regularly, and even Thucydides writes the same for the most part. Otherwise, Attic prose has εἰς. — Φαιήκων stands in attributive apposition to ἀνδρῶν, and thereby takes on the character of an adjective; H. 500 a; C. 361, 11. This use of a national appellative is found in all ages of the Greek language. The order of the two words in the text is by far the more common one in Homer, and is frequent enough later. The phrase "Phaeacian men" is found 8 times in Homer compared to about 70 instances of "Phaeacian" without "men," showing that the latter is rather an ornamental than a necessary adjunct, as in "O men who are generals," etc. For similar expressions, see θ 456, ζ 52, η 103, 347, 20. — δῆμόν may refer to either people or country; θ 157, ν 186, 322, ζ 195, 202.

4. πρὶν ποτ', "in elder days." — εὐρυχόρῳ is used in Homer of the cities Sicyon, Ithaca, Iolcos, Mycalessus, and of the countries Hellas, Elis, Lacedaemon, Hypereia. If the second element is χορός, it refers to the wide dancing-grounds so much in use in the ancient cities; θ 260; or if it be χῶρος, it means wide-spaced, containing wide plains. — Ὑπερείῃ, "the Highland," explained by some as meaning high to the north, by others as containing mountains. Perhaps we may imagine the Phaeacians inhabiting a spacious valley opening towards the sea, like that of Lacedaemon. In the surrounding mountains dwelt the Cyclopes, and in the same land was the home of the Giants, η 58, 206. Homer supplies us with no data for fixing the locality, but it was anciently identified with Sicily.

5. Κυκλώπων. The Cyclopes of Homer are a gigantic race of shepherds of cannibalistic tendencies, dwelling upon the summits of lofty mountains in hollow caves. They possess no cities, nor ships, and, as the height of barbarism, they have neither public assemblies, nor counsellors, nor laws. The little form of government they do possess is patriarchal. They respect neither gods nor men, ι 275. The rights of the stranger, so sacred in the eyes of the Greek and the Phaeacian, are unknown to them. In fact, they are conceived as the exact opposites of the Phaeacians in character and habits, as if the poet had created them for the express

3

50 NOTES.

purpose of making the one the foil of the other. The later legend, found as early as Hesiod, that they were but three in number, and that they were the assistants of Hephaistos, is totally at variance with Homer. The phrase andrōn hyperēnoreontōn (hyperphialōn, Odyssey 9.106), "men of monstrous pride," paints their character as a class.

6. spheas, how scanned? H. 37; G. 10; C. 39. — syneskonto, "kept harrying," the iterative imperfect representing the continued past action as repeated. What other tense and voice use this iterative form? How is it made? H. 410 D.; C. 334; G. 119, 10. It is not confined to Homer, but is found among the epic writers, the Dorians, in Herodotus, and occasionally in the Attic poets. — biēphi . . . ēsan, "for in strength mightier were they." — biēphi; H. 206 D., 609. The Phaeacians are an ease-loving people and care not for the bow and the quiver; Odyssey 8.248, 6.270. Polyphemus stolidly answers Odysseus' appeal to the rights of guestship by declaring that he must be a simpleton or come from afar, if he thinks the Cyclopes regard either Zeus or any of the gods, epeiē poly pherteroí eimen, Odyssey 9.276. This epeiē exemplifies the de of the passage before us, where, as often, it expresses the reason and stands for epei or gar, not only in Homer, but also in later Greek, though less frequently: on Odyssey 6.169.

7. anastēsas, "having made them to rise up." What distinction between the transitive and intransitive tenses of histēmi? H. 416; C. 329. Migration under pressure from more powerful neighbors must have been a strong element among the causes that peopled Europe out of Asia. An historical parallel to the case of the Phaeacians is that of the Phocaeans of Ionia, who, being hard pressed by the Persians under Harpagus, launched their penteconters, embarked their wives and children, household effects and all, and sailed away to Corsica.

8. eisen de Scheriē, "and seated them in Scheria." The omission of the preposition is poetic; H. 612. Even in Homer, where this is most common, it is a comparatively rare construction, and still more so in the lyric and tragic writers. Some read d' en here. The Phaeacians, with their marvellous ships and devotion to the sea, would, like the Phocaeans, think only of removal by sea in order to free themselves from such troublesome neighbors. But

BOOK VI. 51

to be rid of all troublesome neighbors, that they might lead in security their life of unruffled ease, they would be likely to choose an island home. See on ζ 204, η 9, 239. Was Scheria a mere figment of the poet's imagination without a local habitation, or was it the geographical Corcyra, as was popularly believed by the Greeks at least as early as the days of Thucydides? — ἀλφηστάων, not found in the Iliad, and but twice elsewhere in the Odyssey; if derived from ἄλφι, ἔδειν, it is equivalent to "eating grain"; cf. θ 222. But the older interpretation from ἀλφεῖν, to acquire, is "gain-seeking," and the phrase (for it is habitually used with ἄνδρες) is distinctly applied to merchants in the Hymn to Apollo, and in Aeschylus. Thus it has an added significance here, for the Phaeacians are not only remote from all other men, but not even merchants visit them; cf. ζ 205, 278, η 9, θ 161–64.

9. ἀμφὶ . . . πόλει, "and around, a wall he ran for a city." — ἀμφὶ is adverbial; see on ν 119. ἀμφί with the dative has in Homer, like most prepositions, a strong tendency to stand at the beginning of the clause, especially with δέ. While its position is thus fixed, its noun is more or less free to subserve the poet's convenience in the metrical and rhetorical construction of his line; cf. ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρα φίλην βάλεν ἔγχεῖ, φ 433; ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρας δειρῇ βάλλ' Ὀδυσῇι, ψ 207; ἀμφὶ δὲ παιδὶ φίλῳ βάλε πήχεε, ρ 38: also η 142, θ 426, 434. The compound ἀμφελαύνω never came into use. — ἔλασσε: in the figure employed the wall is regarded as a creature to be driven: ζ 82, η 86, 113, 109; on η 29. — πόλει; H. 597, ν 73. — ἐδείματο: why is the final vowel not elided? H. 67 D. a; G. 1, 2; C. 63 D. We may not suppose by the arrangement of this line that the people were left shelterless till the wall was built. It is an example of the common Homeric figure of "the later before the earlier," or putting-the-cart-before-the-horse. In a series of objects closely connected, our poet is fond of naming that first which strikes the eye first or most prominently, in viewing them as a whole: θ 455.

10. νηοὺς. It has been concluded by some from this passage that no Homeric city was without its temples; few, however, are actually mentioned. We have that of Athene at Athens, η 81, and Troy, Z 88; that of Apollo at Pytho, θ 80, Troy, and Chryse. One of Poseidon is implied ζ 266, in Scheria, and another at

52 NOTES.

Helice, Book VIII line 203; cf. Book XVI line 185, Book IV line 347, Book III line 274. Otherwise, the Greeks worshipped at altars and in groves; cf. Book VI lines 162, 291.

11. ἤδη, "already," before the period of our story. — κηρί. Of the various words used by Homer to signify doom or fate, κήρ is nearest to a distinct personification, and is of the darkest color, always implying death. It is also the fate of the individual, not of humanity. Compare Book VII line 197. — "Αἰδόσδε," "Hadesward." In the brevity of a familiar phrase the local particle δε has been appended to the genitive, where it belongs to an accusative that is understood. The fuller form of expression, as found elsewhere in the poems, is "into Hades," "into the house of Hades," "into the halls of Hades." The Aïdes of Homer is always a person, the youngest brother of Zeus, who obtained in the allotment of sovereignty the rule of the world of the dead. The entrance to his "House" is beside the Ocean-Stream, where it empties into the central sea. Hard by the Cimmerians dwell, and the whole region is wrapped forever in cloud and darkness. Odysseus sails thither from Circe's isle, and the shades are sent up for his inspection. The condition of the dead, though without punishment except for great offenders like Tantalus, is pitiable. "Seek not to comfort me in death," exclaims the shade of Achilles; "rather had I the lot of the wretchedest laborer upon earth than be king over all the dead;" Book XI line 488.

12. τότ', at the time of the story, as opposed to that of Nausithous and of the poet; cf. νῦν, Book VII line 68. — θεῶν . . . εἰδώς, "with wisdom from the gods endowed;" on Book VIII line 584. This god-given wisdom is not a favor shown to Alcinous alone; all conspicuous external and internal characteristics, in general, are received directly from on high; Book VIII lines 167, 488, 457, Book VI lines 18, 229. The Homeric man had ever before him the immediate interposition and guiding hand of Providence; on Book VI line 172. — ἄπο; Hadley's Grammar section 102 D. Anastrophe of this preposition occurs also at Book VI line 18, Book VII line 152, Book VIII lines 88, 411, 457; on Book VI line 15.

13. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις 'Αθήνη, "the goddess, luminous-eyed Athene." — γλαυκῶπις belongs to 'Αθήνη, not to θεά, as shown by its frequent occurrence with 'Αθήνη alone, but never with θεά alone. Our poetic translators usually treat this as an epithet of color; but it is more than probable that the idea of color does not enter into it at all. γλαυκός occurs once of the flashing sea, and γλαυκιόων

BOOK VI. 53

describes the eye of a lion, when, reaching the height of his wrath, he makes his rush at the hunters. This is the key to its force in glaukopis, representing the brightening flash of the eye under the influence of feeling. Athene is the goddess of war and the goddess of wisdom. In the one capacity the eye is kindled by martial fury; in the other by the power of mighty conceptions. The poet has developed a phase of it, Iliad 200: "and his eyes shone terribly." Schliemann's "owl-faced" is unproved.

14. "To Odysseus" (dative form): what is this in Attic? Hadley 189 D. The final syllable is lengthened by the probable doubling of the initial liquid of the following word in pronunciation; Hadley 87 D. This in thesis is rare; Iliad E 358. The word megas ("great") and its derivatives quite constantly lengthen a preceding short vowel; Odyssey Book 6, lines 62, 304; Book 7, lines 150, 180; Book 8, lines 9, 42, 227, 434, 520; Book 13, lines 2, 8, 13, 51, 121; cf. Book 7, line 145. — metioosa ("devising"), how is it formed? Hadley 370 D.; Goodwin 120; Curtius 243; on Book 8, line 574.

15. imen ("let us go"), Book 6, line 50. — thalamon ("chamber") is best placed in the second story of the palace; Iliad B 514, Iliad Pi 184. — polydaidalon, "richly wrought;" compare the description of the palace, Book 7, lines 83-97. — eni, Book 8, line 220; Book 11, line 367; on Book 6, lines 12, 262.

16. koimat', "was sleeping." — phuen ("figure"); Hadley 549; on Book 6, line 152.

17. Nausicaa is here introduced for the first time, and the poet has emphasized the fact by placing the name as the first word in the line. — megaletoros ("great-hearted") is Virgil's magnanimus, and is used by Homer not only of Aeneas several times, but of a number of other warriors, both Greeks and Trojans, most constantly of Odysseus. It is also applied to the Trojans as a people, the Paphlagonians, the Phlegyans, Myrmidons, and Eteocretans. It commonly has a good sense, "great-souled." Here it pictures that large-heartedness which Alcinous displays in his hospitality towards Odysseus.

18. par, "near by;" supply koimonto ("they were sleeping"). — The word amphipolos is always feminine, as therapon is masculine; and the former is a slave, while the latter is a freeman. Noble ladies are regularly attended by two amphipoloi, and are always accompanied by them when appearing in public. Here they sleep in the maiden's chamber, one on each side of the door, to guard the entrance. — The Graces of Homer, like his Hours, Fates, and Cyclopes, have no definite number, but are more than three. He conceives them mainly as

54 NOTES.

the attendants and handmaids of Aphrodite, and as such they doubtless came with her worship from Babylonia through Cyprus. Hence their earlier number would be two, as we see them in the Babylonian Isdubar Epic, and some of the Cypriote groups, and as they were worshipped in Lacedaemon and at Athens (Pausanias IX. 35). Elsewhere in Homer it is the gods that bestow beauty, Athene, Hera, and Aphrodite being especially mentioned as possessing that power. Here the beauty conferred by the handmaids of Aphrodite upon the handmaids of Nausicaa is remarkable, but it is inferior to that of the princess (Book VI, lines 108–9), which is the gift of the gods; Book VIII, line 457.

19. "stahmoin," Book VI line 82, Book VIII line 458.—Observe that "hekas" and its derivatives usually have the digamma; Book VI line 8; but not so in Book VII lines 91 and 321.— "epekeinto," "rested thereon," that is, upon the door-posts, which would occur only when closed; for the doors consisted of two valves turning, not upon hinges, like ours, but each upon a pivot running into the lintel above and the threshold below. — "phaeinai"; see Book VII line 84.

20. "But she like a breath of wind sped to the couch of the maiden."— The particle "de" is fully adversative, meaning "but," though the doors were closed. The goddess passes in through the key-hole, along the strap of the key, like the phantom which she sends to comfort Penelope in her dreams, Book IV line 802, when Penelope is suffering a mother's agony at the intelligence that the suitors are plotting the death of Telemachus on his return from Sparta. — "epessunto": what other verb doubles sigma after augment? Hadley's Grammar, section 308 D.

21. "ste ... kephales," the regular formula for assuming a position when addressing a person so reclined; most commonly of dreams, as that of Agamemnon in Book II line 20; but not exclusively. Athene so appears to Odysseus, as he is rolling and tossing on his bed of skins, Book XX line 32; and Eurycleia takes this position when she hastens to awake Penelope and announce the presence of Odysseus after the destruction of the suitors, Book XXIII line 4. Hence it does not mean "hovering in air," as Hayman explains, but standing near the head and bending over it. Virgil applies the expression to Iris as she descends to release the soul of Dido: "She flies down and hovers above the head," Aeneid IV line 702.— "pros" must be taken by tmesis with "eeipen," and the construction of the two accusatives is after the analogy of "prosaoudao," and even "audao." Yet the real compound "proseipon" is

BOOK VI. 55

construed with the accusative of the person only, and the thing, if expressed, becomes the dative. Still, Aristophanes has "I will address a word to you" (προσείπω σ' ἔπος), Pax 520; cf. 522.

23. "they" (οἵ), Nausicaa. — ὁμηλικίη, "a parity of years;" the abstract used for the concrete, ὁμηλικίη in place of ὁμῆλιξ. This usage gives vigor and beauty to the sentence. It is naturally a poetic mode of expression, and therefore is more common in Greek than other languages, as this language grew up under the auspices of poetry (Jelf, G. G.). — κεχάριστο, "was dear," used as an imperfect; H. 712 a; G. 200, 6. A passive sense for deponent verbs, though rare in the present and imperfect, is more common in the other tenses.

24. μιν, in this formula, is governed by προσέφη ("addressed"), not by ἔεισαμ., as is proved by λ 241, where μιν disappears along with προσέφη.

25. Ναυσικάα: why not Ναυσικάη? H. 125 D. — τί νύ, "why, pray?" H. 552 a; G. 160, 2. — ὧδε μεθήμονα, "so remiss." — γείνατο; H. 416, 8. This mode of expression is more forcible than the simple "Why art thou?" since it represents the remissness in the light of an inborn characteristic, and thereby incites the maiden to greater zeal; so N 777, Δ 400, E 800, α 223. Am.

26. τοι, "to thy discredit," the ethical dative, repeated in μοι, 59. — ἀκηδέα is predicate; σιγαλόεντα is attributive to εἵματα ("garments"). σιγαλ. is an example of the standing or fixed epithet, the application of which becomes at times incongruous, because the speaker has in mind the normal and proper state of the object, rather than its condition at the time; cf. 74, θ 41, 378, λ 327, Φ 218. For the expression, as applied to garments, we may compare "gleaming like a star" (ἀστὴρ δ' ὣς ἀπέλαμπεν), ο 108, of the peplus presented by Helen to Telemachus as a memorial of her handiwork. "The king gave his six sons the finest clothes you ever set eyes on, so fine that the light gleamed from them a long way off." Dasent's Tales from the Norse.

27. γάμος, the marriage ceremonies, which appear to have consisted of a wedding feast, celebrated with profuse bounty (λ 414) for the relatives and friends by the father of the bride (α 277, δ 3). The song and the dance accompany the feast (ψ 135). No vow appears to have been taken, and the validity of the marriage consisted in the public avowal in these ceremonies; ζ 288. As evening drew on, the bride was conducted by the groom and

56 NOTES.

his relatives to the house of his father, where young sons customarily lived, and the procession is thus described as wrought by Hephaistos upon the shield of Achilles, two weddings having occurred on the same day:

"And in it he fashioned two fine cities of mortal men. In one there were marriages and feasts, and brides were being led from their chambers through the city beneath blazing torches, and the loud wedding-song arose; young men were whirling in the dance, and among them flutes and lyres sounded; and women stood admiring at each doorway." Iliad 18.490–96.

"And two fair populous towns were sculptured there;
In one were marriage pomp and revelry,
And brides in gay procession through the streets
'Neath blazing torches from their chambers borne,
While frequent rose the hymeneal song.
Youths whirled around in joyous dance, with sound
Of flute and harp; and, standing at their doors,
Admiring women on the pageant gazed." Derby.

ἵνα means "at which," referring to the γάμος [wedding]. — καλά, supply εἵματα [garments]. — αὐτήν, standing for σὲ αὐτήν, as the subject of ἔννυσθαι; this verb, used in the middle voice, retains only the accusative of the thing, while the person is implied by the voice itself.

28. τὰ δέ means "and others," as if τὰ μέν had preceded. A scholiast tells us that it was customary for brides to furnish garments to the friends of the groom. If so, this practice appears nowhere else alluded to. The reference here might be to the dowry, more precisely specified below at line 38; for it seems pointless to deny that some dowry went with the bride, in light of passages at α 277, β 132, δ 736, Ι 148, η 314, Hymn to Aphrodite 140; but see the note on ζ 159. Yet, provision for men's garments to clothe Odysseus seems necessary here, since the device at lines 60–5 is simply intended to develop the character of the princess; and, further, to suppose the bridal procession dressed in garments of the bride's providing gives greater point to the next two lines. — ἄγωνται: see H. 757; G. 232, 3; G. M. 61, 3; C. 554; cf. ζ 159, 262, 297, 303, θ 445, 511, 549, ν 155.

29. ἐκ τούτων means "from these things," that is, from her own fair adornment and ample provision for the groom's friends. — τοι is the dative ethical, meaning "look you," or "you must know." As here, it not unfrequently

BOOK VI. 57

directs the attention of the listener earnestly to some proverbial or general statement; cf. θ 329, 351, ν 130. It corresponds often to our colloquial "you know." — anabaínei, "mounts high among men." — phátis is only less lightly personified than Óssa, B 93, ω 413, and is conceived as rising higher and higher as it advances; cf. "my fame reaches heaven," ι 20, τ 333–34, the description of Eris, Δ 442, and Virgil's Fama, Aeneid IV. 176. The construction of the accusative is unusual, but see ξ 286, Euripides, Hecuba 928, 119.

30. esthle receives a double emphasis by its position at the end of the clause and the beginning of the line. This is a favorite artifice with our poet; see ζ 132, 182, 233, 274, 283, 284, 301, etc.

31. iomen, subjunctive of exhortation, showing the original connecting vowel instead of the later mode sign; Hadley 347 D. For the mode, see ζ 126, η 190, θ 31, 34; for the vowel, ζ 33, 126, 219, 232, 259, 262, etc. — plyneousal; H. 373. This future has the true stem plun-; the present is lengthened by the insertion of iota; H. 328 d. — "at dawn," a frequent Homeric formula, which was handed down in its essence to later Greek, as in Herodotus III. 86, Xenophon, Anabasis II. 3, 1; I. 7, 2. The dative is not used absolutely, as Jelf would have it, but is governed by hama. Homer regularly employs the present participle when speaking of the sun rising, but the aorist of its setting, as A 592; because we can follow the further course of the sun after it has risen, but no mortal eye sees it after it has set. (Classen, Beobachtungen, p. 59.)

32. "I will follow along." The simple dative of accompaniment with hepomai is often more clearly defined in Homer by hama, syn, meta. In like manner other verbs of following. hopedeō has hama in Homer, meta in Hesiod; homarteo, hama in Homer, syn in Sophocles. The Attic akoloutheo takes syn, and meta with the genitive. This tendency is further seen in compounds, such as synepomai, synephepomai, symparepomoi, synepakolutheō, symparakolutheō.

33. The first word of this line and the last are scanned with synizesis. — entyneai is aorist subjunctive. Why may it not contain a dactyl? H. 345, 2. — eti has long ultima; why? H. 87 D.; C. 77 D.

35. Connect "of all the Phaeacians" with "the best men"; cf. ζ 283, θ 36, 390. — hothi . . . autei, "where for thine ownself, too, is thy parentage;" hothi refers to dēmon. — autei is to be connected with toi, and the phrase is strengthened by kai; see 39. hothi has been referred to
3*

58 NOTES.

"aristees" as well as "demon." But, whichever is preferred, it has appeared weak and pointless to tell Nausicaa that she is a Phaeacian, or that she is noble. This has led Bekker and some others to omit the line. But they have not seen that the purpose of the poet here is to hint the fact that the princess is wooed by native suitors, and those only, and thus to intimate at this early stage how distasteful they are to her, and the effect which the coming of Odysseus may produce. For, as Mr. Gladstone has shown (Hom. Studies, III. p. 69), the distinction in Greece between the aristocracy and the royal family was so broad a one that the latter were accustomed to contract a marriage only with royalty beyond their own borders, as is the custom among the reigning families of Europe at the present day. Since Phaeacian life and manners are essentially Greek, simply a trifle more god-favored and effeminate, the same custom may be supposed to obtain in Scheria; and though all communication with the outer world is severed by their remoteness, yet there remains a lingering hope in the family that for the only daughter, the darling of them all, some Nausithous (Book η 56–62) may be thrown in their way by Providence, and she may thus be rescued from the nobles she despises (Book ζ 283), and sustain the dignity of her station. This will explain her secret wish that Odysseus will remain among them (Book ζ 245), the immediate supposition on the part of the gossiping populace (spoken, however, by Nausicaa herself, and so colored by her thought) that a stranger seen with her will become her husband (Book ζ 277), and the startling offer of his daughter's hand which Alcinous makes to a total stranger (Book η 313). Hence the line is not only not weak and pointless, but shows that the poet had in mind when it was composed the passages just cited, which have been the objects of strong suspicion. See further on those passages, and Proceedings of American Philological Association for 1879, p. 8.

36. "eothi pro," "in the morning early."—"pro," temporal adverb like "proi." This construction accords with the sequel, line 48, as also Book Λ 50, where the same phrase is used of a period later than the actual coming of Eos, Book Λ 1. "eothi" is then a temporal dative. If "pro" be made the post-positive preposition, "before" dawn, a double difficulty is assumed—the circumstances of the case, and the

BOOK VI. 59

The fact that θι is mainly a dative termination in its use, though ὅθι = οὗ, and αὐτόθι = αὐτοῦ.

37. ἅμαξαν: H. 65 D. — ἥ κεν ἄγῃσιν is a relative clause of purpose; cf. ζ 58, 114. How would this be expressed in prose, and how is it a sign of archaism? G. M. 65, 1, and Note 2, Rem.; G. 236. — ἄγῃσιν: In Attic, what active endings are dropped, and when? H. 361; G. 112, 2, Note.

38. ζώστρά occurs only here, but is equivalent to ζώνας, an important part of female attire, which here and in general must have been of some woven or knit material, to admit of washing. The only girdles for females whose material is specified by Homer are those of Circe and Calypso. They are of gold, but it is implied that they are of unusual splendor. That of Hera is adorned with a hundred tassels. — The πέπλος is the large uncut garment of the women, corresponding to the χλαῖνα or φᾶρος of the men, and worn like those over the more tightly fitting undergarment, the χιτών. They also served for other purposes, as offerings to the gods, coverings for thrones (η 96, etc.). — ῥήγεα, from the root ῥεγ, to dye, are colored rugs or thick woollen blankets, used commonly for the covering of the bedstead (η 336, ν 73, 118), though they are spread upon the thrones in Circe's palace. They would necessarily form a part of the dowry of a bride for the outfit of a new household, and all material fresh from the loom would need washing.

39. The conveyance is necessary for the vestments, "and in this way, too, for yourself (as the king's daughter) it is far more seemly than to go on foot." — καὶ δέ is an epic collocation; in Attic the words are habitually separated by the emphasized expression; ζ 60, 286, η 213; cf. η 327. — σοὶ αὐτῇ: Homer never compounds these pronouns, even when reflexive, but commonly places their components in juxtaposition, as ζ 60, θ 396. They are sometimes separated by light enclitics or conjunctions and the like (λ 369, 371, θ 211), or by one or more emphatic words (ζ 35, 39, 277). — κάλλιον: how does it differ from the Attic form? H. 222 D. — πόδεσσιν: note the various forms: θ 230, 253, 103.

40. ἀπὸ in the sense of "far from" is common in Homer, and regularly stands directly before its case, as ζ 220, λ 344; cf. ζ 294. Here it is best taken, perhaps, with the verb by tmesis, as ὃν οὐκέτι

60 NOTES.

"I declare that [he will be] away from his loved ones" (Odyssey σ 145). The subject is not uncommonly placed between the preposition and its verb; see η 283, θ 380, 475; on ζ 100. — πλυνοί, "laundry-pits;" on 86. — πόληος; Hadley's Grammar 186 D.; Curtius 157 D.

42. "Where they say the seat of the gods fast forever standeth." Many objections have been urged against the genuineness of lines 42–7. The description of Olympus has been declared inconsistent with that of the Iliad, so that the Chorizontes have found in it confirmation of their belief in the different authorship of the two poems. Mure reconciles this in the following way: "Olympus is here figured as a mountain, the sides and visible summit of which are for the most part enveloped in snow and clouds; while its extreme peak, where the palace of Jove was situated, free from all such atmospheric contamination, enjoyed a perpetual brilliancy and serenity. The confusion between heaven as a mountain and heaven as a sphere equally pervades both poems." Cf. Iliad Θ 19 and following, Τ 126 and following, Ο 18 and following, Odyssey υ 103–4, 113–14. So too, there are numerous inconsistencies in the Homeric picture of Hades and elsewhere, where the marvelous enters largely, as seen also in Virgil, and often in tales of wonder; see note on ζ 329. Again, φασί is said to be strange, applied as it is to a fact elsewhere so fully accepted by the poet; but cf. Ν 631, Ε 635, Ζ 100, Υ 105, 206, Β 783, Ω 615, μ 389–90; Virgil, Aeneid I. 731, III. 416, Conington on IV. 577; Horace, Odes III. 5, 41. It is the real world now and then peeping through the wonder-working element so constantly in sight. The passage has also been called irrelevant, because there is no reason why at this point we should be carried off to divine abodes. Episodes, however, are a striking feature of the Homeric style; and, as a detailed description of the dwelling-place of the gods is to be found nowhere else in the poems, it may be maintained that this splendid picture of the divine seat and the easy life there is but a fitting introduction to that of an earthly community which, in its local surroundings and luxurious living, approaches near to the gods. Set aside this passage altogether, and it might truly be said that the poet has painted a fairer Elysium for the god-connected man in the afterlife (δ 563–69), and a fairer Elysium for the Phaeacian upon earth, than he has anywhere given to his deities in heaven.

BOOK VI. 61

43. The word "ποτ'" connects to both the preceding and following clauses; compare ε 479, δ 566. Note that the subject of the verbs is "the seat of the gods" (θεῶν ἕδος), not Olympus as a whole. These lines are translated by Lucretius (On the Nature of Things, III. 18–22), when he is describing the rapt vision of the student of nature as he gazes out upon the universe unfolding before him: (See Tennyson's "Lucretius.")

The divine power and quiet dwelling-place of the gods becomes visible:
Which no winds shake, nor clouds sprinkle with showers,
Nor does white snow, hardened by sharp frost, falling violate,
And a sky forever cloudless covers it,
And broadly smiles with diffused light.

44. The word "μάλ'" qualifies "ἀνέφελος" (cloudless). Adverbs, even in prose, may be separated from the words they modify; those of place, time, and manner frequently, those of degree at times. Short, Essay, p. lxv. — "αἴθρη" is a feminine form of "αἰθήρ" (clear sky).

45. "πέπταται" means "is outspread," as a garment, ζ 94. The clouds are all below the divine abode, and form the rampart that shuts heaven from earth. Through their self-moving gateway, guarded by the Hours, Athene and Hera pass on their way to Troy, Θ 396, and then Zeus espies them. — "λευκὴ . . . αἴγλη" means "and bright athwart it runs the sunlight." — "λευκὴ" in its original sense, as Ψ 268, of a burnished caldron, κ 94, of the calm. — "αἴγλη," η 84; cf. "αἰγλήεις" of Olympus, Α 532, Ν 243, υ 103; Sophocles, Antigone 610.

46–7. "ἔνι." on 15. — "τέρπονται"; cf. "the gods live easily," Ζ 138, δ 805, ε 122. — "ἔνθ'" is like our "there," used for "thither." — "ἐπεὶ διεπέφραδε" means "after she had told all;" H. 384 D., 706; η 49, θ 68.

48–9. "Ἠὼς" (Dawn) is described not only as "εὔθρονος" (fair-throned), which refers to the seat of her chariot, but also as "χρυσόθρονος" (golden-throned), "κροκόπεπλος" (saffron-robed), and "εὐπλόκαμος" (fair-tressed); on θ 1. — "μιν" has "Ναυσικάαν" in definitive apposition; H. 500 d. — "ἀπεθαύμασ'" means "much she marvelled;" "ἀπ." is intensive.

50. "ἵμεναι," ζ 15, 255, η 14; so also "she went forth to run, to drive." This infinitive, expressing purpose after a verb of motion, is poetic; the future participle is more common; on 134; G. M. 97, Note 1. — "ἀγγείλειε": why optative? H. 739; G. 216; ν 74.

51. "φίλῳ": an adjective belonging to two or more nouns regularly agrees with the first and is usually placed before it, though sometimes after, even in prose. Short, Essay, p. xvi. — "ἔνδον" means within the great hall, "μέγαρον," which served as the common living-

62 NOTES.

room of the family, audience-hall, and dining-room. In shape it was oblong, the shorter side contiguous to the court-yard, and lofty columns supported its ceiling. Its size must have been considerable. In that of Odysseus, 108 suitors daily feasted, each at a separate table, and room was left for their numerous attendants and the slaves, while a large space by the door appears then to have been unoccupied. To the megaron (great hall) of Alcinous scarcely inferior proportions can be assigned. The floor is of native earth, stamped hard, and that of Odysseus is cleaned with scrapers when sodden with the blood of the suitors. Windows are unknown. The wide entrance doors leading from the open courtyard are thrown back during the day, and serve to light the hall in part. In the roof near the farther end is the smoke-vent, no chimney being in use, and this contributed to the lighting of the apartment, as well as the fire itself. But at best the hall is shadowy (Book 13, line 2). The fireplace, eschare, was below the smoke-vent, and nearly level with the floor. Upon it a fire was kept blazing continually, during the day and evening, often perhaps rather for light than heat. About it were the seats of honor. Near-by, in the fire-light, was the position of the housewife's chair, resting against a pillar; see Book 6, lines 305-7, Book 7, lines 153, 169-71. — "being," a supplementary participle, as in Book 7, lines 50, 137; Hadley's Grammar, 799; Goodwin's Grammar, 279; Curtius, 591.

52-3. "The latter," her mother. — "by." The hearth is not large, so that the fire alone is "upon" it, as in Book 5, line 59, Book 13, line 123. —

Helakate are the threads in the process of twisting between the fingers of the right hand, drawn from the flock of wool around the end of the distaff, helakate, held in the left. The operation was doubtless assisted by the spindle-whorl, no mention of which, however, is made in the poems: numbers of them in terra-cotta were found at all depths in the excavations at Troy, and they may be seen among the very ancient objects from Alambra in the Cesnola Collection. In his later excavations at Troy, Dr. Schliemann found, "in the Royal Mansion, twenty-eight feet deep, a distaff eleven inches long, round which is lengthwise wound a large quantity of woollen thread, black like coal." London Athenaeum, Dec. 14, 1878.—

BOOK VI. 63

ἁλιπόρφυρα [sea-purple]; references at ζ 306, ν 108, 85, θ 84, 373, η 337. Doubtless the Phoenician purple from the sea-shell murex is intended, for this was introduced at a very early period into Greece. Yet Mr. Gladstone has shown that the color-sense in the Homeric poems, as in the Vedas, is narrow, weak, indistinct, and confused, though the perceptions of light not decomposed, as varying between light and dark, white and black, are most vivid and effective; accordingly, the descriptions of color generally tend a good deal to range themselves in a scale of degrees, rather than kinds, of light. The word πορφύρεος [porphyreos] is used of blood, dark cloud, the wave of a river when disturbed, the wave of the sea, garments, the rainbow, and death; and the verb πορφύρω [porphyro] of the sea darkening, and of the mind "in a brown study."

54–5. ξύμβλητο [she met him]. Coming from the women's apartments in the rear of the great hall (μέγαρον), she hastens after and overtakes her father before he reaches the door leading into the court. — μετά means "unto;" ζ 133. — βασιλῆας [kings]: there are twelve in the single city of Scheria, θ 390; hence, as in Ithaca, they are the aristocracy rather than the great kings of the Iliad. — The βουλή [council] was the council of elders, η 189, and formed a preliminary meeting to consider the measures to be taken in managing the general assembly of the people, or ἀγορή [public assembly]. — ἵνα means "where," not "whither;" 47, 27. — κάλεον means "were wont to summon him." The chief king, Agamemnon, summons the βουλή in the Iliad. During all the twenty years' absence of Odysseus from Ithaca, no βουλή had been convened. But the Iliad shows us government in the unsettled condition of war, and the council is called together under extraordinary circumstances. In Scheria is depicted a normal state of peace, where the βουλή appears to be a regular senate convened at stated periods, at which it was the duty of the king to be present, a fact intimated by the imperfect tense; cf. o 468. — Φαίηκες ἀγανοί [the gentle Phaeacians], probably meaning the kings; cf. ν 120, 12, θ 428, 389–93.

56. μάλ' ἄγχι [very close], a strong expression, found but four times elsewhere in the poems, though ἄγχι [near] is common enough of one stationing himself near another. Hence it shows the affectionate freedom of the daughter preferring her request, not to the king, but to the father. It accords well with the loving tone of both petition and answer. — φίλον [dear]; see note on θ 178.

BOOK VI. 65

either intentionally introduced or perhaps observed by Homer at all, unless in so far as they may have served, in occasional instances, to enhance the expressive power of his language. That such, apart from musical cadence, is their tendency in many cases, there can be no doubt." The same remark applies to Greek and Roman literature throughout.—This speech of the princess departs perhaps more widely from that of Athene than any other in Homer which follows upon directions given. His usual habit is seen in the opening of Book B, where the Dream receives its orders from Zeus, and imparts them to Agamemnon in several lines of exact repetition; Agamemnon in turn calls the council together, and repeats the words of the dream still more precisely from beginning to end. Throughout the poems there is no compunction about the repetition, not merely of single lines, but of whole passages. Departure from the general custom is due in this case to the admirable conception and depiction of the character of Nausicaa, whose maiden modesty puts carefully aside all reference to marriage, and veils the subject by the natural interest which the only daughter of the house should take in the concerns of the whole family. On line 28.

62. megarois: often in the plural for the palace as a whole; eta 150, theta 227; cf. eta 65, nu 160.

63. hoi du': partitive apposition; H. 500 b.— hoi is the article used as in prose with cardinal numbers when a part is to be distinguished from a whole; H. 528; C. 374; omitted with treis; full form, E 271.— opuiontes, "married;" on theta 254— treis, named at theta 119. F.— ēitheoi thalethontes, like ēitheos thaleros, Delta 474, huiees hēbōontes, Omega 604, young men "unmarried, in the flower of youth." ēitheos corresponds to parthenos of the other sex.

64. hoi d': the last three, who are more closely connected with the duties of Nausicaa than the others, who have wives to care for their raiment. The dance is represented as nearly confined to the unmarried, theta 263, Sigma 593, and the Phaeacians are surpassingly skilful in it, especially Halius and Laodamas, theta 370.— neopluta . . . echontes, as in Paris, Gamma 392–94; cf. theta 249, 392, Sigma 596.

65. ta: demonstrative, "these matters."— memelen, perfect with present sense, as at lines 45, 106, 168, 187, 190, 244, 294, 301, etc. How does the Homeric construction of this verb differ from that of prose? H. 422, 11.

66 NOTES.

66. αἴδετο, "felt abashed," "blushed." What is the prose form? — θαλερὸν . . ., "youth's spring-time marriage openly to name." θαλερός, from θάλλω, "to bloom," indicates that marriage took place in the flower of youth. It was regarded as necessarily accompanying arrival at suitable age. Even the gods assist in bringing it about, as for Neoptolemus and Hermione, δ 7; cf. ζ 180–81. An elderly bachelor or spinster among the freeborn is unheard of in the poems. The sanctity of the marriage tie is held inviolate among the Greeks; polygamy is unknown, and divorce unthought of. Helen resumes her original position in the halls of Menelaus upon her return, as if nothing had happened to disturb the harmony of the household. The Homeric life stands nowhere more vividly and emphatically in contrast with that of the boasted age of Athenian civilization than in the position and estimation of woman. The respect, tenderness, and honor with which she is treated are scarcely less than in our own day, and nowhere in the poems is this more beautifully depicted than in this Phaeacian episode.

67. ὁ δὲ . . ., "but he understood it all;" cf. Iliad A 333, of Achilles when the heralds, come to demand Briseis, were standing abashed before him. Though there existed in the family a strong predilection for a foreign marriage, yet the chances of it appeared so remote that native suitors, drawn by her beauty and loveliness of character, as well as by her station, were already pressing their claims for the hand of the princess with approbation, since she was of marriageable age, and it seemed probable that the same fate awaited her as had befallen her two brothers who had been forced to marry in Scheria. — ἀμείβετο μύθῳ, "made return in speech." The construction ἀμείβεσθαι τόν, τήν, μύθῳ, μύθοις, ἐπέεσσι, is common; cf. the inverted Latin usage with mutare, as "Lucretilem mutat Lycaeo," Horace, C. I. 17, 2.

68. τοι; Hadley 595 b; Goodwin 184, 2. — ἡμιόνων; Hadley 577 a; Goodwin 173.

69. ἔρχευ, like τευ, is an Ionic contraction for what? Hadley 32 D. f. — ἀτάρ; on 2. — ἀπήνην is the same as ἄμαξαν, 37, a four-wheeled wagon drawn by mules or oxen, and used in transporting anything of weight or bulk, as stone, wood from the forest, bodies of the dead, garments. Its epithets are the synonymous εὔτροχος, εὔκυκλος, "with handsome wheels," τετράκυκλος, ὑψηλή, εὔξε-

BOOK VI. 67

...fine, mule-wagon. The two axles were probably connected by a platform stretched across them, forming the wagon-bottom proper. Upon this, heavy articles could be conveyed without additional support, but for lighter ones a wagon-box would be required, consisting of side-boards and end-pieces; or a hamper or box could be strapped on (Odyssey 15.131, 24.267). In the present instance, the word huperterié is probably the wagon-box, for the ancients universally explain it as a rectangle of wood used to hold articles deposited in it for transport. There is nothing to support the hypothesis held by some that it formed a framework-covering for the head, to shield the rider from the beating rays of the sun, as in the later word harmámaxa. If imagined as an open wagon-box, the need for the wrappings mentioned below at line 179, for protection from the dust, can be readily understood.

70. araruian, "furnished." What Homeric peculiarity appears in this form? See Hadley's Grammar, section 338 D.; also Odyssey 7.45, 6.293.

71. ekékleto has both reduplication and syncopation; see Hadley 384 D. Is there such an instance in Attic Greek? What reduplicated 2nd aorist is common there? The words toi and tai occur in Homer as demonstratives as well as relatives. In what dialect were they afterwards used? See Hadley 239 D.

72. ektos, "without" the palace, but within the open courtyard, aulé; Odyssey 7.4, 24.281, 323.

73. ópleon, found only here, with hoplizó being the common form; meaning "made ready," by putting on the wagon-box and the coffer, which served not only as a lunch-box but also as a seat, as the peirins at Odyssey 15.131 serves Telemachus on his journey from Pylos to Sparta and back in Nestor's road-chariot, and as the one strapped to the mule-wagon which Priam takes with him to convey to Achilles the ransom for Hector's body (Iliad 24.267). See how minutely the preparation of the wagon is described there: "and the mules under the yoke they led, and yoked them beneath the wagon." The yoke, often a simple cross-bar, was first tied fast to the end of the pole, then the animals were brought to their places under the yoke (Iliad 5.731), to the ends of which broad straps of leather were already attached; these collar-straps were next put round under the neck of the animal and fastened. The yoke attached to the pole was considered a

68 NOTES.

constituent part of the vehicle; whence, "to fasten under the yoke" was superseded by the phrase "to fasten under the vehicle."

74. φαεινήν is a synonym of σιγαλόεντα at line 26, and is to be explained in the same way.

75. ἐπ' with the dative after a verb of motion, because the state of rest following the action of the verb is the prominent thought; H. 618 a; cf. ν 122.

76. The personal and active participation of the queen and her daughter in these homely labors is a charming sketch of simplicity of manners in the midst of great splendor of position and surroundings. Nor does this belong to the Phaeacian isle alone; it is a truthful depiction of Greek life in the Heroic Age. All the noble women in the poems are skilled at the distaff and the loom, Helen and Penelope notably so. The king is pre-eminent not only in all manly and graceful sports, in the use of arms and in the dangers of the chase, but he also gains knowledge of medicine, and Achilles is skillful with the lyre. Odysseus builds with his own hands a remarkable bedroom and bed in his palace, constructs the vessel with which he sails from Ogygia, and claims that he can reap more grain and run a better furrow down a four-acre field than the best suitor of the band, old as he appears. Indeed, respect for labor, and participation in it as a matter of course, find no exception even among the gods. Zeus and Hera harness, drive, and tend their own horses; Poseidon does the same, or takes and cares for those of Zeus. Athena and the Graces spin and weave ambrosial garments; while Hephaestus hammers and pounds, perspires and grows as begrimed as any blacksmith on earth. See ζ 305–6, η 5, θ 8, 424–38, ν 20. ἐτίθει is a form made with a connecting vowel, but actually more common than the regular ἐτίθη; H. 401 h. The imperfect tense depicts finely the mother's careful preparation and packing of the lunch for the darling of her house, and the supply is so abundant that it suffices in the sequel to satisfy also the ravenous appetite of Odysseus, who had been without food for three days, ζ 250. Another fine picture of a mother's fond anxiety for the little comforts of a child leaving home is that of Thetis in the Iliad, who had stored for Achilles to take with him a coffer full

BOOK VI. 69

of soft doublets and wind-defending mantles and thick woollen blankets, Iliad XVI 221–24. — menoeike, "heart-contenting."

77. en, "therein," adverbial, as referring to kiste. — opsa, "relishes," anything eaten with bread, especially tidbits of meat. On the table of Nestor in the camp stands a patera containing an onion, poto opson, Iliad XI 630. When Peisistratus and Telemachus are setting out from Pylos for Sparta, the housekeeper prepares for their lunch bread and wine and relishes, such as god-nurtured kings eat, Odyssey III 480. Bread is the "marrow of men," the mainstay and principal article of food: all else is a relish to the bread. Homer never mentions any other food on the table by name except bread and meat; but that vegetables were in use is quite certain; Odyssey VII 127. pantoine doubtless includes fruit from the orchard and vineyard, Odyssey VII 115–22, if not vegetables from the garden, Odyssey VII 127. — en before d' oinon goes with echeuen by tmesis; Odyssey XX 260, III 40. To repeat, after a verb compounded with a preposition, the same or a kindred preposition with a noun is common in many languages, but the construction has just begun in Homer; Odyssey VIII 106.— The use of wine by women is spoken of here as if common in the Homeric day; see also on Odyssey XIII 53–8. It was even given to young children, as when Phoenix holds it to the lips of the little Achilles, who spirts it out over his vesture in his childish waywardness, Iliad IX 491; Odyssey XVI 444. A temperate use of the beverage, however, is a characteristic of the age, and its mixture with water served to maintain this. At Rome in early days it was unlawful for women, and even for young men below the age of thirty, to drink wine except at sacrifices. In Egypt the monuments sometimes exhibit the women as indulging in it to excess.

78. asko en: this preposition follows its case in the epic and lyric writers, but is not accented; H. 104. The proclitics ou, hos, ex, follow Hadley's rule, and sometimes es, Odyssey VII 318. The occurrence of the prep. between the noun and its attribute, as here, is common in the Greek poets, and imitated by the Latin. See Odyssey VI 89, VII 77, 79, 85, 193, 254, 279, VIII 53, 80, 211, 220, 232, 257, 420, 456, XI 346. This is the lightest form of the postponement of the preposition. The order aigeio en asko would not be uncommon in prose. — aigeiо. The goat-skin bag was the regular receptacle for wine when transported over the country, but when stored it was

70 NOTES.

kept in large earthen jars, pithoi, ranged round the wall of the store-room, as in that of Odysseus, Book 2, line 340. — epebēset', a mixed aoristic form, sigma of the 1st aorist, epsilon of the 2nd; H. 349 D.; C. 268 D. So Book 6, lines 127, 255, Book 9, line 255. — apēnēs; Book 7, lines 196, 223.

79. dōken returns to mētēr as its subject. — chryseē, two syllables by synizesis. This adjective always has a long upsilon in Homer, but in the lyric poets, and in the lyric parts of tragedy, it is sometimes short. — lēkythō, a small, narrow-mouthed vessel, principally for holding oil for the bath. Later it was generally of earthenware, and many have been discovered in tombs, where they were a favorite vessel for deposit in the coffin beside the dead, especially at Athens. The illustration on the right shows the shape of the Athenian style, and specimens may be seen in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Here the use of dōken, and its emphatic position, seem to imply that the flask was not placed in the coffer, but carried slung over the shoulder or arm, and hence it was pointed at the bottom, like so many in use at an early period. See the vase depicted above on the arm of the Kefa or Phoenician who is represented in an Egyptian tomb as bearing tribute to Thothmes III. — hygron, "liquid," "lissom," as opposed to solid fat. The epithet at Book E, line 903 is applied to milk, where it is contrasted with the curd formed from it.

80. heiōs, in prose heōs, usually means "until;" but here and in Book 4, line 800, Book 9, line 376, Book 19, line 367, it becomes final in meaning, "in order that." These two meanings come together prominently in ophra, and are liable to be confused in other languages; compare the Irish "Come here till I whack yez." Aristophanes, Clouds, line 58.

81. sigaloenta, from the polish given to the leather. In the Iliad mention is made of reins "white with ivory," leuk' elephanti; cf. Book 6, line 316.

BOOK VI. 71

82. μάστιξεν δ' ἐλάαν, "and she plied the whip to start them," a frequent formula; cf. ζ 319–20. — ἐλάαν is the present infinitive of the poetic verb ἐλάω, with stem ἐλα, from which ἐλα-νν-ω = ἐλαύνω is derived; H. 329 d. The infinitive expresses purpose. — καναχὴ . . . ἡμιόνοιιν, "and a rattling was made by the mules." — καναχὴ refers to the clatter of darts showered upon the helmet of Ajax (Π 105), the clank of the visored helm of Achilles as Apollo smites it to the ground from the head of Patroclus (Π 794), and the gnashing of Achilles' teeth when he was mad to revenge the slaughter of his friend (Τ 365). In the present passage it is either the clatter of hoofs or the rattling of the yoke upon the pole. The genitive is one of cause; ν 99.

83. αἱ . . . τανύοντο, "and they unflagging kept on the stretch;" θ 121, ζ 316–20. — φέρον, more commonly ἦγον, for φέρω properly has a personal subject and means to carry on the shoulders or otherwise. F. thinks that the present usage arose from the fact that in the two-wheeled chariot or wagon a large part of the burden fell upon the necks of the animals, so that they literally carried the weight. — αὐτὴν: this pronoun is much used in Homer to emphasize the individual in opposition to anything external to himself, as the sailor in antithesis to his ship, the master to the servant, the warrior to his horses or his arms, the parent to the offspring, the horses to the chariot, the person to his garments, and even the soul to the body.

84. ἅμα. Sentences or notions that are logically one thought should also be represented as such by joining them together by means of conjunctions. When this is not done, an abruptness is created which produces certain rhetorical effects, such as animation, crowding of thought in description, and surprise. Such asyndeton is very common in clauses which define or explain what was indistinctly or generally stated before, and where γάρ or ἄρα would naturally have stood, as γάρ does here. The omission imparts weight and emphasis to the explanatory thought. — καὶ . . . ἄλλαι, "also her attendants went besides." This apparently pleonastic use of ἄλλος is of common occurrence not only in Homer, but in prose Greek, and a similar idiom appears in Latin, German, and French. It springs from a striving after brevity of expression, and may often be translated by adverbs: "also," "besides," "as well."

BOOK VI. 73

or an adjective with "being" (eon); Lambda 350, Zeta 136; on Eta 224. — "dirty things" (rhuponta), supply "garments." The verb rhupao is intransitive, rhupoo (line 59) is transitive. Is hoste used in Homer with an infinitive of result? See G. M. 98, Note 3.

88–9. "Then" (entho), apodosis of "when" (hote), line 85. — "they urged" (seusan): 1st aorist like echeuev, without the tense marker sigma.

90. "to gnaw" (trogein), indicating purpose; line 82. — "agrostis" (the grass-name) has been assigned by different commentators to three distinct genera of grasses: the panicum dactylon, the cynodon dactylon, and the triticum repens. Besides other wide differences, the triticum has five flowers, the panicum two, the cynodon one. The name agrostis is now given by botanists to a fourth genus which includes several species. The triticum repens is our squitch-grass.

91. "by hand" (chersin), instrumental; Theta 68, 84; but cf. Theta 372, Eta 101; on Theta 135. — "they carried in" (esforeon); Theta 529, Eta 6; on Zeta 77, Theta 106. — Homer applies the epithet "dark" (melan) to both river and spring water, but "dark-watered" (melanudros) only to a spring (krene). He also calls water white, as the four fountains of Calypso, and that in which the body of Patroclus is bathed. Light and shade have much to do with the apparent color of water, but some is very dark in itself by reason of impregnation with mineral or vegetable solutions, while some is remarkably clear and transparent.

92. "Swiftly" (thoos) in Homer maintains an invariable position in the line, always following a feminine caesura of the third foot, and with scarcely an exception is construed with a following verb; hence, "in their speed a rivalry displaying."

93. "When" (epei) gives what translation to the aorist? H. 706; C. 493. — pluno means "to wash garments,"louomai "to bathe," nizo "to wash the hands or feet." — "filth" (rhupa); H. 200.

94–5. "Beach" (thin'). What would the accent of the dative have been? H. 160, 100. — "where the sea, dashing on the beach, was wont to scour the pebbles cleanest." — "toward the dry land" (poti chersor) is a pregnant construction involving the idea of motion; Epsilon 402, Zeta 12. The cleanest spot would naturally be sought for the drying, and pluno is the proper verb for cleansing, not for "washing up on shore," as some have construed here.

96. "Having bathed" (loessamevai); Homer uses two stems, lo-F, vocalized lou, lines 210, 216, 219, and lo-Fe, with the digamma not written, as here and lines 221, 227. — lip', only in this elided form in Epic, but some later writers have

4

74 NOTES.

"lipa" (grease/oil); hence probably an adverb meaning "unctuously," though many prefer to consider it a mutilated dative.

97. "deipnon" is the chief meal of the day, as opposed to "ariston," meaning "early breakfast," which the maidens may be supposed to have taken before the start, and "dorpon," the "evening meal," which is prepared for Nausicaa on her return (Odyssey, Book 7, line 13). "epeith'" is in correlation to "epei" implied in the temporal participles preceding; cf. Book 8, lines 377-78; Hadley's Grammar 795a. "ochthesin": When in prose is the movable "n" found? H. 79. What extension does it have in poetry? H. 78c; Goodwin 13; Curtius 68.

98. "heimata," accusative before "tersemenai," is a rare and poetic construction after "meno"; cf. Book 1, line 422, Book 4, line 247. "avge," Book 6, line 305.

99. "sitou": H. 575; G. 172. "tarphten" means "were comforted." Homer uses both "eterphthen" and "etarphthen," from "terpo." The ending "n" here forms an exception to what rule? H. 356c; 355 D.c; C. 293. "dmoai": see note on line 18. "aute," note 83.

100. "sphaire": Nouns in "-ra" are declined like "glossa"; Book 6, line 115. "epaizon" means "began to play." As the imperfect tense implies that a certain action was going on at a specified time, but excludes the assertion that the end of the action was attained, it may often be rendered by "began to" or "proceeded to." "apo," with "balousai": This position for the verbal object, between the preposition and the verb, is a favorite one in Homer; cf. Book 6, lines 21, 77, 140, 212, 228, Book 7, lines 189, 220, 286, Book 8, lines 72, 245, 447, Book 13, line 120. "kredemnon," from "kare" (head) and "deo" (bind), was a head-dress with ends hanging down towards the shoulders in broad bands, and served not only as an ornament, but as a veil to draw before the face upon occasion, as Penelope always does when she appears before the suitors. Andromache, in the wildness of her grief at the death of Hector, tears hers off with the other ornaments of her hair. Ino, the sea-goddess, presents hers to Odysseus to be stretched beneath his breast as a support, when swimming from his wrecked raft to the Phaeacian shore.

101. "tesi" means "for them." "leukoolenos" (white-armed) is the standing epithet of Hera in the Iliad, and it is shown, by its application also to Helen, Andromache, Nausicaa, and her mother Arete, to be ranked high as a description of beauty. In like manner, Aphrodite and Penelope have "white arms." "ercheto molpes" means "led off the sport," which consisted not only of ball-playing, but of the measured movements of the dance following the singing of the leader;

cf. Odyssey θ 370–80. In all choral dances the rhythm required a leader, who was called exarchos, and set the example for the others. Apollo is the Exarchus of the Muses, Achilles of his followers in the lament over Patroclus, and Thetis of the Nereids in the same.

102. "And even as Artemis, the arrow-showerer, glides down from some mountain." — The word oie has for its correlative hos, at line 109, instead of toie; cf. Iliad Χ 317, Odyssey η 108–9. — eisi, not in future sense; so, often in Homer; ζ 131. — kata oureos; note the sense of kata with the genitive; H. 618. For elegance in relation to what follows, some have read ourea. Then the mountain names define appositively the general ourea. But Krüger has remarked the fact that the repetition of the preposition with an appositive is contrary to Homeric usage. — iocheira, from ios, cheo; cf. χ 3, Θ 159. — As was remarked by Valerius Probus (Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae IX. 9), this famous simile is paraphrased by Virgil with greatly diminished effect, since the surroundings of his scene are strangely different from those of the huntress queen. Homer has a maiden amidst her maidens, in a woodland retreat, gliding through the figures of the dance, compared with a maiden goddess surrounded by her nymphs sporting about her, amid the lonely mountains. Virgil, without any material change of scene for the goddess, compares Dido, the widowed queen, as she moves in solemn state through the city, accompanied by a band of counsellors and warriors; while line 108, which is the brightest jewel of the passage in Homer, Virgil is compelled by necessity to omit. Virgil introduces the simile, Aeneid I. 498–504, when Dido is approaching the temple where Aeneas had been tracing with reviving hopes the deeds of his countrymen displayed in painted scenes upon the walls:

As on Eurotas' banks or along the ridges of Cynthus
Diana leads her dances, while a thousand Oreads
Gather here and there around her; she carries her quiver
On her shoulder, and as she strides she overtops all the goddesses:
Joy steals silently through Latona's heart;
Such was Dido, such was the glad bearing she carried
Through the midst of them.

103. "Or along Taygetus the towering, or Erymanthus." Taygetus was the range of mountains lying between Laconia and

the suitors by her charms, makes her more portly as well as taller. The characteristic which clearly marks an ancient statue of Artemis, according to Winckelmann, is its delicate grace of proportion and divine loftiness of bearing, its lightness and slenderness combined with added height. Doubtless the artist borrowed this, as so much else, from Homer: for the stature of Artemis is prominent in this simile, and her slender grace is implied at ζ 163; while among the manifold gifts bestowed upon the daughters of Pandareos, it is Artemis who endows them with height, at υ 71. The accompanying woodcut is from a photograph of the famous antique, the Diana of Versailles, now in the Louvre.

108. "Easily" (ῥείά), ζ 300. — δέ τε, "and furthermore," "although." The beauty of Nausicaa's handmaids has been especially commended, at line 18.

109. "She stood out" (μετέπρεπε), θ 172. — "an unwedded maiden" (παρθένος ἀδμής), "the maiden unwedded," the distinctive trait also of Artemis, and for that reason emphasized in the princess, as a further point in the comparison. The marriage, too, is again brought to mind; on line 35. — ἀδμής, properly of the destined beast of burden, as "an untamed cow, whom no man had yet brought under the yoke," K 293; δ 637. "Whom never husband tamed." Chapman.

110–11. "But when at last she was thinking back homeward to return after yoking the mules, and folding the garments beauteous." The ball-playing had not yet ceased, and lines 252–53 show

78 NOTES.

that the task represented by the participles was still in her thought: "we will return now as soon as we have yoked," etc. The participles are subordinate to "to return" (νέεσθαι), not to "was about to" (ἔμελλε). — νέεσθαι is scarcely an exception to the regular use of the future after μέλλω, since νέομαι, like εἶμι, commonly has a future sense.

112. ἀλλ' ἐνόησε, "of other things took thought," a common formula; ζ 251.

113. ὥς, "that;" ζ 129, θ 21, η 192. — εὐώπιδα, "beauteous-eyed," used exclusively of Nausicaa in Homer.

114. ἥ; on 37. — οἵ, η 22.

115. ἔπειτ', "accordingly," as the result of the determination of Athene, who turns the ball aside so that it may fall into the river and occasion the shout which awakens Odysseus. In the Iliad Athene often turns a spear from its mark, or directs it more unerringly; θ 8. — μετ', 54. — βασίλεια, "the princess." Similarly Virgil calls Ilia regina sacerdos. Sophocles wrote a Satyric drama, now lost, entitled Nausicaa, taking his subject from these scenes. One of his rare appearances on the stage was in this drama, where he won warm plaudits from his audience by his grace and adroitness in ball-playing.

116. ἀμφιπόλου; H. 580; G. 171. — ἅμαρτε: it is Homer's custom to make the person, and not the missile, the subject of this verb. — δίνη; on 75. Its eddies are a characteristic of the river, 89, and a deep eddy would insure the loss of the ball, and cause the louder exclamation.

117. ἐπὶ μακρόν, "afar," "over a wide space," so that the cry is measured, as it were, before the eye. — μακρόν, neuter adjective used substantively. Homer usually estimates sound by distance rather than volume; yet μέγα, sometimes; cf. the curious expression, Λ 462, "she cried out as much as a man's head can hold." — δῖος, root διϜ, original meaning "to shine," then "sky," "sky-god," "related to Zeus," "godlike," "illustrious." The adjective is used of about 30 of the heroes, most constantly of the greatest, Achilles, Hector, and Odysseus; of the last above 100 times. All kings are "of Zeus's lineage" (διογενέες); see Ι 538, and Ψ 346–47 where the relative clause is explanatory of δῖον. Eumaeus is of royal birth, and Philoetius doubtless also, since he holds the title "leader of men" (ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν), elsewhere given only to those of princely race.

BOOK VI. 79

118. ἑζόμενος, "seating himself," i.e., rising to a sitting posture. The fuller idea appears in Book B, when Agamemnon rouses after the dream-visitation. — ὥρμαινε. Homer's faculty of dramatizing his narrative, of transferring from himself to his heroes the duty of developing both the action of the poem and their own characters, is one of the most prominent peculiarities as well as beauties of his style. But exclusively proper to Homer is his art of dramatizing, not merely action, but thought; not merely the intercourse between man and men, but between man and himself, between his passions and his judgment. The mechanism of which the poet here chiefly avails himself is, to exhibit the person under the influence of excited feelings as communing with his own mind, so that the breast of the man seems laid open before us, and, in the literal sense of the term, we read his thoughts as they flit through his bosom. Mure. This self-dialogue is usually depicted by ὁρμαίνω, which denotes the rushing of the thought to and fro in a mind violently agitated.

119. "O woe is me," sc. "I am wretched"; ε 299; "Ah me! luckless I." — μοι, ζ 59. — τέων . . . ἱκάνω; "into the land of what mortals again have I come?" a fitting question after his many wanderings and hairbreadth escapes in unknown places. — τέων; H. 244 D. — ἱκάνω and ἵκω, in Homer, have in the present the sense of the perfect; similarly, what verbs in Attic? H. 698; G. M. 10, Note 4.

120. ὑβρισταί, and ἄγριοι, the insolent and the savage, are opposed to φιλόξεινοι, the hospitable; the Cyclopes and Laestrygonians, to the Phaeacians. — οὐδὲ δίκαιοι, "and unrighteous." οὐδὲ = καὶ οὐ; H. 858. Here the unrighteous is antithetical to the god-fearing man, θεουδής. The stranger is under the special protection of Zeus Xenios, and the man who reveres the deity is the righteous man, and will respect the laws of hospitality. Polyphemus, whose boast is that he fears neither god nor man, becomes the arch-violator of the claims of the suppliant stranger.

121. θεουδής is not θεοειδής, but is compounded of θεός and δFέος, fear, θεοδFής, by transposition and vocalization of F becoming θεουδής. Cf. "having stood in awe of Zeus of strangers," ξ 389.

122. (I say of mortals) "for a feminine cry as of maidens about me came." So when Agamemnon wakes from his dream in the Second Iliad: "a divine voice enveloped him." — ὥστε in its poetic and Ionic use

80 NOTES.

as a particle of comparison; on 87, 84. — thēlus, masculine form for feminine; H. 212 D.

123. nymphaōn, "of nymphs," defining kouraōn more closely. While we are content to contemplate the beauty of nature in its outward forms, and possess a much stronger and more educated taste for the charms of the landscape, the Greek, passing lightly over the external aspect, sought to find the reflection of his own buoyant life within nature's garment, and peopled all nature with a higher life than he saw in the humanity around him. Not only do rivers possess their river-gods, but each spring and grove, mountain-top and grassy meadow contains its indwelling spirit. Homer, however, stopped short of much that is found later — the Hamadryad and the constant nymph-companion of later days, the Satyr. As the daughters of Rain-Zeus, the nymphs haunt mountain, meadow, and grove, doubtless on account of their abundant springs. They are worshipped like the river deities, especially in Ithaca, and their cave there is described at Book 13, line 103.

124. pisea poiēenta, "spring-fed meadows lush with grass." — poiēenta makes the line spondaic. In such cases Homer usually includes the last two feet of the line within one word; cf. Book 6, lines 8, 114, 125, 157, 160, 188; 259; etc.

125. "Surely then, methinks, I am near men of human voice." The punctuation of Ameis, which is favored by Eustathius, is followed here. Most editors have treated it as a question, and several have bracketed lines 123-24 as inconsistent with the rest of the speech. For Odysseus begins with the assumption that he is in a land of mortals, and given this, the declaration that the cry he has heard is of maidens is natural, while that of nymphs would be inconsistent. But this view overlooks the fact that nymphs are most likely to be found in the vicinity of man, since they enjoy the worship accorded them by him. An idea so common would be sufficient for Odysseus to base a supposition upon, one about which he plainly feels uncertain. — audēentōn strengthens the argument for the lines, since it is regularly used to contrast the voice of man with that of the divine race; hence here it contrasts with the supposed cry of the nymphs. The notion of a distinction between the human voice and that of supernatural beings is current in all ages. The cry of Ares and Poseidon

BOOK VI. 81

was like that of nine or ten thousand men, E 860, Ξ 148; cf. "nor does the voice sound human," Virg. Æn. I. 328; "a voice clearer than human," Liv. V. 32. The unnaturally loud, shrill cry of the maidens would easily suggest some such thing.

126. πειρήσομαι [I will try]; on 31; a possible future; η 190, θ 34, ι 174, μ 383; G. M. 87. Such examples show how closely allied the future and subjunctive stand, in the early language especially.

127. θάμνων ὑπεδύσετο [from beneath the shrubs emerged], "from beneath the shrubs emerged." The shelter beneath which Odysseus had sought protection from the chill night air and prowling beasts consisted of two small olive-trees, one wild, the other tame, both growing from the same root, and so thickly intertwined and interleaved that neither sun nor rain could pierce their covert; "which Odysseus had crept beneath," ε 481. These stood in the edge of the wood upon a height overlooking the shore; on 138.

128–29. "And from the dense copse he wrenched with his brawny hand a branch rich in leaves, that this about his person might screen the unseemliness of man." — χειρὶ παχείῃ [with his thick hand], not only of many warriors, but of Penelope and Here; on 107. — φύλλων [of leaves]; H. 560; G. 167, 4. The young sapling or branch would have a thicker foliage than an old one. — ῥύσαιτο [might shield], 113. Exposure of the person was regarded with feelings of repugnance in the Homeric day. When Odysseus would threaten Thersites with the last degree of shameful punishment, he declares that he will strip him to the skin and then flog him to the ships. It was not until much later that the practice of throwing off all covering when entering the arena for gymnastic contest was introduced by the Lacedaemonians; Thucydides says but shortly before his day, and then as a purely gymnastic expedient. "The scene in the Odyssey," remarks Mr. Gladstone, "where Ulysses emerges from his covert on the coast of Scheria, will always be regarded as one of the most careful, and yet most simple and unaffected examples of true modesty contained in the whole circle of literature." Studies, II. p. 466.

130. This simile has been criticised as unseasonably sublime. Mure calls it a good specimen of the "mock heroic," which he finds pervading the whole Phaeacian episode, and says that "no figure can be less appropriate, if taken in a literal sense, or hap-

pier if considered as a travesty of the more dignified epic style." He would characterize it as a parody upon a passage in the Twelfth Iliad where Sarpedon, starting to storm the Greek intrenchments before their ships, glittering in arms and brandishing his weapons, is compared to the lion:

He went forth like a lion bred in the mountains, who long starved of meat is urged on by his proud spirit to make an attempt upon the flocks and enter their well-built fold. Iliad M 299–301.

(He) "Strode onward, as a lion, mountain bred,
Whom, fasting long, his dauntless courage leads
To assail the flock, though in well-guarded fold." Derby.

The opposite point of view has been thus presented by Hayman: "The point of this simile seems to be that the hero moves forth from his covert with forlorn desperation, heedless whom or what he may encounter, even as the hungry lion endures wind and rain, and alike to him comes all prey, wild or tame. Further, the effect produced on the maidens resembles that by the lion on the animals. The constancy of Nausicaa alone is not included in the simile. The simile dignifies a passage which seems to us perhaps to need such relief, but nothing in the whole context is more remarkable than the simple and unruffled gravity of its tone. No later poet could have attempted such a scene save in the Satyric vein." A nice critical discrepancy for the student to weigh and resolve. In considering this, as all Homeric similes, the following principles should be kept in view: No simile can, strictly speaking, be exact. The very nature of comparison implies a difference. But the intellectual age is more likely to work up fully the exact features than the imaginative. To the latter Homer belongs, and often when his similes are descriptive of the mode rather than the degree, we find that he has seized some general feature of resemblance, and has then extended or enlarged the ornamental element of the comparison beyond the limits of the comparison itself. By this means a fair field is gained by the poet for the play of his imagination, and a liveliness and separate picturesqueness are imparted to the description, which are always pleasurable; cf. Odyssey VI 232–35, VIII 521–30. — alkì, a metaplastic form; H. 199. This attribution has nothing to do with the comparison: it is descriptive of the lion, simply.
