132. "daietai," "blaze": the subject "osse" as a neuter takes the same construction as a neuter plural; Iliad 13.466, of Hector, "his eyes blazed with fire."

133. The difference of case in "bousi" (dative) and "elaphous" (accusative), after "met'," vividly marks the character of the animals; the one as slow of foot, and affording no trouble to the lion in seizing; the other swift and wary, giving the pursuer a hard chase before capture; on lines 60, 54. — de; on line 6. — "gaster," 7.216, 6.250.

134. "For the purpose of making an attempt upon the flocks, even going into the stout fold." — "peiresonta" must be construed with "elthein," not "keletai." Of the 57 cases of the future participle in the Iliad, and 63 in the Odyssey, all but Iliad 5.46, 16.343, 20.120, 23.379, Odyssey 11.608, are connected with verbs of motion; see 6.31, 59, 7.229, 324, 8.81, 108, 13.17. Classen.

135. "emelien," "was constrained"; 7.270, 217–20.

136. "mixesthai," "to draw nigh unto." — per; on line 87. This repetition of the overwhelming necessity which conquers all scruples emphasizes the main point of the comparison. — "ikanen," sc. min; line 169. Odysseus' presenting himself to Nausicaa was the subject of a painting by the famous Polygnotus, which was preserved in the Propylaea at Athens, and was seen by Pausanias (I. 22).

137. "And frightful to them did he appear, grimed with sea-dregs." His outward appearance is imitated in the rugged harshness of the line. Dionysius of Halicarnassus remarks upon this passage: "When Homer is to introduce a terrible or unusual image, he rejects the more flowing and harmonious vowels, and makes choice of such consonants as load the syllables, and render the pronunciation difficult." For the reverse, see lines 162–63.

138. "tressan . . . alle," "and they fled trembling, the one here,

84 NOTES.

the other there." — ἄλλυδις is the epic form of ἄλλοσε; the v is Æolic, as in ὄνυμα for ὄνομα. The suffix -δις is only a variant of -δε. — ἠϊόνας refers to the level stretch of sandy shore along the sea upon which they had already spread their garments to dry. The scene so accurately conceived in the poet's mind, whether it had actual existence or not, is that of a river emptying into the sea, upon one side of which rise high cliffs stretching up the sea-coast, while the other bank is a grassy slope running down to the sandy sea-shore, which is an open beach free from rocks. On the river-bank are the laundry-pits hard by the beach. A short distance from the river the land begins to rise into a wooded height, upon which Odysseus has been sleeping. The maidens are playing ball near the river, in the space between the pits and the beach, and as Odysseus descends the slope the attendants flee naturally toward the most open spot away from the intruder, namely along the sea-shore, which, stretching out toward the town, finally swells into a rocky promontory that hides the city from the river-mouth and helps to form one of the harbors. BOOK VI. 85

140–41. ek; on 100. — "holding back," opposed to "they fled in terror." The attendants followed the first impulse and fled; the princess, by the aid of Athene and her own frank and fearless heart, overcame that impulse, and awaited the stranger. Though the poet has seen fit here to introduce his theurgic machinery, it is evident from the character of Nausicaa, as sketched throughout, that Athene's share in the scene was necessary only to destroy the effect of the fear which Odysseus' savage appearance might have produced, not any fear of him as a man, or as a stranger. The fact that she is the only sister among five brothers would tend forcibly to infuse an element of strength and self-possession into her character, and in addition she lives in a court where feminine influence has more than ordinary sway. Mure well says of her: "The portrait of Nausicaa is the most excellent of its kind in either poem. It combines, in the most attractive form, and under such modifications as became her sex, the more favorable characteristics of the Greek nation, frankness, courtesy, and benevolence, with a due share of egotistic loquacity and innocent coquetry." — "She pondered" introduces a favorite Homeric method of describing the workings of the human breast, by way of narrative, instead of soliloquy. The word first exhibits the thoughts in a state of agitation, then follow the various expedients that marshal themselves before the mind, and finally appears the summation expressed by "she resolved."

142. "whether ... or," introducing a double indirect deliberative question; H. 737; G. M. 71; G. 244. — "knees" with "grasping"; H. 574 e. This was the common attitude of the suppliant. Thetis in her solemn prayer to Zeus grasps his knees with one hand, and his chin with the other, Iliad Book 1, line 500, and Priam, presenting himself before Achilles to beg the ransom of Hector, clasps his knees and kisses the dread hands that had slain many a son of his, Iliad Book 24, line 478.

143. "thus," as he was, defined more accurately by "standing at a distance."

144. "in case she would point out," a condition where the conclusion is implied in the context; Odyssey Book 13, line 182; G. M. 53, Note 2. — "garments." Odysseus had doubtless noticed the garments on the beach. This line has been bracketed by many editors as otiose and inapposite, since the question in the mind of

86 NOTES.

the hero was not what he had best ask, but how. His fear was lest, if he approached so near as to clasp her knees, the maiden would be more shocked than propitiated.

145. δοάσσατο . . . εἶναι, "it appeared on the whole to be better," always with some doubt yet remaining in the mind as to complete wisdom in the choice of alternatives. Virgil has employed in his own way this mode of expression for Aeneas, when he receives from Mercury the command of the gods to depart from Carthage, Aen. IV. 285–87:

And now his swift mind darts this way, now that,
And races through all things, weighing every part.
This judgment seemed the better to him as he wavered.

147. μή; η 16, 306, ζ 273, θ 230; H. 743; G. M. 46; G. 218. — Note γοῦνα here, γούνων above. — φρένα; on 106.

148. "Straightway a gracious and winning speech he spake." A speech more admirably contrived to effect its purpose can scarcely be pointed out even in Homer, whose speeches everywhere are wonderful specimens of argument and eloquence. Beginning with the assumption that she is a goddess, he likens her to Artemis, but if she be a mortal, her beauty must be the joy of all her dear ones; for anything comparable with it he never saw save once, a springing palm in Delos. Reverence for her beauty is so mingled with his admiration that it sustains and elevates a flattery which would be too open and unblushing in itself. A skillful hint at his former importance in the world is followed up by an appeal to her sympathies for the forlorn and shipwrecked wanderer whom the very gods are persecuting. He then reminds her of the common obligations of hospitality, in that she is the first whom he has met in the new land, and prefers a request whose very moderation is proof of the true delicacy that accompanies real want. He closes with the wish that the gods who persecute him may shower upon her the choicest blessings they have in store for maiden virtue and maiden hope — a husband, home, and fondest mutual affection.

149. Γουνοῦμαί is chosen, though the suppliant is at a distance, as if to excuse his apparent lack of formality in the position he assumes. — ἄνασσα occurs elsewhere in Homer only of goddesses. Odysseus' original supposition is that he is to meet daughters of

Zeus. Doubtless this idea is shaken by the earthly signs of a homely occupation scattered about; yet he does not free himself wholly from his first expectation, and for rhetorical purposes he does not wish to do so. — "some goddess, then, or mortal art thou?" a double direct question with the particle omitted in the first clause, as at α 226, δ 140, 314, 371. — What parts of the verb "to be" are regularly enclitic? H. 105; G. 27.

150. "of those who." Before a relative referring to a whole class of persons or facts, a genitive plural is often to be supplied in thought.

151. "you yourself": this harsh hiatus is elsewhere found in the second foot, at τ 185, Β 8, Γ 46, Τ 288.

152. "eidos" is beauty of face, "megethos" loftiness of stature, and "phyen" that complete harmony of every limb and part which formed the Greek ideal of beauty, and was afterwards embodied in their masterpieces of art. It may represent massiveness of frame, or slenderness, as here. The poet has already likened Nausicaa to Artemis, and he makes his hero strike upon the same analogy. It is needless, nay, wholly wrong, to suppose that Odysseus had acquired an idea of the appearance of Artemis from statuary or painting. The former of these arts is barely mentioned in the poems, the latter never. Personal communication between man and the deities, especially in the Iliad, is so common that one need not look further. See on ζ 107, η 100, θ 34. — This whole address should be compared with that of Aeneas to Venus when she meets him on the shores of Carthage in the guise of the huntress, Aeneid I. 327–34:

O — by what name shall I call you, maiden? For your face is not mortal, nor does your voice sound human. O surely a goddess; are you Phoebus's sister? or one of the Nymphs? Be gracious, and whatever your power, relieve our toil; tell us under what sky, on what shores of the world we are cast, wandering in ignorance of people and places, driven hither by wind and vast seas: many a victim shall fall before your altars at our hands.

154. Here speaks the heart of him who took no greater pride in any name than in being called the father of Telemachus; Β 260, Δ 354. Virgil's paraphrase, put into the mouth of Aeneas in his first address to Dido, is characteristic:

What ages so happy bore you? What parents so great brought forth such a child?

155–57. μάλα, causal asyndeton: "For deeply, I ween, are their hearts ever with fond gladness warmed because of thee, when beholding such a scion to the dance tripping." — εὐφροσύνησιν: the plural of abstract nouns is especially common in Homer, and occurs more frequently in the Odyssey than the Iliad. What force does it convey? H. 518 c. — λευσσόντων after σφισι has several parallels in the poems, and is variously explained: either the dative is so far equivalent to a genitive that the participle agrees with the implied σφῶν, in preference to the expressed σφισι; or it is an actual genitive absolute with subject suppressed; or the participle is indeed dependent on θυμός, but represents the last stage of development before its full emancipation into the genitive absolute. — εἰσοιχνεῦσαν agrees with the natural gender of θάλος, as referring to the maiden, rather than the grammatical; H. 523. — The joint participation of maiden and youth in the dance, which was a common custom in the Homeric day, exhibits a freedom and independence of manners such as existed later among some of the Dorians and Asiatic Greeks, but stands far removed from the seraglio-like confinement of the sex at Athens. A beautiful picture is drawn of the choral dance as exhibited upon the shield of Achilles:

There youths and maidens worth many cattle were dancing, holding one another by the wrist. The girls wore fine linen garments, and the youths wore well-woven tunics lightly gleaming with oil. The girls had beautiful garlands, and the youths carried golden daggers hanging from silver straps. And sometimes they would run around with skillful feet very nimbly, as when a potter sitting at his wheel tries whether it will spin; and at other times they would run in lines toward one another. A great crowd stood around the lovely dance, delighting in it; and among them a divine bard played the lyre, while two tumblers whirled through the midst of them as the song began. Iliad 593–606.

"There, laying each on other's wrist their hand,
Bright youths and many-suitored maidens danced:
In fair white linen these; in tunics those,
Well woven, shining soft with fragrant oils;

These with fair coronets were crowned, while those
With golden swords from silver belts were girt.
Now whirled they round with nimble practised feet,
Easy, as when a potter, seated, turns
A wheel, new fashioned by his skilful hand,
And spins it round, to prove if true it run;
Now featly moved in well-beseeming ranks.
A numerous crowd, around, the lovely dance
Surveyed, delighted; while an honored bard
Sang, as he struck the lyre, and to the strain

construction, but the two are virtually antagonistic. The superlative includes all of the series, not excepting the happy man, while "of others" expressly excludes him. "Of others" may be translated as if it meant "of all." This inclusion of the object being compared among the objects of comparison is similar to that of including a person or thing among those from whom they are to be distinguished (on 84), and the present time in the past, Odyssey VI.220. Compare Milton's imitation in Paradise Lost, IV.323:

"Adam the goodliest man of men since born
His sons; the fairest of her daughters Eve."

159. "prevailing by his gifts of wooing": "by his gifts prevailing." Aristotle says that the Greeks in early days were accustomed to purchase their wives from each other. The Homeric poems exhibit a transition period in this respect, as in so many others. To make large presents to the father of the bride was still the prevailing custom, and the word for "bride-gifts" for the most part represents these, as here; for the leading thought of the passage is to heighten the estimation in which the maiden is held, and this is best effected by depicting her as the object of ardent competition among numerous suitors who will pay heavily for the boon of her hand. See on 28, 287. "he might lead her home"; on 28. — A poet in the Anthology rises to a still higher flight in his panegyric:

"Happy is he who looks upon you; thrice blessed is he who hears you;
a demigod is he who loves you; and immortal is he who marries you."

161. "man." Homer's truly Greek love of the beautiful in human form has not confined that characteristic to the female sex. All of his heroes possess beauty in a marked degree. Thersites, the most contemptible wretch beneath the walls of Troy, was at the same time the most ugly. Achilles, on the other hand, the greatest of his heroes, possesses an almost superhuman beauty. The poet expressly declares, Odyssey VIII.168, that beauty is one of the three great gifts of god to man; and his reverence for it throughout the poems rises almost to a worship. It entitles Ganymede and Tithonus to immortality. The reverence, therefore, which Odysseus here professes before the maiden, who is plainly the poet's ideal of virgin beauty, must not be attributed merely to his flattering and gain-seeking tongue, but to a genuine admiration, which the plain-spoken hero neither needs nor desires to repress.

BOOK VI. 91

162. Δήλῳ (at Delos); on line 8. No other mention of Delos is found in Homer. Voss has inferred from this passage that Delos in Agamemnon's time possessed the foremost oracle of Apollo for seafarers, as Delphi did for landsmen. This conjecture gives a plausible motive for Odysseus' stopping there on his way to Troy, just as Aeneas does on his voyage to Italy. Doubtless it became a welcome haven at a very early period, for its harbor is one of the best in the Aegean. A scholiast thinks that the palm here is the same one of which much is made in the Homeridean Hymn to Apollo in connection with the birth of that god; but he overlooked the epithet νέον (young/new). In Homer no spot bears any trace of being honored as the birthplace of a god. The Apollo of our poet, in particular, is a deity too lofty and dread to have his birthplace fixed. Indeed, his birth at Delos was an Ionian and Athenian legend, never recognized by the Delphians, Boeotians, or Peloponnesians, except the Messenians. As late, however, as the time of Cicero and Pliny, a palm-tree was shown on the island which was declared to be the one under which Apollo and Artemis were born, and the same one which Odysseus saw; and a palm is found as an emblem of Delos on Greek vases.

163. The use of θάλος (branch) above seems to have suggested the comparison by ἔρνος (shoot) here. θάλος is properly a branch of the tree, ἔρνος a scion which springs from the root. Homer does not use ἔρνος like θάλος of a person, as the later poets do, but he says of Achilles "he shot up like a young plant" (ἀνέδραμεν ἔρνεϊ ἴσος), Iliad XVIII.56. The slender grace of Nausicaa, marked by the comparison with Artemis, is here again emphasized by the young palm shooting up with the straightness of the arrow. — ἐνόησα (I perceived) is also construed in this sense with "eyes" (ὀφθαλμοῖς, ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν).

165. τὴν ὁδόν, "on that journey;" cognate accusative; H. 547; cf. Odyssey VI.261, VIII.107. — ᾗ, "by which." — ἔμελλεν, 135. What other tenses of the infinitive may follow? H. 711; C. 501; G. 118, 6.

166. ὥς δ' αὔτως, "and in the self-same way." This phrase always assumes this form and place in the Homeric verse. Later it becomes ὡσαύτως. As an adverb it corresponds exactly to ὁ αὐτός (the same), αὔτως being the adverb of αὐτός. Buttmann therefore conjectured that the accent should be αὐτῶς, and this is the spelling adopted by Bekker. — ἐτεθήπεα, a pluperfect with the sense of an imperfect.

92 NOTES.

The termination is archaic, with the personal ending ν dropped, as is regularly the case in the 1st aorist; H. 351 D.

167. ἐκ, with γαίης: this is a rather unusual separation of a preposition from its noun, but see θ 149, ι 535, λ 115, and some remarkable prose examples in Prof. Short's Essay, p. lxxxiii. — δόρυ, used in the unusual sense of a standing tree. It is commonly used of the tree once cut and fashioned.

168. ὥς, "as," correlative to ὥς δ' αὔτως, not to τοῖον. The usual order of the correlatives is reversed; cf. γ 218–19, τ 224. — γύναι. From line 153 the assumption of divinity has been abandoned. Given the vividness of the Homeric conception of the scene, it seems scarcely too much to suppose that the poet imagined some gesture of dissent on the part of the maiden to have settled the question. She makes no disclaimer in her speech, as Aphrodite does in answer to Anchises in the Hymn, and as she does to Aeneas in the Aeneid, under similar circumstances. Homer turns his epic into drama more fully and frequently than any other poet. As in an unacted play, we are left to imagine the action, tone, and gesture not only of the speaker, as at ζ 206, 276, η 30, 48, λ 353, but also of the person addressed; see on η 315, and compare ε 205, κ 330, Milton, Paradise Lost, II. 689–95, Anthon on the Aeneid, III. 340. Virgil is usually much more descriptive. Compare Aen. I. 561 with the words of Nausicaa below. — δείδια; H. 319 D.; stem δFι, δέδFια = δείδια; on 121. Under the spell of her beauty he elevates his fear — his reason for assuming the position of a suppliant — onto higher ground than before, at line 147: ἄγαμαί τε τέθηπά τε, "I both revere thee and marvel." Construe σέ with the former verb, not the latter, which is intransitive.

169. δέ, "although," 108. The arrangement of sentences co-ordinately — that is, by employing co-ordinate conjunctions (H. 853, 855–67) to connect them — is doubtless the second stage of development in a language, the arrangement of clauses side by side without conjunctions being the earliest. The Greek language in the Homeric poems had reached the third stage, that of subordination (H. 853 b), but it still reverted with a lingering fondness to the earlier mode, and frequently used it where the logical connection requires a rendering in keeping with the later, full subordination; on 6, 234, θ 389, η 262.

170. χθιζός. The poets are fond of using adjectives for adverbs

BOOK VI. 93

of place, still more frequently for those of time, sometimes those of mode or manner and cause; H. 488 c.; on Book XIII line 75. — "wine-dark" (οἴνοπα) is used by Homer only of the sea and of oxen; XIII 32. "Wine-hued" is its proper sense, and wine is either red (ἐρυθρός), dark (μέλας), or gleaming (αἴθοψ), of which αἴθοψ is flashing, μέλας dark, and ἐρυθρός dark red. See on 53.

171. "And so long continually did the wave keep bearing me on, the sweeping tempests also." — The verb "was bearing" (ἐφόρει) is made to agree with the nearest noun, though referring to "squalls" (θύελλαι) as well. This is often the case even when several subjects stand before the verb, and is regular, as with us when only one precedes. As here, Book IV 628, Book XI 626, XIII 192, Book XXI 186; cf. Book VIII 277. For the thought, compare the words of Aeneas to his mother, Aeneid I. 375:

"We, swept from Troy across diverse seas, have been driven by fortune's own tempest to Libyan shores."

172. The preposition "from" (ἀπ'). Anastrophe does not take place when the preposition suffers elision, nor when "but/and" (δέ) is inserted between the preposition and its case; Book VI 107, 197, Book VIII 85. — "Ogygia's" (Ὠγυγίης) occurs in Homer only with "island" (νῆσος), and takes the same case. It is Calypso's isle, the "navel of the sea" (ὀμφαλὸς θαλάσσης), or centre of the great northern sea; on Book VIII 244. — "but now" (νῦν δ'), "now, however," pointing out the occurrence as beyond expectation; it may also refer to something unwished for, or not resulting in accordance with the circumstances. A succeeding aorist has the force of a perfect. — "has cast down" (κάββαλε), "has flung me down;" H. 73 D. — "divine power" (δαίμων). The idea of divine Providence governing the world and shaping the current of events is generally centred by Homer in Zeus, the father of gods and men, who holds the scales of fate, and on whose floor the two caskets stand which contain the varying incidents of human destiny; on line 188. Often this idea is conveyed by "god" (θεός), "the gods" (θεοί), "the immortals" (ἀθάνατοι), "divine power" (δαίμων), representing either Zeus himself or the gods in their combined action, since the polity of Olympus is founded upon that of the Greek state, and the united action of the ruler, counsellors, and people is the only proper mode of decree; on Book VIII 197.

173. "so that ... some ill" (ὄφρα . . . κακόν), "that doubtless even here I may suffer some ill." — "so that" (ὄφρα) is epic and lyric only. In final clauses the subjunctive is frequent after a leading historical tense, but here the force of "has cast down" (κάββαλε) is such that the subjunctive follows naturally; see Book IX 511, 580, Book XIII 303, Book XVI 233, Book III 15, Book XI 94, Book I 158, Book X 98.

94 NOTES.

174. παύσεσθ': supply κακὸν as subject; on θ 520. When are only diphthongs elided? H. 70 D.; ζ 307, θ 184. — ἀλλ'...: "but still many will the gods work me ere that." — πολλὰ, i.e. κακὰ from κακόν. — τελέουσι: H. 374.

175. ἄνασσ': He still retains the reverential mode of address. — σὲ...ἐς πρώτην: such a separation is strongly emphatic in itself, and still further emphasis is gained by placing σὲ at the head of the sentence, and ἐς πρώτην at the beginning of the line. Less care is taken for effect in the less pressing case ν 228. Cf. η 51–52, 89, 317–18.

177. τήνδε πόλιν, "the city here." What would the prose construction require with this phrase? H. 538; G. 141, Note 1 (c); C. 389. He has seen no city, but infers there must be one near, just as he conjectures that the habitations of men must be near because he hears the cry of nymphs.

178. ἄστυ and πόλιν are scarcely distinguished here, but the former, allied to the Sanskrit root vas, "to dwell," is properly the town considered as a dwelling-place; the latter, connected with πολύς, is the city viewed with reference to its inhabitants, hence the State. — ῥάκος, in Aeolic βράκος, showing Ϝράκος, as needed here by the metre.

179. "If haply some wrap of the vestments thou hadst when hither coming." — σπείρων, the garments for the wash; see on 69. — ἔχες: Why the indicative? H. 745; G. 221; C. 536; G. M. 49; ζ 150, 153, 282, 312, η 199, 320, 321, θ 146, 408.

180. δοίεν: H. 721, 1; G. M. 82. How is this optative distinguished from the potential? H. 722; on ζ 57; cf. 181, 244, 245, η 148, 149, 224, 314, 316, 331, 333. — φρεσὶ, 106, 118, 166, 313.

181–83. "Both a husband and a home, and a noble oneness of heart may they make to follow them; for surely nothing than this is more masterful or happy, than when a husband and wife, one-hearted in their purposes, sway a household." — κρεῖσσον, strong against δυσμενέεσσιν; ἄρειον, happy among εὐμενέτησι. With οὐ, ἄλλο may be supplied, as ν 392; cf. I 401, Soph. O. T. 428. — τοῦγε...ἢ ὅθ': the genitive after the comparative is more clearly defined by the clause introduced by ἢ ὅθ', which is only an enlargement of the demonstrative. This idiom is general from Homer down, in prose as well as poetry, and finds its counterpart in Latin, as

96 NOTES.

For two jars stand on the floor of Zeus's hall, filled with the gifts he gives — one of evils, one of blessings. To the man to whom Zeus who delights in thunder gives a mixed lot, he meets with evil at one time, good at another; but to the man to whom he gives only from the jar of griefs, he makes him an object of contempt, and bitter hunger drives him over the bright earth, and he wanders honored neither by gods nor men. Iliad XXIV, 525-33.

"Such is the thread the gods for mortals spin,
To live in woe, while they from cares are free.
Two coffers lie beside the door of Jove,
With gifts for man: one good, the other ill;
To whom from each the Lord of lightning gives,
Him sometimes evil, sometimes good befalls;
To whom the ill alone, him foul disgrace
And grinding misery o'er the earth pursue:
By god and man alike despised he roams." Derby.

Achilles applies this principle to his father Peleus, whose extraordinary fortune was to be marred by the early death of his son.

187. epei. No proper apodosis for this clause appears. The thought is broken at the end of the line, and when resumed at 191, it is resumed with a change, and epei repeated. See on z 275. — kako has been rightly understood by Eustathius as referring to degree, not moral character; cf. Xi 126, a 411, d 64, th 553.

189. ethelesen; on 37, 183. — hekasto, appositive, as alle, 138.

190. soi: when do the enclitic pronouns retain their accent? Hadley 232. What does Homer use for the enclitic soi? — tag', i.e. kaka. — tetlamen. Homer regularly uses the short -men after a short syllable, the long -nai after a long one, in the infinitive.

191. nun d', 172. "I could wish that Zeus had been more kind to thee, but though he afflict thee, yet will we not."

192. oun, correlative to epei. — deusesai must not be confused with deuterai, 44.

193. "(Of those things) which it is meet a suppliant trial-tried on meeting one (should not lack)." — on; on 150. The case is governed by me deuesthai, to be supplied in the thought. Why me rather than ou? Hadley 837; Goodwin 260, 1, Note 1.

194. ounoma; cf. eta 54, zeta 42, 102, eta 83.

197. "And upon him depend the Phaeacians' strength and

BOOK VI. 97

power." — ek governs tou. Why not ek? on 172. — echetai, middle, "hold themselves," the king being conceived as the stay to which all the people cling for safety and strength; lambda 346, theta 67.

198. He rha, "she spoke accordingly;" theta 186, 416, 469; more fully, theta 46, 482. — keleusen, "called to."

199. stete moi, "stop, I pray you." The ethical moi in this sense, especially with imperative thoughts; eta 208, 303, nu 59. — pose. She implies that the mere fact of seeing a man is no good reason for their flight. Only in the event of his being hostile would their flight be excusable; on 140, eta 10.

200. e me pou . . . phastho, "you do not say to yourselves, I hope, do you?" — e me would be ara me or mon in the Attic. What answer is implied in such questions? H. 829. — phastho; the operation of the mind in thought again represented dramatically, as in the actual self-dialogue of Odysseus above, 119, 141; on 185.

201. "For that man exists not as a living mortal, nor can he even be born," a strong asseveration of the supposition contained in the previous question, that they cannot imagine him to be a foeman. The asyndeton is causal. — houtos aner is quite indefinite. houtos is generally found before a relative sentence, seldom hode; if the latter, it is emphatic. — genetai, epic subjunctive; H. 720 e; G. M. 87; on zeta 126. Its taking ou, not me, shows its close connection with the future; compare pi 437, where Eurymachus, replying to Penelope, who has upbraided the suitors for their plots to slay her son, bids her be of good cheer:

"There is no such man, nor will there be, nor will he come to be,
who would lay hands on Telemachus, your son."

— dieros: Nausicaa has something of her father's fervor; on lambda 349, eta 167; psi 187.

202. For the rhyme, see on 61.

203. She assigns two reasons for their immunity from enemies: the special love and protection of the gods, and their remoteness from the rest of the world.

204. polyklustoi eni pontoi; this phrase occurs again only at delta 354, where it is descriptive of the island Pharos, a day's sail from Egypt, and at tau 277, of the spot in the midst of the sea, at a distance from Thrinakia, where Odysseus' bark founders, and he loses all

5

98 NOTES.

his companions. This seems to bear towards fixing the position of Scheria as insular; on 8, η 239.

205. eschатоi, "the remotest of men." The Ethiopians are likewise called "the remotest of men" at α 23, and they are situated along the stream of Oceanus to the south. The Phaeacians appear to represent loosely great distance in the opposite direction, though all indications place them far from the northern Oceanus.

206. "But some unfortunate yonder in his wanderings hither has come." The man we see yonder is no exception, for he is some unfortunate, who is here simply because he has been driven out of his course, and has reached here by chance. — The word "this here" is frequent, especially in the poets, in the adverbial use of "here," before us; "yonder," at no great distance, accompanied by a gesture indicating the position; on 170; H. 678. — The word for "wretched" is used substantively, as at κ 281, λ 80, 93. — "Wandering" occurs at η 239, θ 28, 14, ζ 278.

207. "The," as relative. The true relation of "pros" here is generally misconceived. As akin to "pro," this preposition has, with the genitive especially, the sense of "in front of," "in the sight of." Donaldson says rightly that "pros theon" means "in the eyes of the gods," "as seen by the gods." Compare our "'fore Heaven." This is further seen from the following passages: Zeus accompanies strangers at η 165; he protects because he accompanies — "Zeus is the guardian of suppliants and strangers, the god of strangers, who attends upon strangers along with those deserving of respect," at ι 270; he takes vengeance upon the one who ill-treats the suppliant, because he has a personal oversight of such an evil-doer — "Zeus of suppliants would punish them, he who watches over all other men and exacts punishment from whoever goes wrong," at ν 213; and he is a witness for suppliants — "suppliants, for whom Zeus is witness," at π 422. Hence the meaning "under the protection" usually assigned here arises from the earlier sense "under the eye of."

208. "Strangers and beggars." The word for "stranger" in its widest sense comprehends not only the suppliant, the one who appears with a suit for shelter and aid under the pressure of some calamity, and the guest proper who needs food and shelter simply because of his absence from home and the lack of inns for accommodation, but also the public beggar, the "beggar of all the people," of whom Irus in the Eighteenth Odyssey is the type. These travel about the country seeking relief in hospitality, and pay for it, in a measure, by im-

BOOK VI. 99

parting the news of which they are the gatherers and bearers. Odysseus appears at his own palace in this guise, and Antinous, the suitor, reproaches Eumaeus for inviting a beggar to the house. The swineherd answers evasively that no one would be so foolish as to invite a beggar, to eat him out of house and home, rho 387. But if the beggar came uninvited, he came as a guest-stranger (xeinos), towards whom the courtesy of the age must be extended. — "oligē..."; "small for the giver, but welcome to the recipient." Scholiast. It is a proverbial expression; xi 58, Alpha 167; Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus 5.

209. Brōsin, posin, dosis denote the result of the action. What is the usual sense of the verbal ending -sis? Hadley 460.

210. Lousate, "give him to bathe," i.e., supply him with the appliances of the bath, so that he may bathe himself. These consisted, under ordinary circumstances, of the water for the bathing-tub, and the oil for anointing, with perhaps a change of clothing. The active lousate is here used in its causative sense; Hadley 686. From what has already been said of the delicacy of the Homeric age respecting the person (note this, in the main, also in archaic art), and from the poet's handling of this whole episode, it would be hard to believe that the meaning of louō here and elsewhere could be simply "go bathe the stranger," the ablution to be performed by the maidens themselves. For this service is not merely rendered by slaves, but in the house of Nestor his youngest daughter attends Telemachus at the bath, and Helen performs a similar office for Odysseus when he enters Troy disguised as a beggar. Gladstone (Studies, II. p. 513 sq.) has shown that such a sense is not only repugnant to the entire tone of Homeric morals, but is inconsistent with the facts and the usage of the words. See eta 296 for an explanation of this use of the active given by the poet himself; and observe that, while the active occurs regularly of the part performed by the attendants, the middle is uniformly employed of the act of bathing whenever it is described; zeta 96, 227, theta 427, 449. — "hothen... anemоio," "where near by there is shelter from the wind." — epi, adverbial. — anemоio; Hadley 565. The shelter would appear from the circumstances of the description, epsilon 400-43, to have been a cliff, forming, by its projection into the sea, a harbor within which the river empties. If the river be conceived as run-

100 NOTES.

ning at an acute angle to the sea-coast on the side opposite the washing-troughs, and the bank there rising to a considerable height, the conditions will be sufficiently complied with; on 138.

211. ἀλλήλησι κέλευσαν, "called to each other." This "is a happy, picturesque touch; it shows each, uneasy under reproof, endeavoring slyly to throw the blame on her fellow, and it indicates that flight had scattered them." Hayman. See on 138, and compare O 658, where the Greeks, hemmed in about their ships by Hector's impetuous valor, after retreat stood closely massed beside their tents: for shame held them back, and fear; for they called out to one another without pause.

212. "And down then Odysseus they seated, taking him to the shelter." — κὰδ; on 100. — The pregnant construction of ἐπὶ with the accusative of motion and a verb of rest requires a verb of motion to be supplied in translation; H. 618 a; θ 469, ζ 218.

213. On 17. Such repetitions of the name and patronymic or its equivalent, so common in Homer, are intended to elevate the style and dignify the individual. The expression is more than ordinarily remarkable here, in that the subject of the formulaic phrase "as he commanded" is added, contrary to the poet's usual custom.

214. πὰρ . . . οἱ: this separation by conjunctions is one of the most common; ζ 248, 197, 230, η 70, 231, ν 27, ζ 207, 29; on 167. — The φᾶρος, like the χλαῖνα, was a large rectangular blanket-like mantle, worn loosely about the person as the outer garment, and caught over

BOOK VI. 101

the shoulder by a clasp, which was often of elaborate and curious workmanship, as that worn by Odysseus when departing for Troy, τ 226. It corresponded to the Roman toga, as the χιτών did to the tunic or under-garment. This was a sort of woollen shirt, shaped to the body, and reaching generally to the knees. It was without sleeves, or had only very short ones. See the accompanying illustration from an archaic statue of the Cesnola Collection. — εἵματα, appositive, "as garments;" a frequent formula; η 234.

216. μιν, subject accusative. — λούσθαι, "to bathe himself." The whole procedure here doubtless gives in full the usual details. After telling him that everything is ready and he can bathe in the stream, they were withdrawing to a distance, when Odysseus forestalls the movement in order to ingratiate himself with the attendants by a display of delicacy, as he had already done with their mistress by his winning courtesy and modest request.

217. δή ῥα τότ', "straightway then." This collocation of particles shows Odysseus' eagerness to anticipate their departure. When only may δή stand at the beginning of a clause? H. 851 c. — The dative of the person with μετανδάω seems to be one of place, since the simple verb regularly has an accusative, but the compound a dative, pointing to the influence of the preposition as determining the case; cf. θ 433.

218. στῆθ' . . . ἀπόπροθεν, "take your stand, going thus to a distance;" on 212. — οὕτω, "thus," as you are now doing, shows that they are already withdrawing. — ὄφρ'; on 80. When is the subjunctive used in such clauses? G. M. 66, 2; ζ 304, η 319, ζ 295, λ 351; η 141, 276, 280. — ἐγὼ αὐτὸς, "I, by myself," so that in the unembarrassed performance of the task I may be free from any hindrance from your possible proximity.

219. ὤμοιιν; 19, 82; 224. — ἀμφὶ; on 9.

220. δηρὸν gives to ἐστιν the force of a perfect; η 152, θ 36; on 158, 250.

221. ἔγωγε, "I at least," whatever a boor might do. — ἄν shifts the positive tone of the future, "I will not," to the more courteous "I would not," because it is repugnant to my feelings; G. M. 37, 2; H. 710 b. κεν is the usual particle with the future; ἄν only here and X 49, 66.

102 NOTES.

222. kourē: properly used of the freeborn, and often of the noble. It is therefore a dignifying word, and by using it here Odysseus further wins the goodwill of the attendants by implying his belief that they are above the common station of amphipoloi (servant-maids).

223. eipon, "told it," that is, his delicate courtesy and the good impression he had made upon them. This, coupled with apaneuthen, shows that the princess had purposely gone to a distance along the seashore where her attendants would join her.

224. ho ek: this hiatus is not unusual, especially after autar ho; Odyssey Book 7, line 230, Book 8, line 396. What words are exempt from elision? Hadley's Grammar, section 70. — ek potamou: The usual custom where conveniences were at hand appears to be illustrated at Book 10, line 361, where Odysseus in the palace of Circe is made to seat himself in the bathing-tub and wash from a large tripod, pouring the water down over head and shoulders. ek potamou and perhaps eisan appear to show conformance with the custom here. — nizeto, with a double accusative like verbs of depriving; see the genitive at line 219; Hadley 553; Goodwin 164; Curtius 402.

225. nota: see note on line 107. — ampexen: why not amphexen? Hadley 65d.

226. atrugeto, "vintageless," "unharvested;" see Book 7, line 124. This is the specific epithet of hals, thalassa, pontos, and of aither, in opposition to the land, which is polyphorbos, polyboteira.

227-28. panta, supply chroa (the whole body). — aleipsen, active, for metrical convenience. — amphi: see note on line 100; "and about him the garments had been thrown."

229. men begins the apodosis of epeide. — Dios: see Hadley 572d. — ekgegauia, like Virgil's "born of Ammon," "son of a goddess," etc.

230-31. "Both taller to look upon and portlier, and down from his head she showered his thick locks, the hyacinth blossom matching." — eisideein: what voice is used in this construction? Goodwin-Middleton 93, 2. How is passona formed from pachion? Hadley 60. This heightening of personal graces for a special purpose is resorted to again on the following morning, when Odysseus is to appear before the critical eyes of the whole Phaeacian people (Book 8, line 19), and on another occasion when he is to be recognized by Penelope (Book 23, line 157). Penelope herself is in like manner adorned by the goddess when she purposes to present herself before the suitors to complain of their omission to offer the customary

gifts, sigma 195; and Laertes is renewed with additional youth after his recognition of Odysseus, omega 369. All these involve no absolute change in the appearance, further than to heighten and reanimate what is already there, fill up the toil-worn or grief-worn limbs, and bring back the springing step and lofty bearing. Flowing hair was a characteristic of the Greeks of the Heroic Age, as of the Spartans later; their care of it is evidenced by the common phrase "long-haired Achaeans." The word oulас, identical in root with holos (whole), is here "thick and heavy," representing the vigorous growth of manly strength. Am. The likeness to the flower of the hyacinth has generally been found in its dark color. But Homer is not accustomed to make his similes turn upon color. They are rich in the use of motion, force, form, sound, symmetry, number; but Mr. Gladstone finds only three color similes out of some two hundred, at Delta 141, Xi 14, and Rho 547. Again, the color which fills the ideal of beauty for the hair, and forms the crowning glory of his great heroes, is blonde or auburn, as that of Menelaus, Achilles, etc. It is true that the extraordinary mental gifts of Odysseus everywhere so far overshadow his bodily qualities that the latter are seldom mentioned; yet it is clear that he lacks but one of the Homeric elements of beauty—stature. He is shorter by a head than the lofty-statured Agamemnon, but he is more stately than Menelaus. Yet at nu 399 and 431 he is distinctly stated to have fair hair; and if those passages are genuine, as is usually conceded, at least for one, the same color must be supposed here; for no change affecting that is made from this point on to the transformation of nu. The difficulty remains, however, that at pi 175, where he is retransformed, to be recognized by his son, we find the expression "he became dark-complexioned, and his beard became dark," which has appeared inconsistent with auburn hair. But it must be remembered that the poet is treating of a change from the white complexion and white beard of decrepit age, nu 430–32, pi 182, sigma 355, to the strength and color of active manhood, and the verb geneto is to be noted, "he became dark-skinned" from white, and his beard "became darkened" from white. The ruddy tan and sunburn of a man much in the open air, and the ruddy beard usual with auburn hair, would satisfy the epithets; cf. mu 243, Virgil, Aeneid VIII. 64, IX. 816. Even light hair with a black-

104 NOTES.

ish beard is a combination sometimes seen. Egyptian paintings represent the Creteward enemies of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Dynasties as fair, with aquiline nose, blue eyes, short red beard, and hair formally curled. Since, therefore, the likeness in the present passage is not assignable to color, there remains the form, so common in the Homeric simile. As the petals of the hyacinth are thick and curly, so was the hair of Odysseus.

232. "gold ... silver" — the verb περιχεύεται (poured around), aorist subjunctive, is most commonly found in Homeric similes, though the present tense also occurs. The comparison is taken from the realm of the metal-worker's art. Just as the craftsman imparts additional splendor to already beautiful silver by plating it with gold, so the art of Athene bestows that same enhancement upon Odysseus. Plating with gold is often mentioned. Nestor gilds the horns of the sacrificial victim he is to offer to Athene; the silver wool-basket of Helen is worked around the rim with gold; see Odyssey θ 403, 430. Gold was more abundant than silver in the Homeric age, yet at the same time more valuable. Numerous objects of silver plated with gold were discovered by Schliemann at Mycenae, but invariably a thin plate of copper was found between the two metals, as if the goldsmith found it easier to plate gold onto copper than directly onto silver.

233. Hephaistos teaches the metal-worker as the god who presides over that particular branch of art; but Athene, as ruler of the wider sphere of all art and handiwork. As a female deity, she particularly imparts skill in spinning, weaving, embroidery, and other accomplishments of her sex; but she also teaches measurement to the carpenter, and presides over industry in general. — δέδαεν (she has taught); θ 481.

234. Since δὲ introduces a clause of result, ὥστε would be substituted for it under full subordination, as at line 30.

235. κεφαλῇ: a poetic construction, partitive apposition to τῷ; see H. 500 b; θ 19, 541. The foregoing passage has been applied by Virgil to Aeneas, as the enveloping cloud dissipates and he stands revealed before Dido, Aeneid I. 588:

Aeneas stood forth, gleaming in the clear light,
Godlike in face and shoulders; for his mother herself had bestowed upon her son
Beauteous flowing hair and the radiance of youth.

BOOK VI. 105

He breathed upon them a rosy joy and gladness to the eyes: as when craftsmen's hands add beauty to ivory, or when silver or Parian marble is set about with yellow gold.

236. Apart from them: he crosses over to the sea-shore where he can be seen by the maidens, but apart from them, and seats himself to await their further attendance in supplying the promised food. This act again exhibits in strong relief the profound refinement that characterizes the entire scene. He does not force himself upon them. He does not even approach them. That might excite repugnance as appearing to show too much familiarity. His action is measured by the feelings of true gentility.
237. Gleaming with beauty. Compare the description of Paris, Iliad III 392, gleaming with beauty and garments, and of the young men in the dance, as quoted on 157. — He marvelled.
239. Hear me: [cross-references to other passages of the Odyssey]. — So that: [cross-references]. — the form "eipō" (I will speak): is this mode regular in sequence? See G. M. 31, 33.
240. "Not without the favor of all the gods." So Virgil makes Venus say to Aeneas, Aeneid I. 387:

Whoever you are, I do not think you breathe the air of heaven without favor, you who have come to the Tyrian city.

More succinctly: "Not without the will of the gods," Iliad II. 777.
241. Of the Phaeacians (with elision). How does the Homeric usage of this elision compare with Attic usage? See H. 70. This occurs in Homer especially after a double sigma.
242. The change wrought in the squalid sea-waif is so great that it must needs have been done by a god; he must therefore be under the protection of the dwellers of Olympus. — "In front of," as applied to place, means "in front of"; see note on 207. We generally view the past as behind us, the future as before us. Homer, on the contrary, conceived the past as in front, the future behind, as in his description of the prophetic powers of Calchas, Iliad A 70: who knew the things that are, the things that will be, and the things that were before. After the present and the future, "that which is in front" must be the past. A vestige of the same view appears in our word "before," which may be employed to translate the Greek word here.
244–45. "Would that such a man might be called my husband, coming here and dwelling, and that it might please him"
5*

106 NOTES.

here to remain." — αἲ γάρ, introducing a wish viewed as attainable; on 180. What other particles are used? H. 721; C. 514; G. 251; G. M. 82. — ἐνθάδε; on 218, 212. These lines were rejected by the grammarian Aristarchus as too bold to suit the maidenly character of Nausicaa; but it is to be observed that they are spoken to her attendants, and the position of the group is such that they are quite out of ear-shot of Odysseus. The thought of her approaching marriage is continually before her, and is naturally a subject of frequent conversation between herself and her maids (on 185), and even Odysseus himself fell upon it in his speech. She despises the aristocracy of the land, who alone are her suitors, and the thought just uttered, that the stranger has been sent by Heaven to their land, awakens a vague hope that he may be the one looked for to bring her deliverance from an alliance beneath her dignity; on 35. But even this springing hope is alluded to as vaguely as it is vaguely conceived. — οἵ may refer to the indefinite τοιόσδε, but it suggests the particular application to the stranger. He has already hinted his former importance in the world, and it is not unusual in the poems to find outer comeliness taken to argue mental and moral qualities of worth, which in this case have been proved as well by his speech as by his bearing throughout. All this conspires to present the thought to her in the light of a possibility, and the frankness of her nature reveals it to her companions, but the poet has been careful that it shall not reach the ears of Odysseus.

247. A frequent formula. — μάλα, "very willingly."

248. πάρ: for such apocopate forms see ζ 18, 212, 214, 230, 253, θ 85, 110, ν 75; in composition, ζ 172, ν 17, 135. — Ὀδυσσῆϊ: the iota of the dative singular is seldom elided even in Homer; here it is not only preserved, but lengthened by the combined arsis and caesura; θ 224, κ 520, λ 28, π 206.

250. "Ravenously; for long without taste of food had he been." — ἁρπαλέως; on 30. — Just as δηρόν above, 220, gave to the present the force of a perfect, so here it makes the imperfect equivalent to a pluperfect. — ἐδητύος; H. 584 b. Odysseus sails seventeen days on his raft from Ogygia, and on the morning of the eighteenth the dusky mountains of Scheria appear in the distance,

BOOK VI. 107

like a shield spread on the sea. He is then espied by Poseidon, who raises the storm that destroys his raft, and Odysseus floats on for two days, till on the twentieth he lands, seeks the covert, and sleeps until the next day when aroused by the maidens. His fast, therefore, has lasted some three days or more.

251–52. On 111, 112.

253. krateronyugas ("strong-clawed"): on eta 2. — an; on 214, 248. What shows that it is not the particle? H. 873, 849.

254. The formula epos ... onomazen ("spoke ... naming") occurs some 43 times in Homer, always before a direct address. Either the name of the person implied in onomazen is expressly added, or else some representative, as xeine ("stranger") here, with the exception of epsilon 181, kappa 319, rho 215, phi 248, Xi 218, Omega 286, where its omission is compensated for each time by the emphatic prominence of the thought. Am.

255. Orseo ... imen, "Arise now, stranger, cityward to go." Odysseus is still sitting; cf. E 13, "he rose up from the ground on foot." What two peculiarities has Orseo? H. 349 D., 345 D. — imen; on 50. — pempsо, "I may conduct."

256. Buttmann's twofold derivation for daiphronos, from dais ("battle") and phren ("mind"), meaning "warlike," for the Iliad, and from daenai ("to learn") and phren, meaning "prudent," for the Odyssey, is very generally rejected, and the latter alone allowed. Properly "well taught," it has a wide application according to circumstances, whether experienced in war, or "accomplished" as host, or what may be; eta 168, theta 8, 13, 18, 56, 373.

257. Phaiеkon ("of the Phaeacians"). When the partitive genitive is dependent upon a relative pronoun, the commonest position for it is immediately before the relative, as theta 204; but sometimes separated from it, as here. If placed after the relative, it is regularly separated from it, as eta 156, 322.

258. mal' hod', "exactly as follows." — hode, as the adverb of hode, usually refers to something yet to be said. — erdein; H. 784; G. M. 101. The infinitive in this use is commonly viewed as a milder form of command than the imperative, Kühner supplying a verb of wishing, as found in Alpha 277. Krüger thinks it a relic of a primitive naïveté. Ameis objects to both of these, and considers it a mark of energetic brevity wholly in the spirit of the Heroic Age, like the German use of the passive participle for the imperative, which Wolf used to call the cartman's imperative. — ouk apinyos-

-sein, 187. He has already exhibited such sure marks of chivalrous feeling, that he will understand and appreciate her desire not to be seen publicly in his company, and so forgive the apparent breach of hospitality in not conducting him quite to the palace.

259. "As long as the fields we are traversing and the tillage of men." — ophr' (so that); on line 28, Odyssey Book 8 line 147. — an and ke, both in the same clause also at Odyssey 5.361, 11.187, 202, 13.127, 24.437, 9.334. — ke is found doubled at 4.733, but an never in Homer, though often in later Greek; G. M. 42, Note 3. — agrous; H. 550. — By agrous the country is meant, whether wild or cultivated; by erga that which is cultivated. Odysseus, having landed in the country of the Laestrygonians, mounts a cliff, and thence sees no signs of man except a curling smoke, "neither the works of oxen nor of men" (Odyssey 10.98); compare Virgil's "glad sowings and the labors of oxen."

260-61. meth' (with), 54. — ercbesthai (to go), as at lines 258, 295, 298, 304, 311, Odyssey 7.222, 8.12. — hodon (road), 165.

262. epen, 28, 297, Odyssey 8.511, 553; of what is it compounded? H. 759. — What two peculiarities appear in the form epibeiomen? H. 400 D. i. — peri; on Odyssey 6.12; cf. Odyssey 7.110, 8.44, 63. — pyrgos, "a turreted wall."

263. hekaterthe (on each side), 19. — poles, 40. The situation is that of a city built upon a peninsula, something like that of New York, with a harbor on each side, and a narrow neck of land connecting the peninsula with the mainland. This neck is the eisithme or entrance to the city from the country. The end of the peninsula towards the sea appears to have been unfitted for landing, by reason of its elevation and ruggedness along shore, or lack of shelter. The dock-yards were consequently built along the low neck of land, and occupied both sides of the single road-way leading into the city, so that the ships, drawn up upon their rests out of the water, as was customary in the Homeric day, seemed to form a rampart along the road-side, and guard the way.

264. lepte (slender), predicate. — Most recent authorities agree upon the meaning "curved" for amphielissai, but some refer it to the sides, others to the ends. They reject altogether the older interpretation, "rowed on both sides," arguing that, as it is applied to a ship when in a state of rest, it is natural to look to its shape as then seen, not to characteristics of motion, for the explanation. Yet it is not always used of a ship at rest: Odyssey 9.9, 252, 9.64, 21.390, 13.174, 15.549. The annexed cuts are from the Ramesseum on the

BOOK VI.                                                    109

west side of the Nile at Thebes, on whose walls is portrayed the great naval battle fought in the mouth of the Nile between the Egyptians under Ramses III. and invaders from Asia Minor, Cyprus, Crete, and the adjacent regions, about 1275 B.C. The upper figure is a ship of the victorious Egyptians; the lower belongs to the "Pelesta of the mid sea" (Pelasgians) and the "Tekkariu"

(Teucri?), and is one of the earliest representations we have of a vessel from Greek localities. Both ends curve up into the neck and head of a water-bird, which certainly gives a definite meaning for the epithet korwnisi (A 170) when compared with koronai enaliai, e 66 (cf. akra korumba, I 241, and the Latin rostrum), and for orthokrairaon, S 3, from a different point of view; and since amphielissa exchanges with these at metrical need, it is probably to be explained in the same way.

265. The word eiruatai; H. 405 D. b. — pasin ... hekasto, "for all (the Phaeacians) have a boat-house each." — pasin; H. 598. — hekasto, 189. — Ammonius, deriving epistion from epi stenai, explains it as a place for the ship to stand upon when drawn out of the water; but the view of the scholiasts, that besides the mere rest there was also a covering over them to shelter from sun and rain, seems more reasonable, as they were for permanent use; on n 77. Yet we must not conceive them as closed houses, for the ships are prominent objects in the scene, e 43.

266. Phaeacian devotion to the sea is marked not only by the fact that every man has a pinnace of his own, but by their establishing their agora hard by the ships, though at Troy it was beside Priam's palace, and in the camp of the Greeks near its centre. The agora then, as later, was the common resort of the men, whether any public business was being done or not. No regular assembly of the people had taken place in Ithaca since the departure of Odysseus, till convoked by Telemachus, b 7, and no other is spoken of from that time till after the death of the suitors; yet Telemachus goes to the agora on the morning following his return from Sparta, evidently expecting to find, and does find, the people gathered there. He does the same on the succeeding morning, as if it were a matter of course. See o 468, k 114. — "around a beautiful shrine of Poseidon." — The word Posideion appears nowhere else in Homer as a substantive, but at B 506 as an adjective, Posideion aglaon alsos. This has probably led one of the scholiasts to interpret it here as a grove or glebe, and Mr. Gladstone urges this view. That, however, accords rather with the unsettled condition of a camp, as before Troy, or a primitive country life, than a wealthy and peaceful city. Furthermore, the poet has expressly stated that Nausithous founded temples when the city was built,

BOOK VI. 111

and we have no other mention of them unless this is one. Gladstone himself says that in the agora "the public solemnities of religion were performed, and there were gathered into a focus the religious as well as the patriotic sentiments of the country." Hence we should naturally look there for a temple, and that too of their tutelary divinity. We can have little doubt who that greatest of the gods would be to a people so pre-eminently devoted to the sea, and the sequel shows that Poseidon regards them as his actual offspring, and it is he that endows them with their miraculous speed upon his element; Book XIII line 130, Book VIII line 35. Virgil unites both grove and temple, Aeneid I. 441. — The word ἀμφὶς stands mostly after its case, but, like ἀμφὶ, it does not shift its accent.

267. "With hauled stones in the earth fast set." Three explanations have been given for this; the first of which, namely, that of a stone pavement, may be rejected at once, not because that would be an anachronism, as Merry says, for Schliemann discovered a paved street at Troy, twenty-five feet below the surface; but because the athletic exercises of Book VIII, performed in the agora, would not have been held on a paved surface. Of the other two, the weight of authority leans towards a wall of Cyclopean architecture enclosing the square. In the only passage where κατωρυχέεσσι occurs elsewhere, it is employed of the stones forming the wall of the court-yard before the cave of Polyphemus. In like manner ῥυτοῖσιν is found only once more, at Book XIV line 10, and there of the stones used by Eumaeus in constructing the enclosure of his court-yard. Others, however, refer the stones to the seats mentioned at Book VIII line 6; cf. Book II line 99, Book XVIII line 504, Book II line 14. Schliemann's excavations in the acropolis of Mycenae unearthed a circular enclosure about one hundred feet in diameter, formed of two rows of slabs set upright in the earth, and dove-tailed together at the top by a third slab covering them. The upright slabs leaned somewhat towards the centre, thus forming both enclosure and seats, and combining the diverse views here, if Schliemann's interpretation of it be accepted. The Phaeacian agora is of great size compared with that. Of porticos and other decorative structures which adorned the agoras of the later Greeks, Homer makes no mention.

268. The word ἔνθα, as at line 266, places us close by the ships, possibly a part of the agora adjacent. — ὅπλα is a general term, including all the tack-

112 NOTES.

ling of the ships, defined more accurately by the appositives
peismata, speira [cables, sail].

269. speira, final syllable lengthened by arsis and caesura; "sails."—
apoxynousin, the reading of all the manuscripts; "they taper." One of
the many details of ship-building is here put for all; but it is a
very important one, since the skill of the Phaeacians in the use
of the oar is set before us frequently; on Book 13, line 81. A newly built
ship is mentioned at Book 8, line 35.

270. Contrast with this the boast of Odysseus, Book 8, lines 215–29. And
yet the bow and the quiver themselves are regarded by the Ho-
meric hero as weapons scarcely worthy of his hands, a fact which
presents the unwarlike habits of the Phaeacians in still stronger
colors; on Book 8, line 220. Besides their passion for the sea, their other
pleasures are enumerated at Book 8, lines 248–49.

273. "From their gossip unpleasant I shrink." In returning
to the town the princess would be compelled to pass by the ships
and through the agora, where she knew that many would be
gathered whether for business or lounging; on Book 13, line 155. The voice
of public opinion is the greatest moral power that the man of the
Homeric day knew. It restrained from crime more even than rev-
erence for the gods; cf. Book 9, lines 459–61, Book 14, line 239, Book 21, line 324. — opisso, "after-
wards;" on line 242. Such a speech would not be uttered by the
churl in her hearing, but would be spread among the people till
it came to the ears of her family, who would then blame her; cf.
ereousi, line 285.

274. momeye; on line 147. — rala . . . demon, "for they are very
uncharitable among the people." This characteristic receives
exemplification from the speech of Euryalus, Book 8, lines 159–64, and is
touched upon by Athena, Book 7, lines 16–17.

275. eipesi, "may say;" G. M. 87; H. 720 e; on lines 126, 201.—
kakoteros; on line 187. Some of the ancient commentators rejected
lines 275–88 as unsuited to the character of the princess. Hayman
has well said: "The more repugnant such female freedom was
to later Greek notions of decorum, the more certain the genuine-
ness of the passage." Goethe, with his true poetic instinct and
clear insight into the workings of the human heart, has divined
the real character of the maiden, and vindicated both the pas-
sage and the purpose of the elder poet. Besides a frankness and

BOOK VI. 113

a naïveté so open that the thoughts which spring in the heart fall naturally from the lips, Homer here develops more fully, though covertly and by the dramatic method, that predilection for Odysseus which has already been seen to be springing up in the maiden's breast. It is this first feeling of love which makes her so sensitive to the thought of the gossiping tongue that would couple her name with Odysseus, and the poet with consummate art has veiled it carefully by causing the maiden to put into the mouth of another what she censures in her words though she wishes in her heart. An engaging forwardness is thus rescued from the verge of boldness by an expedient which Pope declares to be "an instance of the great art of Homer in saying everything properly." The length to which the speech of the supposed churl is carried may be attributed in part perhaps to the artless garrulousness of the princess, seen already in the suspension of the thought at 187 and 262, and in the diffuseness of description there following; but if the theory propounded on 35 be admitted, every word is needed without exception.

276. The particle de expresses emphatic surprise. — "this man here"; on 206.

277. "And where was she so fortunate as to find him? A husband now will she have of her own choice." It is wrong to translate the Greek word as "picked up," as some have done; the verb eurisko means to find what one seeks, and, as Eustathius has said, is here used of a piece of good-fortune. The noun eurhema means a lucky find. By the dramatic method, Nausicaa is returning some of the compliments which Odysseus had paid her in his first speech. She was beautiful as Artemis, possibly a nymph; he is handsome and majestic, nay, perhaps a god. The bitter sarcasm which many have seen in the entire speech is totally at variance with the feelings of the princess, and lies rather in the mind of the commentator than in the language of the poet. No slighting or unkindly words should fall from her lips. — "herself," delta 118; on 282.

278. "Either some one doubtless driven out of his course she has brought from his ship." — "driven wandering"; on 206.

279. If he is a man, he must have arrived in a vessel, and come from afar, for none dwell near us; a variant of 204–5.

280. "Or else to her beseeching some long-prayed-for god has come." Nitzsch, while disposed to retain the remainder of the

114 NOTES.

passage, would reject this and the following line. They are, however, exactly to the point. Despairing of a release from the indignity of a union with native suitors, the maiden's prayer turns even to the gods. Nor need such a prayer be deemed presumptuous on her part. Poseidon himself is her great-grandfather, and the gods are wont to come familiarly to fraternize and feast with the Phaeacians, who are of their kin; Odyssey Book 7, lines 56–66, 199–206. The poet who represents the sea-nymph Thetis as married to Peleus and living for many years in his palace would surely feel no difficulty in the idea of such a union among the semi-divine Phaeacians. In fact we have a similar prayer from the mouth of the Greek Antiope, Book 11, line 261.

281. "and will have her to wife."

282. "All the better is it if she even herself personally going to him has found a husband from abroad" (than that she should remain unwedded as she bids fair to do). The word "better" commonly occurs where two disagreeable alternatives present themselves and the lesser of two evils is chosen. Here the two are, on the one hand, no marriage at all, and on the other, an indelicate forwardness that transgresses the widest limits of decorum. But the latter, bad as it is, is preferable to the unheard-of refusal to marry altogether; see note on line 66. Situated as we are, she ought to abandon all her old notions of caste and wed a Phaeacian; but if she persists in her pride of station, it is better that she find her equal from abroad. The form "herself" stands for "and herself." Both "and" and "even" emphasize "herself." Lines 278–84 appear to be answers to the thoughts contained in 276–77. There are two questions and one assertion. "Who is the stranger?" finds its answer in "some foreigner, or else a god." "Where did she find him?" — "She brought him from some ship, or else he comes from heaven." "Now she will have a husband" is addressed by "better that she should than to go unwedded, even though she has been so unmaidenly as to seek out a husband and make the choice herself." The chief censure lies in "herself" at line 277, and "herself even going to him," as proved by lines 286–88, where the thought is recapitulated.

286. "and I too should be wroth at another maiden." The gossipers would be right, too, for I should say the same of anyone; showing that the bitter sarcasm is far from the

BOOK VI. 115

poet's thought. — νεμεσῶ, a subjunctive used for the Attic optative with ἄν; cf. α 228, ο 69, Ψ 494, the last two illustrating the peculiar modal shift from ῥέξοι to μίσγηται. The subjunctive is regular in formal sequence; the optative appears to follow the thought of the leading verb in its equivalence to an optative. Compare the changes after the historical present; G. M. 32; 63, 4 (b.).

287–88. "Who, namely, against the wish of her friends, her father and mother yet living, mingles with men, before at least her public marriage has come." This is appositive and explanatory to ἥτις τοιαῦτά γε ῥέξοι, to ὀνείδεα ταῦτα, and in fact to everything from line 275. The phrase πατρὸς καὶ μητρὸς ἐόντων particularizes φίλων, and brings the thought of their being still alive clearly into view, so that the sense is, "against the wish of her friends, especially of her father and mother, and they still living." Cf. α 78, θ 148.—How does the Homeric construction of πρίν differ from that of later writers? G. M. 106; G. 274.—This episode doubtless shows that in the choice of a husband greater freedom was allowed the maiden in the heroic age than later at Athens, but the share of the parents and other relatives in defining the limits of that choice was a very important one. The father is most frequently spoken of as giving his daughter to a husband, or the suitor as prevailing by the pound-for-pound weight of his gifts; see 159. The brothers also are mentioned as influential in the matter. All her friends are interested, since the honor and power of the family is at stake, but most of all the father and mother who rejoice at her fair fame, ζ 30, as they would grieve if she failed to comply with the prevailing laws of decorum. As the poet plainly tells us here, she could hold no conversation with men before marriage, except with the consent of her parents. After marriage much greater freedom was permitted. We find Arete in the μέγαρον at various times of the day, ζ 51, 304, η 231, θ 423, λ 335, ν 57; and she appears on the street when she pleases, as do the Trojan matrons often.

291. δήεις, "thou wilt find." What irregularity does this form have? H. 378 D. Others take it as a present with future sense. — Both Ἀθήνης and αἰγείρων depend on ἄλσος, the former as a possessive genitive, the latter as a genitive of material; 321, ν 104. — αἴγειρος is identified by the greater number of commentators with the black

116 NOTES.

poplar (populus nigra). It is characterized by the poet as tall, water-fed, smooth, its boughs growing at the very top of the stem, and is selected by the wheelwright for the felloe of the chariot-wheel, and is pointed out by Calypso to Odysseus together with the alder and fir, among the trees with which he was to build his raft. It grows habitually in moist spots, clustering about fountains or along the sluggish streams of some low-lying swamp-land. Curtius, deriving from the root aig, "to move quickly," makes it the aspen (populus tremula). Others still have thought it the white poplar (populus alba).

292. "in" and "around," both adverbial. The poplars cluster about a fountain within a meadow.

293. temenos has two distinct uses in Homer. It is a tract of land set aside (from the root tem-, "to cut"), either for the service of the gods and sacred to some particular deity, as that of Aphrodite in Cyprus, of Zeus on Mt. Gargarus, of Demeter at Pyrasus, and of the river Spercheius; or for the maintenance and enrichment of the king, forming the crown-lands, as that of Bellerophon, Aeneas, Meleager, Sarpedon, Glaucus, Odysseus. Thucydides tells us, III. 70, that the site of the temenos of Alcinous was pointed out by the Corcyraeans even in his time as a sacred glebe. — "blooming"; on line 70.

294. "So far from the city as calls the shouter," makes himself heard. — "having shouted," in prose "the one who shouted." Compare line 117; as the volume of sound is there measured by distance, here the distance is measured by the volume of sound.

295. "to remain," 261, Book XI line 351; the active of "to remain" alone is in use.

296. "let us go to the city." The harshness of this hiatus seems to suggest the possibility of an initial digamma (F) for the stem elth-; other possible cases of its occurrence in Homer are listed at o 543, r 56, Xi 77, 504, K 62, 444, Phi 62, 231, xi 398, k 331, m 17, g 234, I 403, N 172, X 156, r 105, s 402, M 225, a 168. The Doric form enthen has been compared with our "wend," and the recently deciphered Cypriote inscriptions give the proper name Eufelthon.

298. "and then at length," introducing the apodosis; Book VIII line 262.

301-2. "For by no means like to that are the dwellings of the Phaeacians, since so goodly is the palace of Alcinous the hero." — The word "such as" is equivalent to "because such," and is causal in sense; Book VIII line 155; H.

The purpose of the poet is to magnify the object by an unusual fullness and ruggedness of expression. —"toisi" refers to "domata" (dwellings); hence the plural.—Observe the loving pride with which the princess dwells upon her father, at lines 256, 290, 293, 296, 299, 302, 308–9, 196–97, 57.

303. "heroos": this shortening of a long vowel or diphthong in the body of a word is found elsewhere: several times in "oios," as at eta 312, "huios," as at lambda 270, and "beblenai," Lambda 380.—"an" does not compound with any of the relative conjunctions except "epei" in Homer. 307. "kioni keklimene," "leaning against a pillar." The seat of the housewife was the "klisie" or "klismos," so called because of its having a leaning back which admitted of a partially reclining position for the occupant, "klismo keklimene," rho 97. In consequence, the back of the chair was set against a pillar or wall for firmness of support; eta 95, theta 66, 473, tau 55.—"oi," 131; not with "opisthen."—"eiat'," Attic "entai"; on 174.

Then the thought is one that falls naturally from the lips of the fond and admiring daughter, and at the same time pictures sufficiently the effeminacy of the Phaeacian court; cf. eta 4–5. The caesura falls much more frequently into the last foot in Homer than in Virgil. It occurs about one hundred times in the first twelve books of the

— trochon, a frequentative from trechō ("to run"), as strōphaō from strephō, trōpaō from trepō, nōmaō from nemō.
