321–22. dyseto; on 78; eta 289. — Athenaies; on 291. — hina, 27.

324. Atrytone is only used as an epithet of Athene, and always with Dios tekos ("daughter of Zeus"). Its usual derivation, from a- and tryō, meaning "unwearied one," is peculiarly appropriate to her as the goddess of intellect. Others have connected it with otryno ("to urge on"), indicating her other great function as goddess of war, like laossoos, "the inciter," "folk-stirrer." Hayman suggests that it may be a patronymic from atrytos; but such a repetition after Dios tekos recurring regularly seems too harsh.

325. nyn de per, "now then at last." — Note the use of men akouson, akousas after klythi meu. This is quite unprecedented, and shows the heartfelt earnestness of the prayer, almost a demand that she shall hear him. She had been his patroness and ever-ready assistant so constantly on the plain of Troy, that he

BOOK VI. 119

had come to look upon her aid as due to him by a right of his own. Theirs was a partnership founded upon similarity of character, as the goddess herself declares at lines 296–331 of Book XIII. He there complains that she has abandoned him ever since the fall of Troy; she replies that it was only during his wanderings, and then because she was unwilling to battle with Poseidon.

326. "Me while getting wrecked, when the famous Earthshaker was wrecking me." — The word "rhaiomenou" (being wrecked) may refer to the whole period of his sufferings ever since "the god scattered the Greeks" (line 317 of Book XIII), while the appositive clause "when... Earthshaker" points to the last dread calamity, altogether due to Poseidon, when nearing the Phaeacian land. For a similar appositive clause, see Book VII, line 198.

327. This line, with the substitution of "Achilles" for "Phaeacians," is also spoken by Priam in his invocation to Zeus when setting out from Troy to ransom the dead body of Hector (Iliad, Book XXIV, line 309). See Odyssey Book VIII, lines 21–2, and Book XIII, line 121.

329. "Enantien" means "undisguised." After rejecting lines 320–23 of Book XIII, which have been pronounced spurious on other grounds by all authorities, there is nothing to indicate that Odysseus knows of the presence of Athene until she reveals herself in her own proper form in Ithaca. On other occasions she is accustomed to make herself known to him at once, both on the plains of Troy and in his native land. The strict incognito which she maintains in Scheria is the device by which the poet preserves the dignity of Poseidon, and yet achieves his purpose. Poseidon has himself in effect said at Book V, line 288, that his power over Odysseus ends as soon as he reaches Scheria, but the influence of that deity is so commanding there that Athene is bound to respect his rights outwardly, though she may work her will secretly as best she can. And here we are confronted by another inconsistency, so common in the divine machinery of the poet; see line 42. In theory the gods "know all things" (Book IV, line 379), and "can do all things" (Book X, line 306); but it is in theory only. It may be urged here that it is not from Odysseus that the goddess needs to be concealed, in order to save her uncle's dignity, but from Poseidon. The answer, however, lies in the method of the poet, by which a god is easily made to be ignorant, or to ignore or overlook when necessary. One of the most striking instances is found at the opening of the Thirteenth Book of the Iliad, when the Trojans

120 NOTES.

have broken into the naval encampment of the Greeks, and the destruction of the whole fleet is imminent. The Greeks are disheartened, and Zeus has forbidden all the gods taking part in the fight or encouraging either side, while he, in obedience to his promise to Thetis, has favored the Trojans. The poet's countrymen must be reanimated, and to effect this he makes Zeus, who sits on topmost Gargarus overlooking the field, turn his eyes away, to contemplate the Thracians and just-dealing Abioi. Of this Poseidon takes immediate advantage, hastens to the scene of battle, and infuses new courage into the breast of the two Ajaxes. On Book 13, line 140 — "felt reverence." Homer has taken the greatest care throughout that none of his five highest deities shall come into open conflict with each other, even when they take opposite sides of a question or quarrel. They are bound together by a law of mutual respect, and are never allowed even to be named to mortals as being opposed in strife. In the Theomachy Apollo will not engage with Poseidon, "for he felt reverence at fighting against his father's brother," Book 21, line 468. In the death-scene of Hector, it is not till Apollo quits him that Athene, who was at hand and ready, joins and accompanies Achilles. Besides the general tie of respect, there was, in the case of Athene and Apollo, a deference due to the age of Poseidon in accordance with the feeling so prominent in Homer. Poseidon himself yields to it, though with reluctance, when Zeus orders him from the battle-field; "for," says the messenger Iris, "thou knowest that the Erinyes ever accompany the elder," Book 15, line 204; cf. Book 13, line 141.

330. "Was ferociously enraged." The root means "swell;" cf. our "boiling over with rage." The Homeric Poseidon is chiefly distinguished for two characteristics, the element of vast force, in which he stands second only to Zeus, and a persistent vindictiveness. He hates the Trojans throughout the action of the Iliad, because Laomedon cheated him out of his stipulated reward for building the walls of Troy; and he pursues Odysseus, without relenting, for many years, because that hero had blinded his son Polyphemus. His anger at the perpetrator of this act, committed as it was in pure self-defence, and against a monster who respected neither gods nor man, and involving the least possible moral delinquency, evinces the utter

BOOK VII. 121

lack of moral elevation which, with an absence of intellectual force, also characterizes this deity.

331. How does the Homeric construction of paros differ from that of prin? G. M. 106, 2, Note 5.

2. How is pros formed from proti? H. 76. proti occurs 60 times in Homer, and of these 57 times before the digamma, with astu alone accounting for 33 of these, Ilion 17, and hon 3. — menos hemionoin. Strength and endurance are the two qualities prominent in the Homeric epithets of the mule, as krateronux, entesiergos, talaergos.

3. What does Attic prose use for hou? H. 675 a. — agakluta; on Book VI line 58. — ikanev; on Book VI lines 119, 250.

4. stesen, "she checked the mules;" supply hemionous. The full form hippous estese occurs at E 775, Theta 49; on eta 130, 325, zeta 7. — en prothuroisi, "in the outer gate," a spacious entrance from the street into the aule, or open court, and here the comer usually stopped with the chariot, the animals were unyoked and fed in the adjacent stalls, and the chariot tilted up against the side of the entrance, delta 39 sq. For the dative of prothuron, Homer always employs the plural with en, eni, epi; for the genitive and accusative always the singular. No other cases occur. — amphis, zeta 266.

5. histent'... enaligkioi; on zeta 309, 62, 76, theta 419.

6. heluon; H. 268 b. — te esphoron. Hiatus is sometimes admitted at the end of the fourth foot when a caesura occurs there at the same time, as alpha 60, delta 141, eta 70, kappa 337, 574, mu 75, omicron 425, etc. The caesura here is called the Bucolic, because of its frequent occurrence in the Bucolic poets. The first two Idyls of Theocritus, for instance, comprising 316 lines, contain 261 of these caesuras, or 83 per cent. Homer does not employ it so often, but it is found 205 times in the 331 lines of Book VI, or 62 per cent.; so, in the remainder of these selections, Book VII has 64 per cent., theta .60, lambda .60, nu .54. The Eclogues of Virgil have but 28 per cent. This caesura is not unfrequently accompanied by a pause in the sense, indicated by a comma or colon, rarely a period.

7. thalamon (chamber), zeta 15. — pur (fire), needed not only for light but for warmth, "to give light and warmth," tau 64; for the scene of the Odyssey appears to be laid in the late autumn, when the mornings and evenings are chill. Several passages point to this period of the year. When Odysseus is sailing from Ogygia, no sleep falls upon his eyelids for watching the pilot-stars of the day, the Pleiades, Bootes, the Bear, and Orion, epsilon 271. The month when these were best situated to serve his purpose was November; for they were then visible the whole night through. Again, after landing at the river-mouth, he retires to the wood-sheltered acclivity for fear of the frost, and the chilling breeze that will spring up from the river at early dawn, epsilon 467. The frost and cold of morning are again mentioned at rho 25, when, a few days later, the hero has landed in Ithaca; and that of evening, rho 191; on lambda 373, eta 121.

8. greus Apeiraiē, "an aged dame of Apeire." Those who identify Scheria with Corcyra consider Apeire here to be Epirus, Apeirē being formed from ēpeiros, as Ēmathiē from amathos. This is at variance with zeta 204–5, which see; and the territorial name of Epirus is not mentioned by Homer. He does speak of the Thesprotians, who dwelt in that region, and Odysseus, in one of his false accounts of himself, says that he was landed among them on his way home by the Phaeacians. This, however, only fixes a general northerly or north-westerly direction for the Phaeacians, not at all their proximity to Ithaca. Apeire may be derived from a-, peirar, "the limitless land." — Eurymedousa is a feminine form of Eurymedon, the name of the king of the Giants, 58, and, in the Iliad, of the charioteer of Agamemnon and one of Nestor's attendants. It is significant of high birth, and the inference may doubtless be drawn that she was kidnapped from a home of wealth and station, like the Phoenician nurse of Eumaeus, who, while wandering in the fields, was carried off by Taphian pirates, omicron 427. The chief sources from which the slaves of the Heroic Age were obtained are enumerated at omicron 383: cities sacked, or children left alone among the flocks or herds, and carried off by a sudden descent of enemies from the sea.

10. geras exelon, "as royal due they chose out;" so Briseis was chosen for Achilles by the sons of the Achaeans, Iliad II 56. Some such

. BOOK VII. 123

An article of booty was habitually set aside for the chief, before the regular distribution took place. The present passage points to a descent of Phaeacian ships upon some coastal land, and the seizure of other booty besides the woman; and as she became the nurse of Nausicaa, it belongs to their earlier days in Scheria, soon after their removal from Hypereia, when their disposition was more warlike than at the period of our story. Cf. ν 113. Numerous statements of the poems show that such piratical expeditions were not regarded as disgraceful, but rather as an honorable distinction; Thucydides expressly declares it to have been a characteristic of that day, and to have descended in full force to his own time among the Locrian Ozolae, the Aetolians, and the Acarnanians. Mr. Gladstone's view of our passage is different. Among the revenues of a king he places presents from traders as a consideration for permission to barter their wares, and therefore, "We find that certain traders, sailing to Scheria, made a present to Alcinous, as the sovereign, of the captive Eurymedousa." Perhaps the obscurity which is introduced by the employment of νέες with ἤγαγον, and the omission of the subject of ἔξελον, belongs to the purpose of the poet; on ν 125.

11. οὕνεκα . . . ἄνασσε. Out of the spoils of Tenedos, overrun by Achilles, the Achaeans chose Hecamede for Nestor, because she excelled all in counsel (Λ 627), bringing into prominence the greatness of Nestor in the council, as here the absoluteness of Alcinous in his kingship, a fact several times dwelt upon; 187. — θεοῦ . . . ἄκουεν, "and as to a god did the people hearken unto him." Connect θεοῦ with αὐτοῦ, implied in the thought; ζ 326, η 84. — Why has ὥς the accent? H. 104; G. 29; ζ 309, η 71, θ 467. The use of ἄκουεν in this connection is not common, the ordinary phrase being "like a god he was honored by the people," not only of kings, ξ 205, Λ 58, Ν 218, Κ 33, Ι 155, but of priests, Ε 78, Π 605.

12. ἡ, demonstrative. — τρέφε, "used to nurse." Her position was like that of Eurycleia in the house of Odysseus, where she had been the nurse of Telemachus, and of his father before him, and where she still attends upon Telemachus, though in his twenty-first year, when he retires to rest, α 434–42.

13. ἥ, as η 295; cf. μ 125–26, τ 354–56, Δ 442–44, Φ 276–77. — εἴσω, "within the chamber;" for the princess may not present

herself among the gathered guests in the hall. She does not appear upon the scene again until the following evening, when she bids Odysseus farewell, Book 8, line 457. — "dorpon" (evening meal); on Book 6, line 97. — "ekosmei" (she arranged); the converse at Book 7, line 232. For the tense, see the note on Book 6, line 100.

14. "orto" (she rose); on Book 6, line 50. — "amphi d'" (and around), with Fäsi and Ameis, for the common "autar" (but). This is the reading of Aristarchus. Compare notes 42, 140.

15. "aera" is the divine mantle of invisibility which commonly shrouds the gods themselves, and which they all have power at any time to throw around such persons or objects as they may wish to conceal. It is most often called "aer" (mist/air); sometimes "nephele" (cloud), sometimes "achlys" (haze), and even "nyx" (night), at Book 8, line 562. By means of it, favorites are rescued from danger many times by the gods in the Iliad, and the gods habitually throw it over their horses, chariots, arms, and the like, whenever they leave them temporarily. The poet takes the physical fact that mist, cloud, and darkness conceal things from sight, and, infusing into this a divine element, employs the words that relate to physical phenomena in naming his divine manifestations. For although this mist or darkness may gather and may dissipate like the physical reality, it must be understood to be as invisible itself as the object it shrouds. It may even conceal deity from deity, Book 14 (Xi), line 343, though Athene has recourse to the helmet of Aides to hide her from Ares, Book 5 (Epsilon), line 845. — The word "aer" always in Homer has alpha in the nominative, but eta in the oblique cases. "Eer" is found in the Ionic writer Hipparchus. It is always feminine in Homer and Hesiod, but masculine from Herodotus onward. — The recurrence of the same word, as "Odyssei" (dative) after "Odysseus" (nominative), where we would use a pronoun, is not infrequent in both Greek and Latin; compare Book 6, lines 262–63, Book 8, lines 50–2; Xenophon, Anabasis I.4.12; Cicero, Catilinarians II.12.

16. "megalthymos" (great-spirited) is a common epithet of heroes and of peoples. Here it may be compared with "hyperphialoi" (arrogant ones) at Book 6, line 274, and appears to mean high-spirited in a bad sense — supercilious. In estimating this characteristic of the people, it is necessary to take into account their remoteness from other men (see note on Book 8, line 102), and the great rarity of visits from strangers. Treatment such as is here anticipated might be expected from a flippant and indolent populace, lounging about the market-place, and puffed up with their own conceit. Even the people of Ithaca are scarcely more courteous. Eumaeus, when leaving Odysseus alone outside the palace, warns

BOOK VII. 125

him not to linger long, lest someone should beat him and drive him away, ρ 278. True, Odysseus is there in beggar's disguise, but the stranger and beggar are classed together, ζ 208. Virgil has imitated our passage where Aeneas is entering Carthage:

"But Venus wrapped those walking in a dark mist of air, and the goddess poured around them a thick mantle of cloud, so that no one could see them or touch them, or cause delay, or ask why they had come." Aeneid I. 411.

His hero is shrouded in mist for the same reason as Odysseus, and the necessity for it is confirmed by the treatment received by his companions who had landed in the harbor.

17. εἴη (might be); cf. θ 134, ζ 142.

18. δύσεσθαι (to set), ζ 165.—ἐραννὴν (lovely); on 79.

20. παρθενικῇ νεήνιδι, "a girlish maiden." Observe how minutely the poet sustains ζ 300. Both παρθενικῇ and νεήνιδι are substantives in all other passages in Homer, and are best so treated here; on ζ 3.—κάλπιν, a water-jar borne upon the head or shoulder for carrying water from the fountain to the town. The fountain already mentioned is sufficient for the purpose here; but the townspeople are said, η 131, to obtain their water from the palace. The people of Ithaca and the Laestrygonians were supplied with water from a fountain outside the city, ρ 205, κ 105; so too the Athenians in earlier days (Herodotus VI. 137), and the Eleusinians. Female slaves bring the water for the palace of Odysseus and for that of the father of Eumaeus, but it is the king's daughter who performs this service among the Laestrygonians and Eleusinians (Hymn to Demeter). Sir Charles Fellows, in his account of travels through Lycia during the first half of the present century, speaking of the Island of Kastelorizo, off the Lycian coast, says: "It is perfectly barren of supplies; even the water for the use of the town is collected in large tanks, about a mile up the mountain, whence it is carried by women, who are continually

passing and repassing in most classic groups, with pitchers slung
over their shoulders. The town is inhabited almost entirely by
Greeks."

21. στῆ, "stopped." This action would imply that she intended to address him, as actually takes place after this phrase, E 170, Θ 100; hence δ' is strongly adversative, "but," for Odysseus anticipates her. Virgil makes Venus speak first, Aeneid I. 321.

22. οὐκ ἄν, Book 6 line 57. — ἀνέρος, "hero," as E 649, Δ 194.

23. Ἀλκινόου: the retention of the quantity of the final syllable before the relative ὅς may be explained by arsis and the pause; but ὅς originally had an initial consonant, traces of which are seen more clearly with the adverb, in such phrases as ζ 309, than with the relative itself in Homer. Curtius contends that the vanished consonant is j, not F. — ἀνάσσω in Homer is most frequently construed with the simple dative, whether of persons or places. The dative is either one of place or of interest. The occasional addition of μετά or ἐν throws the weight in favor of the former. The genitive is also found, but mostly with places, only twice with persons.

25. τηλόθεν . . . γαίης, "from afar, out of a distant land;" cf. θ 68, 577. — τῷ, "wherefore;" H. 611. For the metre, see on line 6.

26. ἔργα is substituted for γαῖαν of ζ 177. The ἔργα he has now seen, ζ 259; he had not seen them then.

28. ξεῖνε πάτερ is the respectful address to age, used also by Laodamas, θ 145, and by Euryalus after his lesson in politeness, θ 408. Both words are nouns here, as at line 32; on ζ 3. — ὅν, sc. δεῖξαι; 49.

29. ἐπεί . . ., "since near my noble father it dwells." This poetic usage of ναίω and kindred verbs with islands and other places is frequent in Homer. The house, island, town, is conceived as an actual person, in this instance as a neighbor. Compare ἕδος Ἰθάκης, ν 344; in terra domibus negata, Horace, Odes I. 22, 22; agelli quem habitatum quinque focis, Horace, Epistles I. 14, 2; Sophocles, Ajax, 596–97; Herodotus VII. 140. Touching this feature of the Homeric style, Gladstone has said: "The tendency of the Heroic Age, standing at its maximum in Homer, was to pour life outward, nay, almost to force it into everything. Where we should be passive, he is active, and ever at work with a bolder energy and keener pleasure to vivify. His uplifting and vitalizing process is everywhere at

128 NOTES.

whom "these" (οἵδε) points. Nausicaa herself feels that she may have occasion to rue their ill-manners, and not even the presence of the king and all his court saves Odysseus from the insults of Euryalus, and he a noble too; while Arete fears the crew may lay hands on the effects of the stranger, unless they are well secured, Book 8, lines 443–54.

34. The causal asyndeton advances a reason for their inhospitality. It is conceit of their marvellous speed upon the sea that renders them intolerant of strangers. — "on swift ships ... swift." A standing epithet like "swift" (θοή), occurring so continually as it does with "ship" (νηῦς), must necessarily lose a portion of its vigor. Since, therefore, it was too weak here to characterize the Phaeacian ships, "swift" (ὠκείῃσιν) was added. Compare "wind-footed swift Iris," nine times in the Iliad; "of swift-running ships," Sophocles Ajax, 710; "of a shaggy-haired goat," Theocritus 7, 15. Observe the emphasis thrown on "swift" by its closing a spondaic line, while the following verse dashes through the full measure of dactyls. — "having trusted"; Book 6, line 272.

35. The word laítma, connected with laimós ("throat") and laphýssō ("to swallow"), always carries with it the idea of danger, though not to the Phaeacians; Book 8, line 563.

36. "Their ships are swift as wing or thought." For other estimates of the speed of their ships, see Book 7, line 325; Book 13, lines 81–7. This now hackneyed simile of the rapidity of thought is more fully developed and actually dramatized at Book 15, lines 80–3, where it is descriptive of Hera speeding from Ida to Olympus:

"As when the mind of a man darts swiftly, one who has travelled over much
of the earth and thinks in his keen thoughts,
'I was here, or there,' and ponders many things,
so swiftly did queenly Hera fly in her eagerness."

"Swift as the mind of man, who many a land
Hath travelled o'er, and with reflective thought
Recalls, 'Here was I such a day, or here,'
And in a moment many a scene surveys:
So Juno sped o'er intervening space." Derby.

Gladstone quotes these two passages as the main instances in Homer of ideas properly subjective. The mind of that age was not addicted to turning in upon itself for self-communion, but to pouring itself outward upon the objective world. It is in the Lyric Period that the subjective begins properly to appear.

38. The phrase "follow in the footsteps" (μετ' ἴχνια βαῖνε) occurs only here and at Book 2, line 406; Book 3, line 30; Book 5, line 193. It

BOOK VII. 129

indicates the greatest care in following a guide implicitly, so that the foot is planted in the exact spot, as it were, from which the leader's was just lifted, without deviating to the right or left. Its appropriateness here is obvious. At Book 2, line 406, and Book 3, line 30, where Telemachus follows Athene under the guise of Mentor, it exhibits his yet unformed character and lack of self-reliance. At Book 5, line 193, Odysseus has just been distrusting the motives of Calypso; he now abandons himself to her guidance without reserve.

39. The word "famed for ships" is applied only to the Phaeacians and Phoenicians, and this fact, among others, led Mure to conjecture that the whole Phaeacian episode was intended as a playful satire upon some Phoenician colony of the West. 40. The preposition "through" with the accusative in the sense of "through" is mostly poetic, but usually marks the object as passing only part way through; with the genitive it goes through and passes out. Odysseus would be among them even in the palace. Virgil has,

He wraps himself in cloud and enters—wondrous to tell—
Into their midst, mingles with the men, and is seen by none. Aeneid I. 439.

41. What does the augment of the form "she went" show? See Hadley's Grammar, section 312a. The conception of Athene in Homer is too awe-inspiring and dread to attribute to her those feminine characteristics of beauty which are so common with the other goddesses. Except the "luminous eye," which may be considered beautiful in its intellectual aspect, she has no other ascriptions of the kind save "of beautiful locks" here, and "of lovely hair" three times in Book 6, where she is invoked in her temple at Troy. In both these instances it is in connection with a people much more effeminate than the Greeks, and here it is immediately counteracted by the word "dread."

When the Greeks are driven to their ships, they build a wall about the camp with towers along its circuit, at Book 7, line 436, and in front they run a ditch which is defended on its inner brink by sharp stakes, projecting over it. Here

They commonly accompany the name of the individual or class, and are confined, with one single exception in the Iliad, to the persons of the highest known rank, that of βασιλῆες, or kings. The king, as such, stands in special relation to deity, and it is expressly declared that kings derive the right to rule from Zeus, from whom descended, by successive deliveries, the sceptre of Agamemnon: "His honor is from Zeus, and Zeus the Counselor loves him," Book II line 197. which the Odyssey presents (Book VI, line 54), is the introduction of the titles "mistress" (despoina) and "queen" (basileia), which never occur in the Iliad. The former is applied to Eurydice the wife of Nestor, to Arete, and to Penelope; the latter to Nausicaa, Arete, and Penelope. This title, Queen, betokens political movement, and, in the case of Eurydice and Penelope, the increased influence of women due to the absence of their husbands at Troy, and the cares of state thus devolving upon them. Among the Phaeacians, it shows the habitual power exercised by the women. — kichesai, "thou shalt find," i.e. seek out; the future of mild command; Book VII line 319; H. 710; G.M. 25, Note 5.

54-5. "Now, Arete is her name of commemoration, and she is from progenitors the same that begat Alcinous the king." A name is eponymon when it has been selected for the express purpose of commemorating some circumstance connected with the child or family, as when Autolycus names his grandson Odysseus, the Hater, because he had himself hated so many in his day: "for having hated many I have come to this place; so let the name of Odysseus be his eponym" (Book XIX, line 407). Cf. Book IX, line 561. Herodotus tells us, VI.63, that Demaratus, the Spartan king, was so called (Dem-aratos = he who is prayed for by the people) because a prayer had been offered up by the people that the king, his father, long childless, might be vouchsafed a son. So, Arete is the prayed-for child, like Odysseus, Book XIX, line 404. — The meaning of tokeon (parents) is determined by the following genealogy. — ton auton, the article, as in Attic prose; H. 538b. The attempt made by many critics to explain every instance of the article in Homer as used demonstratively is now generally abandoned. Kruger has well said that the same amount of ingenuity expended upon the Attic article could make that always demonstrative. Indeed, Mr. Paley, one of the latest English editors of the Iliad, has founded upon the proper article use in Homer one branch of his argument for the late authorship of the poems, placing them as far down as 450 B.C. In this point he has been completely refuted by Hayman; not, however, by denying the article use, but by showing from Hesiod, Archilochus, Alcman, Sappho, Alcaeus, Solon, and Tyrtaeus — the earliest writings we have after Homer, and all previous to 500 B.C. — that the real article occurs there with as much frequency as in Homer; in short, "that the language

big as a mountain, though Nausithous evidently is not so. Hesiod even has no trace of the war between the Giants and the gods. He makes them three in number and hundred-handed, and they assist the gods against the Titans. — ἀτάσθαλον applies to deep, deliberate wickedness, attended with an obstinate persistence that must be known to be wrong. For when it is intended to allow for mere weakness, or for solicitation from without, or for a simply foolish blindness, then the word ἄτη, not ἀτασθαλίη, is used. Such is the wickedness of Aegisthus, though warned by Hermes, of the suitors, the Giants, and the crew of Odysseus, who devoured the oxen of the sun. Gladstone.

61–3. ἐμίγη, "was united." — ἐν; eta 23. — Ῥηξήνορά; on theta 110.
64. ἄκουρον, "heirless," as regarded succession to the throne. — βάλ'...Ἀπόλλων. All sudden and unexpected deaths, smiting the person when sound and well, without any visible or premonitory cause, are attributed to the painless arrows of Apollo for men, and of Artemis for women. The former produce the deaths by plague in the First Iliad, that of the pilot of Menelaus at his helm, and of the sons of Niobe in the presence of their mother. In the happy isle of Syrie, where Eumaeus was born, the people never died of disease, but by the gentle arrows of Apollo and Artemis, after passing to a good old age. By Artemis dies the nurse of Eumaeus on the Phoenician ship, the wife of Eetion, the daughters of Niobe, Ariadne, and even Orion. The corpse of Hector, restored by preternatural agency to integrity and freshness after the lacerations it had undergone, is said to become like the body of one slain by Apollo, that is, struck down in the full vigor of health.

65. Aristarchus and another scholar punctuate before ἐν, following the scholiast on P. T. Examples may be found to support either reading; lambda 198, 31, 68, Xi 485.

66. ποιήσατ'; H. 556. Another probable case of the marriage of uncle and niece is that of Cretheus and Tyro. Diomedes probably, and the Trojan Iphidamas certainly, married an aunt. Later, marriages of this kind were much more common at Sparta. Anaxandridas and Leonidas each wedded a niece, and Archidamus his aunt.

80. ἵκετο [she arrived]. As regards locomotion, Athene and Apollo display their majesty by movement that is instantaneous and self-sustained. They start, and their journey is completed. On one occasion only, Athene dons the winged sandals of Hermes, α 96. Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, and Ares habitually employ their chariots and immortal horses. Athene does indeed mount Hera's chariot, but only to accompany that goddess, Θ 389. — Why is Marathon mentioned? Situated on the north-east coast of Attica, it would not lie on the direct route to Athens from Scheria in the supposed north-west. Athene, therefore, goes out of her way, just as Hera does in her flight from Olympus to Ida in the Fourteenth Book of the Iliad, lines 225–83, where the purpose seems to be to represent her passage as made by land, touching the highest peaks that line the path at intervals. Athene, on the contrary, travels by sea (line 79), and the poet appears to have envisioned a northerly route from Scheria by water, connecting with the Aegean through the Hellespont (see η 324, 244), from which direction Marathon would lie directly in her path. But in any case, why is Marathon introduced rather than other places along the route? The easiest answer to Homeric puzzles is always that the passage is an interpolation — in this case inserted after Marathon had become famous from the battle against the Persians. But centuries before that battle set its crown of glory upon it, Marathon had been a place of importance as the head of the Doric Tetrapolis, which under Xuthus defends Attica from the bronze-clad warriors of Chalcis, and from which Ion, the son of Xuthus, becomes ruler at Athens by marrying the daughter of Erechtheus — a union to which the present lines may have some reference. See Curtius, History of Greece, pp. 320, 132, American edition. — Ἀθήνην is the only instance of the city's name occurring in the singular. Other proper names, however, vary between singular and plural forms: Θήβη / Θῆβαι, Μυκήνη / Μυκῆναι, Φηρή / Φηραί, Κρήτη / Κρῆται, Μάλεια / Μάλειαι.

81. Erechtheus, according to Β 547–51, was sprung from the soil, nursed by Athene, and established in Athens in her rich temple, ἐῷ ἐνὶ πίονι νηῷ [in her own rich temple], where the youth of the Athenians propitiate him with bullocks and lambs as the years roll round. The two were worshipped together in the ancient temple on the Acropolis, which also contained the salt-spring and the sacred olive tree, and was destroyed by Xerxes. On the site,

the beautiful Erechtheum was built, considerable remains of

82. ἴε; H. 405 D. — κῆρ; ζ 309, η 7. The poet has arranged the circumstances carefully, so that the goddess may preserve her incognito. She has said that her father's house is close by the palace, thus creating an opportunity for her to withdraw in that direction and escape the notice of Odysseus before vanishing.

83. ὥρμαιν', 133–34. — χάλκεον means either copper or bronze, but which is uncertain. Brass, a compound of copper and zinc, it was not. Pure copper is so easily bruised and battered that some process for tempering it, now unknown (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 612), must be assumed if we take it as the sole material of the numerous weapons and utensils in Homer that are described as χαλκός. Count Caylus did, after long experiment, discover that copper could be hardened by repeated water-baths; and pure copper implements have been recently discovered at Santorini, Troy, in Attica, Cyprus,

138 NOTES.

France, Ireland, and India. In Chaldaea it has been found, though rarely, the most of the objects having a component of tin, which hardens the copper and produces bronze. Two of Dr. Schliemann's Trojan battle-axes had respectively 4 and 9 per cent. of tin, while one of his swords from Mycenae yielded upon analysis 13 per cent., a fragment of a vase-handle 10 per cent., but a copper kettle had only the slightest trace, 0.09 per cent. — "oudon," the threshold of the palace proper. That he has passed the threshold of the aule (courtyard), and stands within the open court, seems certain from "outside the courtyard," lines 112, and 135, 95; besides, from such a standpoint he is able to take in the whole scene, though it would be captious indeed to limit the poet in so general a description merely to what Odysseus could see.

84-5. "For as of the sun was the splendor, or of the moon, throughout the palace high-roofed of great-hearted Alcinous." — hoste, Odyssey Book 6 line 122, Book 7 line 11. The glitter is from the gold, silver, and copper with which the palace is adorned, now lighted up by the latest glories of sunset from without, and the flaming torches within. Compare the description of the palace of Menelaus, emblazoned with the returns of his seven years' wanderings about Cyprus, Phoenicia, Egypt, and Libya, Book 4 lines 72-3:

"The gleam of bronze throughout the echoing halls,
and of gold, electrum, silver, and ivory."

86. Toichoi means "house walls," teichea means "city walls." The men of Hesiod's Third Age, which preceded that of the Heroes, not only were clad in bronze, and used implements of bronze, but dwelt in houses constructed of bronze. Doubtless the poet, in his realm of fantasy, may construct his palace walls of solid bronze or copper; but if we are to look for any real counterpart of the buildings of the day, the walls were only sheathed with metal plates. The so-called Treasury of Atreus at Mycenae, which belongs to a very early period, still shows traces of such sheathing in the bronze nails disposed at regular intervals throughout the interior, attesting the purpose for which they originally served. Of like construction in the historic period was the Temple of Athena "of the Bronze House," at Sparta, begun, it was said, by Tyndareus, and the Treasury of the Sicyonians at Olympia, Pausanias III. 17, 2, VI. 19, 2. Doors of wood, plated with bronze, were found near

BOOK VII. 139

Nimrud in 1879; and when Pizarro conquered Peru, the inner walls of the temple of Cuzco were covered with plates of gold that furnished a heavy contribution to the ransom of the Inca.— "have come" (perfect form); see Book VI, line 9.

87. "a cornice of kuanos" — kuanos is something dark, to contrast with the walls, but whether a paint or a metal it is impossible to determine. Many of the ancients thought it a pigment formed of a native carbonate of copper; others make it bronze, lead, steel. The last is favored by Buchholz, Am., F.; but steel is so quickly eaten into a surface of rust by the action of the weather that it would serve no practical purpose as an outside coping, which this unquestionably is.

88. "were wont to enclose" — when shut for the night; they were now wide open; on Book VI, line 51. The phrase is applied to a city at Σ 512, and an island at Ω 544; cf. ζ 303.

89. "doorposts"; Book VI, line 19. Virgil has lavished his description upon Dido's temple, and with consummate art has introduced the pleasing episode of the pictures, Aeneid I. 448: (The temple) whose bronze thresholds rose on steps linked together, whose beams were of bronze, and whose door-hinge grated on bronze.

90. "thereon," upon the doorposts. — "golden"; Book VI, line 79. — "door-hook," the hook by which the door was drawn to; "and she drew the door shut with its silver hook," referring to the sleeping-apartment of Telemachus, α 441. The contrast of colors in the various metals, and their disposition, should be noticed.

91. "on each side," supply "of the doors"; Book VI, line 19. A pair of gold and a pair of silver dogs guarded the portals.

92–3. "to those who know"; Book VI, line 233. — "to keep watch"; Book VI, line 82.

94. "immortal," properly, as appositive to "dogs," should take its case; but when, between the appositive and the idea to which it belongs, a relative sentence intervenes, the appositive can agree with the relative. This construction is not infrequent among the poets, but in prose occurs noticeably only in Plato. Krüger. — "being." This line has been thought a later addition from the presence of "being" (in one form), instead of the usual earlier form. The MSS. give variant forms at τ 230 and τ 489; but the objectors there either change or excise. Yet precisely analogous forms are seen at θ 580, τ 202, ω 491, Ξ 274. — "ageless all their days,"

140 NOTES.

forevermore." — The word agerāos or agērōs never occurs in Homer except with athanatos ("immortal"), and always of something divine, as the Aegis, Iliad B 447, and the immortal horses of Achilles, Iliad P 444. Penelope is mortal (brotos), but Calypso is "immortal and ageless," Odyssey ε 218; cf. η 257. The epithets, therefore, cannot be said to describe merely the enduring character of the material of which the dogs are fashioned. These porter-dogs must be endowed with the same attributes of life and motion with which the poet invests other works of high art in metal, especially from the hand of Hephaistos, and they furnish the climax of that copious vivifying power which he has poured like a flood through his verse. Hephaistos has twenty tripods in his smithy that move spontaneously to the assembly of the gods, and the two maidens that attend his limping gait are wrought of pure gold, and

"in them is mind within their hearts, and in them voice
and strength, and from the immortal gods they know their craft." Iliad Σ 419.

The arms of Achilles manufactured by Hephaistos, so far from being a weight upon him, seemed like wings to lift him from the ground; and the figures on the shield moved and fought, danced and sang, while the golden furrow darkened into mellow mould behind the plough. The Phaeacian ships, which knew no higher architects than the Phaeacians themselves, were gifted with thought and intelligence, and needed not helmsmen to guide them on their way; Odyssey θ 556–62.

95. "But within." The poet passes now to a description of the interior of the great banqueting-hall, which could be seen by Odysseus through the open doors. — eréredat' ("were fitted"); H. 392 D; C. 287; cf. ζ 308, θ 66, 473.

96. diamperes ("right through"); θ 245. — "whereon;" cf. Ξ 216. — peploi ("robes"); ζ 38.

98–9. hedriōonto, "were wont to sit;" ζ 257, ν 9. — epēetanon gar echeskon, "for store without stint they ever had." So Odysseus, returning to the ship after he has compelled Circe to retransform his companions that had been changed into swine, tells the rest whom he finds there to hasten to the palace that they may see their comrades "eating and drinking; for they have store without stint," κ 427. The word epēetanon in these two passages and in Apollonius Rhodius II. 1179 is a substantive; cf. σ 360.

100. Kouroi, not statues, but "youths;" hence they are doubtless to be considered animate productions of the same hand that wrought the golden hounds. Assyrian art, from which the Greeks borrowed so much, thus far exhibits no work that can justly be called a statue, only five crude figures of stone in the round. On the other hand, sculpture in relief attained there to a high degree of excellence. So it is in the Homeric poems; there is no statuary. The Pallas figure of Z 303 must have been as crude as the oldest Assyrian figure; cf. the seated goddess depicted above, p. 89. The dogs of Alcinous may have been a poetic reflection of something similar to the lions over the gateway at Mycenae, or, rather, like the handmaids of Hephaistos and the torch-bearers here, living creatures, not made of flesh and blood, but produced from the poetic alembic of gold. Of art in relief, however, the poems are often descriptive, notably in the shield of Achilles, where the vivid imagination of the poet doubtless soars high above the art of his day. Schliemann's discoveries at Mycenae show almost nothing in the round, but much in relief. The accompanying figures exhibit two of the half-dozen attempts at representation of the human form in metal among the objects discovered there; these, however, are properly reliefs, since they are stamped out, and each is but half a body. The terra-cotta figures were still more crude, as may be seen by examining similar statuettes in the Cesnola Collection, especially the Venuses from Alambra. — Bomon, "pedestals," an earlier sense than "altar," which, however, occurs

in Hm. At Theta 441 it is a raised platform on which the chariot of Zeus is placed after use.

101. daidas, uniformly in the plural, because, "as appears from ancient marbles and other representations, it was formed of a number of staves or twigs, either bound by a rope wound round them in a spiral form, or surrounded by circular bands at equal distances. The inside of the torch may be supposed to be filled with flax, tow, or other vegetable fibres, the whole being abundantly impregnated with pitch, rosin, wax, oil, and other inflammable substances." Dict. Antiq. Here the encasement is of gold. They are employed in the palace of Odysseus to light the way to bed, to kindle the fire in the braziers, give light to Penelope at her evening task in her chamber, and, in fact, wherever a portable light was needed. The lamp, lychnos, is mentioned but once, at tau 34. Corresponding to the kouroi here, in the hall of Odysseus are the three lampteres, or braziers filled with wood, lighted and kept replenished, at sigma 307.

102. phainontes, intransitively, "giving light," as sigma 308.

103. hoi, the king; on zeta 131. The palace of Odysseus also has fifty female slaves, imitated by Virgil of the household of Dido. The word dmoai is taken up again distributively by the following "some... others," so that no verb is to be supplied; so at alpha 109, eta 129, theta 360, mu 73. The change from the past tenses in the preceding description to the presents that follow, 104-30, is unusual for Hm., who, in narration, regularly uses the present only of facts which may be conceived to be true during the time of the singer himself, as at zeta 42-6, nu 96-112, Beta 751-55. Though the historical present was admitted here and in a few other instances by the scholiasts, some modern critics deny its use altogether in Hm., and hence Friedlander, F., Duntz., characterize the present passage as an interpolation. Note that the presents here are not of the ordinary historical nature, since they all denote the continued wonted act, much like Alpha 163, 168, nu 377, etc.; cf. zeta 87, kappa 349-50, nu 160, xi 165; yet the ground-work appears laid for the later use, and such slight advances as the present passage shows may exhibit the path along which it developed.

104. aletreousin. This was one of the severest tasks imposed upon the slave, and it fell regularly upon the women. Twelve

BOOK VII. 143

are assigned to this duty in the palace of Odysseus. A specified amount must be the grist of each per day, and the hour which released the ox from his yoke brought no rest to one whose feeble strength had not fulfilled her task. It is such a one that in the dawn of the morning hears the thunder-omen sent by Zeus to Odysseus on the day the suitors die, v 105. Among the Egyptians, too, "the maid-servant that is behind the mill" is the lowliest of the land. Exodus xi. 5. The hand-mill consisted of two circular stones, nearly flat, the lower one fixed, while the other turned on a pivot or shaft rising from the centre of that beneath it. The grain, descending through an aperture in the upper stone immediately above the pivot, gradually underwent the process of grinding as it made its way from the centre to the rim. It was turned by the woman seated, holding a handle fixed perpendicularly near the edge. Such a mill is still to be found among the islands of the Aegean, and is the same as the Scottish quern. Schliemann discovered at Troy numerous stones of lava, 13 inches long by 7 broad, which are reasonably conjectured to have been used as mill-stones; they were found also at Mycenae. — The word ἔπι appears at θ 403, 563, λ 367; on ζ 12, the phrase μήλοπα καρπόν, meaning "apple-hued grain," is probably wheat, since barley is called white (λευκόν). The scholiast compares ξανθή, the epithet of Demeter.

106. If ἥμεναι (seated) applies to the weavers as well as the spinners, then some foreign fashion, like the Egyptian, is intended; for the Greeks are habitually represented as moving up and down before the loom (ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένη, A 31) as they wove, a posture necessitated by the upright loom then in use. Yet the phrase κατὰ δῶμα at line 103 makes the description a general one, so that we are not to look for all the slaves in the great hall (μέγαρον, cf. 121, θ 61), where the mill-grinders would be incongruous indeed, and the loom-workers only less so. The mill-maids of Book v are located in the outer court (αὐλή), and the websters belong to the women's apartments (Γ 125, 142, Χ 440). The spinners might properly remain in the hall (δ 121–35) and answer to ζ 307. They are closely linked here with the former because the two tasks are closely allied, and their joint product is the pride and boast of the people (ζ 26–7, 49, 53, 58, 61, 64, 111, 306; η 107–11, 235; θ 249, 392, 425, 441, 455; ν 67, 73, 118). The simile then probably illustrates both words, στρωφῶσιν and ἥμεναι, rapid

motion in working, combined with a fixed position at work; Book VI, line 292.

107. "And from the close-warped linen drops the liquid oil." — ὀθονέων refers to the outer garment of Helen, Book III line 141, when she visits the walls, and of the maidens in the dance, Book XVIII line 595; compare Book XIII line 73. — ἀπολείβεται is explained by some as referring to the oil with which the threads were sprinkled while weaving, to impart a lustre to the cloth, as the so-called weavers' glue is used at the present day; compare Book XVIII line 596, quoted at Book VI line 157. Others insist that it is only a figurative way of indicating that the cloth is as lustrous as oil; or that the weaving is so fine and close that oil will not pass through if poured on. At all events, the cloth has a lustrous surface, Book VI lines 26 and 74, and elsewhere. Compare a somewhat similarly dubious expression in Callimachus, Hymn to Apollo 37–9, and Hymn to Hestia, where it is said of her:
"Ever from your tresses drips the liquid oil."

"Spot more delicious than those gardens feigned
Or of revived Adonis, or renowned
Alcinous, host of old Laertes' son." Paradise Lost, IX. 440.

Regarding the kind of beauty described here, Gladstone, in his treatment of the picturesque in Homer (on page 79), remarks as follows: "I assent entirely, on the other hand, to what Mr. Ruskin has said respecting his sense of orderly beauty in common nature. The Garden of Alcinous is truly Dutch in its quadrangular conceptions; but it is plain that the poet means us to regard it as truly beautiful. Symmetry, serenity, regularity, adopted from the forms of living beauty which were before him, enter largely into Homer's conceptions of one form, at least, of inanimate beauty." Studies, III, p. 420. — The form pephukasin is like lelonkhasin, Book XI, line 304. — telethonta; on Book VI, line 14. Scheria is called "rich in clods," Book V, line 34.

Lines 115–16. Pear-trees, pomegranates, apple-trees, fig-trees, and olive-trees are all trees. — aglaokarpoi, "bright-fruited;" compare nitidae fruges, Lucretius I. 252. These two lines also describe the fruit-trees that hung their branches over the head of Tantalus in the Underworld, but swung them up beyond his reach whenever he tried to pluck their fruit; Book XI, line 589.

Lines 117–18. "Of these, the fruit never decays or fails, winter or summer, lasting through the year." — cheimatos; Hadley 591; Goodwin 179; Curtius 426. Homer divides the year into three seasons only — spring, summer, and winter. Opora, which has been called autumn by some, covers too broad a range, since it begins early in July, and must be taken as a synonym of theros (summer). Buchholz. — epetesios gathers up and reinforces the thought of the preceding. — mal' aiei, "ever unceasing."

Line 119. For a similar "acephalous" line, see Book VIII, line 452, and compare Book VI, line 45, Book VII, line 94. — Zephyrie is properly an adjective; used here alone for Zephyros. This wind is the most prominent in Homer's view. Within the circle of the Aegean and in Ithaca it is a fierce, loud-roaring wind, often bringing storm and destruction to ships. Only in Scheria and Elysium, Book IV, line 567, does it take on the milder character that was afterwards associated with Zephyr when it had

7

146 NOTES.

moved down from the north and become a simple west wind; for its home, when it sweeps down from Thrace, is in the north-west, and so far towards the north that it almost meets with Boreas at times.

120. The fruit is now spoken of. — epi, "upon," "after."

121. The grape belongs properly in the following description of the vineyard, but the poet has anticipated here, in order to declare emphatically that the most essential peculiarity of the orchard, its never-failing supply, also pertains to the vineyard as well. It will be observed that this quality of their climate scarcely squares with the need of fires, eta 7, but we are expressly informed that all here is supernatural and god-given, 132; on zeta 42. The poet has transferred to this one spot everything desirable that nature offers in different places and different climes, or that the fancy can conceive in one wonderful clime. Therefore, as Am. remarks, it is a fruitless task to attempt to bring each several part of the description into accord with actual reality, and to satisfy the critical judgment on every side. Aristotle, when asked his opinion of the city of Athens, wittily quoted this line in allusion to the sycophants.

122–26. hoi, 103. — tes . . . hypoperkázousin, "of which one part, a sunny area in a level spot, is dried by the sun, and then again other grape-clusters they gather, and others they tread; and in front, too, are setting grapes, casting their flower, and others just darkening." — theilopedon, appositive to heteron. The sense runs: In one part of the vineyard, more sunny than the rest, perhaps by reason of elevation (cf. Virgil, Georgics II. 521), or distance from the fruit-trees, the clusters hang till dried to raisins; in another part they gather fruit, and in a third they make the wine. — tersetai is generally understood to refer to a partial drying of the grape for the vinum passum, which was made from such grapes; Ameis argues that no hint of any such wine is to be found in Homer, while the plain sense is more Homeric, and would furnish an additional product for the table, and a further proof of luxuriant profusion. — heteras, sc. staphylas.—Ameis refers paroithe to the extremity of the branches of the vine, because the clusters nearest the parent stock ripen first. — The preposition of hypoperkázousin is usually given the sense of "somewhat." Am. sees in it another

BOOK VII. 147

touch of nature; for the grape begins to color first underneath. Compare with this passage the beautiful picture of the vintage wrought upon the shield of Achilles, Σ 561–72.

127–28. "There, too, well-ordered garden-beds of all kinds along the last row are growing, bright the year through." — The word prasiai, from prason, originally meant a leek or onion garden; see note on ζ 77. The garden of fruit and vegetables appears to have been a common, if not a necessary, adjunct to a household. Odysseus extols in high terms the careful cultivation bestowed upon the orchatos and prasiē of Laertes, ω 244–47: Diomed speaks of many orchatoi among the possessions of his father, Ξ 123; and pease and beans are mentioned in a simile, Ν 589, and the poppy, Θ 306. — Neiaton refers to the last row of vines passing in the order assumed above from trees to vines, and vines to vegetables. — Ganoosai must not be taken in the sense of "bright with flowers," as if this were a flower-garden. Such appears to be the meaning of Mr. Bryant's "beds of plants that all the year bore flowers." As this verb, in the only passages where it otherwise occurs in Homer, pictures the sheen from the polished helmets and breastplates, so here it sets before us the lustre of leaves that are full-fed from the soil and full-watered from the irrigating rivulets. No hint of the cultivation of flowers simply as such is to be found in Homer; for the poppy was undoubtedly an article of food, as we know it to have been in the time of Thucydides, and as it still is in Poland and Russia. The love of flowers, however, was not absent in the Heroic Age, as is evinced by the frequent and loving mention of them bespangling the meadows and hill-tops, and by their selection to adorn objects in metal and tapestry; but this fondness found full gratification in their profusion of wild flowers. Of these the lily, crocus, asphodel, hyacinth, and violet are mentioned in the poems; but, strange to say, the rose, which grows so luxuriantly there, and is so frequent a theme with the later poets, appears only indirectly in the epithets rhododaktylos, rhodoeis, and the proper name Rhodos. The same is the case in Hesiod, and it first meets us in the Hymn to Demeter.

129. En de, in the vegetable garden. — The words he men . . . he d', as above, 104. — Kepon, the same as orchatos above. The orchard-garden of Laertes is called indifferently kepos, orchatos, aloe. Irrigation

148 NOTES.

by artificial channels is made the subject of a simile in the Iliad. Achilles, pursued by the river Scamander, which overflows its banks in the chase, is compared with the man who, letting water into a garden, hastens to clear the stoppages from the channels, and is overtaken by the stream, Phi 257.

130. "ἡ δ'": the other spring is led under the threshold of the court, within which an enclosed fountain, like that of Ithaca (on Eta 20), may be supposed to have been constructed, and from this the townspeople obtained water. "ἵησιν" means "pours"; see note on Eta 4.

131. Ameis is of the opinion that the presents of lines 104–30 are due to the poet's adopting the standpoint of Odysseus as he surveys the scene, but that with "ὑδρεύοντο" this standpoint is abandoned, and he returns to the regular recital; see note on line 50.

132. "Such, then, among the possessions of Alcinous were the splendid gifts of the gods." — "ἐν Ἀλκινόοιο"; Zeta 11. The word "οἴκῳ," the usual word to be supplied, is here to be understood in its widest sense of the house and all belonging to it, so as to include the garden with its wonders, as well as the palace. — "ἔσαν"; Theta 233.

133–34. These lines, with appropriate substitutions, are applied to Hermes when he stops before the Grotto of Calypso to gaze in admiration at the beauties spread before his eyes, Epsilon 75.

135. "οὐδὸν" refers to the house proper. — "δώματος" is governed by "εἴσω"; Theta 290.

136. "ἡγήτορας ἠδὲ μέδοντας," meaning "leaders and guardians," are the standard titles describing the chieftains as a body, in their capacity as leaders and shepherds of the people — on the one hand, taking the initiative in war, and on the other, exercising a patriarchal guardianship and watchfulness over the people. The latter title habitually accompanies the former, and both are regularly joined to some genitive, as here.

137. "Ἀργειφόντῃ" is commonly translated "Argus-slayer," as referring to the myth of Io, but no explanation of the word is given in Homer, Hesiod, or the Hymns, and Io nowhere appears in Homer. Ameis derives it from "ἀργός" and "φαίνω" and translates it as "the courier," following a scholiast who glosses it as "one who appears swiftly and clearly"; others, interpreting "ἀργός" as "bright," render it "the bright shiner," connecting it with the idea of the dawn. "Ἑρμείας" is referred

BOOK VII. 149

by Max Müller to the Sanskrit Sarameias, one of the names for the dawn.

138. σπένδεσκον; Book VI, line 6. Is this a proper conclusion for the conditional relative clause following? Goodwin & Müller, Grammar §62 Rem. Libation is poured to Hermes last, before retiring to rest, because he is the giver of sleep through the agency of his caduceus, as is said in Book V, line 47:

He took his wand, with which he charms the eyes of men
whomsoever he wishes, and rouses again those who are sleeping.

He exercises this influence upon the warders of the Grecian camp when he conducts Priam through their midst to the tent of Achilles, Book XXIV, line 445. — μνησαίατο: Book VI, line 286; Book VIII, lines 70, 87, 90, 220; on Book VI, line 183.

139–41. διὰ δῶμα: Book VI, line 304. — ἠέρ' ἔχων, like a garment; Book VI, line 61: "wrapped in cloud," Virgil's Aeneid I.439. — ἵκετ': why the indicative? Goodwin & Müller §66, 1; Goodell §239. So Book VII, lines 276, 280; cf. Book VI, line 218.

142. ἀμφί: on Book VI, line 9. — Observe the recurrence of the name Odysseus at lines 133, 139, 142, 145, at the end of the line, a favorite position for a proper name if the metre will admit. Of the 73 instances of the occurrence of the name Odysseus in these selections, 47 are at the end of the line, compared to 26 elsewhere. Cf. Book VIII, lines 2, 4, 8, 130–32, 143, 419, 421, 423.

143. "And then, at last, from him back poured the mystic air." — αὐτοῖο: Hadley §580. — πάλιν. The cloud melted back into the transparent atmosphere from which it was formed, as mist vanishes before the morning's sun. For though the veil is divine, the similitude of the natural phenomenon is maintained; and the ancients considered fog to be nothing more than thickened air, while darkness was a very thick fog deceiving the sight. Virgil has expressed this somewhat more accurately: "The cloud that wrapped them suddenly parts and clears away into open sky," Aeneid I.587.

144–45. οἱ δ' ἄνεῳ ἐγένοντο, "and silent they became." — ἄνεῳ is treated as an adjective by most authorities, despite Buttmann's objection. — κάτα: Book VI, line 12. — φῶτα ἰδόντες: Book VI, line 199. — ἐλλιτάνευεν: on Book VI, line 20; Book XIII, line 151.

146. θύγατερ, "daughter," is a more resonant and exalted mode of address than the simple patronymic, which is found but twice among the Phaeacians, Book VIII, lines 114–16. Compare Odysseus' address to Nausicaa, Book VIII, line 464, and that of the suitors to Penelope, Books XVIII, XIX, and XXI, lines 245, 285, and 321 respectively.

147. Observe the art with which the dignity of the king is maintained—

150 NOTES.

held (respecting which he is somewhat touchy, Book XI line 348), by the choice of the word "husband," and its position here. The dignity and brevity of the prayer are admirably adapted to the situation. Compare it with the presentation of his case to Nausicaa. All the eulogistic compliments which comprised one half of the speech to the young lady, and all reference to his former importance in the world, are omitted. His misfortunes are but barely stated, the prayer for their prosperity is abridged, and, instead of the modesty which characterized his request to the maiden, we have the boldness that befits the suppliant to king and court.

148–49. "ολβια ζωέμεναι" means "happiness in their lives;" compare Book VIII line 413, Book VI line 306. — ζωέμεναι is added to contrast with what follows; not only to live happily, but die happily, in the midst of wealth and honors, bequeathing these to their children, not to strangers.

150. "γέρας" may be any prize for honorable services, as an estate (Book VI line 194, Book IX line 578), a female slave, complimentary portions at banquets, presents in general, and even the kingly authority. As regards succession to the last, Gladstone concludes from the evidence offered by the position of Telemachus, that "It was admitted by the suitors that it descended to him from his father. Yet there evidently was some special, if not formal, act to be done, without which he could not be king. Perhaps the expressions of Antinous imply that such a proceeding was much more than formal, and that the accession of Telemachus to the supreme dignity might be arrested by the dissent of the nobles. The answer, too, of the young prince (Book I line 396) seems to be at least in harmony with the idea that a practice either approaching an election, or in some way involving a voluntary action on the part of the subjects, or of a portion of them, had to be gone through." Studies III, p. 51.

151–52. "But for me an escort speed ye my native land to reach." — ἱκέσθαι: compare Book VI lines 82, 90; Book VII line 174; Book VIII line 45; Book IX line 518; Book VI line 58; Book XVII line 362; Book I lines 93–5. — θᾶσσον means "with all haste," a comparative used absolutely, but never for the positive form alone, and always with the imperative, the hortative subjunctive, or sentences of purpose. — ἐπειδή: I speak of haste because I have already been kept so long from home. — δηθά: compare Book VI line 220.

153. ἐπ': compare Book VI line 52. He seats himself by the hearth, because the

BOOK VII. 151

A lowly position would display his personal humility, notwithstanding the boldness of his request, and because it was near the feet of Arete. That a certain degree of sanctity, too, should attach to the family hearth, and the spot near which the guest was seated in honor, is a natural inference; but it was not as yet exalted into divinity. Histie, as a goddess, appears first in Hesiod, where she is a sister of Demeter and Hera; in the Hymn to Aphrodite she is regularly installed over the hearth. The suppliant often takes a seat on the threshold of the room, as Odysseus before Aeolus, Book 10 line 62, and at home as a beggar, Book 17 line 339; so too Penelope, in her agony of grief at the departure of Telemachus, Book 4 line 718. Themistocles, in exile, follows among the Molossians the example of Odysseus here.

154. "by the fire, for him"; Book 6 lines 224, 248, 296. — "hushed in silence;" Book 8 line 234, Book 11 line 333, Book 13 line 1.

155. "but at last, then," mostly after the preceding formulaic line, to which it naturally attaches as introducing the action which some one of the company, more bold or more energetic than the rest, takes upon himself to urge or initiate after a long silence of astonishment, doubt, or fear.

156. "of the Phaeacians"; on Book 6 lines 257, 202. — "an elder," "very aged;" the comparative as "more swiftly," line 152, "more beautiful," line 159.

157. "in words"; H. 609. — "knowing," causal; H. 789 c. Knowledge in the Homeric age must be founded on experience, and experience comes with years. The aged man, with his many-sided experience reaching back into the past of three generations, is the wise man, skilled to speak the word that wins the meed of fairest counsel:

A man who knows many things from of old,
Nestor, whose counsel even then was seen to be best. Book 24, line 51.

159-60. "Not indeed to thee is this fully honorable, nor even is it fitting." — "to sit" defines "this" appositively; H. 766; Book 11 line 359, 364. — "on the ground" may be taken literally (Book 6 line 51, Book 19 line 63) or generally.

161. "But these, thy word awaiting, themselves restrain;" cf. Book 11 lines 342-46. — "these men here," with a gesture to his fellow-kings.

162. "silver-studded," an epithet applied only to the sword (on Book 8 line 406), and to the throne in the palace of Hephaistos, Alcinous, Circe, and once in that of Odysseus; hence something unusually splen-

152 NOTES.

did. Compare the numerous large gold bosses or buttons discovered by Schliemann in the graves of Mycenae.

163. "He directed him to rise" (ζ 7–8). — "to the heralds": on θ 399.

164. The scholiasts are unanimous in giving the sense "anew" to the preposition of επικρῆσαι (to mix again), and this is well suited to the case at hand, since the last libation for the night has been poured and the mixture may well be supposed exhausted. Many recent editors think it describes the addition of wine to the water. — καί, "also," as well as Hermes. — τερπικεραύνῳ (he who delights in the thunderbolt), like ἀστεροπητής (wielder of lightning), ἀργικέραυνος (of the bright thunderbolt), στεροπηγερέτα (gatherer of lightning), ἐριβρεμέτης (loud-thundering), ὑψιβρεμέτης (high-thundering), ἐρίγδουπος (loud-crashing), εὐρύοπα (far-seeing), νεφεληγέρετα (cloud-gatherer), κελαινεφής (dark-clouded), is an epithet of Zeus in his capacity as lord of the atmosphere and its phenomena.

165–66. "Let us pour a libation": on ζ 31. How is σπει- derived from σπενδ-? H. 49, 31. — "suppliants": ζ 207. — "those within" = "those who are inside," the viands ready at hand; 176. This is the custom when a stranger arrives unexpectedly; no fresh meal is prepared.

167. τόγ': why the accusative? H. 576 a. — "the sacred might of Alcinous," meaning "the impetuous ardor of Alcinous." Ameis suggests this rendering for ἱερόν, an archaic meaning supported by the Sanskrit ishiras. Hayman describes Alcinous as "simple, genial, good-natured, garrulous, boastful, and hospitable;" but the main spring from which these characteristics flow is an ardent impetuosity which carries him away quite beyond the limits of sober discretion. He is somewhat slow of perception, and therefore slow to act upon an unexpected emergency; but when the proper course is suggested by others, he is not only quick to acquiesce, but far outstrips the suggestion in his eagerness to adopt it. Astonished at the appearance of Odysseus, he remains speechless with the rest until prodded into action by Echeneus, whose age brings both the wisdom that comprehends the situation and the authority under which his rebukes will be tolerated. Then the king hastens to raise the hero and seat him even upon the throne of his favorite son. When the courtiers have retired, it is Arete who begins the conversation, at line 236, and introduces the usual questions which it was his place to put to the guest; cf. λ 335, and for his impetuosity, η 299–301, 311–16, θ 102, 246, 388, 546, λ 348–53, 375–76, etc. The periphrasis of "the impetuous ardor of Alcinous," for "the impetuous and ardent Alcinous," is common to

BOOK VII. 153

many languages, and personifies that quality which is the essence of the individual; cf. on 187. Of similar phrases Homer has, "the strength of Telemachus," "the might of Castor," "the power of Eetion," "the shaggy heart of Pylaemenes."

168. "of the hand"; ζ 142. — "bold-hearted"; ζ 256. — "of varied cunning," like "of many counsels," "of many devices," "of many turns," "of many thoughts," elsewhere among his epithets.

169–70. What irregularity does "ἐσχαρόφιν" have? H. 206 D. — "manly-spirited," meaning "manly;" for proof of this see his speech to Odysseus, as compared with that of Euryalus; θ 145–64.

171. "but"; on ζ 6; it exchanges with "for," ρ 257. — "him," the son.

172–76 are repeated 4 times in the Odyssey: α 136–40, when Athene, in the guise of Mentes, is received by Telemachus in Ithaca; δ 52–6, when Telemachus and Peisistratus arrive at the palace of Menelaus; κ 368–72, of Odysseus in the halls of Circe; ρ 91–5, of Telemachus with Theoclymenus on his return to his home. It is remarkable that many such repetitions in the poems are descriptive of objects of that homely character which may appear least adapted for poetical embellishment. Yet it is evident that they were agreeable to the poet's audience, as they are, indeed, to modern taste, though foreign to our practice. For us the apparent anomaly has been explained by the charm of antiquarian interest, as the domestic utensils of Pompeii awaken a livelier emotion than the porticos and temples; but for the poet's contemporaries, it must reflect the feelings of a simple and childlike state of society. As the potter

7*

154 NOTES.

soon learns to fashion the common utensils of every-day use into more elegant shapes and to adorn them with various forms of ornamentation, so the poet brings gratification to the popular taste by the embellishment of objects of domestic or familiar interest. — prokhoō is to be construed with "carrying"; cf. Book 3, line 440. The prochoos also serves for dipping the wine from the mixing bowl and filling the cups. The preceding figure shows a prochoos of gold, discovered by Schliemann in one of the tombs at Mycenae.

173. hyper. The hands are held over the basin and washed while the water is poured over them from above, as Muslim custom demands to the present day. This ablution habitually precedes the meal as well as the sacrifice. Fingers, not forks, conveyed the food to the mouth. — lebetos; on Book 13, line 13.

174. nipsasthai; Book 6, line 82. If the infinitive endings -sthai, -menai, and -ai were originally dative case-endings, as many think, we can easily trace the dative sense here, "for washing." — trapezan. A separate table is usually placed before each person at the feast. All were accustomed to sit; reclining at table was a later custom, but when it was introduced is uncertain. The Spartans appear to have followed it at the time of Alcman, but for Greek women and children the ancient custom continued in use.

176–77. eidata; on Book 6, line 77. — charizomene pareonton, "giving freely out of her present store;" H. 574. — pine; Book 6, line 249. Virgil adds an additional touch from his own time:

The servants offer water for the hands, and bring forth Ceres' gifts in baskets, and present napkins of soft-shorn cloth. Aeneid I. 701.

182. Tennyson's "honey-hearted" rightly interprets meliphrona, for the elder poet is personifying, according to his custom; on lines 29, 187. meliphron is also an epithet of wheat, grain, and sleep. — kirnao, kirnemi, like pitnō, show a rare weakening of epsilon to iota, permitted by the strength of the following combination of consonants; H. 334 c.

183. eparksamenos depaeessin, "having performed the initiatory rite in succession with the cups." — eparksamenos is a ritualistic word, but what the rite was it is impossible to determine, whether a formula of words, as the cup is handed to the guest, Book 3 lines 41, 45, 47, Book 19 lines 121, 151, Book 15 line 150, or a slight libation, Book 14 line 447, or a few drops poured into the cup for the guest to make the libation. See

BOOK VII. 155

the lifelike representation of wine-distribution of later days on the sarcophagus from Golgoi in the Cesnola Collection.

184. speisan ("they poured a libation"): of course this is the act of the feasters, whatever the herald does.

186-87. This magniloquent opening, with the appropriate change of persons addressed, falls from the lips of Hector, Antenor, Priam, Zeus twice, Alcinous twice, and Odysseus twice before the suitors. Such association is significant. The simpler form appears at Zeta 239. — The personification of thymos ("spirit/soul"), as something different from the individual himself, is a strong Homeric characteristic; on Zeta 118, Theta 178, 237.

188. daisamenos ("having feasted"): H. 789 c. — katakeíete, "seek ye repose." This form is made an imperative by most authorities. According to H. 378 D., it is a future indicative used like kichesai, Eta 53. Can katakeio-men, in a final sentence after ophra, Sigma 419, be a future? G. M. 44, 1, Note 1; G. 216, 1, Note 1.

189. gerontas ("elders"): on Zeta 55; the title officially applied to the members of the boule ("council"), and it had thus become dissociated from the idea of age, even in Homer, for Nestor was the only old man among the Greek gerontes before Troy. Idomeneus, indeed, was near upon old age, and Odysseus was apparently not under fifty. The majority would seem to have been rather under middle life, Achilles not above thirty, and perhaps much younger. Compare the Spartan gerousia, the Roman senatus, and our alderman. — epi with kalesantes; cf. Zeta 55, Eta 49, Theta 7-11, 41-2. The full number of twelve kings is especially summoned on the morrow.

192. hos ch': H. 741; G. M. 44, 1, Note 2; G. 216, 1, Note 2; Eta 223, Theta 101, 251, Zeta 113. — The article with xeinos ("guest/stranger"), as with geron ("old man"), is formulaic, occurring some 33 times in the Odyssey, far more frequently than with any other word except geron, showing, according to some, the high honor conceded to these. — aneuthe ("apart, without"), without the toil and annoyance that usually accompany a voyage by sea; cf. Eta 318-19, Theta 445, 563, Nu 79-80, 89-92, 119.

194. karpalimos ("swiftly"), placed at the close of the thought for rhetorical and metrical reasons. Except here, Zeta 312, Mu 166, E 904, it stands always (38 times) at the beginning of the verse, whether at the beginning, middle, or end of the clause. — estin, "he is," as proved by the termination -then, and by Zeta 312.

156 NOTES.

195. μηδέ, "and that he may not," connecting πάθησιν with ἵκηται. Why not οὐδέ? — μεσσηγύς γε, "meantime at least;" or it may be local as elsewhere, "in mid passage."

196. "At all events ere he upon his native land sets foot; but there then." Would the infinitive be used here in prose after πρίν? G. M. 67; G. 240.

197–98. "He shall suffer whatever for him at his birth-hour Fate and the Spinners stern spun off with the thread, when him his mother bore." So long as he is under our protection he shall suffer nothing; but once landed on his native shores, our task is done, and he must not look to us further: an intimation thus early of the poet's purpose to make the Phaeacians leave him asleep on the Ithacan coast and return immediately. — ἄσσα; H. 246 D. — Aisa is here a power determining and ruling affairs, and so far is faintly personified. This is a rare use of the word, which more commonly means the destiny of the person as it is determined by the gods, or a moral law for the government of conduct. The Klothes are nowhere else mentioned in Homer, but appear to be a special personification of the fate-determining power which in Hesiod become the three daughters of Night — Klotho, Lachesis, and Atropos. Aisa and the Klothes here perform the functions assigned to Aisa alone, at Y 127, to Moira at Ω 209, to the gods at Ω 525, α 17, λ 139, ν 196, γ 208, θ 579, to Zeus at δ 207, to the divine power at π 64, to Ker at Ψ 78; in all which cases, except the last, the verb ἐπίνέω or ἐπικλώθω represents the act. Hence the process of spinning the destiny of man is performed most frequently by the gods, to whom it properly belongs; and when otherwise assigned, it is a special concentration of a general function upon a single minister, or a minister in conjunction with the gods, as here, for the Klothes may stand for the gods themselves. It was the later Greek mind that elaborated the idea of a Fate apart from and higher than the gods. In Homer, destiny, in whatever form, never fights with the gods, nor, unless it be in the shape of death, defies them; not even the human will is controlled in such a manner as to suggest or sustain the necessitarian theory. — βαρεῖαι; on ζ 188. — γεινομένῳ . . . ὅτε; cf. ζ 326. As an example of parallel passage, entirely distinct from epic commonplace (on η 78), and exhibiting the natural disposition of the same mind to express a

BOOK VII. 157

similar idea in a similar manner, and thus bringing proof of the unity of authorship for Iliad and Odyssey, Mure compares the present passage with Y 126, where the destinies of the other protagonist are thus referred to by Hera:

"So that he may suffer nothing among the Trojans today; but later he shall endure whatever Fate spun for him on the thread at his birth."

199. The extraordinary manner of his appearance before them, his beauty, zeta 230-37, 243, 276, and their remoteness from men make Alcinous doubtful whether he is not a god.

200. "something other (than ordinary) herein." — "this"; zeta 206, 276.

201. The word "to," exactly like the Attic use of the article with adverbs; H. 524. — "they appear"; zeta 220. — "undisguised," in their own proper persons, so as to be easily recognized. This boon is not always granted to the Greeks, as is expressly stated when Athene appears to Odysseus at the hut of Eumaeus, and Telemachus does not see her, pi 161. This infirmity of vision may arise from the supernatural ether habitually enveloping the deity, or from a mist that stands before the person's eyes and must be removed, E 127, or from some disguise assumed by the divine personage, eta 19, theta 8, 193; for it is assumed that the proper persons of the deities are in general well known; on zeta 152.

202. "let us sacrifice"; zeta 183. This word in the great majority of cases does not have the digamma in Homer and Hesiod, though "ergon" does. — The hecatomb, even in Homer, never reaches a hundred victims, and is not always confined to oxen. The greatest number specifically named is in the hecatomb offered to Poseidon by Nestor, gamma 7, when 81 bullocks are sacrificed. Twelve heifers are promised to Athene by the Trojans, Z 93, and Peleus slays 50 sheep to the river Spercheios, Psi 147.

203. "to us"; zeta 205. The Phaeacians, like the Ethiopians, are a race favored by the gods with their presence and familiar intercourse, especially on occasions of solemn and stated sacrifice, when they appear and seat themselves beside them like any guest. At the opening of the Odyssey, Poseidon is among the Ethiopians, "where he was taking his pleasure at the feast, sitting among them," alpha 26, and in Book A all the gods sojourn among them for twelve days in continual feasting.

158 NOTES.

Such intercourse implies more than the mere enjoyment of the savor of the banquet, even to partaking of the food, notwithstanding we are told that the gods eat not bread nor drink the ruddy wine, E 341, both of which Athene does when, disguised as Mentor, she is present at the sacrifice which Nestor is offering to Poseidon. See on Book 6, lines 42 and 329. The tradition of a time when the gods dwelt among men and ruled over them is common to many nations.

204–5. "And if, too, any one of us, a wayfarer, even though journeying alone, haply meets them, no concealment at all do they make, since to them near akin are we." — With "tis" supply "of us." — "kai," even upon ordinary occasions when no sacrifices are being offered. — "xymblētai": on Book 6 line 54, Book 7 line 75. — "katakryptousin" (they conceal themselves).
