Among the Greeks at all periods the notion was prevalent that the gods commonly appear upon earth and travel about in disguise, to watch the good and evil among men, Book 17, lines 485–87. In the Hesiodic Works and Days it is the first or golden race that, after death, perform this service, becoming the unseen police of the gods. A like belief is prevalent elsewhere. In India it is Brahma and Vishnu generally who wander; in the Edda, Odin, Loki, and Hœnir; and throughout the Middle Ages it is Christ and St. Peter. — "eggythen" (near), compared with "anchithéoi" (near to the gods) at Book 5 line 35, and the general expression at Book 13 line 130, appears to mean near in kinship. No such genealogy can be positively traced in Homer except for the royal family. The case is similar with the Cyclopes and the Giants, though Polyphemus is the son of Poseidon. According to Hesiod, the Giants and Cyclopes are sons of Gaia, and Acusilaus and Alcaeus ascribe a similar origin to the Phaeacians.

208. "allo ti" (something else), not the thought that I am a god. — "moi" (to me): on Book 6 line 199.

209. When Athene has retransformed him from his beggar-guise to his proper personality, that he may disclose his identity to his son, and he is taken by the latter for a god, his disclaimer is more simple, Book 16 line 187.

210. "phyen," "shapeliness;" Book 6 line 152. — "thnētoisi brotoisi," "to deathful mortals," a collocation occurring several times; also "thnētoi anthrōpoi, andres" (mortal human beings, men). "brotos" has the same root as "mortal." "mort." by metathesis (H. 57) becomes "mrot.," a combination of initials not admitted in Greek, and therefore beta is inserted as in

160 NOTES.

the expression of St. Paul when he and Barnabas were thought by the people of Lystra to be Mercury and Jupiter, and the priest was about to sacrifice to them: "Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you." Acts xiv. 15.

216. The preposition epi, "beside," is more graphic than the simple genitive after the comparative, since it sets before us the very act of arranging things side by side for ocular comparison. — kunteron; H. 224 D. The superlative also occurs at K 503. The figure receives illustration from the well-known words of Achilles to Agamemnon, "having the eyes of a dog" (A 225), "O utterly shameless one" (158), and the epithet which Helen applies to herself, "dog-faced" (Gamma 180, delta 145).

217. epleto, ekeleusen; on zeta 185. — het' is causal; zeta 302. — With ekeleusen supply tina. The statement is a general one, but is particularized in "as I myself." — anagke; zeta 136.

219–21. hos kai; theta 176. — he de, "but this maw of mine." — mal' aiei, 118. — ek with lethanei, "makes me forget;" on zeta 100. — panton; H. 576. — hosson'; after pas and similar words the regular relative is hosos, not hos. — anogeí; zeta 216.

222–23. humeis d', opposed to eme men, 215. Why the nominative? H. 784; G. 269, Note; C. 577. — am'; zeta 31. — hos k', 192. — ton, Attic article; cf. Euripides, Medea 711, 20. — epibesesthe; on zeta 7.

224. kaiper, the only instance in all of Homer where these particles are found contiguous. Elsewhere they are either separated by one or more words (zeta 282), or kai is used alone (eta 218), or per alone (215, zeta 87). — me ... aion, "me even life may leave," a poetic use of the optative, where the thought is rather a permission than a wish; G. M. 82, Note 1. With a change of idonta to epeita, the same phrase is employed by the wounded Sarpedon, when he begs Hector only to drag him away from the field that he may not become a prey to the Greeks (E 685); and it is found nowhere else; see on 197. Odysseus' heart-sick longing for home meets us at the very opening of the poem, where Athene says of him that he so yearns to see even the smoke curling up from his native land that he wishes he were dead (alpha 58); and Calypso, bearing tidings of his release from her isle, finds him sitting upon the rocks of the seashore weeping his life away, and gazing out towards his home over the sea (epsilon 151). See iota 28, kappa 47–52, eta 260.

225. The expression is a general one, but points to kingly

BOOK VII. 161

power in the possessor, and is intended to convey an intimation of the important position which he held at home, as was done also to Nausicaa, Book VI, line 164. The natural manner in which these hints are introduced gives them additional force, and they are artfully calculated to raise the hero in the estimation of his hearers—a point overlooked by those who think this line an interpolation. Nitzsch suggests that "his household servants, his dear wife, and his infant son" (Book VI, line 366) would have been more suitable. To mention his wife and son would unquestionably have been more pathetic; but any man might have a wife and son that he loved. A king would have possessions and slaves and a palace. — Throughout this speech the prominence which he gives to his sufferings, and to the wretchedness of his present condition, is to be remarked in lines 211–14, in "grieving though I am," "sorely afflicted," "bearing grief," "I have grief," "all I have suffered," "wretched me," "having suffered much."

Lines 226–28. "They approved"; on Book VIII, line 398. — "with fitness," meaning "appropriately." — "But now . . ." is a repetition, in epic style, of line 184, after interruption, in order to gain a resumptive foothold from which to start off anew; cf. Book VII, 233–36; Book XIII, 165–67; Book XIX, 1–2, 51–52; Book I, 45–87; Book V, 3–43.

Line 232. "They cleared away the appliances of the banquet," more fully described at Book XIX, line 60: "The white-armed handmaids came from the hall, and from the tables took away the plentiful food, and the cups." — With "the implements of the feast" compare Virgil's Cerealia arma ("implements of Ceres"), Aeneid I. 177.

Lines 234–36. "She recognized." Ameis suggests that this discovery, made at the very first, was the reason of her silence, because she hoped, after the departure of the guests, to be able to satisfy her curiosity undisturbed. It doubtless connected itself in her mind with Nausicaa's task of the day, and suggested that the garments must have come from her. Should there be anything in the circumstance calculated to provoke the censorious tongue, she was wise enough not to draw it out before the whole company. Nausicaa had not communicated with any one in the great hall since her arrival.—The custom of the matron's weaving with her daughters the clothing for the husband and sons was seized upon by the poets as a favorite means of recognition of lost relatives. Penelope is convinced that the Pseudo-Odysseus has seen her husband; for he describes the very garments she had given him at his departure, Book XIX, line 255. Creusa, in the Ion of Euripides,

162 NOTES.

proves herself to be the mother of Ion by describing the pattern of a shawl in which she had wrapped him as an infant. Iphigeneia recognizes Orestes on one occasion, and Electra knows him on another by the figured clothing he wore.

236. A formulaic line, occurring 52 times.—φωνήσασ' [having spoken]; on Book XIII, line 58. —πτερόεντα [winged] carries with it not only the idea of swiftness, but of flying from the lips as the arrow from the bow, and passing as straight to the mark. The metaphor is doubtless taken from the feathered arrow, ἰοὶ πτερόεντες [winged arrows], Iliad XVI.773, and Pindar talks of the many swift arrows within his quiver that speak to the wise, Olympian II.150; cf. Psalm 64.3. "When the savage and the deaf-mute both express the speaking of truth by passing the extended index directly forward from the lips, and the utterance of falsehood by carrying it crookedly sidewise, there seems to be some natural analogy between the gesture and the thought." Marsh, Lectures on the English Language.

237. πρῶτον [first], "first," before any other question; adjective with τὸ. What would πρώτη mean? H. 488c.—ἐγὼν . . . αὐτή [I myself], independently, without waiting for my husband; on lines 73, 167. The same line is put into the mouth of Penelope when she begins her conversation with the disguised Odysseus, Odyssey XIX.104, and again with a slight change after the interruption occasioned by the foot-bath, XIX.509. Its occurrence nowhere else is significant.

238. τίς πόθεν [who and whence], two questions blended into a single sentence, a favorite idiom of the Greeks, but seldom imitated in Latin; H. 827. The question is one habitually put to strangers after they had broken their fast; Odyssey I.170, X.325, XIV.187, XV.264, XXIV.298, XXI.150.

239. "Did you not say that you came here wandering over the deep?" and how does that accord with the garments you wear? In fact, Odysseus had not said a word in her presence about his coming by sea; but he has spoken of his sufferings away from his friends, and that, coupled with the fact of his being a stranger, was evidence enough to the Phaeacians that he had arrived by sea. The question is so natural that it forms the most convincing, because unconscious, proof that Scheria was conceived of as an island.—οὐ [not]: what answer is expected? H. 829; cf. Book VI, lines 57, 200.

241. "Hard is it, O queen, fully to relate." By this apology

BOOK VII. 163

the poet puts aside the first part of the inquiry, and, as at line 225, does not tell the whole story, so that the interest of the development through the Eighth Book may not flag, and opportunity may be obtained for the complete recital of his hero's wanderings in Books IX–XII. Besides, Odysseus' veracity and honesty have been questioned, and that is the vital point for him to answer in his present situation. He knows as yet nothing of his name being famous among them. Virgil imitates this opening when Aeneas begins his story to Dido: "Unspeakable, O Queen, is the grief you bid me renew."

242. Ouraniones, "the heaven-dwellers;" cf. Book VI, line 150. It is not a patronymic derived from Ouranos, for Homer knows nothing of Ouranos as an arch-god prior to Kronos; Ouranos and Gaia are great and venerable gods, but neither presents the character of predecessor to Kronos and Zeus. The progenitor of all the gods, in Homeric mythology, appears to have been Oceanus, Book XIV, line 201; cf. the cosmogony of the Chaldeans and the philosophy of Thales. It was the later and more systematic theogony of Hesiod that cemented the link between Kronos and Zeus.

244. Ogygie is situated at the "navel of the sea," Book I, line 50, that is, at the midpoint of a sea, just as the navel-boss of a shield is at its centre. This is the great northern sea which Homer supposed to occupy the main part of Europe. Ogygia is northerly, for Hermes, speeding towards it as the bird flies, passes from Olympus over Pieria, and then downward upon the sea, and all the bearings of Odysseus' homeward voyage point that way. Strabo identified it with the island Gaulos, near Malta, and others placed it off the coast of Bruttium. — "From far away," eighteen days' steady sail from Scheria.

245. All that is known of Atlas from Homer is that he is the father of Calypso, is "baneful of mind," and knows the depths of every sea, and personally guards or holds the pillars that keep heaven and earth asunder. — "Deceitful": this characteristic is no unpardonable fault in Homer's eyes, but rather a merit. Odysseus, at the beginning of his recital to Alcinous and his court, proclaims himself one "who is known to all men for his wiles," Book IX, line 20. The poet has given us an example of her artfulness in her attempts to detain Odysseus by gracious and winning words, Book I, line 56; and of her de-

164 NOTES.

...deceitfulness in pretending to him, after she had received the order from Zeus, that she was sending him away of her own election, and out of compassion for his homesickness.

246–47. "nor does she mingle" (οὐδέ...μίσγεται), as at ζ 205, because of remoteness. Hermes tells her that he comes unwillingly, and at the command of Zeus; for no one would of his own free will traverse such a mighty expanse of water, where a god could get no refreshment on the way from the offerings of mortals; ε 100.

248–50. "divine force" (δαίμων); on ζ 172. — ἔλσας ἐκέασσε, "having smitten, clove asunder;" described more fully at μ 403–49. Setting out from Thrinakia, where his companions had brought upon them the vengeance of Zeus by their slaughter of the oxen of the Sun, they are scarcely out of sight of land before a storm arises, and howling Zephyrus snaps the mast, which dashes out the brains of the pilot as it falls. Zeus hurls his thunderbolt, and the ship, quaking from stem to stern, is filled with sulphurous smoke. The crew fall dead into the sea, and Odysseus wanders through the ship till the waves part the sides from the keel, which he then bestrides, lashing to it the mast. The wind shifts, and he is borne back on his route till morning, when he is drawn into the whirlpool of Charybdis. Just as the keel is plunging downward into the abyss, he catches the long branches of an overshadowing fig-tree, and there clings, bat-like, without a footing all the day long. At last the timbers reappear, he drops upon them, paddles out of reach of the maelstrom, and is then borne on to Ogygia.

251. "all" (πάντες), all upon his own vessel, which alone remained to him. Eleven other ships that had set sail with him from Troy were destroyed the year before in the harbor of the Laestrygonians, and his vessel had escaped only through his discretion in remaining outside the harbor till he had ascertained the character of the people. — ἀπέφθιθεν; ζ 99.

252. τρόπιν...ἑλών, "the keel in my arms seizing." So at ε 371, when his raft is blown to pieces he clings to a plank, bestriding it as he would a race-horse, "like a man riding a racehorse" (κέληθ' ὡς ἵππον ἐλαύνων).

253. ἐννῆμαρ...δεκάτῃ, "nine days...on the tenth," a frequent formula in Homer: of Odysseus borne from Malea to the Lotophagi, ι 82; from Aeolus into sight of Ithaca, κ 28; from the vicinity of Crete to the Thesprotians, ξ 314. The pestilence caused by Apollo's arrows lasts nine

BOOK VII. 165

days, and ceases on the tenth; cf. Z 174, Ω 610, 664. The decade is thus a favorite number, but it is at the same time a round number, and, like that of the hecatomb, must not be insisted upon as conveying anything like mathematical accuracy. The preparations for the siege exhaust ten years, the siege itself ten, and the home-coming of Odysseus ten, according to several statements of the poet; yet by strict calculation of the epochs laid down, the last does not exceed nine years. Similar difficulties are met with in Herodotus; and through this inexactness we may account in some measure for the superhuman endurance attributed to the hero. Twice he is said to float for ten days astride a timber without food or drink; he clings to the branches of the fig-tree by his hands alone a whole day, and directs the tiller for eighteen days without closing his eyes. But the real explanation is to be found in that poetic exaggeration which exalts the hero into the demigod, makes Ajax hurl a stone heavier than two ordinary men can lift, makes Ramses II., alone with his charioteer, overthrow 2500 chariots of the Khita with three men to a chariot (Poem of Pentaur), and Richard Coeur-de-Lion, just risen from a sick-bed, smite asunder with a broadsword the steel handle of a mace an inch and a half in thickness (Scott, Talisman).

255. This line after 246 presents the same disagreeable repetition as Odyssey 6.144, and is therefore bracketed; for with this all difficulty vanishes, if, with Nitzsch, "tenderly" is written as a separate word in line 256. The word "lamboussa," in the sense of "having escorted," as in Odyssey 6.278, is extraordinary. Many bracket lines 251-58 without sufficient reason; for not only is some such summary natural, but lines 256-57 are necessary to the sequel; see note on 312.

256. "She loved him"; cf. Odyssey 7.33, 8.208. The verb "she nurtured" exchanges with "she tended" in the same phrase at Odyssey 12.450; cf. 8.453.

257. A scholiast cites this as an example of her deceitfulness, because she was promising what she could not perform, for Zeus alone could confer immortality. This function of Zeus is familiar to us from the story of Tithonus in the Hymn to Aphrodite, but appears to be later than Homer, with whom immortality is produced and maintained simply by a diet of nectar and ambrosia, which Odysseus purposely and stubbornly refuses, desiring rather to return home a mortal than remain a deathless exile;

166 NOTES.

cf. Odyssey ε 196–98, ε 341–42, τ 38; also Pindar, Olympian I. 98–101, Pythian IX. 105–11, Theocritus XV. 106–8, Apollonius of Rhodes IV. 869, Ovid, Metamorphoses XIV. 606. Indeed, of nectar and ambrosia Julius Braun has said: "This is the food which the gods require in order to preserve their immortality. It has come to the west from Central Asia, with the whole company of the Olympian gods; for the root of the conception is the tree of life in the ancient system of Zoroaster. The fruit and sap of this tree of life bestow immortality, and the future Messiah (Sosiosh in the Zend writings) will give some of it to all the faithful, and make them immortal. This hope is fully expressed in the Assyrian sculptures, where the winged genii stand before the holy tree with a vessel containing the juice and fruit." History of Art. Compare the Tree of Life in the Garden of Eden, and that among the Egyptians.

260. dakrysi [tears]. Tears spring from their sources with far greater readiness among the excitable inhabitants of Greece and Italy than in our colder clime and among our more reserved and self-contained people. For the hero to weep was as honorable as for the Mohawk to repress all signs of emotion. But even here, Odysseus, man of iron nerve and soul as he was, has a specialty. — ambrota [immortal]; on lines 210, 214. It is an epithet applied to anything belonging to the gods, made by them, or coming from them.

261–63. de og: One syllable by synizesis — ogdoaton [eighteenth]; Odyssey ζ 170. — kai tote de, "then at length." This use of kai [and], like that of de [but], Odyssey η 47, probably reflects a stage of the language when all coupling of clauses was co-ordinate; cf. on Odyssey ζ 169, θ 389. — autes for heo autes; on Odyssey ζ 27. Calypso says nothing to him of the message from Zeus.

264–66. polydesmon, "well-jointed," both by bolts (gomphoi) and dovetailing (harmoniai); Odyssey ε 248. — proeken [sent forth]; Hadley's Grammar 312. — te [and]; on Odyssey ζ 14. Some think that liaron [warm] has lost an initial chi.

267–69. oktokaidekaте [the eighteenth], so that the two days in the water shall make up the double decade. — skioenta, "shade-covered," because well wooded. Others say shadow-casting, because of their height; cf. "While the shadows of the mountains sweep over the curved slopes" (Virgil, Aeneid I. 607); "Where the sun changes the shadows of the mountains" (Horace, Odes III. 6, 41). Others look to the dimness and haziness lent to the mountains by the dis-

BOOK VII. 167

tance, or the dark color of the foliage and earth. It is an epithet also of clouds and palaces. — φίλον; on θ 178.

270. Refer γὰρ to δυσμόρφω. — ξυνέσεσθαι οἴζυι means "to be fellowshipped with misfortune." — οἴζυι is viewed as an animate existence, a comrade; so a breeze is called "a noble companion," λ 7; on θ 99, 237.

271–74. μοι ἐπώρσε means "upon me set." — μοι ἐφορμήσας means "against me calling up." — κατέδησε κέλευθα means "chained down my advance;" another bold figure, as so many throughout this fine description. The onward journey is conceived as possessed of motion and life, and is caught and fettered like any prisoner. νόστος is treated in the same way, ξ 61. κέλευθος is most commonly the journey, ὁδός the path over which the journey is made. — ὤρινεν . . . φέρεσθαι means "and stirred up the sea immeasurable, nor even a whit did the wave suffer me upon the raft incessantly groaning to be borne along," but swept me off into the sea. He recovers his position, however, upon the raft, and then the sea-nymph Ino comes to his aid and lends him her immortal scarf to assist him in swimming when the raft is destroyed; ε 313–52.

275. θύελλα; it is κῦμα, ε 366, dread and grievous, down-sweeping, which strikes him and scatters the timbers of the raft like chaff upon a threshing-floor.

276–78. τόδε; ζ 276. — ὄφρα; η 141. — ἐπέλασσε; ζ 171. — ἔνθα . . . χέρσου means "there me emerging the wave would have overpowered upon the coast." — μ'. Observe that the regular position in Homer for the enclitic pronouns is close to the head of the clause. — κέ . . . βιήσατο; the condition is implied in ἀλλ' ἀναχασσάμενος; H. 746, 751; G. M. 49, 2, 52; G. 222; C. 537.

279. πρὸς; ζ 89. — βαλὸν means "by hurling me;" H.789 b; on ν 58. — ἀτερπεῖ, applied also to χῶρος, λ 94, of the house of Aïdes; to δαίς, κ 124, of the cannibal feast which the Læstrygonians made of the dead comrades of Odysseus; and to λιμός, hunger.

280. ἀναχασσάμενος πάλιν means "retiring back;" so ἀναχάζομαι with ἄψ, ὀπίσσω, ἐξοπίσω. — πάλιν is always local in Homer. — νῆχον; ζ 100. — εἶος; ζ 80, η 141. He is actually carried by a huge wave towards the shore, and would have been dashed dead against the beetling cliffs had he not caught an outlying rock and held with the grip of death till the wave swept on to the cliff. Its refluent

168 NOTES.

The surge bore him back far from the shore, and then he turned to swim along the coast, watching for a harbor; ε 400–40.

281–82. ἐς appears after ἐπήλθον; cf. N 756; on θ 190. — τῇ . . . ἄριστος, "where, lo! to me there came in sight a spot most admirable." — πετράων; H. 584. — σκέπας; ζ 210.

283. A great desire for brevity has made this line obscure. The details are given at length in ε 451–58. On reaching the mouth of the stream, he prays to the river-god for aid, who stays his outflow, and lands Odysseus safe on the bank, but so exhausted that he falls flat, the water gurgles out of his mouth and nostrils, and he lies for some time breathless and speechless in a faint; at length he begins to breathe again, and into his bosom his spirit is gathered back, "his spirit was gathered back into his chest," ε 458. Hence ἐκ means "when out of the water;" ἔπεσον means "I fell fainting." θυμηγερέων occurs nowhere else, but "his spirit was gathered back into his chest" (also X 475) gives the general sense of returning life after a swoon. If this, then, be taken as a future participle (H. 374), all difficulty vanishes, and the sense is "soon to revive;" or even as a present, equivalent, in the hurry of the moment, to a future. J. Krauss (Rhein. Mus. für Phil. 1877, p. 324) neatly suggests "and having fallen out, I revived."

284. ἀπάνευθε; on ζ 127, η 7. — διιπετέος, a standing epithet of rivers, as nourished by Zeus; on ζ 105, η 164; cf. "Zeus rained," ξ 457. All rivers, the sea, fountains, and wells are said to flow from Oceanus, Φ 196; on ζ 11, η 242.

285–86. κατέδραθον; H. 57. — ἠφυσάμην, elsewhere used of drawing liquids from one vessel into another. He covers himself up with the leaves to keep the night air from him, naked as he was. There was a heap large enough to protect three men in the winter season, and he buries himself in the midst, as a frontiersman hides a live brand deep in the ashes, to keep the seeds of fire alive, ε 482–91. — θεὸς; it is Athene, ε 591, though he does not know it. — ἀπείρονα; no wonder, after twenty days of sleeplessness.

289. We read δείλετο, "was westering," with Buttmann, Nitzsch, Ameis, and Faesi, instead of the common reading δύσετο. The assumption that it was a mere conjecture of Aristarchus is without sufficient foundation. δύσετο cannot be reconciled with ζ 321 and the other circumstances of ζ, unless it be assumed that the sun on that late

BOOK VII. 169

An autumn day might seem to the group in the ravine to have been some time down behind the hills, though it had actually just set when they emerged into the more open region around the city. It is accepted by some, however, with the remark that such discrepancies are explainable by the greater carelessness of detail naturally resulting from oral recitation, since they are found even in Virgil and others who committed their thoughts to writing at once (cf. Longinus, 33). Compare Book XIV, line 344, with the other circumstances of that book. The word deilomai is indeed not found elsewhere, but deieliesas appears in Book XVII, and the analogy of Phi 111 and Iota 56 points to some form of deilē here. — anēken. Sleep is here viewed as a cloud (on eta 15, 143), which pours down at line 286, overpowers, and holds the sleeper a fast prisoner (Psi 17), until it chooses to release him; cf. Zeta 2, Eta 318, "sleep the all-subduer," Omega 5. Sometimes there is complete personification; on Nu 80; sometimes it is a mantle thrown about one, ballein; cf. Sancho Panza's "Blessings on the man that invented sleep; it folds round a man like a cloak."

290–91. Why is teēs older than sēs? — enoēsa; Zeta 163. — paizousas; Zeta 100. — autē; on Zeta 83. — eikuia; Zeta 151.

292. nōēmatos hēmbroten, synonymous with noou deuetai at line 73. She is her own mother's daughter; on Zeta 201. — hēmbroten, from stem hamart- = hamprat- (H. 57) = āmbrat- (H. 53) = āmbrot- (H. 25). Since the probable derivation is alpha privative and the root mer-, "to divide," the aspirate of hamartanō is due to a mistaken analogy, or to a fondness for the aspirate which developed itself prominently in Attic Greek.

293. Supply erxasa in thought before hōs. "(Since she acted) as you would not expect so young a person meeting you to do." — Why an? H. 23 D. Is the conjunction an ever found in Homer? On eta 75. — elpoio contains the indefinite or ideal second person, as if tis. — neōteron; eta 156. At Psi 590, Antilochus, deprecating the anger of Menelaus, throws the blame upon his youth; for "the young are quick in temper, but weak in judgment." Menelaus demands the presence of Priam in the compact for the duel, Gamma 108, "for the minds of the young are ever wavering."

294–6. erxemen: why the future? G. M. 27, Note 3. — aphradeosin, "are inconsiderate." — aithopa, "sparkling," as the light glances

8

170 NOTES.

from the surface. The translation "dark-red" is disproved by μ 19, "the glowing red wine." — "washed"; on ζ 210.

297. "Though in distress"; 215, 218, 224. His forlorn condition has not induced him to depart one jot from the exact truth demanded by Arete's question, however much he might think to gain by a trumped-up story. This is to be compared with the numerous false accounts he gives of himself to Eumaeus, Penelope, and the suitors, for it is truly a most masterly and veracious summary of Books ε and ζ. Eumaeus has had frequent cause to lament the eagerness with which Penelope listens to every stranger; "for roving men in need of hospitality are prone to falsehood, and never wish to speak the truth;" ξ 125, λ 363–66. — "the truth," appositive to "these things"; cf. 200. — "he recounted," as perfect.

299–301. "this . . . my," "in this at least not rightly took my daughter thought," granting in other points what you said about her understanding, 292; on η 167. — "first"; ζ 176.

303–5. "to me"; ζ 199. — "was not willing." This prevarication is ventured upon to shield Nausicaa from the over-zeal displayed by the king. He may know from the habits of the times that she has had no communication with any in the hall, and, from her anxiety not to be seen with him in public, he may think she will be discreet about it in the future. This was enough for a Greek to avail himself of at any time, with the hope of escaping detection; on 245. Even the old archbishop Eustathius says here, "Odysseus falsifies plainly, a thing which the wise man would do upon occasion." It is to be observed that Odysseus' original request was simply that the city be pointed out to him, and he does not intimate that he expected more. — "having been struck with alarm, and feeling a delicacy." The aorist represents the simple act, the present the continuance of the feeling.

306–7. "lest," "at the sight," "lest haply e'en thy spirit might be darkened at the sight." — "frown," properly of the contraction of the brows in anger. — "over hasty." — "for indeed," much like "and indeed," and regularly introducing some such generalizing statement as the present one; θ 169. — "we are"; by the use of the plural and "the race of mankind," Odysseus, with delicate tact, transfers the burden of the censure from Alcinous to the common frailties of the entire human race.

BOOK VII. 171

310. μαψιδίως, "causelessly." — κεχολῶσθαι depends on τοιοῦτον; G. M. 93, 1, Note 1. The construction is more common after the relative; both the demonstrative and relative are found at φ 172. — μαψιδίως points back to δύσζηλοι, κεχολῶσθαι to ἐπισκύσσαιτο. — ἀμείνω . . . πάντα, "nay, better all in measure due." This is the golden mean, aurea mediocritas, the great aim of the Greek, so little practiced by Alcinous. It is expressed more succinctly by the wise Spartan: "nothing in excess."

311. αἲ γάρ; see ζ 244. — Ζεῦ. This invocation, in which the three most powerful gods are addressed together, never appears on occasions connected with any particular rite or function, but simply when the speaker wishes to give utterance with peculiar solemnity or emphasis to some paramount desire — as when Agamemnon wishes he had ten counsellors like Nestor, or that his warriors had the same spirit as the two Ajaxes. By it both Nestor and Laertes wish themselves young again, and Menelaus prays for the appearance of Odysseus among the suitors. A scholiast drew the inference from this form of adjuration that Homer was a native of Athens, because the Athenians were accustomed to use it.

312. οἷός; on ζ 303. — ἐὼν and φρονέων, both causal; cf. Δ 361: "since thou art so noble, and thy sentiments accord so fully with mine." Lines 311–16 fell under the suspicions of Aristarchus, doubtless because of Alcinous' startling offer of his daughter's hand to a total stranger; but the king is plainly quite captivated by the commanding presence and bearing of his guest, and by the eloquence and delicacy of sentiment he has displayed. His high station in life has been directly asserted at line 225, and the immortality which Calypso designed for him suggested a lofty lineage befitting such a fate and such a love; see 256–57. His sentiments have already won the approval of the courtiers at line 226, and though Alcinous disagrees with the idea that he might have been angered at Odysseus' return with Nausicaa, he nonetheless respects and approves the delicacy which prompted the hero's action, to such a degree that he feels assured Odysseus' feelings are in harmony with his bearing and eloquence. To infer kingly station in a stranger from his appearance and comportment alone is not unique to the impetuous Alcinous; cf. δ 63, ν 223, υ 194, ω 253. Indeed,

172 NOTES.

Both father and daughter have suggested that he may be even a god (η 199, ζ 280), and the former distinctly declares (λ 363–67) that he believed him no impostor, but the hero his appearance and words proclaim. Add to all this the strong predilection for a foreign marriage with royalty (ζ 35, 244, 275), and the offer from so impetuous a person loses its startling features and becomes eminently characteristic of the man.

313. παῖδά . . . ἐχέμεν, "my daughter thou hadst to wife." With ἐχέμεν, ἐθέλοις may be supplied with Eustathius, or the infinitive considered as developing more emphatically the abruptness of the ardent wish. The accusative and infinitive in a wish are not uncommon (G. M. 102), but this and ω 379 are the only examples in Homer where the nominative occurs, and in the latter the wish is unattainable, so that ὤφελον would be supplied.

314. μένων: note how the words of the father echo those of the daughter (ζ 244–45). — δέ τ': on ζ 105. — δοίην, "that I might give," continuing the wish from αἱ γὰρ, and showing the nature of the wish implied in ἐχέμεν; cf. θ 339–42.

315. "(As I would do) if willingly at least thou wouldst remain," supplying the conclusion (H. 753). Here a gesture of dissent on the part of Odysseus, settling the question definitively, may be supposed (on ζ 168); for the language immediately changes, and at line 317 the proposition is completely abandoned and never alluded to again, while in the next Book he is assumed to be the possessor of a wife at home (θ 243, 410, 457–62). The probability of the explanation offered by Mure and Hayman, that this change is due simply to the garrulity of Alcinous, is much reduced by the solemnity of the appeal and the wish. By making his hero decline this offer, as well as that of Calypso, the poet extols his constancy and his affection for his wife. — κ'; H. 748; G. M. 50, 2, Note 2 (b.). — δέ, "well."

316–18. μὴ: why not οὐ? H. 834. — τεκμαίρομαι, "I appoint." — εὖ εἰδῆς, know well, and therefore rest content. — αὔριον ἔς is explanatory of ἐς τόδ'. — ἔς by all authorities here, but ἐς at η 254, γ 137, ο 59; εἰς at ο 541. — δεδμημένος: on 289, θ 445, ν 79.

319–20. λέξεαι: on 53. — οἱ, the crew, as opposed to σύ. — ἐλδώσι: η 109, ζ 82. — γαλήνην: ζ 259; θ 563, η 192. — ὄφρ': ζ 218. — καὶ εἴ που, "and wherever else."

BOOK VII. 173

321–22. εἴπερ . . . ἑκαστέρω, "even though very much further." The particle εἴπερ is frequently concessive, whether used with the indicative, as here, at θ 408, ν 138; or with the subjunctive, as at A 580; or with the optative, at ν 42, 49. — οἵ λαῶν: see on ζ 257. — τηλοτάτω: The Phaeacians have already been described as the most remote of men at ζ 205, and this is again reiterated by the claim that a place which is one of the most central in the Greek world was to them the most distant known.

323–24. Ῥαδάμανθυν . . . Τιτυὸν: The allusion here is so obscure that it merely piques our curiosity without leaving anything to satisfy it, nor is it elucidated by later legend. Rhadamanthus is the son of Zeus by a Phoenician maid, and the brother of Minos (Ξ 321); he rules the abodes of Elysium (δ 564), as Minos judges the dead in the House of Hades. The present passage completes all mention of him in Homer. Tityos appears again at λ 576, undergoing punishment in the Underworld for attempting violence against Leto "as she was going to Pytho through Panopeus," a town in Phocis on the route of the sacred processions or embassies from Delos to Delphi through Marathon. Geraestum, in Euboea, is also on this route, and it was sacred to Poseidon (γ 177), the patron god of the Phaeacians. Hence it may be conjectured that, since the verb ἐποψομ. has the special sense in Homer of visiting or overseeing for the purpose of punishment, the semi-divine Phaeacians, dwelling somewhere toward Elysium, serve as the conveyors of Rhadamanthus to visit Tityos at Panopeus after his crime, and determine whether he, given his relation to the gods, shall be transferred to Elysium or Hades; and their leaving him in Euboea would be entirely consistent with their depositing Odysseus in the harbor of Phorcys (ν 96). But Euboea is far out of the way for anyone going to Panopeus along the western side of Greece, Crissa being the usual landing-place. If, therefore, we accept Gladstone's suggestion that the Phaeacians sailed around by the north and entered the Aegean through the Hellespont (on η 80, 244), they are then kept "entirely in their own element as borderers between the world of Greek experience and the world of fable." Studies, III. p. 283.

325–26. ἔνθ': see ζ 47. — With τέλεσσαν and ἀπήνυσαν supply ὁδόν; cf. η 4. — ἤματι τῷ αὐτῷ: see on η 55. Whether this refers to the outward passage only, or to both directions, remains uncertain. The distance is evidently considered greater than that to Ithaca, which is al-

174 NOTES.

ready known to them, Book 13 line 113, and the voyage thither occupies all the night from sunset to dawn. It is customary for them to wait till evening before setting out from home; hence "on the day" (ἤματι) may perhaps be extended through the whole twenty-four hours and limited to the outward journey.

327–28. "you will know" (εἰδήσεις); Book 6 line 257. — "himself" (καὶ αὐτὸς), as well as Rhadamanthus. — "in his heart" (ἐνὶ φρεσὶν); Book 8 line 448. — "how great" (ὅσσον); Book 7 line 108. — "to toss up" (ἀναρρίπτειν); Book 13 line 78.

331–33. "ah!" (αἶθ'); Book 6 line 244. — "grain-giving" (ζείδωρον), personifies "the ploughland." — "unquenchable" (ἄσβεστον), exhibits "glory" (κλέος) under the aspect of an ever-rising flame; cf. clarus, gloria; on Book 6 line 29; Book 8 line 74. Alcinous desires such fame as earnestly as if he were not cut off from the rest of mankind by his isolated position; Book 8 lines 101, 244.

335–38. "he bade" (κέκλετο); Book 6 line 71. — "bed-clothes" (δέμνι'); Book 6 line 20. — "under the portico" (ὑπ' αἰθούσῃ), which ran along the front of the house, and here the bed of the guest was habitually placed, as that of Telemachus at Pylos and Sparta, of Odysseus in Ithaca, and of Priam in the tent of Achilles, who, however, apologizes to Priam for so doing, Book 24 line 650, but the circumstances are quite exceptional. Doubtless we may see in the custom a reminiscence of a period when all strangers were regarded with too much suspicion to be admitted to the house at night. — "coverlets" (ῥήγεα), corresponding to our mattress, as "rugs" (τάπητας) to under sheets, and "cloaks" (χλαίνας) to upper sheet and blanket. The χλαῖνα is also an outer-garment; on Book 6 line 214, Book 8 line 455; hence the use of "to put on" (ἕσασθαι).

339–43. "they went" (ἴσαν); Book 7 line 82. — "torch" (δάος); Book 7 line 101. — "Up!" (Ὄρσο); Book 6 line 255. — "sleeping" (κέων); Book 7 line 229. — "welcome" (ἀσπαστὸν); Book 13 line 35.

345–47. "perforated" (τρητοῖς), with auger-holes in the sides of the bedstead, through which thongs of leather were passed to support the coverlets, etc. Compare the description of the bed made by Odysseus, "I bored it all through with an auger, and stretched across it thongs of ox-hide, dyed crimson," Book 23 line 198; cf. Book 13 line 77. — "resounding" (ἐριδούπῳ), to the tread of passing feet, made more perceptible by the roof flinging back the sound. — "couch . . . bed" (λέχος . . . εὐνήν), "graced his couch and bed." — λέχος is properly the bedstead, εὐνήν all that forms the bed thereon; Book 23 line 179.

BOOK VIII.

1. The word Emos ("at the time when") indicates a more sharply defined point in time than hote ("when"), and accordingly in all thirty-eight passages where it occurs it is joined with the indicative mood, except at delta 400, where the subjunctive is found. — The word erigéneia ("early-born"), derived from its components eri (I 360) and gignomai ("to come into being") (cf. "when the twelfth dawn came," A 493; Xenophon, Anabasis I.10.18; Aristophanes, Clouds 3), appears to mean "early coming." Sometimes Eos is viewed in her purely physical aspect, and may then be said poetically to be born anew every day; but she is more commonly represented as a distinct person with a continuous existence, the wife of Tithonus, rising from his couch each day. "Child of Dawn" cannot stand in any strict sense of the term, for Homer gives us no hint of Eos's parentage, nor any physical description that would accord with such a phrase. The first sign of the breaking day is the morning star Eosphoros, which comes as the herald of light and proclaims the approach of Eos, nu 94. After him follows Eos herself, Psi 226, who, rising from beside Tithonus, mounts into the sky with her team of swift-footed colts from the streams of Oceanus. In Hesiod she is the sister of Helios and Selene, and born of Hyperion and Theia, children of Ouranos and Gaia. — The epithet rhododaktylos ("rosy-fingered") is usually taken to refer to the red rays of the rising sun, which, under certain atmospheric conditions, are seen to spread in divergent bands like the fingers of an outspread hand. It is mostly an epithet of the personal Eos; of the physical phenomenon, see Z 175. How Eos finds her way back to the east is nowhere hinted at, and the same silence is observed with respect to the sun. Later poets, such as Mimnermus, solved this problem for the sun by imagining the return journey to be made along the stream of Oceanus in a golden cup furnished with wings.

2–3. The word hieron ("sacred"): eta 167. — an: zeta 253. — orto ("he rose"): as psi 348; otherwise the imperfect tense describes the act of rising from sleep; cf. omicron 59–61. — ptoliporthos ("sacker of cities"), used only of Achilles and Odysseus among their generation. Achilles boasts that he has captured twelve cities with his ships, and eleven more by land in the region of the Troad, I 328.

176 NOTES.

Odysseus obtains the title of being pre-eminent in counsel, and as the prime cause of the fall of Troy, Book 8, line 494.

4–7. "toísin" [to them]: refers to Odysseus and probably the sons of Alcinous. It may apply to the two only; Book 7, line 47. — "beside the ships": Book 6, line 266. — "was made ready": Book 6, line 301. — "near one another": Book 6, line 267. — "plesion" [near each other], "near each other," as in Book 4, line 21, referring particularly to Alcinous and Odysseus, the proximity emphasizing the honor paid to the latter. — "metoicheto" [had gone upon a quest]. The prefix "met-" points to her search for the men; line 47.

8. "keryki" [as herald]. Athene acts as herald also in Book 2, to still the people, so that Odysseus may be heard by all, and she sets the limit of the discus-throw, Book 8, line 193. The lamp is carried by her to light Odysseus and Telemachus while conveying the weapons from the banqueting-hall, Book 19, line 33, and she restores the whip to Diomed which Apollo had thrown from his hand in the chariot-race, Book 23, line 383. No service is too menial for this mighty goddess to perform for her favorites; on Book 6, line 76. — "daiphronos" [of the fierce-hearted one]: Book 6, line 256.

10–12. "hekasto" [to each], limited by line 11; Book 7, line 189; as in Book 1, line 11. — "Deut'" [Come now!], an adverbial form regularly used with the plural only, "deuro" with the singular; Book 8, lines 133, 145. The present is not an exception, since "age" is purely adverbial and formulaic; Goodwin §253; Goodwin & Middleton §84, Note 1. — "ienai" [to go]; on Book 6, line 261. — "ophra... puthesthe," "that of the stranger ye may hear."

13–15. "neon" [new, fresh]; Hadley §552. — "Hos... hekastou" [So... of each]. This formulaic line occurs here only in the Odyssey, but ten times in the Iliad, where it uniformly follows some stirring appeal to the army inciting to deeds of valor and martial fury. — "menos kai thumon" [ardor and spirit] are there "ardor and spirit" worthy of the soldier; here "ardor and desire" to see and hear of the stranger. Such combinations of closely parallel words, to heighten the force of expression, are common in all languages, as "menos" with "alke, tharsos, psyche"; "thumos" with "phren, kradie, psyche"; Quietum animum mentemque benignam [a calm mind and a kindly spirit], Aeneid I. 304; "Stir your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage," Shakespeare, Julius Caesar.

16–19. "emplethento" [became filled]: Hadley §403 D. — "agorai" [assemblies]; on Book 7, line 44. — "agromenon" [of those who gathered]; the participle is the only form of this aorist that suffers syncopation. — "Daertao" [of Laertes]; other forms? Book 8, line 75; not the ending -ou in Homer. — "kephale" [head]; on Book 6, line 235. This retouching after the same operation performed yesterday shows the character of the change produced. It bears a close analogy to that resulting from the use

BOOK VIII. 177

of the bath, Odyssey gamma 468, which it actually follows, zeta 229, psi 156; hence perhaps the need of its renewal after a heavy night's sleep.

21-3. "That to the Phaeacians all, pleasing he might become, and dread and revered, and might achieve exploits many in number, in which the Phaeacians made trial of Odysseus." — The particle hos ken: see Goodwin 216, Note 2; Goodwin-Moody 44, Note 3. — philos: zeta 327. — deinos t' aidoios, feelings produced by his personal appearance (on zeta 161), by his feat with the discus, and by his general challenge, line 234. — pollous. The sense is, he was able to prove successful in contests many, and it was in contests that they tested him; not the numerous contests which. The sequel shows that he was engaged in the discus-throwing only, but he was challenged to other deeds, 145, and he signified his readiness to meet them in others, 206. The difficulty, more apparent than real, led Zenodotus to reject the line. What obelizing editor of Homer would admit such a criticism as Conington makes upon Virgil, Aeneid V. 68! "Either Virgil has expressed himself loosely, or when he wrote this line he thought of introducing one more game." — tous: H. 549; or perhaps the accusative is chosen here by preference for the antecedent case; cf. theta 100, 145, 184. — Phaiékes ... Odysseos; on eta 15.

24. "But when in consequence they had been gathered, and together were come." This line, recurring five times, describes the act of gathering in from all sides, and the resulting condition of the assembly, seated and intent to hear and judge; on line 15; beta 378.

26-8. keklute; on eta 186. — ouk oid' hostis. Odysseus does not disclose his name or country till the king expressly requests it, and supports his request by the declaration that his destination must be divulged in order that the pilotless ship may know where to direct her course, theta 550. This sustains the interest of the incognito, and exalts the hospitality extended to the unknown stranger. — Observe, in general, oida hos estin, but ouk oida estin, since the indefiniteness which the antecedent clause acquires by the addition of the negative makes the indefinite hostis necessary.

29. e ... e, indirect question dependent on oid', as a fuller explanation of hostis. — eoion ... hesperion. To Homer the horizon is usually divided into two parts only — the sunrise and the sunset,
8*

178 NOTES.

morning and evening, east and west. This may be derived from the line drawn by the bird-diviner, for whom all to the east, the home of the morning and the home of the race, was propitious, all to the west and darkness, ill-omened, M 239–43. North and south are sometimes indicated by the winds; n 110–11.

30–3. empedon, "ratified" by the people, 157, as it has already been promised by the king; e 317, 192, 151. — hos . . . per, "just as heretofore;" th 566, n 180. — oude . . . allos, "for not another, no, not one." This emphatic doubling of the negative displays the impetuosity of the speaker; l 349, e 167. oude gar oude and oude men oude are common in Homer, but are not Attic, though the latter phrase occurs in the poetic style of Xenophon and of Plato's Phaedrus. Krüger. — hotis; e 17, z 28. — enthad'; z 47. — deron; z 220. — heineka pompes, with menei, "for the sake of," to gain.

34. melainan, the usual color for the Homeric ship, probably produced by pitch. The only intimation of the use of paint in the heroic age is for ships, which are either black, melainai, kyanoprooroi, or red-cheeked, miltopareioi, phoinicopareioi. The staining of ivory with purple for the cheek-piece of the bridle is mentioned, D 141, in a simile, as done by a Maeonian or Carian woman. It seems something rare and foreign. In like manner, none of the numerous objects discovered by Schliemann on the site of Troy (1871–73), below the historic stratum, have any signs of paint, except two stray fragments. All ornamentation not in raised work is incised in the pottery while the paste was soft. This is a characteristic of all the most ancient ceramic ware unearthed about the Aegean, and may be seen in that part of the Cesnola Collection which came from Alambra. Still, the accoutrements of the terra-cotta warriors found there are roughly delineated in red and black. The pottery of Mycenae, however, unearthed by Schliemann was of an early painted variety. — dian stands as an epithet of hala almost exclusively in passages where the theme is embarkation. It points to the solemn tone of the sailor's thought at the moment of separation, when he entrusts himself to the god of the sea and offers up a silent prayer for protection; and this pious tone of thought is heightened by the consciousness that that deity dwells along the shore and lingers in its neighborhood. Buchholz.

BOOK VIII. 179

35. πρωτόπλοον: in honor of the guest, and to ensure his safety and the boasted speed. The wagon selected by Priam to convey Hector's ransom to Achilles was described as "first-built" (πρωτοπαγής), at Omega 267. — κούρω: at Zeta 222, the dual form κούρω results from the proximity of δύω. Gladstone conjectures that δύω stands for the two most important men of the crew, the captain and the steersman, and that the less important rowers are not regarded as forming part of the subject of the verb. For fifty was a regular ship's complement of rowers, as in the seven ships of Philoctetes and the fifty of Achilles. We may compare Delta 393, where the Cadmeiones choose for the ambush against Tydeus "fifty young men, with two leaders." In Odysseus' ship, Eurylochus appears to have been a second in command, though probably not the steersman; see Kappa 204–8, 429–41, Lambda 23, Mu 195, 278, 339. Did Homer, like Mr. Gladstone, Ameis, and Düntzer, forget that the Phaeacian vessels have neither rudder nor steersman? See Theta 557–58.

36–7. κρινάσθων: middle imperative, 3rd plural, governing κούρω, with subject indefinite, like the common φασί; or is the subject to be found at Theta 258–59? — δησάμενοι: why middle? H. 689. — ἐπὶ κληΐσιν, "to the rowlocks." The κληΐς in a ship is the upright pin or thole projecting from the upper extremity of the ship's ribs, to which the oar was loosely fastened by a twisted thong of leather, τροπός, line 53. A common rendering of κληΐσιν as "rowing-benches" is pronounced incorrect by Grashof, Doederlein, Seiler, Am., and F.

38. θοὴν, "speedy," quickly prepared, quickly ended. That departure before nightfall was not contemplated is evident from the events of the following day, when the same haste is made by the king to place the presents in the vessel at early dawn (Nu 19), but the whole day is allowed to pass in irksome idleness until evening draws on. Such bustle is characteristic of Alcinous. — ἀλεγύνετε, "do ye lend hand to;" found only in the Odyssey, and with δαῖτα, δαῖτας. Authorities are not agreed as to whether the sense is "prepare" or "partake of;" probably both. At Alpha 374 and Beta 139, it is applied to the suitors, who are told by the herald at Rho 170–82 that it is time for them to cease their exercises before the palace and go in to prepare the feast, which they accordingly do, throwing their mantles

180 NOTES.

on the thrones, and slaughtering the sheep, goats, and swine; cf. Book θ line 61.

39–42. "Plentifully to all." Compare "he provided many sacrificial victims," ξ 250. — "the others" is appositive to the pronoun implied in "let them go." The article with the plural of "other" is formulaic; see lines 107, 204, 212. — "scepter-bearing" is an exclusive epithet of kings; but the sceptre as a badge of authority was borne also by judges, heralds, priests, and seers. — "kings" is appositive to "the others." — "my beautiful halls": for this naïve expression see ζ 58, and on θ 178; compare the old ballad of the Blind Beggar's Daughter of Bednall Greene, where "pretty Bessee" is made to say of herself:

"My father," quoth she, "is plain to be seen,
The simple blind beggar of Bednall Greene,
That day by day sits begging for charity,
He is the good father of pretty Bessee."

43. "The divine bard." The bard was an indispensable member of a royal court in the Homeric day, and his was recognized as an established profession, like that of the herald, the seer, the physician, and the artificer, who were all denominated demiurgoi, handicraftsmen. The bard of Agamemnon was appointed guardian to Clytemnestra in her husband's absence; and it is not until Aegisthus has banished him to a desert isle that the plotter is enabled to gain the confidence of the queen. Homer is careful to tell us, at the first mention of Phemius in the palace of Odysseus, that he appears among the suitors and sings for them only because he is coerced. The bard is "divine" because of his close connection with deity; cf. lines 44, 63, 481, 488, 498–99.

44–9. "God," meaning the Muse; line 63. — "exceedingly"; η 110. — "to delight"; ζ 82. — "wheresoever," meaning "howsoever"; η 72. — "prompts"; line 73. Observe the prominence given to song by the closing words of the last three lines. — "scepter-bearers" used substantively, as in Ξ 93. — "herald," referring to Pontonous; line 65; η 179. — "for the two"; on line 35. — "the shore"; ζ 94, 236.

51–2. "They indeed": emphatic repetition of the subject in the second clause, a common epic construction; η 163, θ 488. It lays a stress upon the clause which our idiom, and for the most part the Attic dialect, does not recognize. — "sail"; on ζ 107, and see the sail of the Pelesta, p. 109. — Notice the repetition in consecutive verses, "ship, ship, ship." So, twice, κ 407–8, 444, 446–47; on η 15.

BOOK VIII. 181

At lambda 1-3 these verses are repeated, but at 9-11 the construction of our idiom is followed, with the forms nea, ten, tes.

53-4. "On the rowing-benches" (tropois); on line 37. — "All" (panta) may be taken adverbially, or "doing" (poieontes) may be supplied; H. 508 b. Iota 342 shows that panta does not belong with "oars" (eretma), but the phrase is a formula of general application, meaning "everything ship-shape." — "They spread out" (ana petassan), "they unrolled," on the vessel, to be in readiness to hoist on the mast; Scholiast B. Q.; on nu 81. These details are formulaic; on eta 172.

55. "And high on the water they moored her," by a cable to the perforated stone, nu 77, and by the anchor stone thrown out ahead. — "Aloft" (hypsou); only so far out as to give floatage, since the stern must be close enough to shore to admit of egress without a small boat, no hint of which occurs in Homer; cf. gamma 11, nu 75. With hypsou compare xi 300, and the nautical phrases meaning "having been swung overhead" and "having held off from this," Herodotus VI. 116, "ships riding at anchor," Thucydides I. 48; "the high seas."

57. The aithousai are the two porticos on opposite sides of the courtyard (aule). — The herkea are the enclosures of the courtyard. — The domoi are the rooms of the house, the great hall (megaron) and vestibule. These terms include, with exaggerated fullness, the whole house open to men.

58. This verse is wanting in several manuscripts, and is condemned by most editors.

59. Alkinoos; on zeta 76. He takes part in person, as do Nestor and his sons, gamma 435-46, where Stratios and Echephron lead up the victim by the horns, Aretos brings the lustral water and the sacrificial barley, Thrasymedes stands ready with the axe, and Perseus holds the bowl for catching the blood. Nestor's duty is to offer the prayer and perform the other initiatory rites. The suitors are similarly engaged, beta 300, in the courtyard, where these preparations for the banquet were habitually made (Lambda 773-76); and there stood the altar of Zeus of the Enclosure (Herkeios), which could be used in the ceremonies. — The word hiereusen ("he sacrificed") exhibits the religious tendencies of the age. To slay an animal for food is in every case to sacrifice it (hiereuein), whether for the solemn and public offerings to the gods, or for the private table of the swineherd. To the gods was always assigned their portion. In early times among the Egyptians, as with the modern Arabs, the master of the house killed whatever was brought to the table. Virgil makes Dido

182 NOTES.

proclaim the thanksgiving at the temples, but she feasts Aeneas at her own palace. The banquet to the ship's crew has its parallel in the bulls, lambs, and swine sent by Dido to Aeneas' companions in the harbor.

60. eilipodas, "rolling-paced," a noticeable characteristic of the gait of the ox, occasioned by the knee and the hoof at each stride describing a semi-gyration about the straight line of the course, so that the foot is swung round, and not lifted and set down squarely like the "high-stepping" horse, aersipous.

61. deron applies only to the beeves and the sheep. The swine are not flayed, but singed (euontas, Book 2, line 300). — erateinen, "delicious." Compare the more labored preparations for the banquet in Dido's palace:

The inner house, splendid with royal luxury, is being prepared, and they set out banquets in the midst of the halls . . . fifty handmaids within, whose long line of duty it is to store the pantry and tend the flames of the Penates; a hundred other maids and an equal number of male servants of matching age, to load the tables with food and set out the cups.

62. enguthen: if the ending -then here retains any of its separative force, it is rather in the sense of coming from a distance so as to be near; see note on line 67. The simple "near" gives its usual force in Homer with verbs both of rest and motion; Book 6 line 279, Book 7 line 112. — erieron, "dearly loved."

63. The Muses are the givers of song to mortals, while the province of Apollo in Homer is to preside over the mechanical art of playing upon the lyre, or of endowing with prophetic instinct; see note on Book 8 line 488. The Muses have no fixed number in Homer, except in the last book of the Odyssey, where they are the conventional nine. Here the Muse confers upon her favorite both the good and the ill which Zeus commingles with the common lot of humanity; Book 6 line 188.

64. Observe the chiastic arrangement of the clauses of this line and the preceding, and the effect of the alliterative delta. Some have supposed that the tradition of the blindness of Homer arose from the careful and sympathetic picture which he has here drawn of the blind bard Demodocus, and the prominence which he has given him beyond any other minstrel in the poems. In the ancient Homeridean Hymn to Apollo, the bard tells the maidens

BOOK VIII. 183

of Delos, if any stranger arrives and asks, "Who is the sweetest singer that comes to delight you," to answer,

"A blind man, who lives in rocky Chios."

This minstrel is called Homer by Thucydides, and, though the hymn is later than the poems, the fact shows the early origin of the tradition which made our poet blind. Some thought that the tradition arose from the word homeros in the Cumaean dialect, meaning blind. The bard Thamyris, B 594–600, is one whom the Muses did not love. He boasted that he could prove victor even though they should contend with him themselves, and he was punished with loss of sight and the power of song.

66. messō, used substantively; on zeta 8. Why the double sigma? The original stem was methio; cf. Sanskrit madhias, Latin medius, English mitten, middle. — ereisas; eta 95.

67. kad ek, "down from," the usual Greek idiom, looking to the result of the action, so that it hung down; on 62, 85. — The phormigx is the same as the kitharis, and the earliest lyra, which last is first mentioned in the Hymn to Hermes, to whom its invention is there attributed. It had two arms curving upward in the familiar shape, and a crossbar near the top, to which the gut-strings, running up from below, were attached. glaphyre, 257, refers to the hollow between the arms and the crossbar. According to the common Greek statement, the phormigx had four strings in the heroic period, and the three others were not added until the time of Terpander, 650 B.C. See the very early Cypriote bronze bowl above, p. 89, and Schliemann, "Troy," p. 25–8. — ligeian, also applied to the wind, to the Muses when singing, and Nestor and Telemachus when speaking.

68. autou, adv. "there," defined in epic manner by hyper kephales. autou is thus followed by en, eni, with the dative thirteen times, para and the dative four times; also epi, pros, meta, kata; cf. theta 577, nu 56. — epephrade; zeta 47, eta 49, theta 142.

69. kaneon, properly a wicker basket, but usually any vessel in which food was served, a broad shallow dish, a patera. At Lambda 630 it is of bronze, and holds the onion on Nestor's table; in Circe's palace it is of gold; at upsilon 300, one holds not bread as usual, but the beef's hoof hurled by Ctesippus at Odysseus; at gamma 442, it contains the sacrificial barley. Observe the prothusteron here; on zeta 9.

70. piein; 45. — anogoi; on eta 138, theta 87, 90. An especial honor

184 NOTES.

Honor is here paid to the bard, as kings have "fuller cups" than others, Iliad 262, 162, 311.

71–2. Formulaic lines occurring often; Book 8, line 484. — "hands"; on Book 7, line 173. Virgil introduces a custom of his own day: "After hunger had been banished from the tables, and the dishes removed," Aeneid I. 216. More closely: "After hunger had been banished and the desire for eating suppressed," VIII. 184.

73. "Inspired" — "glorious deeds of men." The envoys find Achilles singing the same in his tent, Iliad Book 9, line 189; a theme suiting the man and the age. The Virgilian bard is Hesiodic and didactic. Iopas' song is of cosmogony and astronomy, of eclipses, Arcturus, the Hyades; Homer glories in man and his chivalrous deeds.

74. "The path of song, of which" — "of song," genitive by inverse attraction to the relative, for the accusative "song," a construction not uncommon in Homer; H. 817; G. 153, Note 4. — "then even," so soon after the events themselves, the celebrity of the war being so instantaneous that it was seized upon at once by the minstrels of the day as the subject of song. Of the four lays whose subject is given us in the Odyssey, all are upon the Trojan War except one, and in that the scene is laid upon Olympus, not on earth. — "fame reached"; on Book 6, line 29; cf. "fame above the winds to the sky," Aeneid I. 379; 457. The story has spread to the ends of the earth, and hence the Phaeacians must know it, as the bard does in the palace of Odysseus, and the Sirens in their lone isle, Book 12, line 191. Virgil gives the reason why the incidents of the war are so well known to Dido, a Phoenician; it was from the banished Teucer who had sought her father's aid. But Homer gives us no clue, save this of heaven-high fame and the inspiration of the Muse.

75. "Quarrel," more specifically defining "the path of song," "glorious deeds of men."

76. "How once they battled" — "bounteous;" H. 218 D. The ancient authorities mostly refer this quarrel to the period succeeding the death of Hector, with whose burial the Iliad closes. A truce of twelve days had been granted by Achilles to Priam for the celebration of Hector's funeral solemnities; and it is at the end of this period, upon the eve of the resumption of hostilities, that the banquet to the gods is most plausibly set. Here a dispute arises between Achilles and Odysseus touching the future conduct of the war. Achilles is hot for

BOOK VIII. 185

open assault, Odysseus urges stratagem. Frightful words are bandied between them, and Agamemnon is rejoiced because the fulfilment of the prediction touching the fall of Troy seems near at hand.

77–8. "Lord of men" (ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν) is the distinctive title of Agamemnon, given to him 46 times; otherwise, only 6 times; never found after Homer. — νόῳ, "in his soul," not expressing his joy. — ὅτ', ὅτι, causal. Is this elision allowable in Attic? H. 70 D.; G. 12, Note 2. What modes are found in causal sentences? G. M. 81, 1 and 2; what is the usage in Homer? G. M. 81, 2, Note 1.

79. ὥς, "so," gathers into itself with careless ease from the preceding the thought that the great piece of fortune was at hand when the chieftains quarrelled.

80. Pytho (Πυθοῖ) is the most ancient name for Delphi, which does not itself occur in Homer, though it appears often in the Hymn to Apollo. Pytho is mentioned at λ 581, as the destination of Leto; at Β 519, as a city of Phocis; and at Ι 405, where it is used as a synonym for a city of the greatest wealth. — ἠγαθέη is an epithet given to several cities and lands which stand under the immediate protection of some god, as Pylos of Poseidon, Lemnos of Hephaistos, Nysa of Dionysos. — "stepped over the stone threshold" (ὑπέρβη λάϊνον οὐδόν) is a common expression for entering a house, as that of Eumaeus, π 41, of Odysseus, ρ 30, ψ 88; ν 63. Here it is the threshold of the temple, built of stone, according to the Hymn to Apollo, under the direction of the deity himself, by the brothers Trophonius and Agamedes. Pausanias states that it was this temple that was burned 548 B.C. The oracle was unquestionably an ancient one, and of great influence in the Homeric age, as shown by its wealth, which would be gathered from the offerings of consulters, and by the fact that so important an event as the expedition against Troy was referred to its decision. The only other oracle certainly belonging to that age is that of Zeus at Dodona; but see on ζ 162. The more usual and accessible mode of ascertaining the divine will was through the mouths of the various seers, gifted by Apollo with the power of interpreting the significance of the flight of birds, the flashing of lightning, appearance of meteors, etc.

81. "To consult the oracle; for then even was rolling down woe's beginning." — τότε ῥα, like τότ' ἄρα, 74, but referring to the

186 NOTES.

period before the war, when Agamemnon went to Pytho. — "kulindeto," especially of on-sweeping waves; here the wave of woe.

82. "Dios . . . boulas": compare the expression at the opening of the Iliad: "the will of Zeus was being fulfilled," A 5. — "dia," "in pursuance of."

84. "porphyreon": zeta 53. — "pharos": on zeta 214. One end of the ample garment, that was commonly thrown over the shoulder, could readily be drawn over the head to conceal the features.

85. "kak," "down over;" cf. 67. — "prosoopa": on zeta 107. Telemachus, weeping before Menelaus at the latter's touching reference to Odysseus and his family, holds his purple cloak before his eyes with both his hands, delta 115. In the Pompeian fresco depicting the sacrifice of Iphigeneia, Agamemnon is represented with his mantle shrouding his face, as in Euripides, Iphigenia in Aulis 1550; indeed, so characteristic was this as the costume of sorrow that Aristophanes makes Euripides deride Aeschylus for his frequent use of it on the stage; Frogs 912.

86. "Phaeakas," object of "aideto," "before the Phaeacians." Thetis, mourning for the loss of Patroclus, when summoned by Iris to attend the Olympian council, replies that she feels reluctance to mingle with the gods, with such a load of unrepressed sorrow in her heart, Omega 90; and Odysseus says, tau 119, that it ill becomes him to sit grieving in another's house, lest mistress or maid might call his tears the maudlin tears of one overcome with wine; on eta 260.

87-9. "hote": eta 138. — "amphikypellon." Aristotle, in describing the opposite cells of the honeycomb, says that on each side of a common base they have an opening like the "amphikypella." This, then, was a double cup, of which one end would serve as a pedestal while the other was in use, and some have supposed that such cups were in use in the time of the philosopher. Nothing of the kind, however, has ever been discovered, according to Krause, among the vast number of vases and cups from ancient sites (a few have been found among the very ancient remains of Bologna, Italy), and the numerous diverse explanations for the term by the ancients themselves argue against that supposition. Schliemann, comparing gamma 41, 50, 63, claims that the "amphikypellon" is the same as the "aleison" (add omicron 85, 102), and the "aleison" is called "amphooton," chi 10 (cf. chi 17, upsilon 153), or two-handled; of these he finds many kinds both

BOOK VIII. 187

at Troy and Mycenae. The cut above exhibits the double-mouthed and double-handled goblet from the "Trojan Treasure" (see p. 213), and the one below a peculiar style, from Mycenae, with birds on the handles, which the explorer seeks to connect with the famous goblet of Nestor, Iliad XI.634. — The purpose of the libation was naturally the hero's thankfulness to the gods for their bringing him at last to a land where he was so well known to fame that

188 NOTES.

the theme of their song was his own achievements. This not only satisfied his love of glory, and flattered his self-esteem, but gave him fuller assurance of a return to his home. Like the paintings which Aeneas beholds on the walls of Dido's temple, depicting the exploits of himself and of his companions, "here he first dared to hope for safety and to trust better things for his afflicted men," Aeneid I. 451.

90. archοito . . . otryneian [he would begin . . . they would urge him on]: the more prominent thought is placed first, though the reverse is the order of time, as at line 69. The pauses show that the lay was one of considerable length. Is the urging proof of a fixed composition divided into rhapsodies, or of a floating mass, undefined, fashioned at will and continued at command?

91–6. epeessin: not words merely, but theme as well, "lay." — kata with kalypsamenos. They are always separated in Homer. — goasken; H. 410 D. — pantas elanthane: a tribute to the magic power of the bard; theta 532, lambda 334, 368. — epephrasat' ed' enoesen, "noticed and remarked him;" on line 15. — stenachontos; on theta 564. — philereтmοisi, exclusively applied to the Phaeacians and the Taphians.

98. daitos; H. 575. — thymon, not object of the verb; cf. "having satiated himself with wine according to his heart's desire," xi 46. — eises, as the standing epithet of the mind (phrenas), the ship, and the shield, betokens the quality of symmetry of parts which makes "well-proportioned," "evenly balanced," and, for the banquet, "duly portioned," not in the sense of each and all sharing alike, but of each receiving the share due to his position in the community; for the king, M 311, the honored guest, theta 475, the faithful warrior, H 321, receive a larger share than the rest, the servants a smaller; nu 281–82, theta 70.

99. syneoros, "wedded to," "linked with." It is said, rho 271, that the gods made the phorminx "a companion to the feast;" cf. "the lyre, dear to the greatest gods," Horace, Odes I. 32, 14.

100–3. peirethomen; H. 413; cf. theta 120, 126, 205, 213. — hos ch'; eta 192. — enispe; H. 450 D. 8. For the thought, see eta 333, theta 243–44. — hosson; eta 108. The speaker's characteristic impetuosity has again carried him beyond the bounds of prudence; but it is not an unnatural boast of a people so isolated that they conceive a contempt for the outside world through sheer ignorance of its achievements, and, wrapping themselves in their own conceit, regard their littleness with a serene satisfaction (cf. sigma 382–86).

BOOK VIII. 189

Experience with one foreign arm of heroic mould brings retraction of the vaunt, 246.

106–7. ἔξαγεν ἐκ ("led out from"): the same repetition occurs at v 21, B 690, Z 42, H 336, 435, I 331, K 267, Ψ 394; ἐν is repeated at ε 260, τ 10, υ 261, χ 347, B 720, Z 244, H 438, Λ 155, P 570; ἀνά at χ 132, 142, 240, Ψ 717; ἐς at δ 802, Φ 610; on ζ 77, θ 190. — αὐτὴν ὁδόν, "along the same way," is the earlier expression for τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδόν, which occurs in a similar passage of the Iliad, Z 391. — οἱ ἄλλοι, 40. Supply the kindred verb ἥεσαν from ἦρχε. The bard must be honored with the same attention as the others, and would take his pleasure in the games as well as they. The dance does not seem to be contemplated at this time; 254–55.

108. ἀέθλια, as ἄθλα at 160, refers to the games; usually meaning the prizes. — θαυμανέοντες: ζ 134. The description of athletic sports always held a special charm for the Greek hearer; but the poet here treats it with a brevity that seems to presuppose the elaborate and detailed account of the funeral games of Patroclus in the Twenty-third Iliad to be already in his repertoire, and to have been often sung in its proper place. Besides funeral games — of which those following the death of Oedipus and of Amarunkeus of Elis are mentioned in the Iliad — mention is made of those in which Tydeus was victorious at Thebes when he had gone there as an envoy; and the Olympic Games, or something corresponding to them, appear to have been a regular institution in Elis; on ν 81.

109–10. ἔσπετο πουλύς: ζ 164. — μυρίοι: H. 257 D. should read: "Homer uses only μυρίοι, paroxytone, and always in the sense of numberless." — ἵσταντο, imperfect, refers to the whole crowd rising one after the other; ὦρτο refers to the single act of each individual.

111–14. All the Phaeacian names, with the exception of Alcinous, Arete, Laodamas, Rhexenor, Demodocus, and Polybus, reflect their ruling passion for the sea, and this is further illustrated by the very length of the list here, equalled nowhere else in Homer, except by that of the Nereids who rise from the sea with Thetis to sing their lament over Patroclus, Σ 39–49. Many of the names here will be recognized as having equivalents among our own proper names. — Πρυμνεύς and Πρῳρεύς may be respectively the same as the later πρυμνήτης, helmsman, and πρῳ-

190 NOTES.

ράτης: the lookout who stood at the ship's head to give signs to the pilot; see note on line 35.

115–17. ἄν, sc. ἔστη. — βροτολοιγῷ, "man-quelling," is an exclusive epithet of Ares. The whole phrase occurs in the Iliad of Hector, Achilles, and Leonteus. In bodily powers Euryalus appears to be the foremost champion the Phaeacians can boast; see 126–27. We read Ναυβολίδης with La Roche, Bekker, and others, without the traditional θ', considering it a patronymic (as at B 518), referring to Euryalus, thus bringing the following ascription of beauty into connection with Odysseus' words at 174–77. So much description of his personal qualities appears natural in consideration of the important part he plays in the sequel; and since the place of honor in a poetic enumeration is at the extremes, if θ' be read, we have the anticlimax of an unknown person.

118–22. τρεῖς παῖδες; ζ 63. — τοῖσι . . . δρόμος, "and for these from the starting-point the pace was strained to the utmost." δρόμος is not the course but the pace, as at Ψ 375. νύσσης is the scratch-line (νύσσω) from which the race went straight to the goal around which the spectators stood, at line 125. In the Olympic Games the foot-race was originally a straight one, the length of the stadium, and it was not until the 14th Olympiad that it was changed to the δίαυλος, in which the runners went out and came back. See H. 590; G. 179, 2; C. 425.

124–25. "As far as on the fallow it is the custom for mules to range, so far ahead of his competitors did he come in to the people, while they were left behind." The distance meant by οὖρον ἡμιόνοιιν is not known; but from the circumstances of K 344–57 it appears to have been greater than a spear-cast. There, Odysseus and Diomed, out on their nocturnal scouting expedition, hear the Trojan spy Dolon coming towards them. Odysseus proposes to let him pass by a little, and then rush upon and seize him, or else drive him into the camp. As soon as he is past them,

"as far as mules can range over fallow ground — for they are superior to oxen in drawing the fixed plow through deep-soiled land" —

they start after him. Many have thought that οὖρον represents the distance a mule team will outstrip oxen in a specified time.

BOOK VIII. 191

But from Psi 431 it seems best to make it the whole distance the mule team will go at one pull till they stop for breath, and this, the poet's experience has taught him, is greater than that of the ox. Compare the Latin measures actus, versus, and our furlong, ploughgate. Clytoneus comes in so far ahead, because he is best of all at running; cf. Virgil, Aeneid V. 318-19. There is no such distance between the competitors at Psi 754-81. Odysseus is victor at last, but only because Athene makes Ajax slip and fall just at the goal.

126. "agonizing." The spirit of this epithet is well illustrated from the wrestling-match between Ajax and Odysseus, Psi 714-17, where their backs are said to creak beneath the tug and strain of their stout hands, the sweat pours down like rain, and bloody weals leap up along their sides and shoulders. So Scott, Lady of the Lake, V. 23:

"For life is Hugh of Larbert lame;
Scarce better John of Alloa's fare,
Whom senseless home his comrades bear."

127. "all the best men." The victors, paired by lot, contend, two by two, till Euryalus alone remains victor even of those who have proved themselves best in the previous matches. Am. This suits the lengthened description accorded Euryalus, 115-16, and his subsequent arrogance.

129-31. Elatreus: the arm that drives the oar well, hurls the discus furthest. — "they were delighted"; Zeta 99. — "minds": the plural is more common, but cf. Zeta 155. The contests here resemble the later pentathlon, described in the following lines:

The leap of feet, the throw of the discus, and the rushing of the javelin,
and the footrace and wrestling — one end was set for all.

Of these, only the javelin-throwing, in which the Phaeacians are nowise concerned, is omitted, boxing being substituted. In Psi the leap does not appear, but chariot-racing, armed assault, and archery are added, and it is the chariot-race of which the poet makes by far the most. In Scheria we find no mention of the horse at all; neither are there any horses in Ithaca, and the reason alleged, Delta 605, is that Ithaca is a rugged, pent-up island, and no island is fit for horses.

133-34. "Come now"; Theta 11. — For the hiatus before "if," see on Eta 6. —

192 NOTES.

οἶδέ . . . δεδάηκε, "knows and has learned;" on [line] 90. Why the indicative? See G. M. 70, 1, Rem.; on η 17, ζ 239. — γε μέν, "at all events," whether he knows or not.

135–36. The generic word φυήν [physique/stature] is here described with epic minuteness in its various parts, as a connoisseur might run his eye admiringly over the muscles of an athlete. The early poet is fond of such picturesque definiteness in his descriptions. — ὕπερθεν [from above], simply to specify that the hands are higher than the feet. At N 75, he says "feet below and hands above." Compare the language of Scripture: "I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath." Amos, ii. 9. — σθένος [strength], a characteristic addition to the parts, since σθένος is viewed as a member of the body; see on [line] 237.

137–39. συνέρρηκται [has been shattered]; cf. "the Greeks broken by war," Aeneid II. 13; "a soldier broken in limb," Horace, Sat. I. 1, 4. — πολέεσσιν; see ζ 284. — οὐ . . . τί separated, as at η 73, 216. — συγχεῦαι, "to crush." Construe γε with συγχεῦαι, to which it is attracted by its fondness for the first word in its clause. In many points of view there is nothing better than the sea, especially to the oar-loving Phaeacians; but in the one point of utterly crushing a man there is nothing worse. This is Phaeacian observation, rather than experience; see θ 563. — εἴη; η 52. The rendering of these lines has been preserved to us from the Odyssey of Livius Andronicus, which was the first translation of Homer into Latin, and served as a school-book in the days of Horace:

For nothing worse
Wears a man down than the savage sea, however great
His strength, when the relentless waves break over him.
