141–42. μάλα . . . κατὰ μοῖραν [quite in due measure]; see η 227. — αὐτὸς . . . μῦθον: this line was not recognized by Aristarchus, Aristophanes, or Zenodotus; but it must be confessed, as Am. says, that the preceding line, standing alone, renders the answer strangely thin and abrupt. — ἰών [going], like the absolute participles φέρων, ἄγων, ἐλθών, λαβών, ἰδών, παραστάς, is employed to place the whole action more vividly before the eyes of the hearer, on the stage as it were. — πέφραδε μῦθον, "show forth thy saying." According to Aristarchus, φράζω never means in Homer simply to speak, but always to point out, as at [line] 68; but the addition of μῦθον here and at α 273 reveals the tendency

BOOK VIII. 193

to the later meaning already begun. Cf. Odyssey θ 499, and the verb deik-nynai, Latin dic-ere.

145–48. "Come here"; θ 11. — "thou too," as well as ourselves. — "for it is fitting that you should know of feats of strength;" cf. line 134. — idmen is more commonly 1st plural indicative. — "as long as he may live;" on ζ 183, 259, η 94. Note the rhyme esin, eesin; on ζ 61. This sentiment, that man gains no greater glory in all his years than that which rewards the successful competitor in the games, is thoroughly Hellenic, and proves the Phaeacian, though lower in the scale of achievement, to be the equal of the Achaean in enthusiasm for the pursuit.

149. "Make trial," "scatter." The word order would point to action as the proper means of dispelling his anxieties; but "for" at line 150 appears to be causal, and thus to introduce the reason; hence, as in line 90. Laodamas anticipates the objection which Odysseus actually makes, with a sympathetic appreciation for his situation and a manly respect for the hero, which mark every line of his two short speeches, and prove him to be what the poet names him, the goodly son of Alcinous. The tone of his language is no less courteous when beyond the hearing of Odysseus than when addressing him, and he forms a pleasing contrast to the ungentlemanly Euryalus. The challenge is couched in such terms that it is really a compliment to Odysseus, and offers him a chance to leave behind him in the land a reputation for prowess, which was so dear to the Homeric man. Tydeus, visiting the Cadmeiones, even challenges them himself to the contests of the ring. — "away from the heart"; on ζ 167; cf. Υ 341.

153–57. The words of Laodamas, kind and courteous as is their intent, sound to Odysseus, in his situation, like a taunt. The connection of thought in his answer runs much in this wise: Laodamas, why bid me this? you cut me to the heart; for you present to me the pleasing picture of one whose cares are light, and to be thrown aside at will. Would that such lot were mine — that the expectation of departure might give me reason to assume that cheer which victory in the games demands! But games are not for such as I. Care, only, shrouds my mind; for such depths of suffering have I journeyed through in all the past. And now, sitting as suppliant of your people and your king, craving a

9

194 NOTES.

return which is not yet mine, think you I can so lightly rid me of my anxious fears? — "these things" (H. 555); — "to me, it is" ("have I") — "and rather" (Odyssey η 213); "who" (ζ 302); "many" (H. 547c); "after" (η 101, θ 433). Odysseus is too prudent to feel unshaken confidence in mere preparations and promises, and takes advantage of the opportunity to hint at that fact, as well as his longing to depart. — "all the people." Gladstone sees in this phrase a sign of the strong popular infusion in the political ideas of the age. Something similar seems hinted at in the account of the prayer of Tydeus and Polynices for assistance at Argos, Book Δ 380.

158–60. "And dispraised him to his face" — "no, for" (on line 32); "contests" (on 108); contraction, as 164; "many" (η 260, 214, θ 214); "they are" (η 132, θ 233).

161–64. "But to him who, with ship of many a row-lock abiding, a captain of seamen who are traders, fares abroad, both of his cargo heedful and keen-eyed for return wares and profits rapacious; for, athlete thou art not like." The sting of this passage lies not so much in the allegation that Odysseus is a trader as in the suggestion that he has been so devoted to his wares and his gains that his bodily powers and every nobler ambition have been sacrificed to them. It is also the kind of gain made by sharpness of dealing, and by peaceful, though often by illegal, means. See on η 10. The Greeks who are mentioned in the poems as engaged in commerce — the Cretans and the Taphians — are at the same time characterized as high-handed pirates rather than peaceful merchants; but it is the Phoenicians who hold in their hands the chief carrying trade of the Mediterranean, and to them, as a class, the present passage may be supposed to refer, since the poet elsewhere gives them the epithets "greedy knaves" and "very crafty," and in general paints their character as a compound of such greed and cunning as closely matches the picture here. An acquaintance with such traders is here a bit outside of Greek experience, rather than Phaeacian (on η 50, λ 367; cf. Ameis on ο 381), since the possessions of the Phaeacians are the gift of the gods (η 132, λ 341), unless they have gained such knowledge abroad (ν 113), or a ship has been driven there by chance at some point (ζ 202, 278, θ 31, λ 364–65). — "traders." All the crew are traders, and probably have a stake in the venture. Hence the plural is

BOOK VIII. 195

used of the Phoenicians who came to Surie with their wares and corrupted the nurse of Eumaeus, o 415, 456. — φόρτου (cargo). The cargo of the Phoenician ship just mentioned contained countless trinkets (μυρία ἀθύρματα), which may be enumerated as ornaments, decorations, the finest products of the loom, gold, silver, electrum, ivory, tin, etc. In bartering these they remained a whole year, amassing "much substance," which would form the provisions (ὁδαίων) for the return voyage. When ready to leave, they notify the Phoenician nurse of Eumaeus, who steals him away, together with three goblets of gold, and embarks with them. Such gains may be classed among greedy profits (κερδέων ἀρπαλέων). Since one of the scholiasts limits φόρτου μνήμων to keeping in mind the value of each article of the cargo, it has been cited as one of the proofs of the absence of writing in the Homeric day. This by no means necessarily follows, whatever may have been the state of letters at the time. Any careful master would keep a close watch of the cargo, whether he possessed a bill of lading or not; and the manner in which the sales were conducted required an accurate knowledge of the wares, without turning to a price-list. Wolf saw this. Prolegom. XX., Note c. — ἁρπαλέων; ζ 250.

165. ὑπόδρα ἰδών (looking from under his brows), torva tuens, Aeneid VI. 467; acerba tuens, Lucretius V. 33. Mr. Gladstone, so competent a critic in oratory, characterizes the following response of Odysseus as "that wonderful speech in answer to the insolence of Euryalus, which teaches us, more than any other composition with which I am acquainted, up to what point emotion, sarcasm, and indignation can be carried without any loss of self-command." Juv. Mundi, p. 392.

166. οὐ καλόν (not fair), 239, 397, 408. — ἀτασθάλῳ, "presumptuous;" on η 60. — ἔοικας (you seem), retorted from 164.

167. οὕτως, "so we see." οὕτως in this usage regularly points to the person addressed as an example of the case educed. The application is made more fully at 176. — χαρίεντα, "(all) the gifts of charm." The neuter plural is used substantively, as often in Homer, and here implies πάντα (all); Δ 320, Ν 729.

168. φυὴν, φρένας, ἀγορητύν (beauty, mind, eloquence), particularize χαρίεντα as the three great gifts of the gods to man—beauty (and thereunder vigor and strength), the power of thought, and power of speech. — οὔτε, οὔτ', οὔτ', as Ζ 450–52, distinguish the general negation by dividing it

196 NOTES.

into the parts especially to be dwelt upon. No man has all three; one has physique, another intelligence, another eloquence.

169–70. "One man," opposed to "another again," at line 174. — "for" at eta 307. — "feebler." — "flings the crown of charm over his words," morphen used figuratively, as at lambda 367; epesi is the indirect object.

171. "Unfalteringly," with copious flow of language, when the words come thick and fast as snowflakes in the winter storm. Odysseus is describing himself as if he had just been listening to the famous passage from the Third Iliad, when Antenor, looking out upon the battle-field from the watch-tower of Ilium, with Helen, Priam, and the Trojan Elders, gives his reminiscences of the hero who had come to Troy with Menelaus before the war, to demand the restitution of Helen; Gamma 210–24.

172. "With a winning deference," a careful appearance of respect for his audience, which forms a principal grace of the orator. This sometimes takes the form of a little hesitation at the beginning of a speech, and many eminent speakers have practised it merely in order to give the appearance of unpremeditated reply to prepared speeches. — "befits" with "meta"; zeta 109.

173–75. "Like a god"; eta 71–2. — "like the immortals"; eta 5. — "but not for him is grace flung crown-like round about his words." — charis is synonymous with morphen above. — "wreathed all around." According to Bekker, in the 15,694 verses of the Iliad there are 185 which have no caesura in the third foot, and in the 12,101 of the Odyssey there are 71. These are mostly in proper names or in compounds, so that at the end of the first element a kind of caesura occurs, as at zeta 200, and, besides, a caesura regularly falls in the fourth foot. This is prevented by amphiperistr., and by amphiponesometh', Psi 159, so that Am. and F. would separate amphi- from the verb; but cf. Hor. C. I. 18, 16; 37, 5; II. 12, 25; 17, 21.

176–77. "As also in your case," with special application of the thought to the case in hand, as eta 219. — "pre-eminent." — "otherwise," i.e. better. — "neither . . . nor"; on line 32. — "but in judgment profitless art thou." With all his attractive exterior, he has no intellect, and therefore no power of becoming speech.

178. "My dear breast." It has been cus-

tomary to render φίλος in such connections as a possessive pronoun; but this is out of deference to the feelings of a later age, rather than a right appreciation of the earlier. In its use as an attributive, the applications of this word may be divided into two classes. It occurs in the poems between 500 and 600 times, and most frequently by far with words of relationship and the like, father, mother, papa, child, offspring, son, boy, brother-in-law, father-in-law, maternal uncle, husband, wife, wedded, spouse, lord, nurse, nymph, companion, head, stranger, man, old man, god, counsels, earth, ground, fatherland. None of these give offence in the English when connected with dear, and this translation is forced upon us when a limiting genitive, as N 427, O 639, M 355, β 51, ν 259, etc., or a possessive pronoun, as E 314, 318, T 132, Z 474, Π 447, T 4, Φ 330, 378, σ 214, ω 505, Ω 416, ξ 177, ν 413, χ 350, qualifies the same noun; I 555, λ 327, fall under fixed epithet. The evidence for the strength of the domestic affection is cumulative throughout the poems. The second class comprises the mind, life, parts of the body, etc., as spirit, lifetime, heart, heart, chest, throat, hand, knees, limbs, eyelids, garments, gifts, old age, house, home, bed, homecoming. With these, the possessive translation is almost universal; but if we find the possessive pronoun, possessive genitive, or a quasi possessive dative at the same time, this must show that the sense of dear was necessary, and consequently that the same sense was not incompatible when the pronoun was not used. Such are found at ε 297, 406, χ 68, 147, Φ 114, 425, ω 345, δ 703, O 166, 182, δ 270, ι 413, π 274, υ 9, ν 231, N 85, etc. This gives fair ground for the conviction that φίλος to Homer meant dear in both classes, and the explanation of this curious fact is probably this: 1st. In many ways it is the youth of the world that the Homeric poems set before us in their childlike directness of expression, which is quite foreign to ourselves, but often heard from the lips of children before a conventional schooling has repressed the undisguised utterances of the feelings. The Homeric man calls his breast dear, just as he calls his hand stout, μ 174, or his thigh thick, λ 231, or his house beautiful, θ 41, or himself valiant, A 393; ι 19-20, etc. 2d. The fondness of the poet for personification leads him to apply it to the feet, N 75, the hands, ε 434; while the members are sometimes treated as separate and distinct individualities apart from the person himself, as υ 237, 13-22, ε 355,

198 NOTES.

Delta 314. Under this aspect there is as good reason for applying the word "dear" to one's own hand as to that of a second person. The German language exhibits many instances of a similar usage, and English a few. See Proceedings of the American Philological Association, 1878, p. 15–17.

179–81. kata kosmon ("in order"); section 141. — How is mytheiai formed? See Hadley's Grammar, 370 D. b. — emmenai, "that I was," used as an imperfect. What three uses does the present infinitive have? See G. M. 15. — ophr'; cf. 147, zeta 259. — pepoithea; zeta 166.

182–85. echomai, as if by chains. — polla etlen; on eta 225. — andron ... peiron, "through both the wars of men and grievous waves cleaving my way," the one with my sharp sword, the other with my sharp-prowed ship. — alla kai hos, referring to the preceding, is more closely defined by the concessive pathon, and suggests the later use of homos with a participle; cf. lambda 104. — mythos, en.

186. auto pharei, "with cloak and all," a use of autos continued into later Greek; Hadley's Grammar 604. Homer also joins syn with it; nu 118; so also Xenophon, Cyropaedia II. 2, 9. Usually in such trials of strength the cumbersome pharos (cloak) would be thrown aside, and in the boxing and wrestling matches of Book Psi even the chiton (tunic) is doffed, and a loin-cloth only is worn. The scholiasts describe the discus as a circular plate of stone or metal, about a foot in diameter, pierced through the centre by a hole, and thrown by the aid of a strap attached. But nothing in Homer is said about the last two particulars, and the copies of Myron's Discobolus (see illustration) show neither strap nor hole. There the disk, grasped by the hand on one side, extends up the forearm, and is in the act of being released into the air. The object in view was to throw from a fixed point to the greatest distance, as in the Scottish "putting the stone." This exercise was common in the Homeric age as a part of military training; for the heavy stone, ready at hand on the battle-field and hurled by the practiced arm, is often mentioned in the Iliad as a formidable weapon when others were exhausted.

187. "Very large as well as thick, heavier by not even a little." — pacheton, probably a strengthened adjective form of pachys (thick/heavy). — stibaroteron, heavier in consequence of its size and thickness.

BOOK VIII. 199

188. "Than such as the Phaeacians were wont to pitch with against each other." — "with such as" (οἴῳ); H. 607. — "with one another" (ἀλλήλοισιν); H. 602.

189–90. "swinging this round" (τόν ῥα περιστρέψας): "this then swinging round." The motion is that of the baseball pitcher of today, and Zeus employs it when he hurls Ate out of heaven, T 131. — "it hummed" (βόμβησεν), an onomatopoeic word. The whir is heightened by the rotary motion imparted by the twisting impulse, "spinning it flies," Ψ 846. — "and they crouched down against": the preposition κατά in composition is rarely repeated with the accompanying substantive; Λ 493, Τ 25, ρ 86, 179, υ 249; but other prepositions often define the thought more clearly, as ποτὶ here; ἐν at η 285, 345, θ 422, ν 135; ἐπί at ν 70, 74, 76; ἐς at κ 107. So ἀπό with ἐξ at α 270, π 65, σ 260, ω 7, 189, Ν 367; with παρά at Θ 533, Ξ 46, Ο 407; ἀμφί with περί at Ψ 561; on η 281, θ 106.

191. A latent sarcasm might be thought to lurk under this line in this connection; but when compared with its occurrence at 369, ν 166, and the habit of the poet, the evidence inclines toward rejecting such a supposition.

192–93. "but he" (ὁ δ'), the stone. — "the marks" (σήματα): the marks (sticks, stones, or what not) set up to indicate the spot where the discus of each competitor had fallen in the previous contest, 129. Note the mixing of metaphors in "flew past, running" (ὑπέρπτατο, θέων); cf. 247. The verb θέω is also used of a ship, of a rolling stone, of the potter's wheel, a vein, and the rim of a shield. — "Athene set" (ἔθηκε . . . Ἀθήνη): "Athene set the bounds," i.e., fixed the marker (σῆμα), 195, which was to show how far Odysseus had thrown, and would then form a goal for any other who would prove victor by passing beyond it. The word τέρμα, so used, is commonly plural.

195–98. "And . . . feeling around" (Καί . . . ἀμφαφόων): "even a blind man, stranger, could pick out this mark by groping with his hands." — "you may be sure" (τοι); on ζ 131. — "in the throng" (ὁμίλῳ): among the other marks set up before. — "this one here" (τόδε γ') is the reading of Aristarchus, and refers to the σῆμα to which she points. — "will come up to" (ἵξεται): "will reach as far as."

200–1. "a kindly companion" (ἑταῖρον ἐνηέα): "a helpmate well-wishing;" becoming "companion" (ἑταῖρον) by reason of the assistance given Odysseus, just as a fair wind is called "a good companion" (ἐσθλὸς ἑταῖρος) at λ 7. — "at the contest" (ἀγῶνι): like ἀγορῇ, but especially of the assembly for the games. — "more lightly" (κουφότερον): "more lightly," with lighter heart. The success of the cast, and the diversion in his favor among the people, dissipated some of the gloom of his feelings (on 149) which had been visible even in

200 NOTES.

his countenance, and mollified the anger with which he had denounced Euryalus.

202. Τοῦτον, δίσκον: this is the natural expression for him to use from his standpoint, just as τόδε at 198 is used for Athene at the other end of the space; hence τόδε there is better than the other reading, τόν γ'. — τάχα δ' ὕστερον: "and quickly thereafter;" so τάχα always in Homer, and not until later in the sense of "perhaps."

203–6. τοσσοῦτον ἢ . . . μᾶσσον: "so far or still farther," both adverbial. — μᾶσσον: H. 222 D. — τῶν ἄλλων: on ζ 257; as opposed to νέοι, it includes those who do not pride themselves upon their discus-throwing so much as upon the other exercises enumerated at 206. — κραδίη θυμός: on 15. — ἄγε πειρηθήτω: on 11. — καὶ ποσίν: because he is distrustful of his own powers there, and virtually withdraws the challenge, 230.

207–8. πάντων Φαιήκων, defining τῶν ἄλλων: "of all the Phaeacians I say." — αὐτοῦ: "alone," a meaning not infrequent, and obtained by its use in opposition to "others;" more exactly, αὐτὸς οἷος, μόνος. Laodamas appears to be the eldest of the unmarried sons of Alcinous, because he has his seat next to his father (cf. γ 39), is the prime favorite, and takes the lead in challenging Odysseus. He is, then, in a special sense, the representative of the family, and as such is excepted by Odysseus from the number of the challenged; and he is regarded by him as his host more particularly, because, by yielding his seat to the stranger, he placed himself in that relation at the outset, and he has actually proved himself the real host in his speech; cf. γ 36–50, 482. The married sons have no specific mention, except at ζ 63. — φιλέοντι: "with his entertainer," with the added notion of the progress of the act at the time. — μάχοιτο: of the contest in games also at Ψ 621.

209–10. κεῖνός ἀνήρ: as subject. — ξεινοδόκῳ avoids the ambiguity of ξεῖνος. — προφέρηται: ζ 92, 183. The folly of such a course is exemplified in the action of Tydeus, Δ 391, who, though a guest-friend, challenged and defeated all the Cadmeiones in the games. So enraged were they that, as he was returning, they laid an ambush for him, and it was only his wondrous prowess and the aid of Athene that saved him from an ignominious death.

211–15. ἕο . . . κολούει: "for his all he mars." — ἴδμεν, 146; η 327. — πειρηθήμεναι: on 100. — πάντα . . . εἰμι: "for in all things not

BOOK VIII. 201

"worthless am I." — πάντα is limited by "however many contestants there are." — μετ' ἀνδράσιν is in an emphatic position; cf. lines 204, 230, 408, and Book 13, line 143. When compared with line 160, does there appear to be a lurking sarcasm in the phrase regarding the lack among the Phaeacians of the warlike sports which he proceeds to dwell upon? — Why is the hiatus allowed after οἶδα? See Hadley's Grammar 67 D. d; Curtius 63 D.; cf. line 216, Book 13 line 14. — ἀμφαφάασθαι; Hadley 802.

Lines 216–18. "I could be the first to strike my man with my arrow in a throng of hostile men, even though many a comrade stood close beside me using the bow against the warriors." — πρῶτός, before my comrades. His shot is quick and sure, like that of Meriones in the funeral games for Patroclus, who snatches the bow from his competitor, who has cut with his arrow the string confining the dove, and pierces the bird through before it has escaped from his range, Iliad Book 23, line 870. — ἄνδρα: He does not shoot at random into the mass, but selects his mark. — παρασταῖεν; Book 8, line 52.

Line 219. Philoctetes led the Thessalians from Meliboea; but on the way to Troy, while in Lemnos, he was bitten by a serpent that issued from the altar as the chiefs were sacrificing. The wound became so offensive that he was abandoned by his companions, and remained in Lemnos until after the period covered by the Iliad. An oracle came to the Greeks that Troy could not be taken until the arrows of Heracles, which that hero had presented to Philoctetes at his death, were in the Greek camp. Accordingly, an embassy is sent for Philoctetes, who is finally prevailed upon to come to the Troad, where he is healed and slays Paris with his bow.

Line 220. δήμῳ, "land." — τοξαζοίμεθ': This, for the foremost chieftains, would not mean in battle, but in contests of archery, which may be supposed to have received a special impulse from the return of the great archer to the camp. Teucer is the only man of note who makes the bow his regular weapon. The bow is spoken of slightingly, because it did not demand that close hand-to-hand combat in which the Achaeans took pride. See the weapons of the Pelesta as compared with those of the Egyptians, p. 109. In general, these northward maritime enemies of the Egyptians do not use the bow. Odysseus' bow is left at home, and he makes no use of one in the Iliad except in the night-scout of the Doloneia, and then he is supplied with one by Meriones, and actually

202 NOTES.

brings it into play only to lash the horses of Rhesus into camp. His claim here to excellence in its use prepares the mind of the hearer for his great feat in the sequel, when he slays so many of the suitors with his bow.

221–22. eme is an example of what unusual construction? H. 775; C. 569. So H 198, N 269. — ossoi: the hero is comparing himself with men of his own generation. Elsewhere the poet, speaking in his own person, uses hoioi, when contrasting those of his day with the Troic heroes; E 304, M 383. — With "upon the earth" compare "those upon the earth" (epichthonioi), A 272. In these, man is opposed to the gods, who are the "heavenly ones" (Ouraniōnes), eta 242. The same contrast appears in "eating bread" (siton edontes), which is varied in "those who eat the fruit of the plowed land," Z 142, "grain-eater" (sitophagos), iota 191; cf. N 322; "Whoever feeds on the gift of the earth," Hor. C. II. 14, 10. The gods, on the other hand, "eat no bread, drink no sparkling wine," E 341.

223. "With men of former times." The ever-recurring lament for "the good old times of our fathers" has been the constant theme of the pessimist in all ages. Homer touches upon it frequently, especially in extolling the strength of his heroes, of whom Diomed, Hector, Aeneas, hurl stones which two men, "such as mortals now are," could not lift. This fact has been taken by some to prove that the poet must have lived long after the scenes he describes. The weakness of such evidence is apparent in itself, and Homer has refuted it in the present passage, where those who are so much greater than Odysseus are removed from him by one generation only. Heracles was still alive when Odysseus, though a young man, phi 21, meets Iphitus in Messenia, and Eurytus was not long dead; cf. A 262–72. Poetic and popular exaggeration is the main element in such comparisons; on eta 253. — etheleso, "I would wish," a naive expression; cf. theta 210.

224. "He wounded Heracles"; on zeta 248. Heracles wounds both Hera and Hades with his arrows, E 392–409, and his shade, which Odysseus meets and recognizes in the lower world, is armed with bow and arrow, ready in hand, with arrow upon the string, lambda 607. His traditional costume of the club and lion's skin is later than Homer. Pisander of Rhodes, B.C. 600, is said to have been the first thus to accoutre him. The annexed cut, from a colossal statue discovered by Gen. Cesnola in the temple of Golgoi, exhibits him arrayed

BOOK VIII. 203

with bow, club, and lion's skin. Eurytus was king of Oechalia in Thessaly, and, according to the later version, he was the teacher of Heracles in archery, and afterwards slain by his pupil. But the Homeric account states that it was Iphitus, the son of Eurytus, who was slain by Heracles, after he had met Odysseus in Messenia, and presented him with the bow of Eurytus, which had been left to the son by the father at his death. This is the bow which Penelope brings forth from its long resting-place in the treasure-chamber, to make the proposal to the suitors that whoever shall bend it most easily and shoot an arrow through twelve axe-heads set in line shall win her hand. None can even string it till Odysseus gains permission to try, when he handles it with the ease of a master, achieves the feat proposed, and then turns upon the suitors themselves.

225. No tradition was handed down of any such contest on the part of Heracles. His wounding Hera and Aides does not appear to be applicable. The scholiast supposes that the plural is used sylleptically, and applies only to Eurytus. This is very harsh, and, Düntz. declares, impossible. More plausible is the conjecture that some story was alluded to, which, though known to the lays of the poet's contemporaries, fell into oblivion soon after, and was not transmitted to later sources; on Odyssey Book VII, line 324.

226–28. "to him"; Book VII, line 25. — "upon" with "old age"; cf. "he did not reach the threshold of old age, but perished," Odyssey Book XV, line 246. Otherwise, Book XIII, line 59. Dione says of Diomedes, who had wounded her daughter Aphrodite, that the man is not long-lived who battles with the immortals, nor to him returned from warfare do children upon his knees lisp the name of papa, Iliad Book V, line 406; cf. Iliad Book VI, line 131. It is a settled doctrine with Homer, as with later authors, that superhuman self-conceit on the part of man will not long escape

204 NOTES.

punishment from the gods, with whose perfection he provokes impious comparison. Thamyris and the lesser Ajax, together with Eurytus, are his special examples, and Heracles' death is supposed to have been hastened by his temerity in wounding Hera and Hades.

229–30. "another," "he throws"; on 107. With the English long-bow, in the Middle Ages, three shots to the mile was reckoned good shooting. The Homeric bow was doubtless inferior; but even then Odysseus seems to be indulging in something of the boastfulness of his host. — "I fear"; on Book 6, line 168. — "with feet" with "he might pass"; cf. 214.

231–33. "I was subdued shamefully"; 137–39. — "amid many waves," an expression of general import, on the wide sea, as "amid the waves of Amphitrite in the open sea," Book 3, line 91. — "since... unceasing," meaning "since care of my person on shipboard was not continuous." This is fully explained at 451–53; cf. Book 6, line 220. — The word komide never means anything else in Homer but the care which is bestowed for the highest productiveness of the soil, or for the best maintenance of the bodily powers, whether of horses or men; that care, in relation to diet, cleanliness, bathing, sleep, and exercise, which formed so important a feature of Hellenic life, and which would necessarily be interrupted in a great measure during the eighteen days' voyage of Odysseus, when his constant attention day and night was given to the helm. Of food there was abundance on board till his shipwreck, Book 5, lines 265–67. — "dear things"; on 178. — "they are loosened"; Book 7, line 132; Book 13, line 34; cf. "the limbs of Aeneas are loosened," Aeneid I. 92.

236. The word epei finds its apodosis at line 241, and the thought runs thus: Since thy challenge and thy proud claim are spoken with no unkindly spirit, but simply to proclaim the excellence which is properly thine, and to meet the charges of this man who has disparaged thee as no one would dispraise thy prowess who knew the use of language, therefore hear, too, what excellences Zeus has bestowed upon us, as upon our fathers. — "not ungraciously," meaning "not ungraciously."

237. "attends." Excellence, strength, knees, and hands are said to attend upon a man as his faithful followers and obedient servants, ready at all times to render such service as may be commanded of them; on 178, Book 13, line 45. The belly, on the contrary, is his lord and master; Book 6, line 133, Book 7, lines 216–21.

BOOK VIII. 205

238–39. "that," 78. — "in such wise as." So Odysseus indignantly retorts upon Agamemnon, who, in his faint-hearted despair at the success of Hector by the ships, proposes that they shall make their escape homeward by night, Iliad XIV 90–2:

"Be silent, lest some other Achaean hear this
speech, which no man would at all take through his mouth,
whoever knew how to speak fitting words with his own mind."

— "he would take" and "he would benefit" form the conclusion of the conditional relative clause "whoever knew" in both passages. To translate ὡς as "so that," as many have done, breaks up the plain flow of the language by making "being angry ... rebuked" parenthetical, destroys the evident parallelism of construction which the other passage presents, and emphasizes much less strongly the manifest determination of Alcinous to lay the whole blame of the awkwardness of the situation upon Euryalus, where it rightly belongs. The king discerned the greatness of Odysseus directly upon his appearance in the palace, and the judgment which Euryalus passes on him argues neither quickness of perception nor gift of language. Later, when good-humor is again restored, the king makes Euryalus apologize.

240–41. "in one's mind;" Odyssey VII 327. The scholiast is right in paraphrasing "but" by "indeed;" on line 389, VII 47; cf. XIV 149–51. — "from me;" VI 289. — "and to another," not only learn them yourself, but spread my fame by telling it to others.

243. "you feast," with lengthened penult in thesis by metrical exigence; Hadley 28 D. — "to your wife." Odysseus has said nothing of his wife, but his possession of a palace and slaves, and his refusal of Calypso's offer as well as that of Alcinous, raise sufficient presumption to found the supposition upon; VII 315. The statement here shows that the wife was accustomed to feast in the great hall with her husband and guests, as we find Arete VII 141, VIII 420, XI 335, XIII 57; on VI 287–88.

244–45. Connect "what deeds," meaning "what acquirements," closely in thought with "you might say." — "he bestows upon," meaning "bestows;" on VI 100. Homer always uses the present and imperfect of this compound in tmesis. — "upon us as well as you," and, what is more, "distinguished beyond ... from our fathers," meaning "still unimpaired from our sires," to whom we do not confess ourselves inferior, as you do to men of former days in your

206 NOTES.

own land. This is a hit at Odysseus, 223, and is in excellent keeping with the boastfulness of the king. Athene warns Telemachus, Odyssey Book II line 276, that he must needs exert himself if he would prove that he is a worthy son of his mighty sire, "for few sons are equal to their father; the majority are worse, though a few are better."

246. Odysseus took occasion to qualify his original boast of readiness to meet the Phaeacians in any contest, and was not backward in dwelling on those accomplishments in which he knew that the Phaeacians were not versed, and in which, therefore, the field was free to himself. Alcinous now adopts the same policy, and, as usual, outstrips the prudent common-sense of his original. He withdraws his former claim to pre-eminence in boxing and wrestling, line 102, and, waiving competition in these, seizes quickly upon what Odysseus wishes to decline, and enlarges upon other accomplishments in which he feels assured that Odysseus cannot become a competitor, and which were really the best exponents of their easy, secure, and Olympian mode of life.

247–49. "The best" [ἄριστοι], "we are" [εἰμέν]. — "feast" [δαίς]; Book VII line 99, Book XIII line 9. — "lyre-playing" [κίθαρίς]; Book VIII line 67. — "dances" [χοροί]; Book VI line 65, 157, Book VIII lines 264, 371. — "garments for a change" [εἵματά ἐξημοιβά], implying not only neatness and fastidiousness in dress, but the abundance which permits its indulgence; Book VIII line 392, Book VI lines 49, 59, 61, 64. The contrast is supplied us in the statement of Eumaeus to Odysseus that they have no mantles for a change in his steading, but one only for each man, Book XIV line 513. — "soft beds" [εὐναί], of the softness of the bed, as Nestor claims that he has numerous blankets and coverlets, so that one may sleep softly therein, Book III line 350. The tone of these lines is much exaggerated by Horace in his "fat Phaeacia" (pinguis Phæaxque), Epistles I. 15. 24, and,

"Alcinous-like,
Youth too much devoted to grooming the skin,
For whom it was fine to sleep till midday
And lull one's cares to the sound of the lyre." Epistles I. 2, 29.

250–54. "Come now" [ἄγε]; line 11. — "strike up" [παίσατε]: hiatus? on Book VII line 23. — "going" [κιών]. As the aorist participle sometimes encroaches so far on the domains of the present as to represent time coincident with that of the primary verb (on Book VIII line 564, Book XIII line 58), so the present is occasionally used to denote priority of time, chiefly, however, as a picturesque imperfect. Though κιών is probably an aorist, as accent and usual meaning

BOOK VIII. 207

seem to show (see the gnomic form ekion, Hesiod, Works, 345; and Plato's translation of kion, A 35, by apochoresas), yet many authorities insist that it is a present. Kühner classes it among those verbs in which, since no aorist participle occurs, the present is forced to do duty for both; among these he cites ion, theta 142, 144 (eta 204, theta 445), ezomenos, zeta 118, iota 244, kathezomenos, zeta 295, nu 372, hopniontes, zeta 63 ("having taken to themselves wives"), hopniomene, Theta 304; on nu 134, theta 482.

255. oiseto; on zeta 78. Other forms of this aorist imperative in Homer are oise, oisete; of the infinitive, oisemen, oisemenai; oise is also found in Aristophanes. — "probably is lying." The king had left the hall before the herald hung up the lyre and led forth the bard, 104–8. keimai is also used of a chair, footstool, bed.

256–58. He rose ... to bring; on zeta 50. — "hollow;" on 67. — "umpires," "judges;" properly, those who think only of the dues of each contestant, for the purpose of giving an unbiased decision. In the chariot-race of the Iliad, Achilles sends Phoenix to the goal round which they were to turn, "so that he might keep in mind the turnings and report the truth," Psi 361. — "nine in all." The word pas with numerals marks a complete and definite number. In Homer it always stands after the numeral, in Herodotus before; later its position is not fixed.

259. "of the people," chosen from the people, and probably by the people. — "in the assemblies;" agon means only the assembly, or place of assembly; on 200. The meaning "contest" is later. — "were wont carefully to arrange each particular." It is plain from the phrasing that the aisumnētai were regular officers whose duties were fixed and frequently discharged. Though not mentioned before, they were unquestionably engaged in the superintendence of the previous contests, and their introduction onto the scene for the dance marks the prominence which the poet would lend to that leading feature of the Phaeacian accomplishments; on 36, 472.

260. "And they smoothed the dancing-ground," cleared away all the obstructions, as Apollo tells Hector he will go before him and smooth the road for him (O 261) to the Greek camp. The spot is a particular one in the agora, and must have been frequently brought into use for their favorite amusement. The whole agora of the Spar-

208 NOTES.

tans was called χορός — καλὸν . . . ἀγῶνα, "and they widened a fair area;" they made the people that had pushed into the arena retire and leave a wide space for the dancers. — καλὸν seems to limit ἀγῶνα to the place, since its meaning is "serviceable for the end in view," as at ζ 263, and applied to ἄνεμος at ξ 253. Compare, Ipse (Æneas) omnem longo decedere circo infusum populum et campos jubet esse patentes, Æn. V. 551, where Æneas, clearing the field for the evolutions of the boy-cavalry with Ascanius at their head, takes upon himself the duties here assigned to the umpires, and thus especially dignifies that feature of the pageant.

264. "And they beat out the dance divine with their feet." Most authorities agree in taking χορὸν here to mean the dance, instead of the dancing-ground, as at 260. This is supported by the epithet θεῖον, applied to it because the dance was very early connected with the worship of the gods. Virgil takes the same view in his translation, pars pedibus plaudunt choreas, Æn. VI. 644.

265. μαρμαρυγὰς, "twinklings." So, Byron addresses Terpsichore as the "Muse of the many-twinkling feet," and Moore has, "Dancing feet that gleam and shoot, rapid and white, like seabirds o'er the deep." This dance has been supposed by many, in both ancient and modern times, to be of a mimetic character, representing by its movements the scenes described by the bard in the following song of the loves of Ares and Aphrodite. Such dances were in high favor among the Greeks in later times, but were mostly confined to the symposia. In private life, dancing appears to have had the ban of condemnation set against it; and though Plato recommends that the two sexes should be allowed to meet socially in this way, it never found fulfillment in Athenian history; on ζ 157.

266. ἀνεβάλλετο, "struck up a prelude." The playing of the Homeric singer upon the cithara was probably not a continuous accompaniment, but was confined to a prelude sounded to give the key, to the filling-up of the pauses, and to heightening the effect of particular passages. Later the rhapsode discarded all accompaniment.

The comic element of the omitted episode which follows subserves the purpose artfully to allay the angry feelings that had been excited on both sides by the unfortunate speech of Euryalus

BOOK VIII. 209

and the retort of Odysseus, and brings back an era of good feeling that was very important to the success of the poet's plans. Homer presents to us other instances of a similar device resorted to for the same purpose: notably, after the angry scene between Zeus and Hera, Iliad A 584–600, when the halting Hephaistos assumes the office of cup-bearer, and by his words and ungainly actions wins a smile from Hera's lips and hearty laughter from the other gods; and again in the treatment which Thersites receives from Odysseus, and the ridiculous figure he presents after his flogging. The people are just disappointed in the great hope, roused in them by Agamemnon's speech, of seeing soon their homes again; but, though in their grief, they laughed heartily at him, Iliad B 270. Cf. φ 376–77, χ 371. It is greatly to be regretted that the poet did not choose some less objectionable form of restoring good humor in Scheria; but, as has been often remarked, the absence of the female sex from the circle of hearers preserves the dignity of their character as previously sketched.

* * * * * *

367–73. "The same"; 83, 521. — "hearing"; 429. — "with hands"; ζ 91. — "the," relative. — Polybos. The introduction of the name of the inventor or maker is intended to dignify the work; as Hephaistos, η 92, and often; Daedalus, maker of the Chorus, Σ 592; Phereclus, builder of the ships for Paris, E 62; Epeius, θ 493. — "shrewd"; ζ 256.

374–76. "the," demonstrative, introducing the apodosis of "when." — What peculiarity of form in "he used to throw"? H. 410 D. — "shadowy"; η 268. — "bending backward," in order to throw the ball up vertically. — "but"; η 123–26, 129–30, ν 67–9. — "before"; ζ 331. Ball-playing was a favorite amusement and exercise among both Greeks and Romans through all periods of their history. Every complete gymnasium had a room devoted to it, where a special teacher gave instruction in the art. Foot-ball was the favorite game at Sparta. The game of the Phaeacians was common in later times, and was called Ourania. The ball was thrown skyward, and must be seized while the catcher was off his feet. Homer mentions but one catcher; later there were often more. This game was also in vogue among the ancient Egyptians, where ball-

210 NOTES.

playing was considered more particularly adapted to females.

377–80. "in an upward direction," "straight up," as opposed to the following "toward the ground"; others interpret it as "with might and main." — [a word meaning "much-nourishing"]; see note on Book VI, 226, Book XIII, 85. — "frequently interchanging," in the figure of the dance, which is probably accompanied by a throwing and catching of the ball, though Athenaeus thought not. — "beat time," but whether with hands or feet, or both, is not determinable from the passage. To accompany music with a clapping of hands was not unusual among the Egyptians, Assyrians, and Hebrews; see the illustration cut from an Assyrian bass-relief. — [a phrase meaning "was aroused under"]; see note on Book VI, 40.

382. Compare this striking line with the earlier ones where Odysseus addresses Alcinous, Book VII, 208, 303. He has probed the character of his host and adapts himself to the circumstances. Hereafter he always uses this formula in addressing him, Book IX, 2; Book XI, 355, 378; Book XIII, 38, and it never occurs elsewhere, except from the lips of Euryalus, Book VIII, 401. — "pointed out of all people." Compare the words of Lucian in relation to the notoriety gained by Herodotus on reading his History at Olympia: "if he appeared anywhere alone, he would be pointed out by the finger," Herodotus 2. — "most distinguished," like the word meaning "pre-eminent," at line 487, with a partitive genitive, as if functioning as a superlative. — "of the people" takes the place of "of men" as in the Perseus passage, "most distinguished of all men," Book XIV, 320.

212 NOTES.

out, as the name intimates; T 247, Ψ 350, Ω 232; therefore the metal was probably in small and irregular pieces, such as gold-dust, leaf, nuggets, rings, beads, or the like. During excavations at Troy in 1878, Schliemann found in the "Royal Palace," among other treasures in terra-cotta vases, "large and small lumps of gold," "a large nugget of gold and another of silver," "large lumps of melted gold," "one such as found in gold-mines," also "a lump cut from a gold bar;" on ζ 52. No silver talents are mentioned in Homer. The six silver blades discovered by Schliemann in the "Trojan Treasure" may be seen in the plate opposite, on the shelf below the diadems. He calls them talents; and as they weigh about six oz. each, Mr. Head thinks they represent the third of the Hittite mina of silver, or the lesser Babylonian mina, whose use spread early through Asia Minor from Carchemish, together with the Hamathite or Cypriote syllabary, according to Prof. Sayce, and with the civilization presented to us in the traditions of an early Lydian power (London Academy, Nov. 22, 1879). The relative value of gold and silver we do not know for the Homeric period further than has been stated on ζ 232; in the time of Herodotus it was 13:1; but it is plain from the poems that silver lies between gold and bronze, and gold is to bronze as 11⅓:1, according to Z 236. The apparent abundance of gold in the poems, as compared with its scarcity in Greece during the sixth century, is remarkably confirmed by the great quantities deposited with the dead in the sepulchres at Mycenae. See Appendix. — "highly honored" (τιμήεντος); so "of great worth" (ἐριτίμοιο), I 126. Zeus has said that Odysseus shall have copper also, ε 38, but only a part of the gift is now presented, in order that the remainder may seem to be extorted by the greatness of the man; λ 336 sq.

394–97. "Let us bring" (φέρωμεν) may include the speaker by reference to 425–30, or it may be said condescendingly, as at μ 213; on θ 425. — "holding in one's hands" (ἐνὶ χερσὶν . . . ἔχων), of possession in general; but the whole clause is an expression of Homeric naivete which does not hesitate to declare that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush; on 153; cf. α 311, ο 76. — "him for his part" (ἑ αὐτὸν), whether or not you give satisfaction to us who have also been wounded by your affront to the stranger. Am. Düntz. reads the plainer "himself" (αὐτὸς), by conjecture.

214 NOTES.

398–99. "All" [pantes], the twelve kings. — "gave the order" [ekeleyon], as a concurrent vote of the council [boule]; Book η 226. — "to bring" [oisemenai]; on 255. — "herald" [keryka]: each king is attended by one herald at least, who is now dispatched to the several abodes of the lords for the presents; Book Ψ 558–64.

403–5. "All-bronze" [pangchalkon] does not necessarily preclude added ornament; "all of silver" [hapas argyros] is applied to a crater which is gilded about the lips, Book ο 116. Schliemann found in the graves at Mycenae many bronze-bladed swords that had been gilded, and others without gilt. — "upon," "it is upon" [epi, epesti]; 563. — "silver hilt" [kope argyre], like Achilles' sword, Book Α 219. Some of the swords above mentioned from Mycenae had hilts of bronze plated with gold, and some of wood covered with gold, but none with silver hilts appear to have been found. Signor Castellani, however, had in his possession, in 1879, an Egyptian dagger with a blade of bronze gilt, and a silver handle terminating in a kind of flattened knob covered with thin gold plates. At the junction of the blade with the handle, some small silver nails were inserted with exquisite taste. — "scabbard" [koleon]. The material of the scabbard is mentioned only here and Book Α 30, where that of Agamemnon is of silver. Those from Mycenae were mainly of wood, adorned with gold buttons and other ornaments (see illustration); some even of linen. — "newly sawn" [neopristou] here, and "sawn" [pristou] Book σ 196, τ 564, are the sole evidence we have directly from Homer of the use of the saw. — "ivory" [elephantos]. Ivory is quite often mentioned in use for decoration, as that of a key, reins, chair, bedstead, the palace of Menelaus, etc. It came to the Greeks through the channel of Phoenician commerce, and appears early on the

BOOK VIII. 215

Egyptian monuments as tribute from Ethiopia and the East, and from Cyprus also in the time of Thothmes III. It was found in small quantities even in the lowest stratum at Hissarlik, and in still smaller quantities at Mycenae. Pausanias tells us that the elephant itself was not seen in Greece before the time of Alexander the Great. — "encircles" (amphidedinetai). As an instance of a parallel passage (on Odyssey Book 7, line 197), compare Iliad Book 23, lines 560-62, where Achilles is telling Antilochus that he will satisfy Eumelus for the prize that has been wrested from him unfairly. — "so that at a goodly price for him will it be balanced" (poleos...estai). Poleos as a noun. — "worth" (axion), from the verb ago in the sense of weighing. The thought is realistic, as at line 395. The warrior's weapon as a gift emphasizes the retraction of the sneers at line 159; cf. Iliad Book 7, lines 301-3. But the sword is common among presents to noble guests; Odyssey Book 17, line 222, Book 19, line 241.

406-11. "Silver-studded" (argyroelon) represents the nails used to pin the haft to the blade, as in the Castellani dagger; they were also frequently of gold or bronze in the swords from Mycenae. — "joy be with you" (chaire). — "O father" (pater o); this postposition of the vocative particle o occurs several times not only in Homer, but also in the tragedians. — "word" (epos); on line 214. — "suddenly...storms" (aphar...aellai), a proverbial expression, used also by Helen of herself in a wish, Iliad Book 6, line 346; cf. Odyssey Book 4, line 515, Horace, Odes 1.16.4; 1.26.2. — "wife" (alochon); on line 243. — "since" (epeidei...) ; Odyssey Book 7, line 152.

413-15. "Dear" (philos); Iliad Book 8, line 141; mostly poetic. — "blessings" (olbia); Odyssey Book 7, line 148. — "longing" (pothen) is rather "need," longing through pressing want in dire emergency, than longing through regret for ever having made the gift. The retraction of Euryalus is as hearty as his previous words were ungentle, and they are met by Odysseus in the same spirit; the whole line may be considered a specific application of the general "blessings" (olbia).

416-18. "Slung" (theto), by the shoulder-strap, regularly a part of the sword's accoutrement. Some of gold were found at Mycenae. — "both...and" (t'...kai), as at Odyssey Book 7, line 289, Book 6, line 321, exhibiting the early fondness for co-ordination, though in such expressions of time it is sometimes continued into Attic prose. The sense is: by the time the sun had set, the gifts were received. Duntzer queries why they wait in the agora, and do not proceed at once to the palace, now that the games are over. Evidently, in order that the whole proceeding may be a public one, transacted before the eyes of the

216 NOTES.

assembled Phaeacians; cf. Book 8.157, Book 13.14. Thus Odysseus is honored more highly, and the Homeric fondness for visible display is satisfied. In like manner the gifts from Agamemnon to Achilles are first brought and set in the middle of the assembly, Book 19.249, and then removed to his tent, Book 19.279. Compare the setting-forth of the prizes in the Patrocleian games, Book 23.654, 701, 799, 886.

419–21. "Boys": they appear to have accompanied the heralds to the palace, and there they perform the same duties as Book 7.5. — "to her mother"; Book 6.305. The presents are placed in her keeping because she is peculiarly the host of the stranger, Book 7.142, and the housewife is the usual guardian of the valuables in the house. When Helen presents Telemachus with a piece of her own handiwork for his future bride, she tells him, meanwhile, "let it lie dear beside your mother in the hall," Book 15.127. — "to them," meaning Odysseus and the lords.

424. "Chest." The treasure-chamber of Odysseus contained many a coffer well stored with garments, Book 2.338, Book 21.51; likewise that of Priam, Book 24.228. For the chest brought by Achilles to Troy, see the note on Book 6.76. This is described as "beautiful" and "finely wrought," Book 16.222, and the lids of Priam's are "beautiful"; cf. Book 8.438, Book 13.68; hence they were of handsome workmanship, and we may compare the Chest of Cypselus; on Book 6.84. This was made of cedar inlaid with ivory and gold, and was covered with embossed representations of scenes from early Greek legends, with the names of the personages in archaic letters in boustrophedon style. That the chests of the Homeric period were probably of cedar may be inferred from their contents being called odorous, Book 21.52, and the store-room itself being of cedar, Book 24.192; cf. Euripides, Alcestis 160, and Ezekiel, in his apostrophe to Tyre, xxvii.24: "These were thy merchants, . . . in blue clothes and embroidered work, and in chests of rich apparel, bound with cords and made of cedar." — "which is the finest" we have.

425. "To her" (dative), here and at 441, seems certainly the correct reading, supported by Ammonius, Eustathius, and probably Aristarchus, instead of "she herself" (nominative) with Bekker. The mantle and tunic here are the contribution of Alcinous, which he did not send sooner, as appears from lines 399, 428, 440; while the cup, at line 430, takes the place, only more richly, of the talent given by each of the other kings. This resolves all difficulties here, and leaves the mantle and tunic of Book 13.67 to be the gift of Arete

BOOK VIII. 217

herself after her challenge, λ 340. No gift seems to be required from her here, but to omit it after what she says there would be less than gracious. Greater prominence is given to the presents of the king by this isolation from the others (cf. ν 66–7, θ 472), and it offers opportunity for other happy touches.

426–29. "amphì...pyrí" (around the fire): because the legs of the tripod enclose the fire; see a representation of this from the tomb of Ramses III in the annexed illustration. — "chalkon" (bronze), "tripoda" (tripod), 434. — "híēnate" (they sent), plural, including the servants. — "eû," "snugly;" cf. ν 20, π 223. — "akoúōn," in its causal sense, is parallel to the causal dative "daitì"; cf. Δ 60. Alcinous is again characteristic in dwelling with delight upon the pleasure he is conferring on the guest.

430–32. "egō" (I), opposed to "Phaíēkes" (the Phaeacians), 428. — "tód'" (this), raising the cup from the table before him, where the goblet was accustomed to stand, and displaying it to all. — "áleison," regularly of something splendid, and it obtains the epithets "kalón" (beautiful), "perikalléс" (very beautiful), "amphōton" (two-handled); on θ 89. The derivation from "á" and "leîos" (smooth), rough with figures embossed, is suggested by Athenaeus and some of the scholiasts, and accepted by L. and S. This is supported and strengthened by the fact that the larger part of the numerous gold and silver goblets from the graves at Mycenae are embossed with various designs. Compare the silver and gilt bowls of the Cesnola Collection, in the later Phoenician style. — "memnēménos" (remembering), 244. Menelaus uses the same expression when promising an aleison to Telemachus, δ 591; cf. δ 191, ο 54–5. — "spéndē" (to pour a libation). Achilles keeps a goblet for no other use than to pour libation to Zeus; π 225. Thus the tender memory of the guest-friend is lifted higher by its association with the gods, and a prayer goes up with the libation for the prosperity of his former host.

433–34. "metà," 156; ζ 307. — "éeipen," "told them." At ο 76, 93, "eípō" exchanges with "kéleusen." Account for the tense of the following infinitive; G. M. 23, 2, Note 4. — "trípoda" (tripod), as shown by the following line and 437, is a vessel with three legs attached to it, not a vessel with a separate tripod stand. That both kinds were in use is probable, but the proof from the poems is inconclusive.

10

218 NOTES.

Of the former class a fine specimen of copper from the graves of Mycenae is given below. Others of terra-cotta were common in the excavations at Troy, and some small specimens from very early Cypriote tombs may be seen in the Cesnola Collection; see on Book XIII, line 13. — "as quickly as possible": in such expressions are words denoting possibility found with "that"? H. 664 b.

435–37. The word meaning "bath-filling," or "one who fills the bath," is used at Book XIII, line 297 substantively of the slave who performed that task for the stranger or others, and received a fee. This and the next two lines are repeated from Book XVIII, lines 346–48, where the body of Patroclus is bathed for the funeral rites. The scene is now transferred to the interior of the palace, and the imperfect tense meaning "proceeded to place" may represent this; so in Books XVIII, XV, and XIV at the respective lines cited. The departure of the maids is not mentioned; but neither is that of Arete, nor that of her

BOOK VIII. 219

sons from the agora, 419; compare τ 386–92 with 503–5; so, often. The poet varies greatly in the minuteness of his descriptions. Apparently, it is not till the water is in the bath-tub that Odysseus sees it, 450. — ἐλοῦσαι [feminine plural aorist participle, "having bathed/washed"], taking from the pile of wood at hand, which, in the palace of Odysseus, is said to be split in the morning by the servants and laid ready, ν 161; cf. σ 308. The participle gives a more vivid touch to the picture for the supposed spectator, as Ι 216; ἀείρας [lifting], α 141; λαβών [taking], ν 300; on θ 144.

439–41. θαλάμοιο, "store-chamber." That of Odysseus is described, β 338, when Telemachus goes thither to procure provisions for his voyage to Pylos. It contains heaped-up gold and bronze, clothing in chests, and odorous oil, while jars of wine were ranged round the wall. Priam visits his, Ω 191, to select costly objects for the ransom of Hector, and it treasured many a marvel. Menelaus and Helen seek theirs, to procure gifts for Telemachus at his departure, ο 100. — χρυσόν [golden object] doubtless includes the goblet of the king. Menelaus presents to Telemachus a golden goblet and a silver mixer, and Helen gives him a peplos, ο 102 sq. These are conveyed to the vessel at Pylos, where Telemachus stows away, "clothing and gold, all that Menelaus gave him," ο 207, where χρυσόν can refer only to the goblet; cf. ο 448, 469. — ἔδωκαν [they gave] here is to be compared with ἔνεικαν [they brought], 428, ν 12, 120–21. — αὐτῇ [dative, "to her"]; the manuscripts have αὐτή here, though αὐτῇ appears at 425; but this violates the customary formulaic repetition. Arete is simply executing the orders given, 425. For like use of αὐτῇ, see Σ 542, β 389, δ 846, ε 260, ι 21, π 473, ν 97.

443. "Do thou thyself now look to the lid, and quickly thereto a fastening cast;" another touch of realism. She does not want him to blame her in the future if any harm befalls. Among the first thoughts of Odysseus, on awaking in his native isle and finding the Phaeacians gone, is to count the contents of the chest, as well as the other objects, and see if all are safe, ν 215; on η 33. — ἴδε [look] and λάβε [take/fasten] have recessive accent in Homer. What accent later? H. 366. — θοῶς [swiftly]; on 38, ν 19. Homer, in general, is not the poet of slowness, but of life, action, haste; witness merely the frequency of αἶψα [quickly] and αὐτίκα [immediately]. The departure of Odysseus that evening is still expected.

220 NOTES.

444–45. δηλήσεται, "may do it (the chest and contents) mischief;" [Odyssey] ν 124. — αὖτε, "next," "once more," "by-and-by," as [Iliad] H 459–60. There is no idea of repetition, but only an opposition to the present situation. Some have seen an interpolation here, taking αὖτε in the sense of "again," and finding in it a contrast to the occasion when Odysseus, returning from Æolus, after nine nights of watching at the helm, falls asleep, and his companions open the bag of winds, and they are driven back again. Of this Arete must necessarily be ignorant until the story is related in [book] κ. This is making difficulties where there are none. — εὔδησθα; η 318, ν 79; H. 357 D.; C. 233 D. Some of the scholiasts imagined that the Phæacian ships had the magic power to lull the convoyed stranger to sleep. A voyage by night, with their perfect calm and security, η 319, θ 563, appears sufficient to account for the anticipated slumber.

448. ποικίλον, "intricate," "manifold," shows that δεσμὸν refers mainly to the knot. Though keys are mentioned in Homer, φ 47, Z 89, they are only a hooked shank to throw back the cross-bar of the door. It was fastened by a thong. The means of securing the contents of any coffer was the cunning knot, which would baffle ordinary ingenuity to untie, as the famous Gordian Knot, which is called δεσμός by Plutarch. Chests were so fastened by the Tyrians in the days of Ezekiel, and Herodotus speaks of it, III. 123, in the story of Polycrates. The impress of the seal-ring on wax, coming into vogue, relegated the simple knot, in a great measure, to the mystic cystæ. Æolus uses a silver cord to tie the bag of winds, κ 23, and Zeus a gold one about the wrists of Here when he suspends her from the sky, O 19. Schliemann found at Mycenæ two gold boxes whose lids were attached by gold wires, and two gold vases with the wires still remaining. See cut on opposite page. This explains κρήδεμνον [headband/veil], γ 392. A scholiast tells us that the seal-ring was not yet known. It is true that no mention is made of it in the poems, yet Schliemann discovered several at Mycenæ, and the rude lentoid gems of the Ægean isles were doubtless used in part as swivel-rings. The Babylonian cylinder and Egyptian scarab were employed at a very early period for this purpose; see very fine specimens of all of these from Curium in the Cesnola Collection. — φρεσὶ, local dative.

BOOK VIII. 221

as the recipient of the instruction; on η 327. The scholiast suggests that Circe taught him, that he might be prepared against any such emergency as had already befallen him in the adventure with the bag of winds. She is "deceitful" (Book 9, line 32), like Calypso.

449–53. autódion, "forthwith." — asaminthos. The bath-room is placed near the entrance to the megaron. Hayman's supposition, that the preparations for the bath, and the bath itself, took place in the megaron, is absurd. — ar', after he had gone to the bathroom. — aspasíos, with thumo; cf. 395. — komizómenos; H. 801; G. M. 112, 2. — komidé; 232; eta 257. — theo hós; zeta 309.

454–55. lousan; on zeta 210. — khlaínan; on zeta 9. Since it is a pharos that Nausicaa gives him, zeta 214, eta 234, theta 84, 186, is a change of clothing intended? We have no further mention of his garments until nu 399, when Athene is to transform him into a beggar, but we are only told there that she throws about him a filthy rag. When, however, she retransforms him, to be recognized by Telemachus, she gives him a pharos, pi 173. Telemachus, after his bath in Pylos, has a pharos, gamma 467; next day, on arrival at Sparta,

222 NOTES.

He is bathed and receives a cloak (χλαῖνα), at δ 50, again mentioned at δ 115; when next alluded to, on the morning of his departure from Sparta, it is a mantle (φᾶρος), at ο 61. Directly upon reaching home, he goes to the bath, throws off a cloak, and after bathing puts on a cloak, at ρ 86–9; cf. χ 487, ψ 155. This evidence does not prove conclusively (ο 188) that the two words are synonymous, as they are metrical equivalents in the accusative, or that they are plainly distinct. They are surely different things, however, at Ω 230–31, and a change of garments would be quite in keeping with the specialty the Phaeacians show in that direction.

456–57. Wine-drinkers (οἰνοποτῆρας); ζ 309, η 99, ν 8. They appear to be just beginning the banquet, the preparations for which have not been interrupted by the bath given to the stranger. In like manner, Telemachus is tended by Polycaste while Nestor is engaged in the sacrifice, at γ 464, and there, as here, the bath does not take place until the day after arrival. — "of the gods ... holding"; ζ 16, 18, 102, 151, 161.

458. "stood ... beside"; on ζ 212, 218. — "doorpost"; ζ 19, η 89. As the unmarried princess, she may not appear in the hall (η 13), but she now comes from the women's apartments to the door leading into the hall, by which we may suppose Odysseus, returning by the back lane (λαύρη), must pass to reach his seat. This is the post also taken by Penelope whenever she appears before the suitors. Probably knowing from the preparations within that Odysseus is to pass that way, the princess comes to say farewell; cf. ν 387–89.

459. "He marveled"; ζ 237. — "in the eyes." The construction of "in" in this phrase, which is mainly confined to the poets, has been variously explained. Ameis thinks that the poet conceives all before one to be in the eyes, i.e. within the range of vision, as all behind is in one's back, thus connecting it with the poet's conception of time; on ζ 242. Düntzер, with many grammarians, considers it instrumental, because the power of vision lies in the eye, the simple dative being more common. Naegelsbach says that the expression arises from the form of the object being mirrored in the eye. Both Ameis and Düntzer urge the objection to this that it is too subjective for Homer. But the mirrored picture in the eye is a fact observed by all children at a very early age, and that it was known to Homer is shown by his use of γλήνη, the pupil of the eye, in the figurative sense of "doll," from

BOOK VIII. 223

the image; cf. the later kore, applied to the eye by a reverse process.

461–62. "Farewell"; translate as 408. The sense is: Fortune go with thee, that thou mayst hereafter reach thy native land and there remember me. The participial clause contains the prominent thought, as in her speech at zeta 61, 64; yet, like her father at 431, she wishes to be remembered. — "that"; 78. — "first"; zeta 176. — "life's price," meaning the price paid by a prisoner to his captor for saving his life, and occurs once more at Sigma 407, where Hephaistos, who was saved after birth from his mother by Thetis, says, upon her arrival to ask arms for Achilles, that he must needs pay her this life-ransom. — This is the last glimpse we have of Nausicaa. Her dream at zeta 244 has vanished, but it was all too short to leave a sting behind. If the melancholy of a shattered hope lingers round her few and simple words of parting, yet there gleams through it, while claiming return for saving his life, something of the playful archness so winsome from the outset, zeta 57–65. Homer has not handled this episode as many an imitator has done. Here we have none of the Medeas or Didos, whose name is legion in later literature. It was quite within the province of the poet to enchant us with the lovely creation of the Phaeacians, but it must in no way thwart the grander scheme of his greater epic.

465–69. "In that way," with reference to "farewell, having once been," but also more fully explained by the following line. At omicron 180–81, this line and 467 form the entire speech of Telemachus in reply to Helen's interpreting the appearance of the eagle as prophetic of Odysseus' return. — "now," at last after all my wanderings. — "dispose." — "loud-thundering"; eta 164. Here, a goddess so prominent, aggressive, and partisan in the Iliad, disappears almost altogether from the Odyssey, being mentioned only seven times, thrice in the present formula, once as mother of Hebe, and thrice in legend or narrative extraneous to the subject of the poem. — With "to come" supply "me"; on 520. — "in that event," supplies the place of what? H. 751. — "also there," as well as here, with reference to his present thankfulness, and perhaps with a reminiscence of zeta 149. Gladstone, taking this literally, cites it among the evidences that the deification of heroes

224 NOTES.

and benefactors after death appears before us in Homer as begun, yet, at least in the Olympian mythology, as incomplete, though the consummation of the process is imminent, since all the materials are prepared for the extraordinary development which came later. — "thou... O maiden," meaning "for thou didst give me back my life, O maiden."

469–70. The preposition "to"; references at Odyssey ζ 212, θ 458, Ω 553. — "his," referring to the attendants. — "portions": the proper portions of meat assigned to each according to his rank; see note on line 98. Eumaeus, in his steading, preparing supper for the disguised Odysseus, divides the roast into seven parts, one for Hermes and the nymphs, four for his assistants, and one each for himself and the stranger. The portions were cut up by the carver into slices before distribution; see η 173 on "he distributed"; see also note on 456.

472. The entrance of Demodocus at this rather late moment draws all eyes upon him, and gives occasion for the compliment of Odysseus, and his subsequent request for a further display of the poet's gift of poesy; see θ 425.

473–75. "leaning against"; lines 65–6. — "from the loin... was left": meaning "from the tenderloin cutting off a slice, but thereon the greater part was left." The choice piece had been served to Odysseus as a mark of honor, as when he dines with Eumaeus, ξ 437; Menelaus places his beside Telemachus when the latter arrives at his palace, δ 65. In like manner Ajax is honored by Agamemnon after his duel with Hector, Iliad H 321. Among the Spartans, the kings had double portions assigned them at the banquet, Herodotus VI. 57; and this was done, Xenophon tells us, not that they might eat twice as much as the others, but that they might be able to honor any one from it if they wished, as in the case of Menelaus above mentioned. We may suppose the slicing here to be done with the sword presented by Euryalus, as by Theseus in the story of Plutarch. — "upon... was left" is parenthetical, and is doubtless intended to express by the size of the piece the honor paid to the guest. Yet it would be quite characteristic of the poet should it be interpreted to mean that the hero does not rob himself. Instances of such frugal traits may be seen at Iliad B 183, Z 234, Odyssey δ 97, 717, Θ 289, Ω 236, ν 15.

476. "of swine" limits "loin"; see θ 60. — "fat": fat was in high esteem, and its savor in the burning sacrifice was pleasing even to the

BOOK VIII. 225

gods. The body of Patroclus was enveloped in it completely before cremation, and his ashes were covered with a double layer when deposited in the urn, Psi 168, 253. Acorns and black water serve to produce rich fat in swine, nu 410.

477–81. te (dative): how is it formed?—Connect "Demodocus" with "gave."— "and that to him I may offer my embraces;" cf. zeta 146–49.—"and" connects back to "so that."— "to embrace," originally used of a garment, zeta 252; then of folding in one's arms, congratulating.— "grieving though he be"; eta 215, 297.— "among men," local dative, usually with "in."— "partakers," "participants."— "paths," 74.— "taught," "ceased"; on eta 217.

482–86. "bearing"; on 254. This participle occurs some 95 times in the poems, 40 of which represent time prior to the main verb; cf. eta 172, 175. The aorist participle is found but once; on nu 134.— Connect "in his hands" with "he placed," as 406, nu 57.— "hero," a dissyllable also at H 453. Such a dative is the common usage in this phrase, but not invariably, as at Psi 597, where the genitive occurs.— "received," formulaic after a gift, often followed by "rejoicing." The formula is abandoned at Psi 597 for a simile, when Menelaus receives the horse:

And his heart was warmed,
as when the dew falls upon the growing ears of grain
in a ripening field, when the furrows bristle.

"His royal heart was melted,
As in a growing crop of wheat, when all the acres bristle,
A dew, descending genial, the ears doth warm and soften."
Newman.
— "who indeed"; 71.

487–88. "above all"; on 382; in a corresponding line, N 374, "concerning" is substituted for "above all."— "you indeed," equivalent to "you being such," stands for greater emphasis in both clauses.— "Muse...Apollo." Demodocus has been inspired either as a poet by the Muse, or as a prophet by Apollo, since the Homeric Apollo is not the god of song, though he presides over the mechanical art of playing on the cithara. The Muses know all, and can impart all, B 484–91; and the prophet, under the inspiration of Apollo, knows the past as well as the future, A 70; on theta 74.

489–91. "exceedingly...in due order," meaning "for quite in order due," referring both to his truthful portrayal, and to the proper sequence of events; cf. 87, 90, 500.— "fate," "doom"; 81, alpha 350. The following line is a further
10*

226 NOTES.

extension of "woe" (οἶτον), and by its repetitions emphasizes the woe, and indicates the particularity of the bard.— "so that" (ὥστε); on Book VI, line 122.—With "another's" (ἄλλου) supply "being present" (παρεόντος), from παρεών. Düntz. Gladstone, arguing that the poet lived within a generation of the war, thinks that Homer is glancing at his own case in this passage, and adds: "The idea seems here to be conveyed with distinctness that either actual experience, or, at the least, the evidence of those who had possessed it, was a condition of true excellence in historic song." Juv. Mundi, p. 5. On the other hand, Am. sees only a reference to the lively and vivid portrayal of the details.

492. μετάβηθι, "pass on," to another theme; cf. Hymn to Aphrodite 294, "beginning with you I will pass on to another hymn." 489 shows that he is asked to pass on from the earlier recital of the morning, 73. Odysseus is naturally most interested in that of which he has been a great part.— κόσμον, the setting-up of the parts in order, the building. Mure calls attention to the artistic epic arrangement of the following poem, in which the episode of the Wooden Horse ought, historically speaking, to form the introductory scene. But, instead of that, the subsequent operations of the Greek armament are first described, and there is not a word of the horse itself until, on the scene shifting to Troy, it is found already within the walls. Here, then, was the proper place for the description of the fabric and equipment of the horse, with a list of heroes it contained, as a retrospective episode. That this does not appear may be due to the brevity of the epitome, and to other more commanding incidents; so that, as it stands, the Stratagem of the Horse would be the more accurate title, since the poem must have comprised the whole series of events down to the recovery of Helen, as actually treated in the Cyclic Iliupersis.

493–94. δουρατέου ("of wood"); on Book VI, line 30.— Epeus; "Epeus, himself the maker of the trick," Virgil, Aeneid II. 264. In the Patroclean games he is victor in the boxing-match, but he acknowledges himself inferior in battle.— "with Athena" (σὺν Ἀθήνῃ); "they build the horse by divine art of Pallas," Aeneid II. 15; cf. Book VI, line 233.— τὸν, ὅν; two relative pronouns referring to the same antecedent, without connectives, are unusual; but see Book XI, line 382, Book XXIII, line 229.— δόλον, "as a means of deceit." The dative form δόλῳ is the reading of Aristarchus and Aristophanes according to the scholiast, but all MSS. give the accusative δόλον, which appears supported by insidias, Aeneid II. 36, doli, 264; cf.

BOOK VIII. 227

Eur. Tro. 530. — ἤγαγε ("he led"): because he was the originator and prime mover of the enterprise, and upon his firmness and decision its success depended; see δ 284.

495–98. ἐμπλήσας ("having filled"): this line forcibly presents not only the agency of Odysseus, but also the immense bulk of the horse. Virgil goes into greater detail, Aeneid II. 15, 20, 32, 262. — αἴ κεν: see η 75. — μυθήσομαι ("I will tell"): cf. 242, 251. — πρόφρων: "right heartily." — θεὸς ("god"): whether the Muse or Apollo; 488. — θέσπιν: "god-spoken," the poet being only the mouth-piece of the deity.

499–500. δ δ': is this used in Attic prose? H. 525 (γ). — ὁρμηθεὶς θεοῦ: "stirred by the god;" H. 582 a. — φαῖνε: "brought to light," showing plainly that φαίνω and φημί are from the same root; on 142. — ἔνθεν . . . ὥς: "seizing on the theme from the point that tells how," with reference to 492. At the opening of the Odyssey the Muse is called upon to begin ἀμόθεν, "at some point," α 10. — ἐΰσσέλμων: "well-decked," according to Am., Düntz., Aut., F., Seiler. σέλμα does not occur in Homer; ἴκρια, ν 74, is used instead. — Construe ἐπὶ νηῶν with βάντες.

501–3. ἀπέπλειον: "were sailing away," doubtless to Tenedos, as in the Aeneid, and for the same purpose, though not distinctly so stated by Homer. Tenedos, however, is the first halting-place from Troy on the way toward Greece, γ 159. — ἐν: see ζ 116. — κλισίησι: huts of wood, etc., not tents. What anachronism is committed by Virgil, Aeneid I. 469, II. 29? — 'Αργεῖοι resumes οἱ μὲν as explanatory. — τοὶ is opposed to οἱ μὲν. — ἤδη: "already." — εἶατ': imperfect; cf. ζ 307, θ 512. — ἀγορῇ: in both senses, assembly, and place of assembly; for the agora of the Trojans was in the acropolis, H 345, B 788, as were also the palaces of Priam, Hector, and Paris, and the Temple of Athene.

504. αὐτοὶ ("the Trojans themselves"). By what artifice the Trojans were prevailed upon, Homer does not tell us. The story of Sinon appears first, so far as is known, in the Sack of Troy (Ilii-persis) of Arctinus. Heyne is supported by Conington in the conjecture that this story may have arisen from the account at δ 243–58, of the visit made to Troy by Odysseus in disguise, when he is recognized by Helen, and relates to her "the whole plan of the Greeks." This visit seems to have preceded the Stratagem of the Horse by only a short time, and to have been undertaken to gain "information," δ 258, leading to that

BOOK VIII. 229

Odyssey ζ 303. — ὅθ', ὅθι, "wherein." — πάντες: Homer names Odysseus, Tydides, Menelaus, and Antilochus, in book δ, and Neoptolemus, in book λ. Virgil gives other names, Aeneid II. 261–64. Stesichorus says they were a hundred.

514–16. ὡς; θ 76, 498, 500, ω 237. "The three forms of indirect speech (oratio obliqua) develop in the following order: First, the infinitive form; secondly, the optative form, which is chiefly post-Homeric, the optative for the indicative in Homer being restricted to a narrow class, the interrogative; and, thirdly, ὡς with the participle." Prof. Gildersleeve, "On the Articular Infinitive," Transactions of the American Philological Association, 1878, p. 9. — διέπραθον: what two changes in the verb-form for this? H. 383 D. — ἱππόθεν; "The horse, thrown open, gives them to the air, and joyfully they pour forth from its hollow belly, sliding down by the lowered rope," Aeneid II. 260. — ἐκχύμενοι, ἐκπρολιπόντες: when two or more participles are arranged without connectives, the order of time regularly follows that of their sequence; cf. 526–27. — ἄλλον falls back to the earlier idiom.

517. After the death of Hector and Paris, the chief command of the Trojans appears to have devolved upon Deiphobus, who, with his brother Helenus, commanded one of the five brigades marshalled against the Greek defences, Iliad M 94, and who follows Helen when she visits the horse at nightfall, δ 276. This would account for Odysseus' seeking his palace, and the heaviest battle taking place there: but the Lesser Iliad made Deiphobus marry Helen after the death of Paris; and though Homer nowhere says this, he has nothing inconsistent with it, so that it may be accepted as probably his view of the case. A special appropriateness is thus given to the presence of Menelaus there.

518–20. Ἄρηα; 115. — αἰνότατον πόλεμον. Virgil also takes Odysseus and Menelaus to the house of Deiphobus, but, with his usual tendency to degrade the character of Odysseus, he makes the death of Deiphobus a cowardly murder in his bedchamber, Aeneid VI. 521. — φάτο, the bard said; with a change of subject to Odysseus for the following infinitive.
