Such omissions of the subject of the infinitive, even when it is not the same as that of the primary verb, are frequent in Homer; cf. ζ 174, η 274, θ 466, ν 30; sometimes introducing obscurity, as θ 569, ν 177. — καὶ ἔπειτα, "then too," as well as on so many other occasions by her aid. When

230 NOTES.

she appears to him on landing in Ithaca, he entreats her to aid him in wreaking vengeance on the suitors, and begs her to stand by him, "as when we loosed the shining coronal of Troy;" Odyssey Book 13, line 388.

Lines 522–25. "Was melted:" the figure is from the melting of snow, as it is actually drawn out into a simile at Odyssey Book 19, line 205, when the tears of Penelope are described, as she is told by the disguised Odysseus how he had entertained her husband in Crete. — "she wept" (klaiesi): what peculiarities are there in the use of this subjunctive? See Goodwin and Middleton, Grammar 62, Note 3; on Book 6, line 183. — "husband" (posin) depends on the verb, but is also to be supplied with the participle. — "falling with her arms about:" — "in defence of," not "in front." The scene is plainly laid within the city after the enemy have passed the walls and the death-struggle is come. The preceding song naturally leads up to such a picture; but the presence of the wife on the battle-field among the foremost combatants, as usually interpreted, is not readily accounted for. Aeschylus, describing the sack of Troy, says: "for some had fallen around the bodies of men," Agamemnon line 326; cf. Euripides, Hecuba line 937; Iliad X 463, T 292, I 593–94. — "amunon:" present tense of attempted action.

Lines 526–28. "ton:" not the article; Odyssey Book 13, line 78. — "aspairont':" regularly of the gasping death-throes. — "chymene" exhibits the wildness of her abandonment to grief. — "hoi:" the foe. — "koptontes:" "smiting." No such maltreatment of captive women is directly mentioned elsewhere in Homer, but it is doubtless implied at Iliad Z 465, I 594. It was no soft-hearted age. Odysseus threatens Melantho, a female servant, that he will have Telemachus cut her limb from limb, Odyssey Book 19, line 339; and after the slaughter of the suitors, twelve of the serving-women are strung up in the yard, Odyssey Book 22, line 467. Antinous threatens Irus with deportation to Echetus, who will cut off his nose and ears, and otherwise mutilate him; and this punishment is actually inflicted on Melanthius, whose hands and feet are also docked, Odyssey Book 22, line 475. Zeus declares that Hera could eat the Trojans raw, Iliad Book 4, line 35. To Menelaus, inclined to spare Adrastus, Agamemnon shouts: "Spare none of the accursed race, not even the babe in the mother's womb!" Iliad Z 58; and he slays and lops off the head and hands of a suppliant, Iliad Book 11, line 146. Achilles wishes he could eat Hector raw, Iliad X 347; and, boring his dead feet through, he drags him behind his car, Iliad X 396. He promises to give Hector's body to the dogs to eat raw, and to slay twelve Trojan youths on the funeral pyre

BOOK VIII. 231

of Patroclus. Hecuba wishes she had the core of Achilles' heart to eat (Omega 213); and Priam asks whether Achilles has cut Hector's body to pieces and thrown it to the dogs (Omega 409).

529–30. "eireron" occurs only here, but contains the root ser of the Latin servus. — "eisanagoysi": the preposition ana here has been thought to intimate that the attacking party returns home by sea, as the Greeks from Troy, or to some high-perched citadel. — "both." — "ekhemen"; Zeta 82. — "tes" with "pareiai." This simile is remarkable even among Homeric similes for the prolongation of the picture, which extends even into the period of slavery; on Zeta 130.

531–35. "eleeinon," meaning "pitiable," exciting compassion; 530, Zeta 327. It does produce this effect on Alcinous; cf. Odysseus' own words, 489–90. The four following lines are repeated from 93–6. In consequence, the excisionists, as usual, suspect the whole passage. The more generous criticism of Ameis, Hartel, and Hermann sees no motive more naturally and poetically conceived for introducing the personal narrative of Odysseus than the lay of Demodocus, nor for the tears of the hero when reminded of all that he had done and suffered in company with his old-time comrades.

537–41. "skhethetô," meaning "stay," "hush"; Lambda 334. What peculiarities does this form have? H. 411. — "ou pôs," meaning "by no means," as read by thirteen manuscripts; not "ou pô," which always means "not yet." Am. Others admit that "oupô" may take the meaning of "oupôs." — "ex...aoidos," meaning "from what time we were supping, and the heavenly bard awoke the song." It seems best to take "dorpeomen" as imperfect, and "ôrore" as aorist, transitive as usual; on Eta 4. — "oizuroio," like "eleeinon," 531. — "phrenas"; cf. Zeta 235. — "amphibibêken," as the cloud about the Cyanean Cliffs; Mu 74.

543–47. "kallion"; Zeta 39, Eta 159. — "tetuktai," meaning "have been made ready"; Nu 40. — "pompê...dôra," explain "tad'." — "anti," meaning "in the place of." — "tetuktai," meaning "stands"; 384. The asyndeton is causal. The ethical tone of the Heroic Age stands at its highest, perhaps, in the strength of the domestic affections; on 178. The tenderness of this relation between brother and brother is exemplified especially by Agamemnon and Menelaus, Telemonian Ajax and Teucer. In the case of friends, the expressions are of the warmest. Achilles avers of the death of Patroclus that nothing worse could have befallen him, not even the death of his father,

232 NOTES.

T 321; and Ajax, seeing his comrade Lycophron fall, declares that he honored him as he did his beloved parents, O 439; cf. θ 585. — "ever so lightly touches aught with his mind" (oligon ... prapidесsin); though he skims but the surface, possessing no depth of thought and no depth of feeling; whose mind is but a weakling weapon (cf. 556, λ 344) that may strike the surface, but never penetrate beyond. With epipsauē, tinos may be supplied, to accord with the idiom as exhibited later.

548–49. "therefore" (tō); η 25; since our deeds and thoughts are so kindly. — "now" (nun), perhaps with reference to the way Arete's inquiry was met; on η 241. — "with thoughts of guile" (noēmasi kerdaleosin). Deceit and falsehood were common traits of the Greek character at all periods, and the frequent exhortation, throughout the poems, to speak truthfully shows that tone to be the prevailing one then. Odysseus, awakened from sleep after landing in Ithaca, being met by Athene, tells her a long story about his being a Cretan. She is delighted at his craft, and asserts that deceitful words are dear to him from the very bottom of his heart. On the other hand, Achilles stoutly maintains that the man is hateful as the gates of hell who hides one thing in his heart and another speaks, I 312; and much the same words are put into the mouth of Odysseus, ξ 156; cf. η 297, λ 364.

550–54. "eipt": why this accent? H. 100. — "that" (hotti); H. 556. — "there" (keithi), in its indefiniteness something like "that woman there" (tēnde), ζ 177. — "at all" (pampan) with "no one" (ou tis), as usual with a negative. It is a reduplicated form like the vulgar "at all, at all." — "bad" (kakos); ζ 187. The public beggar in Ithaca had been called Arnaios by his mother, but the young men nicknamed him Irus. — "when first" (epēn ta prōta), cum primum. The words epei, epeidē, to prōton, ta prōta, for metrical convenience, in Homer take the place of the usual prose epei takhista. — "they place upon" (epi tithentai), sc. a name (onoma). The naming of the child is here the joint act of the parents, as was customary, no doubt; I 561; but Irus is named by his mother, Odysseus by his grandfather, Scamandrius by his father. In Homer the individual name of the son is habitually distinct from that of the father, so that the patronymic is necessarily in frequent use for explicitness. Later, the name of the father or grandfather was often handed down; then, too, the father mostly chose the name, and it was conferred on the seventh day or the tenth.

BOOK VIII. 233

556–63. τῇ, "thither." — τιτυσκόμεναι φρεσὶ, "aiming sure in mind;" on line 547. — οὐ γάρ: on θ 35. — ἴσασι is used 10 times by Homer with the initial syllable long, 8 times short. For the thought, see on η 94. The common poetic personification of the ship, as at ι 127, is here carried to the extent that the galley understands the wishes of the crew, and takes them where they will. We may compare the winged steed of Oceanus which he directs "by the will of his mouth, without a bridle" (Aeschylus, Prometheus 287); and in modern times the Flying Dutchman, and the canoe of Hiawatha. — ἠέρι: on η 15. — ἐπί: θ 403, λ 367. Cf. η 192, 195, 319, 117. Yet the Phaeacians do have storms in the adjacent sea, as that which wrecks the raft of Odysseus, and they know its terrors; θ 138; on ζ 329, 42, θ 160–64.

564. "But as to that, in this wise once I heard my father speak." — τόδ' is an adverbial accusative, referring to the thought of the preceding line, the ship's immunity from harm; β 169, ξ 166. — εἰπόντος. The aorist participle regularly represents action which is past with reference to the time of the leading verb; G. M. 24; H. 717; accordingly, the natural meaning here would be, "I heard from another of my father's having said." In fact, this is the meaning assigned by Welcker, Mus. Phil. 1833. Nothing in the context will determine the matter; but in ι 497, φ 210, κ 276, ρ 492, the context does show beyond a doubt that the act of hearing is an immediate one, and that the aorist participle is coincident in time with that of the primary verb (G. M. 24, Note 1 and 2; H. 717 a.), a usage which Curtius claims to be the proper and original one, from which the other was developed (Eluc. p. 217); so Leo Meyer, Griech. Aoriste, p. 125, with special reference to ν 319, Δ 99. The Homeric instances of participial construction after ἀκούω, and the kindred verbs κλύω, αἴω, πυνθάνομαι, ξυνίημι, may be grouped under two heads: A. where the perception is immediate — one hears with his own ears; B. where it is mediate — one hears from another. Belonging to A., we have the aorist at θ 564, ι 497, φ 210, κ 276, ρ 492, Υ 380, Β 182, κ 47, Π 76, δ 505, Α 381, 453, Π 531, 236, Ζ 281, γ 337; the present at Ο 506, 199, κ 221, Α 396, Φ 475, θ 95, 534, δ 76, κ 189, Λ 463, μ 265, Π 515, ζ 325, Ι 509, Τ 79, β 423, τ 419. Belonging to B., the aorist at δ 728, 748, β 375, Ρ 379, 427, Ν 521, Τ 322, 337, ρ 115; the present at λ 458, α 289, β 220, Ω 490, π 301, Η 129, γ 94, δ 324, 732, Α 257; the infinitive at Ζ 386, Ω 543; cf.

234 NOTES.

π 242, σ 127. All the aorists of A. may be considered coincident, being distinguished from the presents by their conceiving the action as transient, instead of continuing. In B., the customary distinction of tense is fully maintained. This coincident aorist after verbs of hearing is properly a Homeric construction, but is sometimes imitated by the later poets, as Hymn to Demeter 27, Xenophanes 6, Aristophanes Clouds 291, 963, Apollonius Rhodius I. 278, Theocritus 13, 62, Babrius 73, Sophocles Philoctetes 615 (Kühn. Gr. 482, 1). The prose-writers employ the present regularly; but cf. Herodotus V. 93, Xenophon Symposium III. 13, Lucian Timon 30; on ν 58. See Proceedings of the American Philological Association 1877, p. 4–5.

565–69. ἀπήμονές ("unharmed"), with reference to line 563; cf. 32, ν 39. The subject of φῆ is Nausithous, with a change to Poseidon for the infinitive; on 520. — ποτὲ retains its accent because it begins the infinitive clause to which it belongs; similarly, Euripides Phoenissae 401, Orestes 44, where see Paley's note. — μέγα ("greatly"); on ν 152.

570–71. γέρων ("old man"), Nausithous. As he is the son of Poseidon, he may be supposed to have had his father's purpose imparted to him by the god himself; η 201; but divination is not confined in the Homeric age to professed prophets any more than it is later; Xenophon Cyropaedia I. 6, 2. Helen interprets an omen, ο 172; and the aged man, by his wide reach over the past, becomes ever more fitted to divine the future; α 200, η 157, Γ 109. — τὰ . . . θυμῷ, "and that the deity may possibly bring to pass, or it may remain unfulfilled, even as it is wont to be dear to him in his heart." The optative expresses the possibility cautiously, and with a nonchalance that is highly characteristic. — ἔπλετο; on ζ 185; H. 424 D. 35. — θυμῷ, 450, ν 145. The objection has been urged to the passage 564–71 that it is in the main a repetition of ν 173–78, and does not belong here; that Alcinous would not have sent Odysseus home after recalling the prophecy here, when he learns, as he does from Odysseus' own lips, that Poseidon is hostile to that hero. Such a conclusion to all the king's professions and promises would be lame indeed, proving him to be quite a different person from what he is otherwise sketched by the poet. It is plain that the expectation of the fulfillment of the prophecy in his lifetime rests but lightly on the mind of Alcinous (cf. μ 266), and the manner in which he dismisses it is so like him that it would be but poor

BOOK VIII. 235

recompense to barter such a trait for a blank. Most prophets are Cassandras till their utterances come true. Achilles rushes into battle, though warned by his horses that his death is near, T 409; cf. Herodotus I. 13, Virgil Aeneid IV. 464, III. 184; Odyssey ι 535, λ 115.

572–76. atrekeos ("accurately"); on line 548. — hoppe apeplangchthes, "in what way thou wast driven out of thy course." — choras, autous, polias, severally take the place of gaian, demon, polin, of line 555. — naietaosas; on η 29. What irregularity of form? Hadley's Grammar 370 D. Prof. Allen, arguing against the statement that contraction takes place and then duplication, lays down the following rule as containing the latest views on the subject: "The verbs in -ao, when uncontracted, commonly show an assimilation of the two concurrent vowels, so as to give for ae or ae a double a-sound, and for ao or ao a double o-sound. This assimilation is usually accompanied by a lengthening of one or both of the vowels." Transactions of the American Philological Association, 1873, p. 16. — chalepo i ("difficult"); ζ 120.

577–80. ho ti ("what"); Hadley 549. — endothi thumo ("within his heart"); on line 68. — The collocation "of the Argives and Danaans" is nowhere else found in Homer. Argeia occurs as an epithet of Helen and Here, and is probably used as such here. — epeklosaonto ("they spun out"); η 198. — anthropois, Greeks and Trojans. — hina ... aoide, "that there might be even for them of aftertime a theme of song." Upon the gods rests the blame of the war, and man should endure their inflictions with resignation; on ζ 187. It accords well with the tone of 570–71 to say that the war was scarcely worthy of tears (α 350), because its main purpose was to give to singers a theme for song. The author of the Cyclic Cypria says that Zeus ordained it in order to lighten Mother Earth of her burdensome weight of mortals; so Euripides, Helen 38. Herodotus maintains that the deity brought it to pass to show to men that great crimes were visited with heavy punishment by the gods, II. 120. — hina: since to the early Greek, as well as the Hebrew, the guiding hand of God was in all the ways of life (ζ 12), hina, ophra, hos, hopos, in such passages as the present, represent purpose only, not at all result; cf. ι 13, μ 428, π 195, λ 214, α 158, β 359, ζ 357; χ 373, κ 236. The rule thus established extends broadly later on, but probably holds to purpose throughout: see the question fully discussed by Tittmann, Winer, and the New-Testament commentators. — esi; form, η 94; mode, G. M. 44, 2; θ 511, ζ 173.

236 NOTES.

581–83. ἦ; H. 831. — τίς is accented from τοι. — πηός, from πάομαι, means a relative by affinity, not by blood; for such relationships, Homer has special names for father-in-law, mother-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, son-in-law, daughter-in-law, and a husband's sister-in-law, for which we have no single word. — πρό; Book VI, line 36. — γαμβρός: how is it formed? See H. 53. — οἵτε . . . αὐτῶν, "who are wont to be by far the nearest, after one's own blood and race." — μάλιστα, often used with the superlative; H. 665 b; cf. Book I, line 641.

584–86. κεχαρισμένα εἰδώς; Book VI, lines 12, 23; so εἰδέναι φίλα, Book III, line 277, χάριν, Book XIV, line 235, ἤπια, Book XIII, line 405; in general, for Homer, knowledge presupposes the feeling (Book VIII, line 547), or the action properly arising from it; to know what is pleasing to another is to act upon that knowledge by doing what will please (φίλα ἔρδοι, Book XV, line 360). This usage survived later in the phrase χάριν εἰδέναι, and we may compare the principle laid down by Socrates, that whoever knows what is right will do what is right. See Book VII, lines 111, 75, and Book XIX, lines 329–32. — πεπνυμένα, line 388. Note the delicacy with which Alcinous chooses to mention not the nearest and dearest, the blood relations. "The closing lines express the strong genius for friendship which animates Alcinous. No example of such an unselfish disposition is shown by any whom Odysseus had encountered; the friendship of all others who befriend him is somehow tarnished. Circe is cruel, Calypso selfish, Aeolus impatient and testy. Alcinous alone is the very jewel of friendship, and he appears just at the right time. The poet, no doubt, had in view the rarity of disinterestedness when he thus drew the characters which illustrate it." Hayman.

Here closes the Eighth Book. The Ninth opens with the narrative of Odysseus in which he discloses his name and relates his adventures among the Ciconians, Lotophagi, and Cyclopes, with Aeolus, among the Laestrygonians, and on the island of Circe; see the Summary for Books IX and X. At the opening of the Eleventh Book he sails to the mouth of Oceanus, near which he finds the entrance to the Underworld, from which the spirits of the dead come trooping up to be seen and questioned. First comes the seer Teiresias, to question whom has been the main purpose of his journey; then come the spirits of heroines of the past, among them his own mother. After he has told how these passed in review be-

BOOK XI. 237

Before him, the hero breaks off his recital with the words which open our short extract from the Eleventh Book.

BOOK XI.

328–30. ἄν; ζ 221, 126. The line is formulaic, as B 488, to introduce the Catalogue of Ships; δ 240, where Helen is speaking of the exploits of Odysseus; and λ 517, as Odysseus is relating to the shade of Achilles the valor of Neoptolemus. — ἀλόχους [wives], incorporated, as usual in the line following the preceding formula; η 214. — πρίν [before], as πάροιθεν, ζ 174. — φθίτ' [perished]: what peculiarity? H. 401 D. 1. — ἄμβροτος [immortal]; η 260, 283. — ὤρη [time]: the omission of ἐστί [is] in this phrase is regular. Compare the words of Aeneas when beginning the story of his labors: "And now damp night rushes headlong from the sky, and the falling stars urge sleep." Aen. II. 8.

331–35. ἐλθόντ' [having come]; on ζ 60. — ἑταίρους [companions], as θ 151. He has been promised departure that night, or, at all events, his departure is expected; η 317, θ 445; and he now reminds them of this in polite terms, and of his hunger for home. The general character of the language in which the wish is couched is purposely selected. — αὐτοῦ [here], a courteous addition. — θεοῖς ὑμῖν τε [to the gods and to you]: in such phrases the poet exhorts man to do all in his power, and then leave the issue to the will of the gods; ρ 601, P 514–15, Ψ 724, Hdt. VIII. 65. — μελήσει [shall be a charge], "shall be a charge;" η 53. This is a slightly milder form than the imperative uniformly in Homer, and is sometimes preceded by that mode, as E 429. — ἀκήν [in silence]; η 154. — κηληθμῷ δ' ἔσχοντο [and they were held in enchantment], "for with rapture were they spell-bound;" 368. — Ἀρήτη [Arete]; η 237.

336. "Phaeacians, how gifted does our hero here show himself to be?" Where an adverb occurs with the verb "to be," it may be translated by an adjective, πῶς [how] here being equivalent to ὁποῖος [of what sort], as the scholiast suggests; but, in fact, εἰμί is not the mere copula in such phrases; it has rather the sense, to be circumstanced so and so, to be in such and such a condition, the translation to be determined by the context; see Ameis on A 416. The construction is poetic; the adverb with ἔχω is prosaic. — ὕμμιν [to you (pl.)]; ζ 205.

238 NOTES.

337. The particle "ide" throws the main force on the last of the series, so that we have, in effect, "not only . . . and . . . but also." — See "endon" at Book VIII, 577. — See "eisas" at Book VIII, 98. With the whole thought, compare Dido's words after Aeneas has finished his recital, Aeneid IV. 10:

"What new guest has come to take his place among us here, / How nobly he presents himself, how brave in chest and arms!"

Like that, the expression of Arete is more of an exclamation than a question; one full of triumph, too, and of delight that he, whose outward appearance has won all, proves himself as commanding in intellectual gifts and in wondrous exploits; see Book VII, 312. Her whole speech has this tenor: What think you of this man now? Do you not perceive that he is the illustrious hero he seems, and who has been so often the theme of our minstrel's song? I see clearly by your looks that you do. It is true that he is my guest, and proud am I of the honor; but each one of you shares in it as well. His greatness demands from us all a fuller recognition. Wherefore, let him not depart in haste, and stint not your gifts to one so needy; for many are the treasures that lie in your halls through the gift of the gods.

338–41. The phrase "d' aut'," meaning "and furthermore," connects its sentence back to the approving answer to her question which plainly appears in their looks and gestures; see Book VI, 168. — See "emos" at Book VII, 142. — Account for the double-mu in "emmore"; Hadley's Grammar, 319 D. Poseidon says that when the allotment of the universe between Zeus, Aides, and himself took place, it was divided into three parts: "each one received his share of honor," Book XV, 189. — The word "ta" draws close to the Attic use of the article as a weak possessive, allowable instances of which in Homer, according to Krüger, are at Iliad IV, 399; XI, 763; XXIII, 75; Odyssey XI, 492; yet here it points to the gifts already presented and lying by her. — See "ioteti" at Book VII, 132.

342–46. See "Echeneos" at Book VII, 155. — See "hos"; this line is not found in some manuscripts, but the balance of authority for its genuineness is about even. — To what dialect does "man" belong? Hadley's Grammar, 852. — When is "hemin" written with eta, and when with short e? Hadley's Grammar, 232. — See "apo . . . doxes": "wide of the mark, nor wide of our expectation of her." — See "skopou": the figure is that of the common phrase "winged words," Book VII, 236; cf. Book VIII, 556, 547. — "Apo doxes" became later "para doxan." — "Periphron" occurs only here of Arete. It is the characteristic epithet of Penelope, occurring 48 times. Otherwise it is used of the trusty nurse and

BOOK XI. 239

housekeeper Eurycleia 4 times; in the Iliad, once of Aigialeia, the wife of Diomed. — "but" (alla); on θ 389. — "of Alcinous"; ζ 197. — "but" — "work . . . word," i.e., it is his to decree, and his to execute; η 161.

348–51. "this . . . I shall rule," "that, indeed, exactly so shall stand as a decree, if I at least, a live man, among the Phaeacians fond of the oar shall continue to rule." — "thus," as θ 465, and alluding to Arete's suggestion. — "it shall be," as 336. — "alive," with strong emphasis; on η 167, ζ 201, Α 88, η 147. — "longing for"; θ 156. — "yet at all events"; the word "then" is resumptive after the partially parenthetical clause, and the two answer to the prosaic "but then." — "to remain"; ζ 295. — "until tomorrow"; η 318. — "until"; ζ 295, ν 59.

352–53. "all . . . I shall complete," "the entire gift I shall complete;" referring to the promise implied in the word "word/promise," but with a cast of language as if he had had it in mind all the time to make the gift larger, which evidently he had not; cf. ν 40, Ι 598. This is quite in harmony with the trait θ 102, 246. — "escort . . . people." The development of this formula in the poems is a curious instance of that perpetual grafting of one set of words on another, that determination to dwell in familiar cadences, and run new matter in the same moulds, which Mr. Hayman has thought to mark the purely recitative poet, ever trading on his fund of memory. The simplest form of the present expression occurs Υ 137, where Poseidon says to Here, urging that both withdraw from the battle, "war shall be a care to men." To Andromache, begging Hector to pity her and abstain from battle, he replies: "Go thou home to thy tasks," "war shall be a care to all men, and most of all to me, who were born at Ilium," Ζ 492. So Telemachus ends his speech to his mother, who has appeared in the megaron to beg the bard to cease his mournful lay of the return of the Achaeans, with, "Go thou to thy room and thy tasks," "speech shall be a care to all men, and most of all to me; for the authority is mine in this house," α 358; and again, after the trial of the bow in her presence, he uses the same language precisely, with the substitution of "bow" for "speech," φ 352. In all these passages there is an opposition strongly marked; in the first, between gods and men, and in all the rest between woman's sphere and man's; cf. Aeneid VII. 444. So here: as to the gift, as Arete says; but the stranger's convoy home is the proper province of

240 NOTES.

us men. — "ἀνδρεσσι πᾶσι" may be explained from Hector's words, "those who were born in Scheria"; cf. 361. — The πομπή (escorting) of a stranger, according to the etiquette of the time, was the special charge of the lord of the house, as is plain from the words of Penelope, τ 312–16. — τοῦ, with a gesture indicating himself. — "κράτος . . . δήμῳ"; η 62, 23; "Kings are to be feared in their own flocks, for power is theirs," Horace, Odes III. 1, 5.

356–57. ἀνώγοιτ', ὀτρύνοιτε, διδοῖτε are continuative presents, meaning keep urging, keep preparing, keep giving. The statement is something of a pleasantry, but is in full harmony with the feelings of the age with respect to gifts, in which direction Odysseus has what we should call an especial weakness. No stronger inducement could be held out to him to remain. He has just been telling how his comrades were anxious to leave the Cyclops' den as soon as they ascertained the character of its possessor. But Odysseus must needs stay "to see, and get the meed of guest-ship." Menelaus grows rich beyond Greek experience by the presents he receives in his eight years' wanderings, and he suggests to Telemachus the wisdom of their making a tour about Greece before he returns to Ithaca, that he may gather a goodly store for future need. Even Achilles accepts the gifts of Agamemnon at their reconciliation. — εἰς ἐνιαυτόν ("for a year") is proverbial in the language of exaggeration; ξ 196, δ 595.

358–61. καί τὸ, "even that," with previous reference, as is most usual with ὁ. — Find the subject of εἴη in the following line. — αἰδοιότερος; θ 22. — ἰδοίατο; cf. θ 240.

363–66. Odysseus has now been persuaded to defer his departure, and the king accordingly proceeds in flattering terms to beg him to go on with his story, one main purpose of their urgency to have him remain. — τὸ . . . ἴδοιτο, "this, indeed, by no means did we think thee on seeing thee, namely, that thou wast a liar and an impostor, like as many the dark earth is wont to feed, men thick sown and ever fashioning falsehoods, whence one could not even see." — With τὸ supply ἔμεν, to which σ' is subject and τὸ predicate. τὸ here points forward, and is explained by the following line. — εἴσκομεν; on η 312. — πολυσπερέας describes πολλούς more fully; the figure is a common one, and supported by the preceding words. — Whether the reference in ὅθεν is to place

BOOK XI. 241

or material is doubtful; perhaps the sense is that the materials out of which the stories are woven have so little foundation in fact that they are like the net-threads Hephaistos spread about his couch — "not even one would see it" (θ 280); cf. ν 386; on η 297.

367–72. "To you," emphatic. — epi (upon); θ 563, Γ 45. — "form"; θ 170. —eni (within) for eneisi, and opposed to epi. The impostor might have the outward show of the glib speaker, but Odysseus possesses not only grace of language, but the inward worth as well. — "even as a bard;" no ellipse need be supplied. The expression is formulaic, like that of η 36. The poet is praising his own work. Eumaeus uses similar language to Penelope when describing the stories that Odysseus had been relating to him, ρ 518. Virgil so far forgets himself as to make Dido say of Aeneas' recital, "What battles she had sung to exhaustion" (Aen. IV. 14); on η 50. — "sagely," "right sagely." — "of all," limited to his immediate followers, somewhat as 353, θ 580. — "you saw," among the Shades. So far he had told only of the heroines, except Teiresias. — "along, along they went," analogous to the repetition of the preposition after a verb compounded with the same; on ζ 32.

373–75. "long"; on η 7: in the opposite season of the year, the spring, it is the days that are long, σ 367, κ 470. — "unspeakable," the impetuous language of the insatiate story-devourer. — "not even yet," "not even yet." How many a child, wide-eyed at a story half-told, has answered warnings like those of Odysseus, 330, in the same words! and Alcinous has much of the child about him. So Eumaeus amidst the fervor of story-telling, ο 392; cf. ο 494. — "but"; on θ 389. — "I could contain myself," be content. — "if so long;" on θ 240; cf. ε 189, ν 391, τ 589.

379. "There is time, it is true, for many words, but it is time also for sleep." Odysseus grants that the night is not so far spent but there is yet time for further story; but he still adheres to his original statement, in deferential language. Yet, if they are so anxious to have him proceed, he will comply.

380–84. "if indeed":

But if your desire is so great to learn of our misfortunes
And to hear briefly of Troy's final agony,
Though my mind shudders to remember, and shrinks back in grief,
I will begin.                                    Aen. II. 10.

242 NOTES.

—"if ... you desire": what irregularity of construction in this hypothetical sentence? H. 750; G. M. 54. — "of these" with "more pitiable," not with "I begrudge." — "to you" with "to speak," as "to me," 374. — "they," "they"; on Book VIII, 493. — "afterwards," explained in the following lines; Book VI, 174. — "escaped"; Book VI, 88. — "of the woman": Clytemnestra, as shown by the succeeding recital of the death of Agamemnon at her hands.

Odysseus here resumes the thread of his story, and tells of the heroes he saw among the Shades, till, terrified, he retreats to his ship and returns to Circe's abode. This closes the Eleventh Book. In the Twelfth, he tells how he left Circe, sailed on by the Sirens and the Cyanean Rocks, passed between Scylla and Charybdis, reached Thrinakia, where his comrades slay the oxen of the Sun, for which they are all destroyed on setting sail thence, leaving the hero alone, to be wafted back on the ship's keel, till he arrives at the isle of Calypso. Here his story connects with the account which he had given of himself in Book VII. He ceases, and the first twelve books of the Odyssey are ended.


BOOK XIII.

1–6. "Thus"; Book XI, 333. — "of bronze threshold": "of bronze threshold," Book VII, 83. This is otherwise an exclusive epithet of the palace of Zeus and that of Hephaistos on Olympus; hence, unusually splendid, as the rest of the palace. The threshold of the palace of Odysseus was of stone overlaid with wood. — "therefore ... you have suffered": "therefore by no means do I think that thou, in baffling courses driven, wilt return back home, even though very deeply thou hast suffered." — "therefore," correlative to "since," like "and so." — "driven far off course" is the emphatic word; cf. Book VIII, 461; not as thou didst go to the land of the Cyclopes, swept far away by all kinds of winds, over the mighty waste of sea, by another way, by other paths, Book IX, 259; but straight as thought reaches (Book VII, 36; Book VIII, 556) shalt thou go, because thou hast come where my ships can give thee convoy. — "even if": thy great sufferings in the past might argue thee to be beneath the ban of Heaven, as Aeolus said, Book X, 74 (cf. Book XIII, 331), and

BOOK XIII. 243

might promise still other perils on the deep; but nothing such waits those that I despatch.

7–9. ἀνδρὶ and τάδε belong to both verb and participle. — εἴρω, present tense of the common ἐρῶ, occurs only here and at β 162, λ 137. — γερούσιον, "Elders'," such as is set apart for the γέροντες, η 189; it is called ἔξαιτον, M 320. — αἰεὶ πίνετ', "always drinking"; η 99. On the first occasion, θ 390, he calls upon them to contribute on the ground that they are kings of the land; now, because they are habitual recipients of his hospitality. — Note the emphatic position of ἐμοῖσιν, "my own."

10–12. εὐξέστη exhibits what irregularity? H. 209; G. 63. Homer uses it 10 times to 4 of the other form; ζ 75. — χηλῷ; θ 424. — As πολυδαίδαλος is an epithet confined to objects highly ornamented, such as armor, necklaces, thrones, the chamber of Nausicaa (ζ 15), it seems to limit χρυσὸς to the goblet presented by Alcinous, θ 430; on θ 440. This leaves ἄλλα πάντα δῶρ', "all the other gifts," for the talents contributed by the others, but with a pompous sort of indefiniteness truly characteristic of the speaker. It is quite in keeping for him to single out his own gift separately; on θ 425. — ὅσα; θ 428; on θ 440.

13–15. τρίποδα; θ 434. — λέβητα: the lebes is used for boiling, as is the tripod, but, unlike that, it is also a wash-basin for the feet, τ 387, and the hands, η 173. It is doubtless the smaller vessel. The annexed cuts show a tripod-stand in the Cesnola Collection, from the vaults at Curium, and a lebes (see following page) from one of the sepulchres at Mycenae. — ἀνδρακάς, "man by man," severally. Observe the language, differing from θ 389–93, in order to include the speaker. — ἡμεῖς . . ., "and we hereafter, levying for ourselves among the people, will repay ourselves; for burdensome is it that one without recompense should bestow lavishly." — ἀγειρόμενοι, indirect middle; H. 689; G. 199, 2; commonly

244 NOTES.

This verb falls under H. 688; G. 199, 1. The first contribution was considered all that custom demanded; and since the one now asked for was something extraordinary, he proposes to distribute the burden among the people. In like manner, Odysseus tells Penelope that he, as the brother of Idomeneus, had entertained her husband in Crete on his way to Troy, giving to him and his force of twelve ships barley and dark wine after he had gathered it among the people, "from the people having collected," Odyssey 19.197. In this way, too, Odysseus says he will make up for the riot of the suitors, Odyssey 23.358; cf. 2.77, 22.55. The estimate placed upon the entire gifts of the Phaeacians may be seen from Odyssey 13.137–38. — "one," used indefinitely of a small number, as "one and two," Iliad 2.346. — "as a free gift," later form used adverbially. Scholiast. — "to grant as a favor," Odyssey 7.176, 17.452. When Glaucus exchanges his armor of gold, worth a hundred oxen, for that of Diomed, of copper, and worth nine oxen, the poet declares that Zeus had deprived him of his senses, Iliad 6.234.

16–19. "was pleasing," Odyssey 8.506. — "who," Odyssey 7.229. — "when," Odyssey 8.1. — "came rushing upon," Odyssey 8.38, 417. — "manly," personifying its noun; cf. Iliad 13.191, 4.420, Odyssey 8.507. Elsewhere in our poet it is applied to wine only, and there a similar personification is intended; on Odyssey 7.182. Here it is the material, bronze, rather than the vessels, that is held in view. In its strength, temper, cutting qualities, and boundless use, bronze well deserves to be called the manly among its companion metals, gold, silver, and lead.

BOOK XIII. 245

20–3. "well" (εὖ); θ 427, 439. — "himself" (αὐτὸς); on ζ 76. — Construe "under the yoke" (ὑπὸ ζυγὰ) with "he placed" (κατέθηχ'). In the same place the lotus-charmed scouts of Odysseus are bestowed bound, ι 99. — "companions" (ἑταίρων); θ 151. — "they might hamper" (βλάπτοι). The care bestowed upon the presents is shown by "well" (εὖ); thoughtfulness for the rowers harmonizes with θ 39, ν 69. A clear field is also assured for a display of their speed, which he is so anxious to prove to his guest; θ 247. — "they might be speeding them" (σπερχοίατ'); cf. 115. — "heed" (ἀλέγυνον); θ 38.

24–30. "To these" (Τοῖσι); θ 59. — "to Zeus" (Ζηνὶ); η 164. — "having kindled" (κήαντες) lacks what element? H. 381 D. For the brevity with which this second sacrifice and feast in honor of the guest (λ 338) is despatched, we may compare the description of the games of θ, after the space allotted to them in the Iliad; on θ 108. — "of wide renown" (ἐρικυδέα), an epithet regularly of the gods, or that connected with them; on ζ 58. — "sang" (ἐμέλπετο); ζ 101. — "honored" (τετιμένος); θ 472. — "turned" (τρέπε), from the bard sitting midway of the hall, θ 66, 93, against a pillar where he would be out of the direct line of vision through the open doorway, over against which the sun seems to have been conceived as setting; on η 84, 289. — "shining all around" (παμφανόωντα); H. 472, Rem. k. — "to set" (δῦναι), subject "him" (αὐτὸν), the sun; on θ 520.

31–2. "all day long" (πανῆμαρ). Odysseus, challenging Eurymachus to a ploughing match for a hard day's work, takes it for granted that they shall be hungry till dark, σ 370. The woodcutter of Λ 86, however, takes a lunch at noon; on the Shield, the harvesters have a dinner in the field, Σ 558, and the ploughmen receive a cup of wine at the end of each round furrow, Σ 545. — "fallow field" (νειὸν); θ 124. — "then" (ἀν'); on ζ 172. — "they might draw" (ἕλκητον); on ζ 183. — "two oxen" (βόε): at σ 372 the "points" of a yoke of oxen are given: tawny, large, both having grazed their fill of grass, of the same age, matched in strength. In Ν 703, we have the simile of the two Ajaxes supporting each other side by side, like two oxen before the plough. — "fitted together" (πηκτὸν): Hesiod distinguishes two kinds of plough, the fitted plough (πηκτὸν) and the self-grown plough (αὐτόγυον), both of which the farmer ought to have on hand, so that if one breaks, the other may be put to service. The former is made of three pieces—the handle of live oak, the share of common oak, and the pole of bay or elm; the latter is all of a single piece as it came from the forest.

33–7. "went down" (κατέδυ); on ζ 185, η 217. — "to go to" (ἐποίχεσθαι); η 174. — "suffers harm" (βλάβεται); so the soldier who goes hungry and thirsty to battle, Τ 166.

246 NOTES.

Virgil applies the phrase to Entellus, "the knees tremble and give way slowly" (Aeneid V. 431). The knees are commonly regarded as a seat of strength. — "To Odysseus"; on zeta 248; H. 189 D. — "especially addressing himself;" on theta 499.

39–43. "Unharmed"; theta 566, eta 266. — "Farewell"; theta 408. In the time of the scholiast the formula of farewell was "be safe." — "Has been accomplished"; theta 544, lambda 352. — "Dear friend"; theta 178. — "The send-off" doubtless includes the preparations for departure, the farewell banquet, etc., so that it may be loosely included in the subject of "has been accomplished." — "Heavenly ones"; eta 242. — "Blessed"; eta 148, theta 413. — "blameless ... dear ones," "and my spotless wife at home on having returned may I find, together with my dear ones safe." Finding his wife at home was to find her unwedded. If wedded, she would have gone elsewhere to the house of her husband; lambda 178, omicron 15, pi 33, phi 77. — "Blameless" is merely a standing epithet, not a predicate; the thought is different, Aeschylus, Agamemnon 606. — "Dear ones" refers to Telemachus, Laertes, etc.

44–6. "Make happy." — "Excellence/prosperity," meaning prosperity, good fortune and health, especially the outer good things of life. Under the rule of the just, god-fearing king, the dark earth bears wheat and barley in plenty, laden are the trees with fruit, the flocks bring forth without fail, the sea offers its fishes, "and the people flourish," tau 114. — "Evil," opposed to "prosperity/excellence"; cf. theta 414.

47–52. "Thus"; eta 226. — "And"; eta 178. — "Having prayed," where we should expect "having made libation," 39, 55; but a prayer of some kind habitually accompanied the libation; cf. iota 172–77, pi 227–31, gamma 394, omicron 258. In the last two passages "to pour a libation" and "to pray" occur together. — "Let us send"; eta 193, theta 556.

53–7. "Thus"; eta 182–83. — "In turn," stopping by each. — "From their places," defined more accurately by "from their seats"; cf. theta 68. At their meals it was customary to make the libation as they sat; the exception, gamma 341, is in consequence of the special occasion. Their sitting is mentioned here to point the contrast in the act of Odysseus; so Agamemnon is said to sit in the assembly, contrary to the usual custom, when he speaks, Tau 77. He sits because of a severe wound, Tau 52. — "Arete"; theta 478. Rightly are his last words addressed to her as his first had been, eta 146. — "In the hands": guests in Homer pledge their hosts, as Odysseus does Achilles, Iota 224. The scholiast notes: Odysseus, when

BOOK XIII. 247

pledged by Antinous, σ 121, pours a libation, drinks, and returns the cup, σ 151. — δέπας [cup]; θ 89.

58. When Classen would make φωνήσας [having spoken] before a speech — alongside φθεγξάμενος [having uttered], K 139, αὔσας [having called out], Δ 508, ὁμοκλήσας [having shouted at], E 439, ἐπευξάμενος [having prayed], Z 475, ἀπειλήσας [having threatened], H 225 — as inceptive only, his range is too narrow. In the field of the circumstantial participle, these are good examples of the coincident aorist; on θ 564. Their time is that of the primary verb, and they represent the manner in which the act of the primary verb is performed, or the means, so that φωνῇ [with his voice] replaces φωνήσας, Γ 161; see ω 530–35, Δ 508, ξ 492, Ω 170, "φωνήσας φωνῇ μεγάλη εἶπε" [he spoke aloud with a great voice], Luke xxiii. 46; on θ 499; η 279, θ 15, Acts i. 24. It is noticeable that Herodotus, who so persistently turns Homeric into his own prosaic expressions, habitually says "ἔφη λέγων" [he said, speaking], "ἔφησε λέγων," "ἔλεγε φάς," "εἶπε φάς," "ἔλεξε φάμενος," just as he turns ἀπειλήσας of H 225 into ἀπειλέων (I. 128).

59–62. Χαῖρέ [Farewell], as θ 461. — μοι, "is my prayer;" on ζ 199. — διαμπερὲς [forever]; θ 245. — πέλονται [it comes to be]; death, the universal, not even the gods are able to keep from a human being, however dear, γ 236. — ἐγὼ [I], opposed to σύ [you]; νέομαι [I shall return], to τέρπεο ἐνί [take joy in]. — τέρπεο, "ever be happy," in thought a passive to εὐφραίνοιτε [may he rejoice], 44. For the sentiment, compare his words to Nausicaa, ζ 180–85, θ 467–68.

63–9. οὐδὸν [threshold]; η 135. — προΐει [sent forth]; θ 399. — ἐπὶ [upon]; θ 50. — δμωὰς [handmaids]; η 103. — τὴν [the]; θ 374–75. — φᾶρος [robe]; on θ 425. — χηλὸν [chest], a good stout load, one may well think, with its thirteen full suits, not to mention the gold; cf. χ 142–45. — σῖτόν [food]: Odysseus is expected to sleep through the voyage (η 318, θ 445, λ 331), and therefore the remark of the scholiast that the food is intended for the crew on their way home is natural. They do not take it from the vessel, ν 120, nor does Odysseus miss it when, upon waking, he counts his treasures so anxiously, ν 217–19. It is another mark of Arete's careful housewifery (ζ 76), and that kindly thoughtfulness for others which has made her the idol of all her people; η 71–4; cf. also θ 39.

70–3. Αὐτὰρ [But]; θ 50. — πομπῆες [escorts]; θ 35. — κατέθεντο [they stowed]: this middle form is habitually used of one's own possessions, garments or armor, and here, accordingly, it is selected with special reference to the food and drink as intended for the escort; and upon this the thought is made to dwell altogether in the following words. πόσιν καὶ βρῶσιν [drink and food], therefore, form only a loose appositive to τάγ' [provisions]. — ἅπασαν is made by Düntz. equivalent to παντοίην [of every kind], as πᾶσαν

248 NOTES.

"food, such as men eat," epsilon 196; cf. iota 222, Alpha 5. — "they spread out": eta 336–37. — "linen," also a part of the bed prepared for Phoenix in the tent of Achilles, Iota 661.

74. "From the deck": there were two decks in each ship, one fore and one aft, covering only part of the space, the rest being occupied by the crew; see the ship of the Pelesta above, p. 109. It is upon the after-deck that Telemachus sits with Athene on the voyage from Ithaca to Pylos, and with Theoclymenos on his return. There, too, he was to have slept, had he not been entertained by Nestor in his palace, gamma 353; cf. mu 206, 217, 229, 412. This deck was probably more spacious, and the fore-deck may have been kept free for the lookout.

75–7. "At the stern": used as an adjective with "ship" at zeta 170. — alpha-nu; zeta 253; at theta 55. — "upon"; theta 37. — "each one"; zeta 189; the singular is most frequent, as there, the plural occurring quite rarely, except in the neuter. — "in order," unusual for the formulaic "in succession." — "the mooring cable"; zeta 269; it passed through the hole in a post set in the dock, and moored the stern of the vessel close to shore; theta 55. — "of the pierced stone," showing the conveniences of the regular dock. At kappa 96, Odysseus, warily keeping outside the harbor of the Laestrygonians until he learns their character, ties the stern cable to a rock.

78. "Throwing themselves back": The poet has not selected for his point of view the first motion, leaning forward to catch the water, as he has done at iota 489, when the rock hurled by the Cyclops has fallen in front of the vessel and the wave is driving them back to land. Then Odysseus says he ordered them to put in the oars... and they, falling forward, rowed; cf. kappa 129, mu 194. So Virgil in his phrases, "we surge with oars," Aeneid III. 207, V. 189; "bending to the oars," III. 668; "leaning on the oars," V. 15; "they lean forward," V. 198. But "with muscles drawn back," V. 141, and "oars pulled back," VIII. 689, present the opposite point of view — that moment, as in the text, when, with the oar swept through the water, the greatest impetus for that stroke is given to the vessel; cf. Ovid, Metamorphoses XI. 461, "They draw back the oars in double rows toward their strong chests." — "they kept throwing back" presents what unusual form? Hadley 370 D, b; Goodwin 120, 2.

79–80. "Nēdumos": uncertain in both derivation and meaning. Sweet, refreshing, fettering, painless — these are some of the meanings derived from it; cf. the note on eta 289, and Virgil's imitation describing

BOOK XIII. 249

the last sleep of Deiphobus: "Sweet and deep rest, most like to peaceful death," Aeneid VI. 522. — "closest to Death": in the Iliad, Sleep is the twin brother of Death, Ξ 231, Π 672.

81–3. The word "which" (ἥ), referring to the ship, stands without grammatical construction, since "stern" (πρύμνη) at line 84 takes its place. — "as on a plain four yoked male horses, all started together under the blows of the lash, high leaping quickly accomplish the course." In this simile the prime point of comparison is not the swiftness, which is indeed implied, but the bounding of the ship over her course. The moment selected at the outset is kept in view throughout. As the ship is then under the strongest impulse forward, the prow would be ploughing into the water and the stern raised. When, however, the oars are lifted from the water and thrown back for a new stroke, the prow rises, to be again depressed by the force of the stroke. The continuous wave-like curve thus formed is like that of the horses bounding over the plain. The alternate rising of stern and prow would be much more noticeable under the alternate stroke and cessation in rowing than with sail spread. The description throughout seems to imply that the mast and sail of θ 52 were not used. If the statement of η 319 be taken literally, this would necessarily be the case; in fact, it is the skill and strength in rowing that are kept in sight through all the Phaeacian episode, and are the great pride and boast of the king; ζ 269, η 109, 319, 328, θ 37, 53, 112, 247, 253, 386, ν 115. So far as can be gathered, rowing and sailing at the same time are contrary to the practice of the Homeric voyager; he may employ the oar in getting out of a harbor, λ 640, or in entering it, Α 435, or on the high sea when the wind fails him, μ 169–72; but he is only too glad when the wind springs up to relieve him from his toil. Here, however, the purpose of the poet is a different one, and he uses language quite distinct from that for a ship under sail, β 428, Α 481. — "four-horsed": in the chariot-race, two horses were habitually employed; so, too, in war, though a third as outrigger is sometimes mentioned. Aristarchus rejected the line Θ 185, where the names of four horses are given as those of Hector's war-chariot, and at Λ 699 the language renders it doubtful whether one chariot with four or two with a pair to each are sent to the games. Hence some have

250 NOTES.

considered the use of four horses to the car as post-Homeric, and our present passage a late addition. Many customs of the Homeric day are known only from his similes. Herodotus states, IV. 189, that "the Greeks learned from the Libyans to yoke four horses to the chariot," but at what time he does not say. Rawlinson thinks the usage originated in Egypt, and passed thence to Libya and Greece, and asks, "Can Herodotus intend to assert a connection between Greece and Libya proper in the ante-Homeric times?"—a pertinent question in the light that has recently been thrown, by the decipherment of Egyptian records, upon the presence of Aryans in Libya long before that period. The four-horse chariot is said to have been introduced into the Olympic Games 676 B.C. — ἄρσενες [males]. The superiority which the Greeks, in general, were accustomed to concede to the mare above the male horse does not yet appear in Homer. On the contrary, the latter is more highly esteemed. The divine horses of Achilles are male, and those too of Diomedes taken from Aeneas, and those of Antilochus and Rhesus; so also those cut in relief on the stelae above the sepulchres at Mycenae. The mares of Eumelus are highly praised; but Agamemnon's mare Aithe is spoken of as if it would be a disgrace to be passed by her, only a mare. — ἅμ' [together], so that their motions are all in unison, like those of the rowers. — πληγῆσιν [with blows]; they are struck on the fore-shoulder, O 352, Psi 500. — ὑψόσ' [upward]; theta 375, Psi 500.

84–7. πρύμνη [stern]: beginning with the whole vessel, the poet now returns to the point of view assumed in ἀνακλινθέντες [reclining]. — κῦμα . . . θαλάσσης [wave of the sea]; cf. the formulaic line for the ship under sail: "and around the prow the dark-blue wave roared loudly as the ship moved," A 481, beta 427; there the prow, here the stern. — πολυφλοίσβοιο [of the loud-roaring sea], a standing epithet here, as nu 220, Psi 59; cf. zeta 26, theta 378. — ἡ . . . ἔμπεδον, "she very steadily ran on without ceasing." — ἀσφαλέως [steadily]; theta 171. — ἔμπεδον [steadily]; eta 259. The same expression of a stone dislodged from a height and bounding downhill, N 141. — ἴρηξ [hawk], the genus, more closely defined by the species κίρκος [falcon]; the order is reversed in our "gyrfalcon," i.e. gyrating falcon. Sailing in circles is characteristic of the hawk family. ἴρηξ and κίρκος are elsewhere used separately by the poet, but he does not distinguish sharply between them. The former represents in similes the speed of Apollo, Poseidon,

BOOK XIII. 251

and Thetis. They are both the enemies of doves, starlings, and daws. The kirkos is the swift messenger of Apollo, at o 526, as the bird of omen, and the derivation of irex from hieros indicates the same. Virgil calls the hawk sacer ales; and the Egyptians had a hawk-headed deity, a symbol of the sun.

88–92. "Running" (theοusa); theta 193. — "To the gods" (theois); H. 603a. — "Having no plans" (mede' echonta); zeta 18, 12; the fuller form is seen at tau 353, "holding shrewd plans in mind" (pukina phresi mede' ech.); cf. eta 218, lambda 445; "Odysseus, equal to Zeus in counsel" (Odyssea Dii metin atalanion), B 169. — "Who" (hos); theta 155, 182–83. — "Then indeed" (de tote) corresponds to "now then" (nun de), theta 156; the phrase is unusual, but has its exact parallel at o 228. — "He slept" (eude). An apt allusion is made to this passage by Antileon, one of the Ten Thousand. After all the dangers and toils of their wearisome march to the sea had come to a close at Trapezus, the force assembled to consider plans for the remainder of the journey. Antileon declared himself tired of packing up and walking and running and carrying arms and marching in ranks and keeping guard and fighting; he longed to cease from these toils, and to sail the rest of the way to Greece, "stretched out like Odysseus sleeping" (ektatheis hosper Odysseus katheudon), Anab. V. 1, 2.

93–5. "Star" (aster), named the Dawn-bearer (Heosphoros), Psi 226; on theta 1. — "Rose above" (huperesxe), "had uprisen;" so of the sun, Lambda 735; zeta 107. — "Will announce" (angellон): the future participle is the regular form in such expressions, as "will say" (ereousa), B 49, "will say" (ereon), Psi 226; on zeta 50. The scholiast on Chi 318, citing this passage, writes angeleon.

96. Phorcys is said, at alpha 72, to be the father of the nymph Thoosa who bore Polyphemus to Poseidon, and he is there also a ruler of the sea. In Hesiod he is son of Pontos and Gaia, and the Graiai are born to him from Ceto. Virgil mentions him, V. 240. — "Harbor" (limen): some have found this in the north end of Ithaca, others in the small bay on the south side of the great gulf that runs in from the east, and severs the island nearly in twain. The two schools have been able to fix all the places mentioned in the Odyssey about either spot. The poet's knowledge of Ithaca appears actually to have been rather vague. — "Old man of the sea" (haliοio gerontos), also of Nereus, Lambda 556, and Proteus, delta 384; they belong to the same class of deities. Hesiod says, "they call Nereus 'the old man' (geron), because of his soothfastness, kindness, and justice;" Theog. 235.

97–101. "Two... from outside" (duo... ektothen), "and in it are two jutting crags precipitous, towards the harbor crouching, which set a shelter against

252 NOTES.

the huge wave raised by danger-breathing winds without." The point of view is from the sea, and as one looks shoreward he sees two forelands shoot boldly out from the coast, but soon, changing direction, they sweep round towards each other till their heads nearly meet, as if their early bravery had paled before the fury of the sea, and they had shrunk back like the Phaeacians beneath the whir of the discus (Odyssey Book 8, line 190), or the fledglings through terror of the snake (Iliad Book 2, line 312). In Virgil's imitation (Aeneid III.535), the coast is personified and said to throw out its arms to enclose the harbor; here each promontory is a separate individual personified. — "aneemon" (of winds): causal genitive, as in Iliad Book 2, line 397. — "entosthen" (within): contrasted, both in position and in sense, with "ektothen" (without). — "desmooio" (of the anchorage): line 77; Book 8, line 55; cf. "Here no chains hold the weary ships" (Aeneid I.168), where the present passage has been imitated as a whole. — "hormou metron" (the limit of the roadstead): here "metron" is used, like "telos" and "terma," of the point where the measure ends.

Lines 102–4. "tanuphyllos" (long-leaved): Six principal sorts of the olive have been distinguished, of which the long-leaved is chiefly cultivated in France, the broad-leaved in Spain. This tree appears to have been purposely selected here, because of its close connection with Athene. It is at its foot that she seats herself (Book 13, line 372), and then it is called "hiere" (sacred). — "eperaton" (lovely): of the picturesque scenery of Ithaca itself (Book 4, line 606); on Book 7, line 79. — "eerooeides" (misty, dim): line 150. The cave of Scylla has the same epithet (Book 12, line 80). — "nymphaon" (of the nymphs): Book 6, lines 322, 123. To these nymphs Odysseus had been wont, in happier days, to sacrifice (Book 13, line 350), for they had a special worship in Ithaca; on Book 8, line 469.

Lines 105–6. "amphiphoreis": usually a large two-handled jar for wine, flour, honey, or oil. The ashes of Patroclus are deposited in one of gold. — "lainoi" (of stone): F. suggests that the conception may have had its origin from the fanciful shapes of some stalactite cave that had fallen under the poet's observation. — "entha d' epeita" (and there too): "epeita" introduces an additional point in the description, as in Book 5, line 73. — "tithaibosssousi" (store their combs): Buchholz infers from this that the domestication of the bee was well known in the Homeric age. Whether or not the inference is legitimate, the fact seems more than probable from the frequent mention of honey and wax in the poems. Honey was their only means of sweeten-

BOOK XIII. 253

ing. Mention of the close connection between bees and nymphs is frequent among both Greeks and Romans. See especially the story of the nymph Melissa, and that of Aristaeus in Virgil's Fourth Georgic.

107–8. en, as at 105, 109, within the cave. — histoi, "looms." Virgil, in his "living rock seats, home of the Nymphs" (Aeneid I. 167), omits such wonders, and follows rather Odyssey mu 318, "where there were beautiful dancing-grounds of nymphs and seats." As the nymphs here, so Circe, Calypso, and even Athene practise weaving. In the German stories, too, the water-nymphs are generally so employed. — haliporphyra; zeta 53.

110–12. hai, plural, because thyra is usually so, though of a single entrance, as at zeta 19. The entrance alone here is meant, the cave being a natural one. Athene closes it with a stone after the valuables have been hidden within it, nu 370. — pros, over against, "fronting;" on zeta 207. — kataibatai, "entered." katabaino is the idiomatic word for passing any threshold into a room. This entrance faces the sea, and may be used by men at any time; but the other, deep in the recesses of the hills, has never been discovered by man. Known to the immortals, it is more used by them than the other; hence theoterai is fully comparative in that sense. — keini, "thereby." — athanaton, here primarily of the nymphs, secondarily of any of the gods; for the gender see kappa 462–63. The nymphs are immortal in Homer; Hesiod limits their existence to 9720 times the life of a man; on zeta 123. Porphyrius, a philosopher of the third century A.D., wrote a volume, still extant, entirely allegorizing the description of the cave. It is a curious specimen of a kind of criticism of Homer that often meets us in the scholia, and upon which much ingenuity of the philosophers of all schools was expended. Porphyrius is of opinion that the cave means the world; it is called gloomy, but agreeable, because it was made out of darkness, and afterwards set in this agreeable order by the hand of the Deity. It is consecrated to the nymphs, i.e., it is destined to the habitation of spiritual substances united to the body: the bowls and urns of living stone are the bodies that are formed out of the earth; the bees that make their honey in the cave are the souls of men, which perform all their operations in the body, and animate it; the beams on

254 NOTES.

which the nymphs roll their webs are the bones, over which the admirable embroidery of nerves, veins, and arteries is spread; the fountains are the seas, rivers, and lakes of the world; the two gates are the two poles—through the northern the souls descend from heaven to animate the body, through the southern they ascend to heaven after death.

113–15. "There" — "they drove in"; Book 7, line 109 — "knowing it before." The poet takes it for granted that Ithaca is well known to them, as Odysseus gives them no directions touching their course, and all that Alcinous asks for, Book 8, lines 555–60, is the name of his country. The knowledge which the ships possess is at the same time predicated of the rowers. So, apparently, of Euboea, Book 7, line 322. — The relative pronoun referring to the omitted object of "they drove in." — "beached." — "as much as"; Book 7, line 108. — "up to the half;" used as a substantive. — "hastening," line 22; on line 81. The ships of Odysseus, sailing on in the deep night, beach unexpectedly on the island off the coast of the Cyclopes, Book 9, line 148.

116–19. "well-yoked," stoutly built, with beams passing across from side to side to strengthen the vessel; these may have served for rowing-benches also. — "with it itself"; Book 8, line 186. — "having been built"; Book 7, line 318. — "down," "upon." The status of the preposition in Homer has been well exhibited by Prof. W. S. Tyler, Transactions of the American Philological Association, 1874, pp. 5–14, from which the following is taken, with statistics added to cover the selections here printed. The prepositions were originally and properly adverbs, expressing such essential relations as up and down, over and under, etc., and would, in the nature of the case, gradually pass from mere adverbs, denoting the direction of motion or action, into prepositions expressing the relations between such motions or actions and the places, persons, and things affected by them. In Homer we see this class of words in the transition stage between adverbs and prepositions, sometimes standing alone, with a fully adverbial force, and even when prefixed to a noun or compounded with a verb sometimes hovering between the office and force of the adverb and preposition. 121-24. διὰ, "through the instigation of;" θ 520; at ν 305, the goddess says it was done "by my will and purpose" (ἐμῇ βουλῇ τε νόῳ τε). — παρὰ; θ 458. — ὁδοῦ: the spot where they land is plainly at some distance from the city, and out of sight of it; yet a road is conceived as running thence past the cave, occasionally used by wayfarers, ν 221, and by those offering sacrifices to the nymphs at the cave. Bypaths also lead up over the hills, one of which Odysseus follows to the hut of Eumaeus. In another anchorage, also remote from the town, Telemachus lands to visit Eumaeus on his return, while his companions proceed to the city, ο 497; and Athene, α 185, pretends that her vessel has been left at a distance, not in the city harbor; cf. ω 308. — μή; θ 444. — πρίν; on ζ 331. — ἔγρεσθαι violates what rule of accent? H. 367 D. — δηλήσαιτο: the articles are evidently screened by their position from the casual observation of the chance passer, though Odysseus sees them at once on waking, ν 203.

125. Why the poet brings Odysseus to his home asleep, and makes the Phaeacians depart without waking him, is an old question. Aristotle, Poetics 24, says that the passage is so full of absurdities that they would be intolerable in a bad poet; but Homer has concealed them under an infinity of admirable beauties which he has crowded together here, as so many charms to prevent our perceiving the defects of the story. Among these beauties may be numbered the similes of the ship, the cave with its marvels, the dialogue of the deities, the transformation of the pinnace into stone, and the final picture with which the episode closes.

256 NOTES.

Heraclides Ponticus, a contemporary of Aristotle, thought that a settled policy of the Phaeacians was revealed. They pretended to lavish hospitality, and made speedy departures for anyone cast among them, and that, too, by night, so that their location in the world might be kept secret from all enterprising pirates. They leave Odysseus asleep so that he may not know what direction they take on the return trip. The scholiast V. gives other reasons for not waking him: that they might not seem to be asking repayment for the escort, or that they might not be detained by him, or that the poet arranged things this way on account of what follows, since Odysseus would have been slain by the suitors if he had returned openly. Plutarch, De Audiendis Poetis 8, cites a tradition of the Tyrrenians that Odysseus was of a remarkably drowsy disposition; but Plutarch himself thinks that his sleep here was feigned, so that he might not have to dismiss the Phaeacians without hospitality. Pope considers Aristotle's criticism justified. Mure sees in the conduct of the crew the true spirit of the practical joker, and they doubtless indulge in a hearty laugh at Odysseus' expense, imagining his consternation at waking and finding himself alone in what seems a strange land; on Odyssey Z 130. Wordsworth, in Picturesque Greece, says: "Homer felt unequal to the task of describing the raptures of Odysseus in approaching his native land, and therefore he very wisely landed him asleep. This is quite consistent with the usual course of nature, which sometimes collapses from exhaustion at times of greatest excitement." See the note on line 92.

126-27. ἀπειλάων [with threats]. When Polyphemus, standing on the shore, learns who has destroyed his eye, he stretches out his hands to his father, and prays that if it is fated for Odysseus to reach home, he may do so only after long years, in wretched condition, all his comrades lost, on a foreign ship, and find evils in his house. And Poseidon heard his prayer, Odyssey I 532: by which it is implied that the prayer is repeated by the deity as a threat; cf. Z 330, L 102. Poseidon's power to harm Odysseus himself has now ceased, but it is quite in keeping with his customary vindictiveness to wish to vent his spite on someone, and this he does upon the Phaeacians, settling an old score in the final reckoning. — τὰς . . . ἐπηπείλησε [he threatened them]; A 319. — Διὸς . . . βουλήν [the will of Zeus]; the same phrase of Poseidon, Y 15, when he has been summoned to the assembly of the gods,

BOOK XIII. 257

and he rises there to ask why they are gathered. His present purpose is to ascertain whether any decree of the gods stands in the way of his wishes; cf. α 20–95, ε 286.

128–30. "Father" (πάτερ) is a common appellation of the gods in many languages, but with Zeus it is formulaic. Poseidon uses it again at H 446, Here at E 757, and Helios at μ 371. — "when" (ὅτε), passing into the sense of "since." — τοι: see ζ 29. — γενέθλης: on η 205, 56; δ 232.

131–33. "And indeed" (καὶ γάρ): and true it is that the Phaeacians do not honor me, for while I said to myself that Odysseus should return at this time, and I never meant anything different, yet I did mean that he should find no release from his sufferings till he had set foot in Ithaca. But these Phaeacians not only received and entertained him magnificently, but they gave him untold gifts, and, what is unpardonable, over my element they bore him asleep, and asleep they landed him in Ithaca. — "now" (νῦν), used with the infinitive "to come" (ἐλεύσεσθαι). Düntz.—The main emphasis in the sentence is on "having suffered many evils" (κακὰ πολλὰ παθόντα); on θ 461. — Note the emphatic position of "return" (νόστον) and "utterly" (πάγχυ); cf. α 75. — "since" (ἐπεί), "from the time that" (ἐξ οὗ); θ 539. — "first" (πρῶτον), as at 127. The poet says nothing directly about this elsewhere, but the assent of Zeus to his acceptance of the prayer of Polyphemus is implied, at ι 553, where Odysseus' sacrifices to Zeus are rejected by that deity, for he was pondering how to destroy all the hero's ships and companions; cf. α 65–79.

134–39. "They" (οἵ), my descendants, bound by all the ties of blood and by countless blessings showered upon them to honor me and punish whom I punish. — "sleeping" (εὔδοντ'), not suffering, as I meant, but "having forgotten all that he had endured" (λελασμένος ὅσσ' ἐπεπόνθει), 92. — "bringing" (ἄγοντες); on θ 254. The aorist participle of this verb occurs only 6 times; the present 51 times, 27 of which are used as in the passage before us. — "bronze ... his share" (χαλκόν . . . αἴσαν) are the words of Zeus, ε 38–40. — ἄν: η 278. — "having obtained from the booty his share" (λαχὼν . . . αἴσαν). — "cloud-gatherer" (νεφεληγερέτα); H. 136 D.

140. "O wonders!" (ὦ πόποι) is an interjection expressing astonishment mingled with displeasure; akin to παπαῖ, "fie." — "Earth-shaker" (ἐννοσίγαι') is well illustrated by N 18, where Poseidon, kept from the battlefield by the orders of Zeus, is watching it from the topmost height of Samothrace, whence all Ida and Troy and the ships of the Achaeans lay spread out before him. The moment

Zeus turns his eyes away toward Thrace (on ζ 329), Poseidon leaves the mountain-top for his palace at Aegae, to equip himself to appear on the battle-field. Four steps he takes, and he is at Aegae; "the long mountains and forest trembled beneath the feet of Poseidon as he went." — εὐρυσθενὲς, "of wide-reaching power." — οἶον, exclamatory, as often. Compare the sentiments of this speech and the preceding with H 445–63, where Poseidon complains to Zeus that his achievements in building the wall of Troy will be eclipsed by those of the Achaeans in their camp-wall, and he evidently wishes them punished for their temerity; but Zeus simply tells him that he shall level the wall as soon as the Achaeans depart.

141–42. ἀτιμάζουσι; ζ 283. — χαλεπὸν, "perilous," Bryant; "a work of pain," Chapman. It combines the ideas "difficult" and "unfeeling;" cf. θ 575, ζ 120, δ 651, κ 305; on ζ 329. — πρεσβύτατον. In Homer, Zeus is the eldest of the three brothers, N 355, O 187, and Aides the youngest; Hesiod reverses the order, making Zeus the youngest. Here it may be said that Zeus, as supreme arbiter, does not include himself among the gods who could be guilty of such an act; or, with the scholiast, πρεσβύτατον may be taken in the derived sense of "most honored;" cf. Euripides, Trojan Women 48–9. — ἀτιμίησιν ἰάλλειν, "into dishonor to thrust." — ἀτιμίησιν is usually made a dative of means, but the expression appears to be an inverted one, like μ' ἀχέεσσί γε δώσεις, τ 167; cf. ο 198, α 95, θ 71. For the quantity of the penult, see on θ 243.

143–45. ἀνδρῶν; θ 408. — εἴπερ . . . οὔτι τίει: οὔτι, not μήτι, because the negative belongs closely with τίει, as if ἀτιμάζει (141). So β 274, μ 382, τ 85, Γ 289, Δ 55, 160, Ο 162, 178, 492, Υ 129, 139, Ω 296; mostly after εἰ δέ in antitheses. The negative is not commonly separated from its word, but we have οὐκέτι νόστιμος, τ 85; cf. O 162, 178, Y 129; H. 842; C. 616, Obs. 1; G. M. 47, 3, Note. — βίη . . . κάρτεϊ; ζ 197, 6; on θ 237, 178; here the insolence, begotten of pride of strength and power, to whose continual urging the better nature yields at last. This is the hubris so much dreaded by the Greek, as bringing speedy punishment from Heaven. πιθήσας and ἐπισπόμενοι also occur with similar phrases. — σοὶ, a god so honored and powerful. — δ'; on η 47. — καὶ ἐξοπίσω, "surely thereafter," if not before; the sentence is wholly general. — ἔπλετο; θ 571.

147–49. αἶψα . . . ἔρξαιμι, "quickly would I do," on each occasion that might arise, should I have your permission. The optative borders closely on the future indicative, and in fact the two are combined at μ 347; cf. γ 365–67, ο 506, θ 595–98; G. M. 52, 2, Note; H. 722 b. — ὡς ἀγορεύεις, i.e., punish those that make light of me. — θυμόν, "wrath." — ὀπίζομαι, "look up to," "regard." — ἀλεείνω; ζ 273. — νῦν αὖ, "now, however," since I have your consent. — περικαλλέα; θ 567.

151–52. ῥαῖσαι, "to shatter," break in pieces. At ψ 235, a simile presents to us the picture of a vessel so shattered by Poseidon, and the poet tells us that but few escape to land, exhausted by swimming. The same verb is used of dashing out a man's brains and of splintering a spear. — ἤδη σχῶνται, "now they may check themselves." If the middle voice here is pressed, it will prove that Poseidon's purpose was not to destroy the town; and this is strengthened by the following words, which on any other supposition would form as grim a pleasantry in tone as that of the Cyclops who tells Odysseus that, as a special favor, he will eat him last, ι 369. — ἀπολλήξωσι; cf. η 145, ζ 20, θ 87; on ζ 14. — μέγα . . . ἀμφικαλύψαι, "and a huge mountain for them around their city enwrap." The statement is ambiguous, like so many prophecies, of which this was originally one; but the intention appears to have been to block up the harbors and shut them off from seafaring in that way. — ἀμφι-, properly "on two sides," may be compared with the two harbors. The construction is an inverted one, as at 142. The figure is taken from a cloud or mantle that enfolds and conceals, Ξ 343, Θ 331, θ 503.

154–55. ὦ πέπον, "O mellow heart;" a figure from ripened fruit; of frequent occurrence in the Iliad as an affectionate term of endearment. Twice it stands in the plural, but then takes on the declining sense of soft-hearted weaklings. — ὡς is the reading of all the manuscripts, though some of the scholiasts had ὥς before them, and that was the reading adopted by Wolf. — μέν, for the emphatic μήν. — ἐμῷ θυμῷ, instead of the more usual μοι, to display the strong feeling with which he expresses his opinion. — ὅπ-ποτε; ζ 303, θ 444. — πάντες: observe the touch; all turned out by the docks or in the agora awaiting her return; still the busy idlers, eager for anything new; the convoy and home-coming

260 NOTES.

a great event in their little world. — "being driven along": supply "ship," as at line 113.

156–58. "to place" . . . "to cover over": these infinitives depend by anacoluthon on "it seems good," as if the "as" clause were absent; this is the earliest instance of a construction quite common in Herodotus, and found occasionally in the Attic writers. Others prefer to consider the "as" clause parenthetical, and the infinitives used imperatively. With "to place" supply "him," as at line 163. The ordinary verb is "to make," as at Omega 611, where Zeus has turned into stone the people of Niobe; but "he made it a stone" is used of the prodigy of the serpent at Aulis, at B 319. — "may marvel at": as those who saw the serpent changed to stone, B 320. — "all": lambda 353. — "a great thing indeed." Poseidon's wish is to give the Phaeacians a lesson for their insolence, and punish them by the destruction of their galley on the deep, and by cutting them off from maritime facilities. Zeus tells him that the prodigy of the vessel turned to stone before their eyes will be the most impressive lesson, standing as an everlasting memorial, and wreaking vengeance on them in ship and crew. Permission is also granted to plant his mountain there if he choose; so that the full warranty of line 145 is maintained, and the agency of Zeus is simply to alter his plan as to the ship. A higher poetic interest is thus, in the sequel, thrown about the fate of the Phaeacians, as they are left standing about the altar. Aristophanes read "and not," changing the thought greatly.

160–62. "they have come to dwell": when the scholiasts say here that this is wrongly used for "they are dwelling," because the Phaeacians have come from Hypereia, they must either forget that it is the poet who is now speaking, or else make the form a historical present, unless they place the poet very close to the period of his story. Even at the time of the story the removal must have been so distant that a generation, at least, has been born in Scheria. But in every other instance where this form occurs in Homer, it may have the sense "are living," or simply "are": at zeta 62, kappa 5, epsilon 35, iota 118, tau 279, omega 84, Delta 325; and necessarily so in all but the first two. Iota 118 refers to the goats on the island before the land of the Cyclopes, and may be quite as applicable to the time of the poet as to the period of the story. Hence, if the historic present be disallowed (on eta 103), the poet must have imagined the Phaeacians as still
